News.title: Cops release CCTV after ‘attempted sexual assault’ at Home Bargains in UK city
News.content:
SHOP HORROR Cops release CCTV after ‘attempted sexual assault’ at Home Bargains in UK city







Next

COPS have released CCTV after an alleged attempted sexual assault at a Home Bargains in a UK city.

Police have launched a probe after the incident, which took place between 12.50pm and 1.10pm on September 3 in a Wakefield store, was reported.



Officers are keen to identify the man in the images, captured wearing glasses and a mask, as they believe he has information that can help their enquiries.

Anyone with information is urged to to contact police via 101.



A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said: “Officers have released CCTV images of a man they are keen to speak to in connection with an attempt sexual assault report in Wakefield.

“An investigation is ongoing in relation to an attempt sexual assault which took place between 12.50pm and 1.10pm on 3 September at Home Bargains on Ings Road, Wakefield.

“Officers are keen to identify the man pictured in the CCTV images.

“Anyone with information or who knows the man in the picture is asked to contact police via 101 or use the live chat facility at http://www.westyorkshire.police.uk/livechat quoting reference number 13260504565.”

News.title: Four yobs who left passengers vomiting blood and gasping for air after spraying tear gas at Heathrow Airport are jailed
News.content:
LOCKED UP Four yobs who left passengers vomiting blood and gasping for air after spraying tear gas at Heathrow Airport are jailed







Next

FOUR yobs who left passengers vomiting blood after spraying tear gas at Heathrow Airport have been jailed.

Anton Clarke-Butcher, 25, Tyrone Richards, 31, Omoneke Whyte, 31, and 29-year-old Denzel Eduardo injured 21 holidaymakers in the horror.



Three of the thugs, who were wearing face coverings and dark clothing, sprayed the substance into a lift at an airport car park.

Two women and two men who met them after their flight from Johannesburg were in the elevator at the time.



They were then followed by the defendants and had their suitcases stolen.

Meanwhile, the CS spray was released from the lift and spread through the entrance to Terminal 3 – including at a nearby Caffe Nero.

A barista began coughing and vomiting blood shortly after being exposed to the substance.

Others were taken to hospital for treatment, while some passengers reported feeling dizzy and struggled to breathe.

The attack on December 7 last year sparked widespread delay after Terminal 3 was closed.

Richards, Clarke-Butcher, Whyte and Eduardo pleaded guilty to affray at Isleworth Crown Court.



Sentencing the gang today, Judge Kwame Inyundo said: “Individuals were targeted by you as a group and the violence used in the incident was serious and sustained.”

Richards was jailed for 27 months, while White and Eduardo were each jailed for 23 months.

Clarke-Butcher was sentenced to 21 months’ imprisonment.



Prosecutor Gary Rutter said he “could not say exactly what led to this incident”, but “one may suspect what was going on”.

He added that the incident left “members of the public, coughing, vomiting, and some vomited blood”.

The barista at Caffè Nero, who started to cough and vomit blood, told the court she was “scared” as she “felt fine one minute and then almost instantly unwell”.



A customer service agent said the incident was “terrifying”, adding she “felt dizzy and like I was going to pass out”.

She also told how a woman in a wheelchair she was assisting “was struggling to breathe and using an inhaler”.

A mum who arrived from a flight from South Africa with her 14-month-old son said her child started to cough, telling the court: “I was immediately afraid for my baby’s safety and my own safety”.

While a man who was ordering a taxi from the airport’s car park said “20 to 30 people were all coughing” after the incident and he was “struggling to breathe”.

Richards was arrested while still at the airport and the other three defendants were later identified and arrested separately.



Genevieve Moss, representing Eduardo, said the CS gas “was discharged by the rival group”, adding that he has asthma and this would have had a “dangerous impact on him”.

The lawyer said Eduardo, who has 12 previous convictions for 18 offences, would have “not agreed to take part in any activity involving such a substance” and expressed “deep remorse”.

Rushnay Sikander, representing Whyte, said he was “very remorseful”, adding he had a “traumatic childhood” including his father being murdered when he was five years old and that he had been the victim of three separate stabbings.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shanda McAteer, representing Clarke-Butcher, who has 14 convictions for 31 offences, said he denied releasing the gas and “genuinely expresses remorse”.

Patrick Harte, representing Richards, who has three previous convictions, said he was “not present when the first spray was released” and was “sorry to innocent bystanders suffering anguish”.

News.title: Disgraced TV cop who created ‘toxic’ WhatsApp culture and asked colleague to send sex video of female suspect jailed
News.content:
VILE COP Disgraced TV cop who created ‘toxic’ WhatsApp culture and asked colleague to send sex video of female suspect jailed







Next

A DISGRACED celebrity police officer who created a “toxic” WhatsApp culture has been jailed after asking for a female suspect’s sex video.

Paul Street, 41, found fame in television crime shows on the BBC and Channel 4 and was known for getting “impressive results” through his “robust” style.



But anti-corruption officers began investigating him and uncovered his two WhatsApp groups in 2021 after a new police officer reported him.

He encouraged colleagues to “bully” a teenage detainee and asked a workmate to send him a sex video of a female suspect.



The vile offences were committed while working at Cambridgeshire Constabulary leading a unit at Cambourne Police Station, mainly dealing with county lines drug supply and organised crime.

Street has now been jailed for four years after he was found guilty of two charges of misconduct in a public office.

The cop also admitted two offences of unlawful disclosure of personal data relating to information and screenshots he sent to his partner in 2020.

Eleven other officers were investigated over their conduct arising from the “toxic” culture Street had fostered.

Of those, two resigned, one was dismissed for gross misconduct, one received a final warning, two received written warnings, and five others were dealt with for low level performance issues.

Prosecutor Anne Whyte KC had described how Street “created a culture of bragging and intolerance towards suspects”, and a “zero-tolerance attitude to anyone on his team who disagreed with his methods and sentiments”.



She had said: “He was not just promoting inappropriate attitudes, he was positively creating a toxic culture which junior officers would find difficult to challenge and likely to adopt.”

In April 2020, Street called on his team to “bully” a 17-year-old detainee – encouraging them to “please hit him” and “smash his head in”.

In the autumn of 2020, PC Josh Williams was tasked with examining the phone of a female suspect he told Street was “quite fit”.

Street asked him if there were “any nudes”, and Williams replied there was a video of the woman committing a sexual act.

Williams went on to send Street a photo from the woman’s phone depicting her in underwear.



The following year, Street asked on WhatsApp if Williams still had the intimate private video because he wanted to show it to “the lads from footy”.

When he was interviewed about it, Street claimed he wanted to see the images to reassure himself the woman, who was released without charge, was not the victim of exploitative behaviour.

But jurors were told it was not Williams’s job to discuss or share the private images, and neither was it Street’s job to ask for nudes or the sex video.

Giving evidence, Street admitted his messages on WhatsApp were “poor” but said the language was “gallows humour” and part of the culture at the time.

He also told jurors that being successful in his job had made him “arrogant”.



Street had previously appeared on BBC show Britain’s Teenage Drug Runners in 2017, and in 2019 was on Channel 4’s Famous And Fighting Crime documentary.

Williams, 38, was sentenced to 16 months’ imprisonment today.

Lisa Rose, Senior Specialist Prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service’s Special Crime Division, said: “This case exposed a sustained pattern of unacceptable conduct by a police officer who abused his position of trust.

“Paul Street repeatedly crossed clear professional boundaries, by encouraging the mistreatment of detainees and seeking access to intimate material that had no place in a criminal investigation.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Police officers are entrusted with significant powers and are expected to uphold the highest standards at all times. Members of the public should have confidence that any personal material obtained during an investigation will be handled lawfully and appropriately.



“The actions of Paul Street and Joshua Williams represented a serious breach of that trust.”

News.title: Moment furious shopper smashes up £9,000 worth of wine in shocking rampage after his card was declined
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment a raging shopper smashes up to £9,000 worth of wine after his card was declined.

Bizarre footage shows the man rampage around a shop, grabbing bottles of plonk off the shelves and throwing them to the ground.



The 29-year-old man can be seen using a motorbike helmet to sweep entire rows of bottles onto the floor.

He throws one through a glass door, smashing it completely.



The man yells as he grabs bottle after bottle of booze and hurls them across the shop.

Workers at the supermarket in Dourado, Brazil were left terrified as wine and shards of glass flew everywhere.

Shoppers and staff back away from the chaos in the dramatic video.

A huge sea of red wine could be seen filling the shop floor.



The alarming rampage began after his card was declined, according to the shop’s manager Aparecido Donizete Ballan.

He allegedly threatened both staff and customers.



Before he entered the shop and began hurling bottles, witnesses said the man knocked over a motorbike outside and kicked a sign.

Damage to the wine stock left by the incident was estimated to be around £8,658.

Manager Ballan said: “We just want something to be done about it, to get someone like this off the streets.

“Now all we can do is wait for justice to take its course.”



He said it was the second incident involving the same customer, who had allegedly previously damaged a tree sapling by the business.

The man left the the shop after causing two-and-a-half minutes of terror and surrendered himself to police officers.

Detective João Fernando Baptista said he suspects the man was having a psychotic episode.

The 29-year-old reportedly has a history of incidents in the town but no criminal record.

He was detained by cops but later released after giving a statement.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Baptista, who is leading the investigation, said: “We need a few reports, including one to establish whether he was actually in full possession of his mental faculties.”

A court will decide if he can be held criminally responsible for the smashing spree.

News.title: Boffins baffled by 25 mysterious stone structures in submerged 14th-century UK town swallowed by sea 700 years ago
News.content:
SUNKEN SECRETS Boffins baffled by 25 mysterious stone structures in submerged 14th-century UK town swallowed by sea 700 years ago







Next

DIVERS have found a series of strange structures at the site of a 14th-century town which was claimed by the sea 700 years ago.

The flint-built remains were discovered several hundred metres off the coastline at Cromer, Norfolk.



They are thought to form part of Shipden, a once-thriving lost medieval settlement which was gradually consumed by the advancing North Sea.

Now divers have photographed a collection of human-built features – but boffins still havn’t worked out their exact history or use.



They include a line of flint structures, lower sections of stone caissons and other pieces of cut stone.

Some remain standing between eight and ten courses high despite having spent centuries underwater.



Specialist photography has also allowed preliminary 3D models of the finds to be created.

The mysterious town has been the subject of myths in Norfolk, with local legend claiming Shipden’s church tower survived beneath the waves.



Some accounts said the ruins could be glimpsed at particularly low tides, while legend claimed its bell could still be heard tolling during storms or warning fishermen not to go to sea.

Researchers now believe Church Rock may not have been the church at all, with St Peter’s thought to have stood further north and west.

Peter Stibbons, chairman of the Friends of Cromer Museum and director of the project, said: “Those of us brought up in Cromer have always known the story of Church Rock, so it’s a big step to saying the legend may be incorrect.

“We’re busy going through the medieval documentation and matching it to the physical finds to date, to suggest a better understanding of Shipden.



“For the present we’re putting forward ideas rather than conclusions.”

Shipden was once a thriving settlement on the north Norfolk coast.

The Domesday Book recorded it in 1086 as having 117 residents, three acres of meadow, woodland capable of supporting 36 pigs, a harbour and two churches.

Its name gradually fell out of use during the 13th and 14th centuries and was replaced in records by Cromer.



Centuries of erosion consumed the original settlement, with the devastating North Sea storm of January 1362 among those to batter the coastline.

Researchers are investigating whether the caissons formed part of a 14th-century attempt to hold back the sea.

They could alternatively be connected to a pier authorised in 1390, although the Alfred Savin project stressed that these remain theories rather than firm conclusions.

News.title: Scandal-hit ex MP left £98k to kids after death aged 59 – just 2 years after quitting over ‘sex & drugs’ sting
News.content:
FINAL FORTUNE Scandal-hit ex MP left £98k to kids after death aged 59 – just 2 years after quitting over ‘sex & drugs’ sting







Next

A FORMER MP who was embroiled in a career-ending sex and cocaine scandal has left just £98,000 to his children following his death last year.

A coroner previously ruled 59-year-old David Warburton died of natural causes at his home in Chelsea, London, in August 2025.



It has now emerged that he left an estate worth £97,639 after debts.

He signed a will in March last year which placed his wealth in a trust for his two children.



Mr Warburton lost the Tory whip in 2022 after The Sunday Times published a picture of him next to lines of cocaine, which he admitted to snorting.

The woman who took the photo alleged he then followed her into the bedroom and stripped naked, before grinding on her.



The shamed MP for Somerton & Frome also faced accusations of sexual misconduct, bullying and harassment from two young women working within the parliamentary estate.

An investigation resulted in two complaints of sexual harassment being upheld, prompting Mr Warburton to resign.



An appeal panel ruled investigations into the claims were materially flawed.

The ex-politician denied he had a fair hearing and insisted the MeToo movement had gone “too far”.

He claimed he had been the victim of a “honey trap”, although he acknowledged he had “been naive and incredibly stupid”.

He went on to take a job as a long-distance lorry driver before moving to Capenex Energy Group as its chief executive.

Paramedics were called to his home on the morning of August 26 and found him dead at the scene.



The Met Police treated the death as unexpected but not suspicious.

News.title: Houthi rebels ‘fire drone at Mecca’ as Saudi Arabia warns attempted attack on holy city is a ‘red line’
News.content:
Next

THE Houthis have been accused of launching a drone towards Saudi Arabia’s holy city of Mecca.

Riyadh warned the Iranian-backed terror group’s alleged attack – the latest in a series of tit-for-tat strikes – was a “red line”.



Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has come under fire in recent weeks from Houthi invasions and air assaults.

One of the Arab Kingdom’s most critical oil pipelines has been forced to shut down for weeks following an attack by the Iranian proxy.



Fears are mounting the spiralling conflict could spark another global energy crisis – with the Houthis extending further control of the Red Sea, one of the planet’s most important shipping lanes.

Sat between the Suez Canal and the Bab al-Mandab strait, the chokepoint is a crucial artery Saudi Arabia needs to export oil.



Their export process has already been put under severe strain by the Strait of Hormuz saga between Iran and the US.

Oil prices have shot up above $100 a barrel in recent days as the Houthis continue to seize more Yemeni government-controlled territories, ports and islands.



The Houthis have denied firing drones toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometers from Yemen’s border.

The Saudis said they intercepted and destroyed the drone before it entered the area’s airspace.

6 Credit: EPA

Mecca is the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad and considered the holiest city in Islam.



Muslims are usually required to make a pilgrimage to the city at least once in their lifetime – with millions travelling there each year.

The Saudi-led Coalition Forces said: “This hostile attempt will also remain a black mark in the record of violations by the extremist terrorist Houthi militia, as a deliberate act intended to provoke the feelings of millions of Muslims.”

They vowed to take any “necessary and deterrent measures” against the Iranian proxy.

It comes as the Houthis claimed to have shot down a Saudi fighter jet.

The militia claimed: “The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah’s aid and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations in support of its military mobilisations in the airspace of Marib province.”



On Monday, the Houthi rebels tightened their grip on the Red Sea by seizing two key islands, Greater and Lesser Hanish.

And last week, the group launched an attack on Saudi Arabia‘s East-West Pipeline – a 1,200km pump that spans the width of the country.

The critical conduit moves crude production from Gulf ports to places like Yanbu on the Red Sea, where it is loaded onto vessels for export.

Riyadh was forced to close down the pipeline due to the attack which is believed to have been inflicted by drones.

Around 2.6 million to 4 million barrels per day have moved through the pipeline since August.



Saudi Arabian oil supplies have also been rocked by Iran-led strikes as UK pump prices continue to spiral.

British petrol and diesel prices – which have already leapt by 5p-per-litre over the past week – are set to carry on climbing as the terror state and its comrades cripple supply routes.

Long term knock-on effects for British householders include higher interest rates and mortgages plus consumer goods hikes as Iran declared war on Western economies.

The Houthis also took Perim island last week – another critical territory key to controlling the Red Sea.

Its capture marked the Houthis’ biggest territorial gain in years and put them in a strong position to threaten vessels in the Bab al-Mandab strait.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Markets fear the latest developments could lead to a terrifying triple blockade that would spark an economic meltdown.

Oil exported from the Gulf now has to travel through three huge barriers to reach Europe – the US blockade of Iranian ports, the IRGC blockade of Hormuz and the threat from the Houthis in the Gate of Tears.

News.title: Widow discovers late husband’s biscuit tin stash hidden for 50 years that’s now worth over £100,000 MORE
News.content:
Next

A WIDOW was left stunned after discovering a fortune inside a biscuit tin stashed in her shed.

Left by her late husband over 50 years ago, the hidden contents of the tin were found to be worth over £100,000.

Over £113,000 worth of gold coins were found inside a ‘Granola Digestive Biscuits’ box after her husband invested in a collection of gold bullion back in the mid-1970s.



Back when prices of gold were low due to ongoing recession, he purchased 41 South African gold Krugerrand coins and 21 gold sovereigns.



After spending between £70 and £80 each on the gold Krugerrand back in 1975, the coins were hidden away for 50 years.

It was only during a clearout of the couple’s home in Penzance, Cornwall, that the true value of the unassuming biscuit tin was revealed.

Opening the lid unveiled an initial layer of silver coins, but digging deeper uncovered the true treasure – the individually packaged gold coins, complete with the original proof of purchase.

Having skyrocketed in value since the mid-1970s, the collection of 22-carat South African Krugerrands and British sovereigns was sold at Lay’s Auctioneers in Penzance.

In total, the Krugerrands fetched a total of £100,000, and the British sovereigns £13,000 – a staggering £100,000 more than the few thousand pounds spent on them originally.



Auctioneer of the coins, David Lay, said: “The lady was thinking of downsizing and I went into her home to look at some items.

“One of the last places I looked was this workshop and there was a biscuit tin inside which was very heavy.

“I plonked it down and looked inside and saw silver coins.”

After the coins were passed on to Lay’s coin expert, the gold was found – a result that Lay calls “astonishing” and “remarkable”.



Another spokesperson for Lay’s added: “You hear about people keeping money under the mattress or under the floorboards because people didn’t trust banks back then but you just don’t expect that to happen now.

“The price of gold has is astronomical at the moment so it was an amazing investment by this man.

“What a shrewd chap her husband was.”

News.title: Men behind Heathrow tear gas attack that left people 'vomiting blood' jailed
News.content:
Men behind Heathrow tear gas attack that left people 'vomiting blood' jailed

Heathrow Terminal 3 was shut down for hours after tear gas was sprayed leaving people hospitalised and bystanders coughing, choking and 'vomiting blood'

View 2 Images Emergency services rushed to the scene at Heathrow after the tear gas attack (Image: PA)

Four men have been jailed after tear gas was sprayed inside a terminal at Heathrow Airport leaving passengers coughing, choking and "vomiting blood".

‌



A woman who was sprayed in the face with tear gas before having her suitcase taken was among five of 21 people assaulted needing medical treatment. The attack caused travel chaos as Terminal 3 remained closed for hours after the incident with major delays for train and shuttle bus passengers.

‌



Tyrone Richards, 31, Anton Clarke-Butcher, 25, Omoneke Whyte, 31, and Denzel Eduardo, 29, were handed prison sentences at Isleworth Crown Court today. The four men all pleaded guilty to affray at the west London court in June.

‌



Richards, who appeared by video link from HMP Wayland in Norfolk, was jailed for 27 months. White and Eduardo, who were at HMP Wormwood Scrubs on video link, were each jailed for 23 months and Clarke-Butcher, who was at the same prison, was sentenced to 21 months’ imprisonment.

Sentencing the four on Wednesday, Judge Kwame Inyundo said: "Individuals were targeted by you as a group and the violence used in the incident was serious and sustained."

The hearing was previously told how masked men sprayed what was "believed to be CS spray" into a lift at an airport car park at 8am on December 7 last year.

‌



View 2 Images Armed police made arrests at Heathrow Airport after the spray attack (Image: Hudaifa Yunis / SWNS)

In the lift were two women who had arrived on a flight from Johannesburg in South Africa and two men who had met them at the airport.

The court heard that the defendants were prevented from entering by the group as "innocent parties ran away from the lift in some distress". Once the lift was on the ground floor, gas was sprayed, causing "difficulties for people at a Caffè Nero nearby".

‌



One of the baristas at the café explained she started coughing and vomiting blood, telling the court she was scared as she "felt fine one minute and then almost instantly unwell".

People in the vicinity needed hospital treatment after coming into contact with the substance, which is widely used by police forces as tear gas to incapacitate people.

The court was told the defendants followed the two women to an airport taxi forecourt and took their suitcases, which were never recovered. One of the women was then left "coughing and choking" after she was sprayed in the face with CS gas at close range.

‌



The judge said it became apparent that the group of men "had a particular and determined interest" in the women’s suitcases.

"Your group followed and confronted the pair (of women) who tried to get a taxi," Judge Inyundo said. "Your group threatened violence to them and took the suitcases from them."

A customer service agent at Terminal 3 said the incident was "terrifying", adding she "felt dizzy and like I was going to pass out" and that a woman in a wheelchair she was assisting "was struggling to breathe and using an inhaler".

‌



A mother who arrived from a flight from South Africa with her 14-month-old son said her child started to cough, telling the court: "I was immediately afraid for my baby's safety and my own safety".

A man who was ordering a taxi from the airport's car park said "20 to 30 people were all coughing" after the incident and he was "struggling to breathe". Prosecutor Gary Rutter said he "could not say exactly what led to this incident", but "one may suspect what was going on". He added that the incident left "members of the public, coughing, vomiting, and some vomited blood".

Richards was arrested while still at the airport and the other three defendants were later identified and arrested separately.

‌



The defence barrister for Eduardo, Genevieve Moss, told the court the CS gas "was discharged by the rival group", adding that he has asthma and this would have had a "dangerous impact on him".

Eduardo has 12 previous convictions for 18 offences and the lawyer said he would have "not agreed to take part in any activity involving such a substance". He also expressed "deep remorse".

Rushnay Sikander, representing Whyte, said he was "very remorseful". The lawyer also told the court that Whyte had a "traumatic childhood" which saw his father being murdered when he was five. He has also been the victim of three separate stabbings.

‌



Shanda McAteer, representing Clarke-Butcher, who has 14 convictions for 31 offences, said he denied releasing the gas and "genuinely expresses remorse".

Patrick Harte, representing Richards, who has three previous convictions, said he was "not present when the first spray was released" and was "sorry to innocent bystanders suffering anguish".

Richards, who appeared by video link from HMP Wayland in Norfolk, was jailed for 27 months.

White and Eduardo, who were at HMP Wormwood Scrubs on video link, were each jailed for 23 months and Clarke-Butcher, who was at the same prison, was sentenced to 21 months’ imprisonment.

News.title: B&M's 'relaxing' £20 room item that similar to £50 Next version
News.content:
B&M's 'relaxing' £20 room item that similar to £50 Next version

The brand claims this small addition to homes will 'complement any space'

View 3 Images B&M has brought back the item in stores across the UK (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Homeowners can create a "subtle and relaxing atmosphere" in their rooms with a homeware item currently on sale at B&M. It's said to have the added bonus of getting rid of household odours and replacing them with something that's "great for setting the mood".

‌



The Naeo Tortoiseshell Glass Aroma Diffuser is available for £20 in B&M stores nationwide. It comes in two colour options - black or white - featuring a speckled design with hints of gold dotted throughout the pattern.

‌



Describing it online, B&M said: "The diffuser showcases a captivating tortoise shell pattern with a golden shimmer on its glass cover, adding an elegant touch to its design. When in use, the diffuser emits a comforting warm white light that shines through the unique artwork, creating an inviting atmosphere that complements any space.

‌



"First, pour water into the tank, then add a few drops of essential oils. With its ultrasound diffusion system, the Tortoiseshell Glass Aroma Diffuser will gently release a scented cold fine mist into the air. Great for setting the mood or for combatting household smells."

View 3 Images The Naeo Tortoiseshell Glass Aroma Diffuser (Image: B&M)

Videos on social media show that similar versions of the diffusers were stocked last year, reports the Liverpool Echo, with shoppers who missed out now getting another opportunity to snap one up. TikTok clip (@Hannahjayne) said: "RUN don't walk to BandM Stores for this gorgeous new aroma diffuser, similar to the other VIRAL diffuser they did."

‌



The B&M deal on the diffuser could be viewed as a budget-friendly choice when compared to other branded options. For instance, Next has a similar-looking Glass Confetti White Electric Diffuser on its website for £50, and Argos has its Habitat Confetti Glass Electric Diffuser on sale for £30.

B&M doesn't provide home delivery or click-and-collect for most homeware products like this. Customers will need to visit their local stores to check availability.

For a "spa-like" atmosphere at home, B&M shoppers might be interested in the Naeo Himalayan Salt Lamp for just £8. Customers can pick between two styles - a moon or a star - for a light that adds warmth to their living areas.

‌



View 3 Images Shoppers can pick from the black or white versions (Image: B&M)

Describing the lamp on its website, B&M said its "calming glow" filters through the "authentic" and "handcrafted" lamp via its USB-powered feature. There are plenty of other options for people looking to bring a more calming presence into home decor.

Another example includes the Restore Himalayan Rock Salt Lamp and Essential Oil Set. Priced at £12.99 (but included in B&M's ongoing two for £20 sale), the set creates a "perfect space for relaxing", according to B&M.

Article continues below

It adds: "The minerals contained in the Himalayan rock salts give the lamp its beautiful pink tones colour, and when coupled with the LED lights, it creates a soothing and calming ambience. This set comes with the Restore Sweet Orange Essential Oil, simply sprinkle a few drops of the essential oil onto the rock salt for a fresh mood and boosting fragrance."

To save yourself a wasted journey, it's advisable to call your nearest store first to confirm whether the item is available. You can locate contact information and opening hours for your local branch by using the Store Locator tool on the B&M website.

News.title: Charlie Kirk's family claims security failures to blame for his assassination
News.content:
Charlie Kirk's family claims security failures to blame for his assassination

Lawyers representing Mr Kirk’s family say a string of 'reckless decisions' by officials at Utah Valley University are to blame for the death of the conservative activist who was killed by a sniper

View 4 Images A memorial for Charlie Kirk left at Utah Valley University (Image: AP)

The family of Charlie Kirk have said university officials failed to prevent the conservative activist’s assassination in a move that may lead to a possible lawsuit.

‌



Lawyers representing Mr Kirk’s family have blamed a string of "reckless decisions" by officials at Utah Valley University for the death of the prominent conservative activist. They claimed Mr Kirk was left vulnerable to the rooftop sniper, who fired the fatal shot from more than 400 feet away on September 10, 2025.

‌



Mr Kirk, 31, had been in an outdoor courtyard surrounded by tall buildings during one of his debate events when he was gunned down in front of a crowd of around three thousand.

‌



An Associated Press review following the shooting showed the campus in Orem did not use several public safety practices that have become standard safeguards at such large events.

Campus police numbers were well below recommended levels for a school of that size and authorities failed to use a drone to monitor rooftops. There was also allegedly a lack of coordination with local law enforcement and no bag checks or metal detectors.

View 4 Images Erika Kirk leaves the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah on July 6 after a hearing for Tyler Robinson (Image: AP Photo/Marielle Scott)

‌



"The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk’s close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," the Kirk family attorney D Loren Washburn wrote in the notice to state and university officials.

The wrongful death notice, dated September 9, a day before the one-year anniversary of Mr Kirk's death, is a required step under state law before his family can file a formal claim or lawsuit.

It names Utah Valley University as well as its then-president, Astrid Tuminez, along with the campus police department and its chief, Jeffrey Long; and the state of Utah.

‌



Attorneys for Mr Kirk’s family alleged officials also failed to carry out an adequate risk assessment before approving the event, establish a secure perimeter or have first responders immediately available. The lack of on-site medics meant Mr Kirk had to be taken to a nearby hospital in a private vehicle rather than an ambulance after he was shot, the notice said.

View 4 Images Charlie Kirk's parents Kathryn and Robert arrive at court for the preliminary hearing in the Tyler Robinson case (Image: Charles McClintock Wilson/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

“Tragically, the UVU Parties took none of these safety measures — steps only they had the authority to take — resulting in a situation that rendered Mr. Kirk helpless before his assassin,” Mr Washburn wrote.

‌



Six campus officers had staffed the event and coordinated with Kirk’s eight-person private security team, Jeffrey Long said after the shooting. The university has since announced it will expand its police force.

The Utah Attorney General’s Office said it does not comment on potential litigation. Utah resident Tyler Robinson turned himself in a day after Mr Kirk’s killing. Prosecutors say he told his romantic partner that he “had enough of his (Kirk’s) hatred”.

Robinson is charged with aggravated murder, making him eligible for the death penalty if convicted. A judge on September 1 ordered the case to proceed toward trial. A date has not yet been set.

‌



View 4 Images Erika Kirk, the widow of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, pictured during a heartbreaking tribute her late husband (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Prosecutors during a preliminary hearing in July presented what they characterised as overwhelming evidence against Robinson. That includes surveillance video of Robinson on the campus, DNA tests linking him to a rifle found near the assassination site and a handwritten note he allegedly left for his romantic partner that read, “I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it”.

Mr Kirk’s parents, Robert and Kathryn Kirk, and widow, Erika Kirk, attended the hearings.

Article continues below

State law allows heirs or personal representatives of people who die to file lawsuits seeking damages if the death was caused by a wrongful act or negligence.

The notice from Mr Kirk’s family did not specify what damages they may seek.

News.title: Southport attack victims, survivors and families hit by Ministry of Justice data breach
News.content:
Southport attack victims, survivors and families hit by Ministry of Justice data breach

The Ministry of Justice has been slammed by the parents of a Southport survivor after court files were were accessed without authorisation as part of a data breach

View 2 Images Court files about the Southport attack victims and families were accessed in data breach (Image: Liverpool Echo)

Parents of a Southport attack survivor said they were "devastated" following a data breach which saw "confidential information downloaded".

‌



Court files about the victims, survivors and families of the Southport stabbing attack were accessed without authorisation, the Ministry of Justice said. It is understood the data breach was discovered during a review of the department's digital systems. Earlier this year it emerged the North West Ambulance Service was looking into whether staff inappropriately accessed the records of Southport victims.

‌



The parents of a Southport survivor, referred to as C1, slammed the MoJ and said: "In recent weeks our family has once again been devastated by two data breaches that involve our daughter; NWAS and now the MoJ.

‌



Sheffield streets on lockdown as bomb squad deployed and homes evacuated READ MORE :

View 2 Images Bebe King, Elsie Dot Stancombe and Alice da Silva Aguiar were killed in the attack (Image: Merseyside Police/PA Wire)

"This culture of snooping across agencies and services must end and that will only happen if those individuals are held to account and not protected by the very confidentiality laws they flouted to access our daughter's information."

The parents said they "expect each of these despicable individuals to lose their jobs" while calling for "full transparency" from both the MoJ and the NWAS.

‌



In May it also emerged that dozens of workers at the University Hospitals of Liverpool Group, where some of the wounded were treated, had looked at records with no good reason.

The parents of the survivor today said: "Two years on our focus should be on our daughter's continuing recovery, not having to manage further failures by the state that have put our daughter at risk once again. Like all the other survivors, our daughter will spend the rest of her life navigating the trauma of what happened to her."

They also claimed that confidential information "has been downloaded without her consent", adding: "Now she is at risk of being confronted by photographs of her injuries or deeply personal information. As her parents, our worst fear is that this could be used to profit or gain in future and could derail her ongoing recovery.

‌



"We are exhausted by apologies. We are exhausted by offers to meet with government ministers and CEOs; all of which amount to nothing. It is not acceptable anymore to continue to heap more risk and stress on to our family and the other families affected.”

The MoJ did not reveal how many people were impacted by this data breach and said there was no evidence personal data was shared with third parties.

Nicola Ryan-Donnelly, Partner at Fletchers Solicitors, which represents 22 of the 23 surviving children, said: "Week after week we are learning of a new data breach against victims who have endured the worst atrocities this country has ever seen.

‌



"It is disgraceful that these public bodies have known of these breaches for months and only choose to disclose them as the media pressure mounts and their internal investigations are all but over. These families have suffered enough trauma, they need transparency and accountability now.

"For our clients affected by the Nottingham and Southport attack, and for all others whose data has been breached inappropriately, we want to see the government launch a full independent investigation to address this grim voyeuristic culture, and ensure private details of victims are properly protected in the future."

The incident has been referred to data watchdog the Information Commissioner's Office and a spokesperson for the MoJ said the government department was "appalled".

Article continues below

The spokesperson said: "We are appalled that this happened and recognise the distress it will have caused victims, survivors, and their families. We apologise to those affected – unauthorised access to court files is completely unacceptable. This is now being investigated urgently, and the Prime Minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee this. All wrongdoing will be met with extremely firm action."

The Prisons and Probation Service and the Courts and Tribunals Service has launched a probe into the data breach, and anyone impacted will be notified directly. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee the matter.

Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine; Bebe King, six; and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, were killed at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport on July 29 2024. Eight other children, dance teacher Leanne Lucas and businessman John Hayes were injured in the attack.

News.title: Dad reunited with heroes who saved him after sudden cardiac arrest
News.content:
Dad reunited with heroes who saved him after sudden cardiac arrest

The dramatic rescue has highlighted how vital confidence with defibrillators can be, with new research suggesting many people would still hesitate to use one in an emergency

View 4 Images Michael and Richard helped keep Marvin alive until paramedics arrived (Image: Collect/PA Real Life)

A dad who suffered a cardiac arrest and was unconscious for 22 minutes has been reunited with the two men who helped save his life.

‌



Marvin Joseph-Daay, 39, collapsed without warning just 15 minutes into a football match before referee Michael Mcdonaugh began CPR and Richard Witt rushed over with a defibrillator. The dad-of-three was later told he had been without oxygen for six minutes and needed four shocks before a faint pulse returned.

‌



Just days after leaving hospital, Marvin met Michael and Richard at a pub in Reading so he could thank them face-to-face.

‌



Marvin, from Hounslow, said: “I heard about what they had done and I just needed to meet them and say thank you. One thing I will say is my ribs were still really sore and I felt like I’d been in a ring with Mike Tyson.

“Then when I saw the size of Richard, I understood. I was definitely very, very thankful to them (after going through) an overwhelming experience where I was that close to death.”

View 4 Images Marvin was unconscious for 22 minutes (Image: Collect/PA Real Life)

‌



Residents told to push bins half a mile as road has too many potholes for lorry READ MORE :

Copies of Earl Spencer's bombshell new book on Princess Diana stolen in Dutch lorry raid READ MORE :

Marvin, who works at Gatwick Airport, had been playing goalkeeper for Englefield Eagles Football Club at Sol Joel Park in Reading on December 14, 2025. He said there had been no sign anything was wrong when he woke up that morning or during the warm-up.

Marvin said: “I felt fit, healthy and ready to go, which is the most frightening part of the situation because I didn’t feel anything was off.”

Around 15 minutes into the game, he suddenly collapsed. Marvin said: “You think you’d get a twinge (of pain) or something or you’re not feeling well, but I had absolutely nothing.”

‌



Michael immediately began CPR while someone nearby ran to find help. Richard, 42, a social inclusion manager at Reading Football Club who had first-aid training through his job, rushed over from a neighbouring pitch. He told PA Real Life: “Marvin was on the floor on his back, eyes wide open, not breathing at all.

“Everyone else was standing around not knowing what to do, panicking, crying on the phone to the ambulance. So I asked if anybody had gone for a defib yet.”

View 4 Images Richard was not supposed to be at the football club (Image: Collect/PA Real Life)

‌



A defibrillator was brought from the pavilion and Richard took over chest compressions before attaching the pads to Marvin’s chest. Richard said: “The machine is loud. It talks clearly, it gives you great instruction, it tells you when to stand back and it tells you when we need to recharge for the next shock.

“And we were talking to Marvin all the way through, even though he wasn’t awake.”

After four shocks, Richard said he was “relieved” to feel Marvin’s “very faint” pulse. Paramedics arrived shortly afterwards and continued emergency treatment before taking Marvin to Royal Berkshire Hospital in Reading.

‌



Richard said he was told Marvin’s chances were still “50-50”. Marvin was later placed in an induced coma and woke around 24 hours later.

Recalling his first memory after waking up, Marvin said: “I was lying there with all these wires coming out and listening to the sounds of the hospital room. I was a bit confused and shocked… it was quite traumatising to be honest.”

View 4 Images The dad-of-three said the experience left him "close to death" (Image: Collect/PA Real Life)

‌



Within two days, Marvin had a defibrillator device fitted to help treat dangerous heart rhythms and was discharged on Christmas Eve. He had previously suffered a heart attack in 2019, aged 32, and was later diagnosed with heart failure and high blood pressure.

Marvin said: “But otherwise, everything was quite plain sailing. I felt healthy in myself, the pills were working and I was getting regular check-ups.”

Since the cardiac arrest, he has undergone physiotherapy and talking therapy as he continues his recovery. Marvin said: “I’m incredibly grateful to Michael and Richard for their fast thinking and what they did.

‌



“I definitely feel very lucky that I’m able to walk out of that situation and I’m happy that these football pitches were equipped with defibs and somebody had the courage to use them. Otherwise I wouldn’t be here now.”

The British Heart Foundation says more than 40,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests happen in the UK each year and fewer than one in 10 people survive. New research from the charity found 69% of football fans believe fear could stop them from using a defibrillator during a cardiac arrest.

Richard said: “People need to be aware that the (defibrillator) machines are not something to be scared of. Having more of them across the country will save lives, just like it did with Marvin’s.”

Article continues below

The British Heart Foundation and Sky Bet are using their Every Minute Matters campaign to tackle fears around defibrillator use, with 400 community machines being funded over three years.

News.title: Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci convicted of war crimes including murder and torture
News.content:
Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci convicted of war crimes including murder and torture

Hashim Thaci has been convicted of war crimes committed during Kosovo's war for independence from Serbia

View Image Hashim Thaci (Image: ANP/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Former Kosovo president Hashim Thaci has been convicted of war crimes, including murder and torture.

‌



The 58-year-old has been sentenced to 25 years in prison after being convicted of four counts of war crimes committed during Kosovo's war for independence from Serbia. Thaci resigned from his role almost six years ago to face the charges.

‌



He was convicted by a panel of judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague, the Netherlands, of murder, torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention. This was during his role as top commander of the ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) in the 1990s.

‌



Wearing a suit and tie, Thaci, who can appeal against his conviction, stood in silence as Presiding Judge Charles Smith read out the sentence. Mr Smith said Thaci "used his position, leadership, authority and standing" to encourage crimes.

The American judge said, however, that the trial was "not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army" or its ultimate goal of securing independence for Kosovo, which at the time was a province in Serbia. Three other former KLA leaders who fought Serbian forces in the 1998-1999 war also faced similar war crimes accusations.

The four were all acquitted on six charges of crimes against humanity because the judges said the prosecutors failed to prove that crimes were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians. The prosecutors had asked for a maximum 45-year prison sentence for Thaci and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi.

‌



All denied the charges against them. Veseli was sentenced to 18 years, Selimi to 13 years and Krasniqi to 25 years in prison. All four were found guilty for the war crimes of arbitrary illegal detention against 385 people, torture of 303 people, cruel treatment against 49 people and murder of 96 political opponents.

All four are widely regarded as national heroes in Kosovo and thousands rallied in Prisina - Kosovo's capital - over the weekend in the defendants' support. The protesters filled a central square in the capital, many carrying red and black Albanian flags.

Portraits of the four former KLA fighters have been plastered across the city along with a huge digital clock counting down to today's verdicts. There was no immediate reaction from Thaci’s supporters who packed the court’s public gallery.

‌



Hundreds more supporters were waiting outside the courthouse in The Hague. In Pristina, thousands of people watched the reading of the verdict live on a huge screen and were stunned at the sentence.

Some started shouting "UCK", the Albanian-language acronym for the Kosovo Liberation Army that Thaci once led before entering politics. One supporter, Bekim Fetahu, said the verdict was "a catastrophic decision".

He said: "They (judges) have put the victims together with the aggressors." As his trial ended in February, Thaci told judges: "Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice."

‌



He also faces a separate trial on charges of intimidating witnesses, due to begin later this month. Thaci, a student at the time, returned from what he described as political exile in Switzerland to join Kosovo's struggle for independence.

He was nicknamed "the Snake" for his ability to evade Serbian forces during the conflict. Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians.

A 78-day campaign of NATO airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About one million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.

Article continues below

In 2008, Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia, a move that Belgrade - the Serbian capital - refuses to recognise. Ties between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense, despite years of negotiations mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.

News.title: Mrs Hinch fans 14p drying clothes method that avoids Martin Lewis 'demon appliance'
News.content:
Mrs Hinch fans 14p drying clothes method that avoids Martin Lewis 'demon appliance'

The weather has turned but some appliances cost almost £1.50 an hour to run

View Image Homeowners are trying to find ways to dry clothes without using the 'demon appliance' (Image: Getty)

It’s the time of year when chilldren are back at school generating masses of washing - but the weather has taken a turn for the worse. Just a month or so ago it was so hot and dry that parents could hang the wet clothes outside and they’d be bone dry in an hour.

‌



People may be tempted to use the tumble dryer - but Martin Lewis has described it as a ‘demon appliance’ and one which uses far too much power. This winter people are facing massive fuel bill rises -

‌



From 1 October 2026, Ofgem’s energy price cap will increase by 3.6% (around £60 a year), raising the annual bill for a typical household paying by Direct Debit from £1,663 to £1,723. Mr Lewis warned that the January price cap is presently forecast to climb by approximately 10 per cent to 15 per cent compared to the cap taking effect this October, with the Iran war blamed.

‌



At £1.46 per cycle for some dryers the amount spent on energy drying clothes can be considerable and add up in winter months. A dehumidifier can cost around 14p an hour to run.

On the Mrs Hinch Made Me Do It Facebook page fans have been discussing the best ways to dry washing. One parent said: “Hello, looking for advice for dying clothes. Don’t have a tumble drier and have 2 kids under 2 so have lots of washings. I have a heated clothes airer (Lakeland) but clothes still very damp even after 8 hours? Also have radiator racks but clothes don’t dry on them either. I have seen a lot of you talk about dehumidifiers. Would this solve my problems? Really don’t have spare cash to fork out for one if it’s hardly going to work.”

People described a ‘game changer’ which transforms the performance of clothes horses and heaters. According to experts people advocate getting a dehumidifier - and using an old duvet cover or sheet.

‌



One said: “Airer, put an old double duvet cover over radiator and airer, tuck it in. My clothes dry in couple of hours. Do a extra spin first.”

Martin Lewis advice to anyone with £5,000 or less in Premium Bonds READ MORE :

A follower said: “I saw a post the other day a woman put a sheet over the clothes on the heated airer and did the same with ones on the radiator. I tried worked brilliantly.”

Some advocate dehumidifyers: “I’ve got one and highly recommend it, mine has a laundry dry function and can dry heavy jeans and work trousers In about 3 hours, costs 8p an hour to run. Mine keeps the whole house condensation free. While it was a fair amount to pay out initially it is paying for itself as the whole house is warmer with it running so I’m not needing heating on no where near as much as usual”

‌



A homeowner said: “Massive difference using dehumidifier cuts drying time right down also noticed a difference in the house temperature.”

“I use a dehumidifier, it cost me £40, I plug it in under the airer, also prevents damp because it draws in the water. I also got one for my daughter in Uni to save her money on drying costs.”

Mr Lewis pinpointed the tumble dryer as the appliance households should limit using wherever feasible, highlighting its £1-per-load running cost. He said: “Do you know what the real ‘demon appliance’ is in most people’s houses - the one that you don’t want to use because it’s really expensive. Tumble dryers.

Article continues below

“You’re typically paying up to a quid per load, so dry your clothes on an airer outside, to shorten the amount of time you’re using your tumble dryer, or avoid using it completely. Those who have dehumidifiers can take some of the moisture out of the air. It’s less wattage than a tumble dryer, so it can be more cost-effective.”

News.title: Full list as seven bank holidays confirmed to move in 2027
News.content:
Full list as seven bank holidays confirmed to move in 2027

There will be eight bank holidays in England and Wales next year

View Image Many people get bank holidays off work (Image: Busà Photography/Getty)

The full list of 2027 bank holidays has been confirmed, with seven of those observed by England and Wales to change dates next year.

‌



Christmas Day and Boxing Day fall on a Saturday and Sunday in 2027, so this will see "substitute" bank holidays observed on Monday, December 27, and Tuesday, December 28. It isn't just weekends that determine when bank holidays fall, either, as the ever-moving Easter date also means Good Friday and Easter Monday move year on year.

‌



There will be eight bank holidays across England and Wales in 2027, with the first being New Year's Day on January 1. Good Friday will fall on Friday, March 26, with Easter Monday following on Monday, March 29 – considerably earlier than the 2026 dates of Friday, April 3, and Monday, April 6.

‌



May's first bank holiday will arrive a day sooner, as these always occur on a Monday, while the second will come later. In 2027, the Early May bank holiday takes place on May 3, with the Spring bank holiday on May 31.

The summer bank holiday, which generally coincides with the end of the school summer break, will be on Monday, August 30, one day earlier than this year's date of August 31.

And to round off the year, the Christmas Day and Boxing Day bank holidays will be recognised on December 27 and 28, as mentioned earlier.

‌



Full list of 2027 bank holidays for England and Wales

Friday, January 1 - New Year's Day

Friday, March 26 - Good Friday

Monday, March 29 - Easter Monday

‌



Monday, May 3 - Early May bank holiday

Monday, May 31 - Spring bank holiday

Monday, August 30 - Summer bank holiday

Article continues below

Monday, December 27 - Christmas Day (substitute day)

Tuesday, December 28 - Boxing Day (substitute day)

News.title: Petrol and diesel price rises push UK inflation higher
News.content:
Rises in petrol, diesel and airfares pushed UK inflation up to its highest level in five months in the year to August.

Inflation accelerated to 3.1% from 2.9%, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The cost of filling up a vehicle soared in August as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt global oil supplies. Petrol prices jumped to their highest for nearly four years, the ONS said, while diesel also rocketed.

Meanwhile, the cost of flying jumped during the key month for summer getaways.

Overall, motor fuel prices rose by 23% compared to August last year.

Oil hit more than $91 a barrel as the US-Israel war with Iran went on. That compares to around $73 just before hostilities began earlier this year.

As a result, average petrol prices have continued to climb and between July and August, they rose by 9.1p to 161.3p per litre.

"This is the highest price recorded since November 2022," said the ONS. At that point, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine had pushed up global energy costs.

News.title: How being music's Mr Nice Guy contributed to biggest crisis of Ed Sheeran's career
News.content:
Singer Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his career after a storm over a decision to drop support act Macklemore from his US stadium tour following the rapper's on-stage pro-Palestinian comments.

Sheeran is one of the most successful songwriters of all time. He has sold more than 120 million records and spent more than 1,000 weeks on the US album charts.

Part of his appeal - apart from those insidiously catchy songs - is his everyman persona. He looks and dresses like a fan on the train home from Glastonbury, rather than one of the festival's headliners.

He has carefully cultivated a non-threatening, everyone welcome public image. In 2014, he donated his entire wardrobe to charity shops. The same year, he adopted a one-month-old kitten, saving it from euthanasia, and named it Graham. Today, he runs a charity providing music lessons to under-18s in his home county of Sussex.

He tries to stay out of politics - usually only getting involved to campaign for issues like copyright protection and ticket touting, or to raise concerns over the impact of Brexit on touring musicians.

But like most artists, he leans left. In 2017, he said he supported then-Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, despite not endorsing him at the stump.

"People thought that, because I didn't put myself behind him, I wasn't a Corbyn supporter," Sheeran told the Sunday Times. "If you knew me as a person, and listened to my music, you would be able to make a pretty educated guess that he would be the kind of person I really dig."

When it comes to non-musical issues, Sheeran prefers to remain circumspect. His reasoning, he says, is that music should unite. He views his concerts as a "place of safety and sanctuary" built on shared humanity.

This week, that argument has come crumbling down - creating a crisis for his reputation and career.

News.title: Village votes to leave UK over asylum housing plan in symbolic referendum
News.content:
Residents of an Oxfordshire village have voted to become independent from the UK in a symbolic referendum held in protest at plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at a former military base.

Villagers in Piddington, near Bicester, voted on Tuesday over Home Office proposals to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at nearby MoD Bicester.

The referendum was organised by the parish council and out of 312 votes cast, 285 voted to leave, 26 voted no, and one ballot paper was spoiled.

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy told BBC Breakfast the government would not reconsider the migrant housing proposal.

Piddington's 350 residents were invited to cast their ballot in a small box outside the village hall.

Delivering the result, parish council vice chair Susannah Parden said: "We are Piddington the village that roars."

Parish council chair Tim McNally added: "This is an example of democracy in operation.

"We went into this village hall as the underdogs - we had a plucky idea. We have given a message to the world."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he understood the village's "strength of feeling" but there needed to be fairness across the country.

"The only thing to do is to get the numbers down, the number of crossings down," he said. "And they are significantly down. They are now at a seven-year low.

"We also made a commitment to people to end the use of hotels to house refugees and asylum seekers, and that commitment needs to be honoured, and I think the vast majority of people say 'yeah, that really does need to proceed'.

"So this involves difficult difficult decisions. It's about fairness across the country. I'm not saying that only one part of the country or one group of communities should do all of the work."

Nandy said that reconsidering the MoD Bicester plan would not be fair.

"The alternative would be to ask communities who have already seen their local community quadruple in size to take more of the load - and I think that's deeply unfair," she said.

Nandy said Piddington was "not actually" unusual, adding: "In my constituency there are particular streets where that has happened to the community."

But she said the government was listening to the Piddington campaigners.

"I do really understand that when changes are made that affect your community it can be very distressing.

"We inherited an enormous asylum backlog, we are processing claims much more quickly, we are removing people who don't have the right to be here.

"Small boat crossings fell this summer for the first time in many years because of the action we have taken.

"While we get a grip on the asylum chaos that we inherited we do need to make sure that we live up to our obligations and house people coming to this country seeking safety."

News.content:
The head of AI company Anthropic has called for the pace of development of artificial intelligence models to slow down and to be closely monitored, and other AI leaders have joined him. But US President Donald Trump is opposing calls to regulate the technology.

The BBC's North America editor Sarah Smith explains the two reasons that are keeping the US president from regulating AI.
