News.title: Lucy Letby: Families' solicitor blames hospital bosses for police delay
News.content:
A solicitor representing seven of the families affected by Lucy Letby's crimes has said responsibility for the delay in contacting the police "lies squarely" with hospital executives.

On Tuesday, the Thirlwall Inquiry report revealed bosses at the Countess of Chester Hospital repeatedly failed in their duty of candour to parents, investigators and regulators.

Tamlin Bolton said each of the 1,100 pages of Lady Justice Thirlwall's findings contained "another opportunity where action could have been taken".

In a statement, former hospital executives named in the report said they were reviewing its findings and recommendations, but could not comment further while investigations remained under way.

Lucy Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms for the murder of seven babies and the attempted murder of seven others, including one baby whom she tried to murder twice.

The offences took place between 2015 and 2016, but concerns raised by consultants were not reported to police until May 2017.

News.title: Kosovo's former president sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
News.content:
The former president of Kosovo, Hashim Thaci, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison after being found guilty of war crimes.

A hearing at The Hague on Wednesday sentenced the 58-year-old for crimes during Kosovo's independence war against Serbia in the 1990s, in which more than 10,000 people died.

He was convicted after a three-year trial of crimes including murder, illegal arrests, torture and cruel treatment. A number of other allegations against him were not proven.

Thaci was a co-founder and commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), a group that fought for independence. He is regarded as a hero in Kosovo.

He was accused of killing nearly 100 people and of committing other atrocities including enforced disappearances.

Thaci was facing trial alongside three former commanders of the KLA who faced similar charges.

News.title: Burnham thanks well-wishers following his father's death
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has thanked party leaders for their support following the death of his father, Roy, on Monday.

All opposition leaders sent condolences to him as he cancelled engagements earlier this week.

Burnham had previously spoken about the fact his dad did not know he had become prime minister, due to his advanced Alzheimer's.

Posting on social media, he thanked, external "everyone who has shared a kind message about my dad, particularly the leaders of the other parties".

Burnham added: "My family and I have been helped though this difficult time by people's warmth and compassion. It means a great deal to us and we wanted to say thank you."

Speaking to journalists on his first day back at work on Wednesday, Burnham thanked all those who had sent "so many lovely messages" to him and his family.

"It's hard and it will be hard for a little while but better to get back to the job," he said.

"I also want to thank the leaders of the other parties, all of whom sent a message, and it shows there is decency in British politics still and that's lovely to see, so thank you from us all, the whole family.

"But my dad would want me to be back out there bringing some of the changes that he always pushed me to make."

He has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

News.title: Watch: Will Ed Sheeran cancel his tour as support acts quit?
News.content:
Ed Sheeran's backing band and all of his support acts have pulled out of the artist's US tour.

It began when rapper Macklemore was dropped from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian comments on stage.

Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was made by his tour promoter, not him.

The BBC's Mark Savage looks at how this change may impact Sheeran's upcoming gigs.

News.title: UK in talks about joining global defence bank led by Canada
News.content:
The UK government is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

Chancellor John Healey is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Treasury officials stressed that no decision has been made. A government spokesperson said it was "fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity."

Before he cancelled commitments due to the death of his father, Prime Minister Andy Burnham had been due to meet Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney in the UK on Wednesday.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte is also travelling to the UK for his first meeting with the prime minister.

He is giving a speech in Oxfordshire, where he is expected to say the UK is "serious about security" and praise the country's efforts supporting Ukraine.

He will also say that Nato will "not be intimidated by Russia's campaign of hostile actions.

"Russia wants to stop us helping Ukraine â but their actions will only lead us to do more for Ukraine."

It comes after Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high amid Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

And on Tuesday Denmark also accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.

The DSRB is a multilateral bank aimed at providing cheaper loans to fund defence projects and has backing from Albania, Bulgaria, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine.

Membership of the bank for the UK and other G7 countries would come with an upfront investment cost of around Â£870m spread over three years.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

The government has so far avoided committing to raising defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030, only repeating the longer term goal of 3.5% by 2035.

News.title: Nandy pledges crackdown on 'doxxing' after RNLI volunteers see personal details online
News.content:
Lisa Nandy has vowed to strengthen the law on "doxxing" after lifeboat volunteers involved in migrant crossing rescues had their personal details published online.

The culture secretary said she would "tighten up the law" to make doxxing, which involves leaking people's home addresses, a criminal offence.

Currently, she said this kind of behaviour is only illegal if it is done with clear intent to cause fear, harm and distress.

Nandy convened a meeting with social media firms on Tuesday afternoon to discuss such abuse, but she called social media company X a "disgrace" for failing to turn up.

Last week, the chief executive of the RNLI - the Royal National Lifeboat Institute - condemned online and physical abuse volunteers for the charity had received over English Channel migrant crossings.

That followed protests after 120 people landed on Portsmouth's shores from France with the RNLI's assistance.

Nandy told BBC Breakfast she was "appalled" that the likes of RNLI volunteers, police officers, social workers and journalists were "being doxxed online" - having their names, photos and addresses published.

In her meeting with social media companies, she said she found "wildly varying standards" from them on doxxing material.

TikTok told her it would automatically remove such posts while Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said it would not, she said.

"And frankly, X didn't even bother to turn up yesterday which shows real contempt for people's safety and security and their obligations to society," she added.

She said the government "will not hesitate to take action" to make clear that "where people's addresses are being published online, that is an offence and action has to be taken swiftly".

A source close to Meta said it removes content that shares, offers or solicits personally identifiable information that could lead to physical harm.

It is undersood the Crown Prosecution Service can currently treat doxxing under offences such as malicious communications if a victim is threatened or harassed.

BBC Verify found viral social media posts about those involved in migrant crossing operations, some of which wrongly identified RNLI crew members and called for their families to be tracked down.

The RNLI has said only 109 of its 9,058 lifeboat launches last year were for people "in distress in the Channel" - 1.2% of its total rescue work.

The charity's chief executive added around 95% of small boats were intercepted by the UK Border Force.

Nandy has also taken aim at "incredibly slow" progress with enforcement of the Online Safety Act, the government's flagship law to tackle online abuse, as she called for regulator Ofcom to move faster.

Describing the "major challenges" with enforcing the Act, she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme two penalties had so far been issued to companies but no fines had yet been paid.

News.title: Judge explains compassionate release of murderer who failed to return to NI jail
News.content:
Speaking on Wednesday, Justice Minister Naomi Long said she believed the prison service had reached "the right conclusion" in relation to Anderson's release.

"They have the experience of doing these assessments on an ongoing basis. They felt it wasn't safe on this occasion for him to be released," Long said.

"But he has rights. He was able to exercise those rights in the court and a judge with that information reached a different conclusion."

That, the minster said, is "part of the process" and "entirely legitimate".

Long said the majority of prisoners on short term release return to custody as required.

"This is an unusual situation that we find ourselves in but it is a deeply concerning one," she said.

"It is not about apportioning blame, it is about trying to find out how we ensure this doesn't happen again but also how we get this person back into custody."

The minister, who urged Anderson to hand himself over to police, said he is "a threat to the public and he is potentially also at risk."

However, the DUP MLA Trevor Clarke, who sits on the policing board, said the whole process needed looked at.

"I think there's clear evidence that there was an issue in this case and that's now been borne out because this person hasn't come back," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.

"All of the things that the courts have involved themselves in this one, I think, has been wrong.

"A chaperone as opposed to a proper prison guard, this is an individual who cannot even handcuff the person while they're chaperoned, so all of the safeguards that could have been put in place weren't put in place."

On Wednesday, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed that Anderson was last seen in the Eastway area of Creggan in Derry.

They also confirmed that they were liaising with An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na (Irish police).

News.title: Colonel cleared over handling of soldier abuse case
News.content:
A senior Army officer has been cleared of failing to properly deal with abuse allegations made by a teenage soldier who took her own life.

Col Samantha Shepherd has been on trial at Military Court Centre at Catterick Garrison in North Yorkshire, in connection with the handling of concerns raised by Gunner Jaysley Beck, from Cumbria.

The 19-year-old took her own life at Larkhill Camp in Wiltshire in 2021 after former Battery Sgt Michael Webber "pinned her down" and sexually assaulted her.

A board - which consisted of an Air Commodore, a Royal Navy captain and an Army colonel - returned a not guilty verdict for Shepherd, on the directions of a judge.

News.title: Husband who drugged and raped wife for 20 years no longer part of trial
News.content:
A man who drugged and raped his wife for more than 20 years without her knowledge will no longer be involved in a trial involving other defendants, a jury has heard.

The husband, aged in his 60s and from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, has admitted a total of 60 offences against the woman including rape, assault by penetration, administering a substance with intent and sharing indecent images without her consent.

Twelve other men are still due to go on trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court accused of serious sexual offences - including rape - against the same woman.

The nine women and three men of the jury, plus two female reserve jurors, have been asked to return to court on 5 October.

The court has heard the husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, has admitted abusing his wife since 2004.

He had already pleaded guilty to 15 offences against her going back to 2022, but admitted to a further 45 counts on Monday.

His wife, who was comforted by other members of her family, watched from the public gallery as he answered "guilty" to dozens of charges.

News.title: Parents of Southport attack victim 'devastated' by data breach
News.content:
The parents of a child injured in the Southport attack have said they are "devastated" after court files were accessed without authorisation.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said an urgent investigation had been launched after court files detailing victims, their families and survivors of the attack on the dance class in July 2024 were accessed without authorisation.

It comes after it emerged earlier this year that the North West Ambulance Service (NWAS) was looking into whether staff inappropriately accessed the records of victims.

The parents of one of the injured children said: "Our family has once again been devastated by two data breaches that involve our daughter, NWAS and now the MoJ."

The parents, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, continued: "This culture of snooping across agencies and services must end and that will only happen if those individuals are held to account and not protected by the very confidentiality laws they flouted to access our daughter's information.

"We expect each of these despicable individuals to lose their jobs, and full transparency from NWAS and the MoJ about what happened to the information they stole.

"Two years on, our focus should be on our daughter's continuing recovery, not having to manage further failures by the state that have put our daughter at risk once again."

News.title: Third Heathrow runway should only go ahead if airlines pay for cleaner flying, say advisers
News.content:
Heathrow's third runway cannot be approved without changes to current climate policies, the government's advisers have said.

The Climate Change Committee (CCC) , externalsaid expansion can still go ahead but only if the aviation industry funds cleaner fuels and pays for machines that suck carbon dioxide out of the air.

Making the industry pay could push up the cost of flying with a return trip to Alicante costing around Â£150 more by 2050, and a return to New York up Â£400 in today's prices, it said.

Once built, the expanded airport would produce more carbon dioxide than any other single sector of the economy by 2050. Heathrow said expansion and climate goals were "not a choice" and it would deliver both.

"Our advice today is clear - Heathrow expansion is not currently compatible with the UK's Net Zero target," said Nigel Topping, the CCC chair.

"Government needs to ensure that the aviation industry takes responsibility for the emissions it creates and bears the costs of decarbonisation. Those conditions do not exist today."

The CCC report cannot block a new runway but it wants the government to pass legislation pushing responsibility for the long-term clean-up of aviation onto the industry.

The government would "carefully consider" the advice alongside other responses to its consultation according to the Department for Transport (DfT).

The government has an ongoing consultation which aims to judge any expansion against four tests - economy, climate, air quality and noise.

It does not approve a runway - that will come in a Commons vote expected later this year.

The Â£33bn project would raise Heathrow's capacity to 150 million passengers a year - up from 85 million.

A DfT spokesperson said any expansion would need to align with the country's climate targets, but added it "could deliver around Â£40bn to the economy and support up to 60,000 local jobs".

News.title: Baby born during Harry Potter screening has 'Cineworld' on birth certificate
News.content:
Molly said that when she went to register the newborn, she was asked where the baby was born.

"We had to say Cineworld in Broughton, and it does say on her birth certificate, Cineworld Broughton," she said.

Molly went to the cinema with her parents and Alfie on 28 August, the day after her due date, having attended a midwife appointment for a sweep earlier that afternoon.

But about 40 to 45 minutes into the film, the labour pains began.

Molly said: "I can remember the scene I was watching when I walked out. It was when Hagrid and Harry are buying his stuff to go to Hogwarts.

"I thought, 'something doesn't feel right'. It was getting more and more intense, and I didn't want anything to go wrong.

"At that point I think my body just went into shock and it was pure adrenalin."

Cineworld manager Michelle McClean and team leader Leah Prytherch were among those who helped as staff called 999 and gathered towels and sheets.

Molly said: "The staff at Cineworld and Starbucks were absolutely amazing.

"They shielded me with towels and sheets so no-one could see. They were absolutely amazing."

Describing the moment she gave birth, she said: "I said to my mum, 'I feel like I need to push,' and she said, 'you can't'.

"I said, 'I can't, I need to. I've got to'. Two pushes and my daughter was out."

Molly gave birth to Elsie Lamb at 16:57 BST.

There were no medical professionals present at the moment Elsie arrived, with Molly's mum picking her granddaughter up and placing her on Molly's chest.

A rapid response paramedic arrived moments later.

Animal rights activists are trying to stop the proposed relocation of four young elephants from India’s northeast to be given as “gifts” to Hindu temples in the south, a process that will involve an arduous journey of thousands of kilometres by road.

The elephants due to be transferred have been identified as Rupsing, 13; Shiva, 6; Hiralal, 8; and Bijuli, 5, according to the non-profit People for Cattle in India (PFCI), which has raised serious questions over the circumstances surrounding the relocations.

PFCI said the elephants face a journey of nearly 3,000km (1800 miles) by road from Assam to Tamil Nadu, raising concerns over the welfare implications of subjecting young animals to such a lengthy travel.

open image in gallery Durga was left Assam on the night of 7 September and reached Madurai on the night of 13 September, covering approximately 3,000 km in around six days ( Supplied )

One elephant, five-year-old Durga, has already been moved from Assam’s Manas National Park area to the Madurai Meenakshi Amman Temple in Tamil Nadu. Durga arrived at the temple on Sunday, six days after leaving Assam on 7 September.

A video released by the Meenakshi Temple Management appears to show the young elephant swaying from side to side, with her front two legs chained.

The Independent has reached out to the Madurai Meenakshi Amman Temple for comment.

Arun Prasanna G, founder of the Chennai-based PFCI, tells The Independent the transfer of elephants should be investigated, including questions surrounding their ownership, the basis for their transfer, and the parties involved in their acquisition.

“We are already horrified with the transfer of Durga, who is appearing distressed in the video after she arrived at her destination following a journey of six days,” he says.

“She’s already chained on her legs. She’s so anxious. When she was loaded onto the vehicle, the mother was heard screaming,” he says, citing locals and reports.

open image in gallery Durga is among five elephants set to be moved from Assam to Tamil Nadu ( Supplied )

“What kind of welfare is this?” he asks.

He says Durga, who was allegedly transferred discreetly without adequate public disclosure, travelled an average of nearly 500km per day.

“This raises an extremely serious welfare and legal question in light of the Kerala High Court’s 13 November 2024 directions prescribing a maximum of 125km of elephant transportation per day, along with limits on vehicle travel time and speed,” Prasanna says.

“The authorities must disclose Durga’s complete journey log, including the vehicle’s movement, kilometres travelled each day, driving hours, speed, rest periods and halts, and explain how a journey averaging around 500km per day complied with the applicable safeguard,” he adds.

Animal welfare groups and conservationists have long raised concerns over the treatment and commercialisation of elephants in India, where the animals are widely used in tourism, temple rituals, festivals, safaris and entertainment, despite being protected under wildlife laws.

Both Hindu and Buddhist traditions give elephants an elevated status. They are used to give blessings and perform sacred duties. In Hinduism, elephants are closely linked to the elephant-headed deity Ganesh.

Indian laws make it illegal to capture, hunt, trade, or harm elephants, but those that were born in captivity or captive before the laws came into place continue to be used for a range of purposes which rights activists say amount to abuse. They exist in a kind of legal grey zone – they cannot be sold, but non-commercial “transfers” of ownership are permitted.

The transfer of Durga was cleared by the Tamil Nadu Forest Department last week. Clearance for the other four is awaited, according to The Hindu newspaper.

Tamil Nadu chief wildlife warden, Rakesh Kumar Dogra, says the “No Objection Certificate” (NOC) for the transfer was issued last week.

“Before the NOC, the District Captive Elephant Management Committee (a local regulatory body) inspected the premises and checked the availability of facilities such as mud bath, water bath and walking space,” he says.

The proposed transfer of the five elephants was challenged in court by another Chennai-based organisation, Seva Trust.

open image in gallery Animal rights activists have claimed Durga looks distressed in videos released by temple ( Supplied )

The court was informed that Durga’s transfer to the Meenakshi temple had received clearance, while applications concerning the other four elephants were still pending. The court directed the state to take a decision on the pending applications within a week and posted the matter for 16 September.

State authorities have said the privately held elephants are being donated to the temples.

PFCI and other welfare organisations have questioned the ownership claims and alleged that the animals are being moved from national parks and reserves rather than being given up by previous owners.

“If you want to give up your animals, normally what people do when they can’t keep their pets is give their animals up for adoption, or to boarding facilities, shelters and sanctuaries. Why would somebody transfer these elephants 3,000km away?” Prasanna says.

The Independent has reached out to the Tamil Nadu forest department for comment.

“The elephants are being ripped [away] from their mothers at such a young age. If the owner is donating them, did the mother also abandon them? What happens to the well-being of the mother, who would be distressed?” he asks.

He also questions the speed with which the transfer paperwork was processed, alleging that the required documentation had been completed within hours.

“The striking part is, the entire paperwork was done in 7.5 hours. The forest department never does any paperwork in less than 15 days. How did they process the paperwork in seven and a half hours?” he says.

Prasanna alleges that the circumstances surrounding the transfers pointed to a wider network involved in the movement and possible trade of elephants.

open image in gallery Mahouts wait with decorated elephants during Jal Yatra, a Hindu religious procession from Lord Jagannath temple to Sabarmati riverfront in Ahmedabad on June 29, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

“So there is a big nexus involved. There are middlemen. There are brokers. Elephant trading is happening big time. Both governments are turning a blind eye, or are part of it. This is a big scam,” he says.

He argues that the animals could face decades of confinement at temples. “An elephant can live for 70 or 80 years. From five or six years old now until she dies, she’s going to be in the temple in confinement,” he said.

The campaigner challenged the claim that the transfers were intended to provide the elephants with better care.

“You are saying the elephant is sent to some other place for better upkeep. What is better upkeep in a temple?” he says.

According to a letter dated 7 September, seen by The Independent, the Assam Forest Department assigned four officials to conduct the transportation of Durga from Manas National Park to the Madhurai temple.

Assam-based conservationist Rohit Choudhury has urged a Supreme Court-appointed committee to immediately halt the transfer, raising questions over the legality, purpose and welfare implications of moving the elephants out of Assam.

Shurthi Vinodraj, former member of Tamil Nadu Animal Welfare Board (TNAWB), has also raised objections to moving the elephants. “This is a clear violation of standing Supreme Court guidelines and rules. We don’t know who is giving instructions to flout rules. This has to be stopped immediately,'' she said.

open image in gallery Hindu devotees gather around an adorned robotic elephant, newly donated by the Voice for Asian Elephants Society (VFAES) for religious rituals at the Chakkamparambu Bhagavathy temple in Thrissur, in India's Kerala state ( AFP/Getty )

P Chokkalingam, chief executive officer, TNAWB, also said that they had not given any assent to bringing in these elephants.

“We came to know about the incident only through some Whatsapp complaints. Since these elephants are being transported crossing various state borders, they must have to get approval from the Animal Welfare Board of India. We will inquire into the incident and report to the government about the incident,'' he says.

Andy Burnham is facing calls to ensure the UK does not fall behind its international allies after the European Union opened the door to Canada becoming its first 'associate member'.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed the new status as Canada and the EU both deal with the fallout from Donald Trump’s trade tariffs.

She said the EU and Canada would work together across sectors from manufacturing to AI, critical minerals and energy, although the details of the arrangement would have to be negotiated.

open image in gallery European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed the new status for Canada ( AP )

Experts say up to 8 per cent of GDP has been wiped off the UK economy by Brexit, through lost trade and increased red tape.

Andy Burnham has said he wants to be “bolder” than his predecessor in resetting relations with the bloc, but has also vowed to honour Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to rule out rejoining the customs union and single market or allowing free movement of people, Labour’s so-called ‘red lines’.

Nick Boles, the former Tory minister who helped to prepare Labour for office before it entered government in 2024, said the idea of associate membership was “very positive and it is definitely something the UK should explore”.

Last month Mr Boles published a blueprint he believes could see Britain strike a deal with EU leaders that would protect the continent and offer the UK a much-needed economic boost, by effectively trading defence capability and access to the single market in a new European confederation.

He questioned if the new status would provide material economic benefits, address security questions and the EU’s “own concerns about granting freedom of movement to Ukrainians, Albanians etc?”

But he added: “If the answer to those questions is ‘yes’, associate membership is definitely something the UK should embrace.”

Mark English, from campaign group European Movement UK, called on the UK to follow Canada’s “proactive example” when it comes to a relationship with the bloc.

open image in gallery Canadian PM Mark Carney is due to meet Andy Burnham ( AFP/Getty )

"Canada's positive and rapidly developing transatlantic relationship with the EU is a win for both sides,” he told The Independent. “It shows the EU is a powerful and attractive power for good in the world, and it shows the value of democracies standing together against illiberal forces.

“The UK’s relationship with the EU, from right next door, is even more economically and geopolitically important. So we need to follow Canada's proactive example and get it moving again, by sewing up deals on youth experience, food and energy, and then going further."

Naomi Smith, the chief executive of Best for Britain, which campaigns for the UK to restore its EU membership, said that while the PM and Canadian PM Mark Carney are due to watch Everton play later there is “more than football our two countries have in common”.

Both economies “are being squeezed by the inflationary impact of Trump's trade wars, deepening the cost of living crisis for their citizens, and neither can count on the US as a reliable trading partner, and both are threatened by an authoritarian in Moscow determined to destroy our liberal democracies,” she said.

“Carney is treating the EU as the strategic asset it is, and the UK must do the same, going much further than the status quo to signal our intention to apply for membership. Voters want it, our economy needs it, and Burnham can deliver it.”

News.title: 12 best dry shampoos for fresher-looking hair, tried and tested
News.content:
Your questions about dry shampoo answered

What is the best dry shampoo?

After weeks of testing, K18’s airwash emerged as the best dry shampoo, even with its sky-high price taken into account. Unlike traditional powder-heavy formulas, its liquid spray left both of our heads of hair feeling freshly washed and without the stiffness, chalkiness or scalp build-up that so often comes with dry shampoos. We were both impressed by how little product was needed, how weightless it felt and how effectively it revived oily roots while adding moveable volume. Ultimately, all its many merits made the steep price tag feel easier to justify, especially given that one bottle lasted more than six months in testing.

Elsewhere, Batiste’s colour dry shampoo proved a reliable budget buy, Living Proof’s original PhD formula delivered the deepest clean, Sam McKnight’s lazy girl dry shampoo excelled on fine hair thanks to its undetectable texture, while Typebea’s scalp-focused formula stood out for its lightweight texture.

How we tested dry shampoos

To find the best dry shampoos, I tested a wide range of aerosols, liquid sprays and powder applicators across several months (and, in some cases, years), assessing how well they refreshed oily roots, boosted volume and held up throughout the day.

I called on a tester with brunette hair to judge residue levels and blendability across deeper hues, while I focused on how the formulas fared on my fine, blonde hair prone to flattening, clumping and oiliness. Specifically, we took the following factors into consideration:

Oil absorption: We assessed how effectively each formula disguised greasy roots and whether hair looked noticeably cleaner after application.

We assessed how effectively each formula disguised greasy roots and whether hair looked noticeably cleaner after application. Texture: We considered whether the dry shampoo left strands soft and touchable or stiff, chalky and cloying

We considered whether the dry shampoo left strands soft and touchable or stiff, chalky and cloying White cast: We noted how visible each formula appeared on both blonde and brunette hair, and how easy it was to blend in.

We noted how visible each formula appeared on both blonde and brunette hair, and how easy it was to blend in. Volume: We tested whether formulas added noticeable lift and body, particularly at the roots and crown

We tested whether formulas added noticeable lift and body, particularly at the roots and crown Longevity: We monitored how long results lasted before hair began looking oily or flat again.

We monitored how long results lasted before hair began looking oily or flat again. Scent: We took into account the various dry shampoo fragrances, both immediately and, where applicable, as they developed throughout the day.

We took into account the various dry shampoo fragrances, both immediately and, where applicable, as they developed throughout the day. Ease of application: We considered how evenly the product dispersed and how convenient the packaging felt

We considered how evenly the product dispersed and how convenient the packaging felt Value for money: We weighed up performance against price, factoring in how much product was needed per use and how quickly bottles ran out.

What is the best dry shampoo for fine hair?

“For fine hair, you want a dry shampoo that refreshes the scalp without coating the strands too heavily,” reveals hair stylist Lorraine Dublin. Specifically, she suggests looking out for the following buzzwords on product packaging:

Lightweight

Invisible finish

Volume boosting

Weightless

She tells me about the ingredients fine hair types should keep an eye out for when shopping dry shampoos, particularly “rice starch and tapioca starch.”

“Try to avoid formulas with heavy oils, thick powders or overly fragranced ingredients, especially if your scalp is sensitive or prone to buildup,” she cautions.

“Personally, I love the pale Ouai dry shampoo and the Living Proof dry shampoo,” feeds in hair stylist Joe Kelly, “I use both regularly on clients because they give that airy, fluffy texture without making the hair feel sticky or overloaded with product.”

How to use dry shampoo

“You can use dry shampoo from the roots all the way through to the ends, depending on the effect you want to achieve,” advises Kelly.

Breaking down the different ways of using dry shampoo, he lists:

“If it’s just to absorb oil or grease, apply it mainly at the scalp and roots. A practical guideline would be around 2–3 sprays.”

“If you want texture, movement, and a more lived-in finish, spray it throughout the hair. Around 3-4 sprays.”

Expanding on Kelly’s advice, Dublin feeds in, “Massage the dry shampoo gently with your fingertips or brush through to evenly distribute the product. Let it sit for a minute or two so the product has time to absorb oil properly.”

“Applying dry shampoo the night before can actually work really well because it gives the product time to absorb oil overnight and leaves the hair looking fresher by morning,” she adds.

Is dry shampoo bad for hair?

“Dry shampoo itself is not bad for the hair when used correctly and in moderation,” clarifies Dublin. She continues, “The issue usually comes from overuse or not cleansing the scalp properly between applications.”

This is because, she elaborates, “A healthy scalp environment matters and dry shampoo should be seen as a styling and refresh product, not a replacement for washing the hair.”

Can dry shampoo cause hair loss?

“Dry shampoo doesn’t directly cause hair loss,” reassures Kelly, who tells me that “overusing it can irritate the scalp and contribute to issues like buildup, dryness, dandruff or breakage, especially if you already have a dry or sensitive scalp.”

Why you can trust IndyBest reviews

Lucy Smith is a senior shopping writer for IndyBest and is well versed on a number of haircare products, from the best shampoos and conditioners to the best hair brushes. She regularly speaks to hair stylists and trichologists to inform her reviews and, as someone who suffers with oily roots regularly, she was up to the task of testing the very best dry shampoos.

Daisy Lester was IndyBest’s senior shopping writer and has covered all manner of hair treatments, including the Olaplex no.3 plus perfector and the £5 gloss treatment to rival Color Wow’s dream coat. Daisy regularly attends new product launches and expert masterclasses, she’s across all the industry’s movers and shakers. Plus, she’s been using dry shampoos for years and – prior to testing, even – had a good gauge on which brands and formulas were the cream of the crop.

A desperate search is underway to find missing three-year-old Noah Woods who was last seen running away from a playground in Suffolk.

The little boy was last seen at 3pm on Tuesday, Suffolk Police said, when he became separated from a relative after visiting the play area in the village of Brantham.

Hundreds of people are now searching for him, including dozens of volunteers, but as of Wednesday morning on the second day of the search, there were no known sightings of the young boy.

Here, the Independent looks at everything we know about the search for Noah.

open image in gallery Members of a search and rescue team continue their search near Merriam Close, Brantham ( PA )

Who is Noah Woods?

Noah, 3, is described as white with curly ginger hair.

He was last seen wearing a white T-shirt with the TV character Bluey on it, shorts and black Vans trainers with a white stripe.

His father has said he is mildly autistic and has partial hearing loss but is capable of everyday tasks.

open image in gallery The little boy was last seen on Tuesday afternoon ( Family handout/Suffolk Police )

“To clear things up because people really do make up their own stories, he is only mildly autistic and has partial hearing loss, he is fully capable of every day tasks,” Rhys Woods wrote on Facebook.

Suffolk Police said Noah is “described as non-verbal, has partial hearing loss and is currently undergoing an assessment for autism”.

The force said that he will not respond to his name.

When and where did Noah go missing?

Noah was last seen on Tuesday at 3pm, when he became separated from a relative after a visit to Merriam Close playground in Brantham, near Manningtree.

He is believed to have run off down the alleyway beside the playground towards the new build housing estate, police said.

The village has a population of around 2,300 people and is located in the parish of Babergh, Suffolk.

It is on the border of Essex, around 9 miles from Ipswich, and is located near the River Stour, surrounded by picturesque countryside. Nearby villages include Stutton, Tattingstone, East Bergholt and Flatford.

What is the latest on the search?

In an update at 5.40am on Wednesday, Brantham parish council said there had been no confirmed sightings of Noah.

Police said specially trained officers and dog units have been searching the village, located near the estuary of the River Stour.

They have been supported by helicopters from the National Police Air Service and the coastguard, with further support on the ground provided by other agencies and a vast number of members of the public, including local search and rescue teams.

Police earlier asked local residents to thoroughly check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings or any potential areas where a child might hide.

Anyone with private CCTV or doorbell cameras in the village, or who were driving through the area with a dashcam, are asked to review the footage from 3pm yesterday afternoon onwards for any possible sightings of Noah.

open image in gallery Local residents join police officers as they continue their search near Merriam Close, Brantham ( PA )

However, Noah’s father has asked volunteers to avoid searching near the pond close to the playground that he went missing from yesterday.

Mr Woods said the pond had been searched “thoroughly” and the amount of people in the area was “making it hard to pick up the infrared signal we need”.

He said: “We still have nothing, all the emergency services and all of you have shown how strong this community is, with people coming from far and wide also, the emergency services are very confident that the high risk areas (decoy pond, railway lines) are all clear.

“Thank you again for all your help, and I’m praying we find him,” he added.

open image in gallery Local residents wait outside Brantham Village Hall ( PA )

What have the police said?

Suffolk Police have said they are “very concerned” about Noah’s welfare and need to find him as a matter of urgency.

Superintendent Pete Partridge said in a statement:“A vast number of resources have been deployed by ourselves, our emergency services colleagues and volunteers from SULSAR.

These resources have been bolstered by members of the public who have turned out in large numbers to assist and we are incredibly grateful for their help and support.

“Given that fast-moving nature of the investigation, it is important that any public searches are coordinated with police to ensure we are working together, and that our resources are directed where they can be most effective.”

He asked local residents not to “put themselves at risk or undertake independent searches overnight”, adding: “We will continue to keep Noah’s family and the public updated on the progress of our searches and investigation.”

First CCTV images released of Noah

In an update on Wednesday afternoon, police released the first CCTV images and footage of Noah’s last movements at the play park.

Superintendent Tom Pearse said his disappearance is being treated as a missing person investigation and there is nothing to indicate anything sinister or any element of criminality has taken place.

He said: “It has now been around 24 hours since Noah was reported as missing to us and we are doing everything we can to find him.

“We are extremely grateful for the support shown by the public. If you are helping please report into the co-ordination centre to ensure the search continues to be done in a systematic and co-ordinated fashion. This will ensure we can carefully plan and take account of people supporting the search. We politely ask people to avoid open waters and railways – these are areas that require specialist and professional expertise. We also ask that personal drones are not used as these can interfere with specialist search equipment.

“There may also be times when officers may need to restrict access to certain areas or move away from search locations. Please do not be offended if this happens; it is necessary to allow us to carry out our enquiries and search activity as effectively as possible.

“There may also be times when officers may need to restrict access to certain areas or move away from search locations. Please do not be offended if this happens; it is necessary to allow us to carry out our enquiries and search activity as effectively as possible.

“This is being treated as a missing person investigation at this stage and there is nothing to indicate anything sinister or any element of criminality has taken place although we keep an open mind as to the circumstances.

“We continue to call on local residents to please check your gardens, sheds and outbuildings, or any other place a child may have be hidden or sought shelter. Please also review CCTV or doorbell cameras, and for motorists travelling in and around Brantham to review any dashcam footage from 3pm yesterday.”

News.title: 13 best hair oils for smooth, shiny hair – tested on three different hair types
News.content:
Your questions about hair oil answered

What is the best hair oil?

After months of testing across our straight, curly and coily hair types, we concluded that Olaplex’s no.7 bonding oil was the best hair oil, thanks to its frizz-smoothing, shine-boosting and damage-softening abilities. Dyson’s omega hydrating hair oil also seriously impressed us, particularly on Aidan’s curls, thanks to its featherlight but nourishing finish. Meanwhile K18’s molecular repair oil stood out after I saw my damaged lengths begin to look healthier after repeat use. And lastly, for a more affordable option, L’Oreal Paris’s elvive extraordinary oil punched well above its price point.

How we tested hair oils

Hair oils are deeply personal and what works beautifully on coarser strands can easily overwhelm fine hair types. To properly put a variety of formulas through their paces, I called on two expert testers with type 3 and 4 hair textures to join my own type 1C/2A strands. Together, we used the oils through numerous wash days, in-between wash days, styling sessions and workouts to assess how the formulas performed in normal life. Specifically, we considered the following criteria:

Weight: We noted how heavy or lightweight each oil felt on our different hair types, and whether it caused our strands to look greasy, limp or stringy.

We noted how heavy or lightweight each oil felt on our different hair types, and whether it caused our strands to look greasy, limp or stringy. Shine : We assessed whether the oils gave our hair a healthy gloss or a slick, unsightly finish.

: We assessed whether the oils gave our hair a healthy gloss or a slick, unsightly finish. Nourishment : We looked at how effectively each formula softened dryness, smoothed split ends and improved manageability.

: We looked at how effectively each formula softened dryness, smoothed split ends and improved manageability. Frizz control: We monitored how well the oils tamed flyaways and held up in humidity, wind and during/after a workout.

We monitored how well the oils tamed flyaways and held up in humidity, wind and during/after a workout. Curl and coil compatibility: On textured hair, we considered how the oils affected definition, bounce and moisture retention.

On textured hair, we considered how the oils affected definition, bounce and moisture retention. Longevity: We tracked how hair looked and felt after washing and in the days after, paying attention to greasiness, dryness and overall shape retention.

We tracked how hair looked and felt after washing and in the days after, paying attention to greasiness, dryness and overall shape retention. Texture and application: We considered dispenser design, how easily the oils spread through the hair and whether the formulas layered well with other styling products.

We considered dispenser design, how easily the oils spread through the hair and whether the formulas layered well with other styling products. Value for money: We factored in bottle size, how much product was needed per use and, ultimately, whether the performance justified the price.

What hair oil should I use for my hair type

“I recommend oils based on things like hair thickness, porosity, dryness or whether someone has loose fine curls versus thick, dense coils,” reveals Dublin.

Expanding on this, she tells me, “On looser curls, I go for something really lightweight, like an argan oil or anything with that soft slip. It gives shine without dragging the curl down.

“For medium textures, things like coconut or rosemary oils give a good dose of nourishment but still feel wearable. They add moisture without making the hair feel coated.

“Thick, coarse or very curly hair usually drinks up richer oils. Castor oil or a blend with heavier ingredients (like a mask) tend to smooth, hydrate and really bring out the curl definition.”

Is argan oil good for hair?

“Argan is packed with vitamins and healthy fats, so it softens the hair, calms flyaways and gives a nice sheen without weighing anything down,” reveals Dublin. Personally, she explains “[she’ll] use it as a pre-treatment on the scalp, leave it on for 10-15 minutes before washing, especially on clients with really dry scalps.”

Meanwhile, if styling the hair, she recommends “rubbing a small amount between the palms and targeting the drier areas, then finishing with a tiny bit on the ends.”

Is coconut oil good for hair?

“I personally don’t use coconut oil on my clients because I find it can actually be drying,” warns Dublin. It can work for some medium textures however, so it’s worth experimenting to see if it suits your hair type.

Is castor oil good for hair?

“Castor is heavier, but it’s great for coating all the hair and really hydrating the scalp before braiding,” touts Dublin. As for how to use it, she suggests: “After a wash, put a small amount on before braiding as a treatment. It helps lock moisture in and keeps the scalp happy.”

Is rosemary oil good for hair growth?

“Rosemary mixed with a bit of peppermint works really well for dry scalps and can support hair growth,” confirms Dublin. In her experience, “It leaves the scalp feeling fresh and clean, almost like a face mask, but for your roots. It’s great for resetting the scalp without adding heaviness.”

Why you can trust IndyBest reviews

As a senior shopping writer, Lucy Smith is frequently testing the latest in haircare, and often speaks to trichologists and stylists to inform her reviews. For instance, she’s covered the best leave-in conditioners, the best shampoos and conditioners and compiled an expert guide to choosing the best leave-in conditioners.

Alongside writing about beauty for IndyBest, Ateh Jewel is herself a beauty brand founder. She lent a hand to the team’s review of the best beauty advent calendars last year and, recently contributed to a new round-up of the best foundations. She’s often speaking about afro hair and proper coil care, and was the perfect person to test hair oils from a type 4 texture perspective.

Aidan Milan has plenty of experience in the field of haircare and has covered numerous products for curly hair from the likes of Cantu, Colour Wow and more. With her own head of seriously healthy curls, she was well placed to put all manner of hair oils through their paces.

News.title: Emmys suffer major ratings blow as viewing figures fall almost 10 per cent
News.content:

Viewing figures for the Emmy Awards have dropped by almost 10 per cent compared to last year, ending a brief two-year recovery in audience numbers.

Network figures published on Tuesday showed that approximately 6.7 million people watched the 78th primetime ceremony, which was broadcast by NBC.

The ceremony, presented by Law & Order: Special Victims Unit actor Mariska Hargitay, was dominated by Apple TV’s Widow's Bay, which scooped a record-breaking 14 awards for a comedy series. Meanwhile, The Pitt secured the best drama title for a second consecutive year.

Organisers faced fierce competition for viewers on Monday night, with ESPN broadcasting the opening Monday Night Football fixture of the season between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Denver Broncos.

By comparison, the ceremony attracted an estimated 6.87 million viewers when shown on ABC in 2024, following a 7.42 million audience for CBS the previous year.

Nevertheless, this year’s total remained well above the record low of 4.3 million recorded during Fox’s January 2024 broadcast, which suffered a multi-month delay amid Hollywood's industry-wide writers' and actors' strikes.

Matthew Rhys poses with the two actor awards that he won at the Emmys ( Reuters )

Coverage of the event cycles each year across four major television networks.

The Emmys consistently trail behind rival awards galas, attracting less than half the audience of the Oscars or Grammys and falling substantially short of the Golden Globes.

Scheduled regularly in September, the broadcast inevitably clashes with American football, which remains one of the few live televised events capable of sustaining massive national viewing figures.

To accommodate NBC's broadcast of Sunday Night Football, the ceremony shifted from Sunday to Monday evening, as is standard practice for the channel. This decision placed the telecast in direct competition with ESPN’s football coverage, while depriving the network of a sports lead-in to boost viewer numbers beforehand.

In the modern era of streaming and prestige television, critical acclaim does not guarantee vast audiences for nominated shows. During the 1990s, series like Seinfeld and ER combined critical success and Emmy victories with huge viewing figures, a feat that current winners such as Widow’s Bay and The Pitt fail to replicate.

The Emmys last crossed the 10 million milestone in 2018, drawing an audience of 10.2 million. At the turn of the century in 2000, the ceremony generated almost 22 million viewers—a height the broadcast is unlikely to reach ever again.

News.title: European Union opens door for Canada to become its first associate member
News.content:

The European Union will open the door for Canada to become its first "associate member", European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday as Ottawa seeks out closer ties with Europe amid a deepening spat with Washington.

"Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system," Ms von der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

"We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics. And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all...Europe and Canada believe in democracy."

Overtures to a new alliance follows a sharp deterioration in ties between Canada and the United States under US president Donald Trump, who has threatened to make Canada the 51st American state and imposed hefty tariffs on Canadian goods.

open image in gallery Carney's European trip follows a historic breakdown in Canada-US relations after trade talks collapsed last month, sparking a series of tit-for-tat tariff measures. ( AFP/Getty )

Ms von der Leyen was careful to state that “this is a partnership not against anyone else” in a possible effort to avoid antagonising president Trump.

Mr Carney has framed the Trump administration as trying to “break us so America can own us” and vowed “never [to] forget the lessons” of what he termed “American betrayal” amid a deepening rift in the relationship worth some £640bn in trade.

He has pledged to double Canada’s non-US trade in the next decade as the country pivots away from its southern neighbour amid an increasingly acrimonious trade war.

Ms von der Leyen’s comments also mark a significant shift in EU policy as the bloc has historically resisted flexible categories, although critics say it remains unclear what such an arrangement could look like.

She argued that Europe and Canada were aligned in their fundamental belief in democracy, urging that new partnerships were needed “in the cold fragility of today’s world”.

open image in gallery The Canadian PM imposed ‘dollar for dollar’ retaliatory tariffs after the US president launched new levies against its neighbour ( Reuters )

She added that the EU and Canada will work together across sectors from manufacturing to AI, critical minerals and energy.

“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said.

One EU diplomat expressed surprise at von der Leyen's proposal on Wednesday, saying "nobody really knows what it means." The diplomat added there were concerns that the European Commission chief "is overpromising and won't be able to deliver."

And significant obstacles remain to ramping up trade. Mark Manger, a professor of political economy and global affairs at the University of Toronto, said EU officials have been frustrated by Canada’s refusal to open two industries it protects at great expense: telecommunications and dairy.

Ms von der Leyen invited Mr Carney to join her in Strasbourg, and he will make his own address on Thursday.

open image in gallery Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen ( Reuters )

The 27-nation bloc faces war at its borders, with Russia's invasion of Ukraine. On trade and other issues, it is also facing stiff rivalry from the administration of US President Donald Trump and from an increasingly assertive China.

It will be up to EU member states whether von der Leyen's proposal goes ahead.

EU members were lukewarm in reacting to Germany's proposal in May of associate membership for Ukraine as a stepping stone to full accession.

Leading sports barrister Nick De Marco has highlighted the “most incredible delay” in reaching an outcome in the key Manchester City legal case.

Wednesday marks two years to the day since an independent commission hearing began to examine more than 100 charges laid against City by the Premier League in relation to alleged breaches of its financial rules.

The charges were first laid in February 2023, with the Premier League’s investigation having begun in 2018, but still no outcome has been announced. City strenuously deny any wrongdoing.

De Marco, who has worked on a number of high-profile football cases, including on behalf of Leicester in their dispute with the Premier League over alleged rule breaches, wrote on X on Wednesday: “It is a most incredible delay. So much for those who argue that one of the advantages of sports arbitration is it is speedier and more efficient than using the courts….”

De Marco is not involved in the City case, although Lord David Pannick, another barrister at the same firm, Blackstone Chambers, has worked for City on the case.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters conceded last month the process in the City case had taken longer than he expected, however he said it was not something which regularly came up when he spoke to top-flight clubs.

“I obviously speak to clubs all the time. It’s not necessarily a topic of conversation that is top of the list,” he said at a media briefing on the eve of the new season.

“(There are) lots of other things to talk about and do. As you say, the Premier League moves on. It’s starting (again) on Friday evening.”

Richard Masters conceded last month the process in the City case had taken longer than he expected ( PA Wire )

Masters was asked if there was a danger that the case may never be resolved, and replied: “It will resolve itself. I literally can’t say a thing about it. There’s only one available option, which is to allow the process to reach its natural conclusion.

“I can’t talk about the substance of the case. I can’t talk about the timing of the case. Our rules are very clear about that.”

Asked whether the league should implement rules to cap the length of time deliberations could take, or to look at using full-time panellists, Masters said: “We’ve always said that the commission need the time and space to do their work.

“In the end, as you know, it’s the league’s job as the regulator, provided the evidence is there, to put serious allegations in front of independent commissions, that independent process to establish the truth.

“In the end, that process shouldn’t really be qualified by the amount of time it’s going to take to establish the truth.”

News.title: Spurs finally score... but still lose
News.content:
“But that is why we cannot say it does not work for anyone. There are players who play every three days with no issues. They are very robust, their performances do not change too much. There are other players where the risk is bigger and the performances are different. I have to learn who is ready to play games every three days and who needs a rest so their performance level is not affected. I thought I had it quite clear in my mind with some, but with others, it is new, even for them, because they have not played as many games. We are learning.”

Liverpool were knocked out in the fourth round of this competition last season, losing 3-0 at home against Crystal Palace. Joe Gomez returns to the squad for the hosts tonight after an injury early in pre-season but Giovanni Leoni, Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Federico Chiesa remain out.

Tottenham are still without a league win or goal this season. Their 0-0 draw at home against Everton Saturday means they sit just above the relegation zone. Tottenham overcame Charlton in the second round, convincingly winning 5-1 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium last month.

“I think we are working well,” Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi said. “We played 30 minutes, 25 minutes very well [against Everton]. In that moment we could score two goals. Then we lost maybe the confidence because we did not score. For sure we have to improve. For sure I have big confidence in my players, they are very good players.

“We have to improve, yes. We can say the coach has responsibility if we do not score, yes, I accept, no problem. We did not win any game so far, yes. We are disappointed, sorry for that. But we have other positive things, like I said we did not [concede goals] in the last two games and the things we have to improve, we start our work. Nothing changed in my project and my idea.”

News.title: England cruise to victory led by ‘absolute freak’ Brook
News.content:
Whatever his returns, there has been an extra focus to Brook’s approach this summer, possibly because he has learnt from a grievous indiscretion in Wellington last winter. While others chase the Indian Premier League, he is totally committed to England, taking his break while that tournament is on and playing every match in all formats for his country.

Brook had come to the crease at the fall of the first wicket and, while it is early days, England appear to have added another arrow to their quiver. They handed a debut to opener Aneurin Donald, with his cap presented in the pre-match huddle by Pietersen, the new “specialist mentor”.

Donald has been selected as an “intent merchant”, charged with going extremely hard from the first over, aping Phil Salt, who is missing with a quad injury. He did what he was asked to do, smearing his first ball for two, then pulling six to leg and hammering four through the offside before the first over was out. Another big shot, off Wellalage, in the second saw him well caught in the deep, but 12 off five had kickstarted the innings.

News.title: Max Dowman-mania could make League Cup hottest ticket in town
News.content:
At this rate, Arsenal supporters will be looking forward to Carabao Cup matches as eagerly as any Premier League or Champions League game, simply because it will be a chance to watch Dowman again. The forward’s age and inexperience means he is still used sparingly in those high-priority competitions. The League Cup, by contrast, may prove to be his domain over the coming months.

Dowman’s double at Portman Road made him just the second 16-year-old to score two goals in a game for a Premier League side. The first was Wayne Rooney, for Everton against Wrexham in 2002.

The two goals underlined why there is so much excitement around Dowman. The first was a demonstration of his prodigious dribbling ability, as he weaved through Ipswich’s defence and buried his shot with the weaker right foot. The second showed his composure: a slotted finish, rolled in with ease.

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit 19-year high as global bond rout intensifies
News.content:
The cost of UK government borrowing hit its highest level since 2007 in a fresh global debt sell-off.

The yield on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money, rose from 5.37pc to a fresh 19-year high of 5.41pc on Tuesday as rising oil prices risk reigniting inflation.

Mortgage experts have warned that residential and buy-to-let mortgage rates are set to climb towards 5pc, as market turmoil threatens to filter through to household finances.

Short-term debt costs have also jumped, with the yield on two-year UK bonds surpassing 4.9pc for the first time in three years.

The bond chaos came as Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, warned that Labour risked becoming “just a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”.

He told LBC that John Healey’s original plan for a “low drama budget” had been “torpedoed” by higher borrowing costs and “events over the last couple of weeks”.

He said: “I think that [the bond market turmoil] will mean some hard choices next month at the Budget.”

“Few hard choices so far, but one is looming on the horizon, how any hole to the budget headroom is made good on. Is that a question of tax rises, or is it a question of taking the knife to public spending.”

Mr Haldane has been advising Labour since Andy Burnham took power.

It comes as the US Federal Reserve and the Bank of England face pressure to raise interest rates this week to combat rising prices.

Anthony Brinkman, a portfolio manager at Principal Asset Management, said: “The recent gilt market movements seem to be intent on showing central banks they are out of time – the market is expecting action.”

Borrowing costs around the world are rising after a 20pc surge in oil prices so far this month.

Brent crude tipped above $109 a barrel this week after Houthi rebels in Yemen, considered a proxy for Iran’s forces, seized control of a key port in the Red Sea, threatening shipping.

The US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates on Wednesday in the face of the inflation threat.

As a result, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds has surged above 5pc for the first time since 2007.

News.title: AI could transform global inequalities or ‘widen the gap’, warns Bill Gates
News.content:
“AI could be a great equaliser, or [it could] widen the gap”, says Mr Gates. “This is not a long-range prediction. It’s a present-tense choice”.

“We can harness AI for good. But it won’t happen by accident. After all, the market is an extraordinary engine of innovation, but a terrible guarantor of equal opportunity.

“With AI, the gap could grow even faster … That is what makes this moment so urgent. Things are changing rapidly, and the window to shape who benefits from AI, and how soon, is short”.

The key issue holding back the deployment of AI in the developing world revolves around the availability of local data and, in turn, the ability for the technology to scale in environments very different from where it is currently being created.

An app that is trained on billions of hours of American English, will struggle at first with British English (see your spell check) but is next to useless if your local language is Swahili or Chichewa.

More profoundly, an AI tool that allows a farmer in Hampshire to control his combine harvester remotely, will offer little to a smallholder in South Sudan who works the land by hand and faces a completely different array of pests, weather conditions and costs.

The same is true for health. “A community health worker in Rwanda examining a baby with a fever faces different questions than a clinician in a well-resourced hospital - and the AI supporting her needs to reflect that”, says Mr Gates.

He adds: “Most of the world is invisible to today’s AI models. These AI systems were trained primarily on what exists on the internet – and the internet reflects a deeply unequal world. More than 90 percent of the data used to train early, large language models came from English-language sources. The communities that stand the most to gain from AI are largely absent from the knowledge base these tools are built on. They are not just underserved. They are not in the picture at all”.

The new investment aims to help correct that. Mark Suzman, CEO of the Gates Foundation, says investments are already being made with companies including Microsoft and Google to build databases of a much wider range of languages, for instance.

Africa alone has more than 2,000 languages, and for AI’s to be effective there they have to understand what and how people actually speak - “their dialects, accents, and slang, too”.

The investments, he says, are being made on the condition that the intelligence and knowledge they accumulate are made freely available for others to use.

Languages for AI “are true public goods, almost definitional public goods. They need to be freely available to everybody. Once they’re created, they are public goods that can be uploaded onto any AI,” said Mr Suzman.

News.title: Reynolds refuses four times to rule out tax raid on state pensioners
News.content:
The Business Secretary refused four times to rule out retirees paying tax on the state pension from next year.

Jonathan Reynolds declined to reassure pensioners that they would not pay income tax on the benefit for the first time, saying it was a question for the Chancellor.

The comments on Tuesday raised concern for millions of retired people expecting to see their state pension surpass £13,000 from April, forcing them to pay income tax.

However, pensions minister Torsten Bell later insisted Labour would not put up taxes on people who rely on the state pension.

It is still unclear how this will be implemented given the complexity of separating the tax arrangements of different groups of pensioners.

The rise under the triple lock guarantee would drag many pensioners into paying income tax for the first time because their state income would surpass the personal allowance of £12,570.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, said last year that people solely reliant on the state pension would not have to pay the tax.

However, Mr Reynolds was repeatedly asked on BBC Breakfast whether Labour would honour this commitment after the next increase in the state pension in April. He declined to answer four times.

He said: “I’m sorry, that is for the Chancellor and for a Budget.

“The majority of pensioners in this country don’t just rely on the state pensions. Some do, I accept that, but the majority don’t.

“Sometimes when this is looked at, we’re focusing just on the state pension side of this. You’ve got to consider the full range of income retired people in the UK have.”

However Mr Bell, the pensions minister, walked back from Mr Reynolds comments.

He said: “In line with the commitment made at Budget 2025, pensioners who only just exceed the personal allowance will not have the administrative burden of paying small amounts of tax in this Parliament.

“The Chancellor will set out further details on how that commitment will be delivered at the Budget.”

Former pensions minister Sir Steve Webb said only one in 16 pensioners would benefit from this policy.

He said: “Those on the new state pension can expect to see an increase of nearly £500 per year next April.

“But the sting in the tail is that this will take the standard rate of the new state pension above the tax threshold.”

The comments came after official figures on Tuesday indicated the triple lock will rise by 3.9pc from April.

Under the triple lock, the state pension rises each April in line with inflation, average wages or 2.5pc, whichever is highest.

Total pay, including bonuses, rose by 3.9pc in the three months to July, down from 4.2pc in the three months to June.

Pensioners may yet receive a bigger increase if September’s inflation figure is higher than 3.9pc. That will be revealed next month but a higher figure is thought to be unlikely.

News.title: Outstanding Leeds cut short Jaissle’s Newcastle honeymoon
News.content:
The foundations are being put in around the stadium for a cavernous new West Stand, and Farke’s remit is to ensure that Leeds will be firmly established in the Premier League by the time it is completed in the summer of 2028.

To be fair to Farke, he has laid a sturdy base for this team to thrive and it felt before kick-off that this was going to be a big evening for Leeds, who had made a quietly encouraging start to the campaign and had negotiated three challenging away trips without defeat.

Big? It turned out to be spectacular. The first half was so one-sided that a boxing referee would not have allowed Newcastle to come out for the second, such was the pummelling they received; wave after wave of white-shirted raids left the visitors black and blue.

Aside from one little rick inside the opening 10 minutes, when James Trafford dithered and presented Yoane Wissa with a chance to mug him, Leeds were every bit as sensational as Newcastle were shocking, seizing on the opportunity to go on a rampage.

Leeds would have been in front after 11 minutes but Ethan Ampadu’s fierce drive battered into Calvert-Lewin’s legs and bounced away. Normally in such circumstances, players will wave an arm to berate their bad luck, but Ampadu, celebrating his 26th birthday, smiled: he, like everyone else, sensed what was coming.

Jayden Bogle, Justin and Nico Elvedi all had opportunities to open the scoring earlier, but eventually, they found the weak spot. Newcastle, who had lost the influential Nico González to a potential concussion, had replaced him with Sean Steur and what an influence he would have on matters.

On the half hour, Steur was a fraction too late getting out to close down Tanaka, whose shot ricocheted off him and to Lewis Miley, before looping away from Lukas Hornicek and dropping into the corner of the net in dam-busting fashion.

Sports.title: Uefa in England ticket climbdown as 100 lucky fans get permission to watch Three Lions vs Croatia in near-empty stadium
Sports.content:
Next

ENGLAND have been allowed to have 100 fans at next month’s Nations League game in Croatia – after a minor climbdown by Uefa.

Euro chiefs announced in February that the game, to be played in Rijeka on October 3, would be played behind closed doors.



That was a punishment after crowd trouble at Croatia’s last games under Uefa jurisdiction, their Nations League quarter-final ties with France in March 2025.

Croatia were also banned from having any fans in their opening game in the Czech Republic on September 26.



But FA chiefs took up the case with Uefa, arguing that England fans, many of whom travel to every game, were being punished for incidents that were nothing to do with them.

England’s previous away game in Croatia – played in Rijeka again in 2018 – was also played behind closed doors because of fan violence.

And Wembley lobbying has had a small success with Uefa agreeing that 100 Three Lions fans will now be allowed to attend.

The official England Supporters Travel Club said: “We’re pleased to confirm that, following discussions with UEFA, a small delegation of England Supporters Travel Club members will be permitted to attend England’s UEFA Nations League fixture against Croatia on Saturday 3 October.

“The match will be played behind closed doors following a UEFA sanction against Croatia.

“However, we have been granted permission to allocate 100 complimentary tickets to active 2026-2028 England Supporters Travel Club members, giving a small number of our supporters the opportunity to attend the fixture.”

The Travel Club said members have until noon on Friday to register, with priority given to fans with the highest number of previous “caps” for attending overseas games.

It added: “We appreciate that this is a very limited allocation and that demand will significantly exceed the number of tickets available.

“Members will be invited to register themselves only.

“As the allocation is extremely limited, tickets will be allocated based on members’ all-time caps totals, with active caps used as the differentiator where members have the same all-time caps total.”

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca swipes Man City are still waiting on their own apology from Howard Webb after Man Utd error acknowledged
Sports.content:
Next

ENZO MARESCA says Manchester City are still waiting for their own apology from referees chief Howard Webb – three years after a controversial derby goal went against them.

Pro Ref have said sorry to United for allowing Erling Haaland’s second half winner to stand in Sunday’s game at Old Trafford – despite the fact Enzo Fernandez was clearly offside.



Yet new boss Maresca was part of Pep Guardiola’s backroom staff in the same fixture back in January 2023.

And back then an equaliser from Bruno Fernandes was allowed to stand despite the fact Marcus Rashford – who shielded the ball for him – was in an offside position.



No apology was forthcoming on that occasion and City dusted themselves down to go on and do the treble.

The new Etihad boss said it is just a part of football – and the team who feel aggrieved just have to accept it.

Maresca said: “Three years ago when I was here, it happened exactly the same against Man Utd. We lost the derby there.

“The goal was not a regular goal, if you remember.

“And to be honest, no one apologised. We are still waiting for the apology for that goal,

“Sometimes it happens for you, sometimes it happens against you. It’s football.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Maresca felt the controversy had overshadowed an incredible win for his team who had played for three quarters of the game with 10 men.

He said: “Talking about one episode or one moment after that game when we played for 75 minutes with 10 men is quite poor. The performance was unbelievable.”

VAR Matt Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus have been dropped from their Prem matches this weekend as a result of the blunders.

But Maresca defended the pair, saying: “It’s not easy, I think, for the VAR, for the people that are in front of the screen, and in 10 seconds, 20 seconds, they have to make a decision.



“Sometimes they make some mistakes, I make mistakes, players make mistakes. I think it’s part of our job.”

The goal was not the only disputed moment of the derby – Phil Foden was sent off midway through the first half for kicking out at United skipper Fernandes.

City decided not to appeal so will miss the next three matches, including the Carabao Cup clash with Norwich on Thursday night.

Maresca said: “At half-time he was very sad and very upset because he knew it was something wrong, then after the game he was a little bit more relieved and happy.

“On Monday he was really good. Phil knows the reaction was not a good one but it’s finished and we move on.”
