Sports.title: Former Premier League star, 35, makes shock retirement decision just days after signing for new club on free transfer
Sports.content:
Next

JAMES RODRIGUEZ has retired from Colombia duty after 15 years playing for his national team.

The former Everton and Real Madrid star, 35, made his debut for Los Cafeteros in 2011 against Bolivia.



He went on to collect 131 caps and his last match came during their penalty shootout defeat to Switzerland at the 2026 World Cup.

Rodriguez became a cult figure in Colombia after starring at the 2014 World Cup, where he was the tournament’s top scorer.



But he has now called time on his international career and called it “one of the great honours of my life”.

He said: “The moment has come. Thank you for every match, every joy, every tear, and every dream we shared together.

“Representing the Colombian national team was one of the greatest honours of my life. Thank you, Colombia, and forever.”

Rodriguez scored a total of 31 goals for Colombia and played at three World Cups.

The playmaker is heading towards the end of his career after joining his eighth club in the last six years.

Rodriguez has returned to Colombia for the first time since leaving the country as a teenager to sign for Atletico Nacional.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

In their announcement, Atletico said: “This isn’t an announcement. It is a labour of love for this team.

“It is the work of many people, day in and day out, done quietly to ensure Nacional grows ever greater.

“When a club works for the sake of the club, greatness isn’t just a discussion – it is a consequence.



“They trusted. They believed. It was inevitable. James Rodriguez is Atlético Nacional. The greatest of the greatest.”

Previously he was playing for MLS side Minnesota United but only played eight games.

He has also had spells with Qatar side Al-Rayyan, Olympiacos, Sao Paulo, Rayo Vallecano and Mexican side Leon since leaving Everton in 2021.

Sports.title: Premier League duo, Chelsea legend and World Cup history maker become latest stars to graduate from PFA Business School
Sports.content:

CAPS and gowns were in order for several football stars following the PFA Business School 2026 graduation on Monday.

Chelsea legend Cesar Azpilicueta joined Everton favourites Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Tim Cahill on the stage as they were presented with their diplomas.



Lazio star Megan Connolly was also among the players who graduated.

Coventry City’s Nigerian forward Taiwo Awoniyi also became a grad, alongside ex-Liverpool striker Fabio Borini and former Stoke duo James Chester and Jacob Brown.



Awoniyi celebrated his Postgraduate Diploma in Global Football Sport Directorship with Merit on Instagram, where he wrote: “Another proud moment for me off the pitch.

“I have always believed that being a footballer shouldn’t stop you from being a student of the game and education has become an important part of that journey for me.

“Still playing. Still learning. The journey continues.”

And Everton took a moment to celebrate Cahill, who boasts 226 Premier League appearances and 56 goals.



They wrote: “Congratulations on your Diploma in Global Football Sport Directorship Tim.”

Meanwhile, Fabio Borini said: “Done!!! Global football business management.

Sports.title: ‘Impeccable timing’ – Fans celebrate as Man Utd announce three new signings just hours after JJ Gabriel asks to leave
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED fans were celebrating the club’s “impeccable timing” after they announced THREE new academy signings just hours after JJ Gabriel asked to leave.

The Red Devils confirmed the arrival of a trio of promising youngsters as they continue to strengthen their famed academy ranks.



The arrival of teenagers Dante Plunkett, Fred Heath and Will Murdock could hardly have come at a more eye-catching time.

It arrived just hours after news broke that 15-year-old sensation Gabriel had formally asked to quit Old Trafford with immediate effect.



United announced their latest academy recruits on social media, prompting supporters to immediately draw comparisons with the uncertainty surrounding one of their biggest young talents.

One fan joked: “Impeccable timing.”

Another celebrated the club continuing to bring young talent through the doors at Carrington.

While other supporters saw the announcement as a reminder that United’s academy recruitment will continue regardless of the uncertainty surrounding Gabriel.

The teenager’s bombshell request stunned officials at Old Trafford after he formally asked for his registration to be cancelled.

Gabriel has been at United since the age of 11 and is regarded as one of the brightest prospects to emerge from the club’s academy in recent years.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Nicknamed “Kid Messi”, he further enhanced his reputation last week when he scored a stunning hat-trick against Sabah in the Uefa Youth League.

That made Gabriel the youngest United player to score a European hat-trick, aged just 15.

He had also been in contention to make his senior competitive debut against Brighton in the League Cup tonight.

Doing so would see Gabriel become the youngest player ever to represent United’s first team.

Goalkeeper David Gaskell currently holds that record after making his debut aged 16 years and 19 days in 1956.



But Gabriel’s shock request has thrown his immediate United future into serious doubt.

The youngster cannot sign a scholarship until he turns 16 on October 6 and is not eligible to sign professional terms until he is 17.

His current registration cannot simply be cancelled unilaterally, with agreement required between the player, his parent or guardian and United.



Should they fail to reach an agreement, the matter can be referred to the Premier League.

United chiefs are understood to have been shocked by Gabriel’s decision and remain hopeful the situation can be resolved.

The forward has already trained regularly with Michael Carrick‘s senior squad and was handed his first-team bow during pre-season against Atletico Madrid.

He was also named the club’s Jimmy Murphy Young Player of the Year last season following his sensational performances at youth level.

Gabriel scored 23 times in 23 Under-18 matches on his way to becoming the youngest player to win the prestigious award.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

United now face a fight to keep hold of their academy jewel.

But the club’s announcement of another crop of youngsters prompted plenty of amusement among fans given the dramatic events of the previous few hours.

Sports.title: Differential options for Gameweek 5: Liam Delap among brave selections
Sports.content:
Next

YOU will have to wait until tomorrow for our sensible transfer recommendations for Gameweek 5.

For now, allow us to put forward some fun differential options that most Dream Team managers are simply too scared to pursue.

Liam Delap (£3m)

A measly return of one goal in 28 league appearances made the 23-year-old something of a laughing stock in Chelsea colours last season.



But this suggestion stems from sound Dream Team logic.



Nottingham Forest are scheduled to face to Coventry this Saturday which has to be considered the most favourable match-up the Premier League has to offer right now.

The Sky Blues sit 20th in the table with a goal difference of -10 having failed to earn a point (or score a goal) across their first four outings since their return to the top flight.

0.7%-owned Delap, who converted one of his six shots against Aston Villa last weekend, will be licking his lips at the prospect of taking on such a vulnerable opponent.

Oliver Glasner was full of praise for his striker’s performance at Villa Park.

Looking further ahead, Forest will take on Crystal Palace in Gameweek 6 — the Eagles have the worst defensive record in the league at the time of writing.

Matheus Nunes (£4.9m)

Manchester City’s right-back finished fourth among defenders last season with a huge tally of 288 points.



In fact, Nunes was the only player in his position to register 10+ assists.

The Portugal international was not 100% fit at the start of the current campaign and Enzo Maresca deployed Abdukodir Khusanov (£4.4m) on the right of his back four but Nunes has since completed 90 minutes against Porto and Manchester United.

He was City’s joint-top performer at Old Trafford with an 11-point haul via a clean sheet and three bonus points.

Enzo Maresca’s team selections are still a little difficult to predict but the Italian will have noted that Nunes is more comfortable at right-back than Khusanov, who is more effective in the middle of defence.

Man City will host Sunderland in Gameweek 5 and have two fixtures to fulfil in Gameweek 6, albeit tricky ones: Liverpool (a) & PSG (h).



Nunes currently features in 0.6% of teams.

Jayden Bogle (£2.8m)

You may think this is a futile case of chasing lost points after the Leeds wing-back’s surprising haul against Newcastle on Monday night.

Bogle was credited with the Whites’ second goal, registered three shots on target, and was substituted a few minutes before the Magpies’ late consolation goal (meaning he claimed a clean sheet) for a total return of 17 points.

It would be unrealistic to expect the same again from the 26-year-old in Gameweek 5 but he’s perfectly capable of another double-digit haul against Crystal Palace at Elland Road this Sunday.



Daniel Farke’s side have started the campaign well and boast a formidable home record whereas the Eagles have struggled and will head to Yorkshire three days after their first Europa League game of the season (vs Lech Poznan).

Bogle (1.3% ownership) is among the most attack-minded defenders in Dream Team and those who recruit him before Friday’s deadline will get ahead of a tasty price increase.

But be warned, he is probably just a one-week punt as Leeds are due to face Arsenal at the Emirates immediately after the international break.

Sports.title: F1 announce 2027 calendar and increase in Sprint rounds
Sports.content:
Formula 1 has announced its 2027 calendar and an increase in the number of Sprint weekends from six to 10, with the season starting in Bahrain.

For a fourth consecutive year, there are 24 rounds scheduled with Portugal's Portimao and Turkey's Istanbul Park returning to the calendar.

As expected, the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort falls off the schedule while the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya moves into a rotational deal with Spa-Francorchamps that will see the Spanish event held in even numbered years from 2028 and the Belgian Grand Prix held in odd numbered years from 2027.

2027 Formula 1 - Race Calendar 1 Bahrain* March 12-14 13 Hungary July 30-Aug 1 2 Saudi Arabia March 19-21 14 Italy* September 3-5 3 Australia* April 2-4 15 Spain September 10-12 4 Japan* April 9-11 16 Azerbaijan September 24-26 5 China April 16-18 17 Turkey October 1-3 6 Miami Apr 30-May 2 18 Singapore October 8-10 7 Canada* May 21-23 19 USA October 22-24 8 Monaco* June 4-6 20 Mexico October 29-31 9 Portugal June 18-20 21 Brazil* November 5-7 10 Great Britain* July 2-4 22 Las Vegas November 19-21 11 Austria July 9-11 23 Qatar* December 3-5 12 Belgium July 23-25 24 Abu Dhabi* December 10-12

*denotes Sprint weekend

F1 had delayed its calendar announcement for next year due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has created uncertainty over the end of the current season with Qatar and Abu Dhabi still currently scheduled to take place later this year.

Bahrain will host a four-day pre-season test on February 24-27 before holding the 2027 season-opener on March 12-14 and it will be a Sprint weekend, with the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix a week later.

Australia reverts to the third round of the season in early April and will also host a Sprint, as will the next race in Japan before China rounds off a triple-header.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton and George Russell tussle for the lead of the 2026 Chinese GP Sprint

Miami retains its slot in the first weekend of May before Sprint rounds in Canada and, for the first time, Monaco, with F1 highlighting fans are "set to enjoy two thrilling qualifying sessions" around the streets of Monte Carlo.

The returning Portuguese Grand Prix slots into mid-June and is followed by a Sprint weekend at the British Grand Prix on July 2-4, with Austria moving to after Silverstone.

Back-to-back weekends in Belgium and Hungary will take the F1 circus to the summer break.

F1 2027 Calendar and Sprint announcement - key points Portuguese and Turkish Grands Prix return to calendar for first time since 2021

Season-opener returns to Bahrain for first time since 2024 and it will be a Sprint weekend

Number of Sprint weekends increased from six to 10

British Grand Prix is on July 2-4

Season to conclude in Abu Dhabi on December 10-12

A sprint round at Monza in early September will be the first event back after four weeks off with the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid a week later.

Azerbaijan, Turkey and Singapore form part of a triple-header before the usual Americas triple-header in Austin, Mexico and Brazil, which is a Sprint weekend.

Las Vegas will host the only Saturday race of 2027, although it will be Sunday morning in the UK, then two Sprint weekends in Qatar and Abu Dhabi on December 10-12 conclude the season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Look back at some of the most dramatic moments to have taken place at the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix

"The 2027 calendar brings together some of the most iconic circuits and vibrant cities in the world, creating an incredible stage for another unforgettable season of Formula 1," said F1 president Stefano Domenicali.

"We are thrilled to welcome Portugal and Turkey to the championship and to expand Sprint racing to 10 events, giving our fans even more intensity, drama, and the wheel-to-wheel action that make our sport so special.

"Formula 1 continues to go from strength-to-strength, attracting new audiences around the globe. Week after week, the world's greatest drivers will battle on some of the most challenging tracks in motorsport, supported by F1's outstanding teams, world-class manufacturers, and global partners. Together, they create a spectacle unlike anything else in sport. As we continue this remarkable journey of growth, I want to thank our fans around the world as their passion drives everything we do."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch back to the 2020 Turkish Grand Prix where Lewis Hamilton claimed his seventh world title in a chaotic rain-hit race

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem added: "The 2027 FIA Formula One World Championship calendar is a strong reflection of the global appeal and continued growth of our sport.

"With 24 Grands Prix across five continents, the return of Portugal and Turkey, and the opportunity for an expanded Sprint programme, the calendar combines tradition, innovation, and fan engagement while maintaining the highest sporting standards."

Sports.title: Donnarumma: Man City are not in transition, it's going to be a great season
Sports.content:
"This is who we are. This is our team. This is City."

It's been a few days since the Manchester Derby victory but sat at Man City's training ground, Gianluigi Donnarumma is still basking in the glory.

He's not interested in Erling Haaland's controversial winner - though he's still annoyed Phil Foden was "harshly" sent off earlier in the game - as something else pleased him. A man down, everything going against them - City showed mettle and won.

"I loved my team-mates' performance, it was sublime," he tells Sky Sports. "The capacity to stay in the game and to react to difficult moments - no one can take that away from us.

"We will give everything for this shirt, for this club that gives us so much and offers us so much great support. It has a great history, and we need to give a lot back to it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from Manchester United’s match against Manchester City in the Premier League.

Not many had City down to hold a 100 per cent record this season ahead of the upcoming, lengthy international break - especially after losing the core of a successful era in Pep Guardiola, Bernardo Silva, John Stones and Rodri.

City have not been entirely convincing in certain areas - even Donnarumma says there is still lots to learn despite the faultless start to the Enzo Maresca era. But this was meant to be a transition season at City.

"I don't really like the word 'transition.'" he adds. "The club's objective is to win. This team's objective is to win. We'll certainly give everything we can to achieve that.

"We could reach the end of the season having won something, or having won nothing. But what's important is having a winning mentality, going out there and trying to win everything we possibly can."

Part of that winning mentality is being driven by Donnarumma - who is part of a newly-formed leadership group that replaced the likes of Bernardo, Stones and Rodri.

Donnarumma sits alongside Ruben Dias in the leadership pecking order, along with Haaland and Marc Guehi. All four players have one thing in common: they all have won trophies both at City and at other clubs in their careers.

Image: Man City have won four games from four at the start of this Premier League season

So as the likes of Ayyoub Bouaddi, Elliot Anderson and Ilimian Ndiaye settle into their new team - tasked with making an immediate impact in a non-transition year - the leadership quartet are there to drive the standards.

"We've changed a few players. A few new ones have arrived," says Donnarumma. "They're all top players who are used to playing on the biggest stages, dealing with certain situations, and playing in the Premier League.

"It's not easy at the beginning when you move to a new club, a new organisation, a new city. But they're adapting well, and we're making them feel comfortable.

"The players who were already here are helping them a lot. I think we're going to have a great season.

"The objective is to get to the end and compete for everything there is to compete for - in addition to the Premier League, there's the Champions League and the two domestic cups."

It's a clear warning from City that anything is possible when it comes to this team. But when it comes to Donnarumma's aim of challenging for the Premier League and the Champions League, one team stands in the way: Arsenal.

Mikel Arteta's side have also started the season with five straight wins - and have the added recent psychological boost of pipping City to the Premier League post last May.

The recent Guardiola documentary showed down and disappointed scenes from City players as they slipped up at Bournemouth to hand the Gunners the title. Donnarumma - who had won the league title in each of the previous five seasons before last term - was one of them.

Image: Donnarumma missed out on the league title to Arsenal

"It's difficult, but that's football, that's life. You're not on your own," he says about that disappointment. "There are other strong teams, especially in the Premier League.

"It's not that if you don't win there isn't disappointment - of course there is - but it can happen because there are other teams as well, just like in the Champions League.

"It's important to go into every game trying to win it. Certainly, our objective will be to win, but there are other teams too.

"You have to compete, you have to work, and you have to do everything possible because the history of this club demands it."

Will it be City and Arsenal again competing at the top come May? "I don't know. We're only four games into the season," says the Italian goalkeeper.

But the stall has been set out. "Our focus right now has to be on working and trying to win every game. That has to be our objective.

"Whether we achieve it in the end or not, only time will tell."

Sports.title: Eating grass, meditation and more – What Tuchel said in viral documentary
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel wishes he'd eaten grass from the Azteca pitch after England's World Cup win over Mexico this summer.

That's just one of the statements from the England boss which has drawn attention across social media, following the FA releasing a new documentary called 'Reflections: England's World Cup Journey'.

In the documentary, Tuchel sits alongside former England international and Sky Sports pundit Daniel Sturridge to look back on England's campaign, which ultimately saw the team finish third, having lost in the semi-finals to Argentina.

England's standout performance of the tournament came in the last-16 win over Mexico in Mexico City, where they played for over 35 minutes with 10 men but prevailed 3-2.

"I texted a friend after the match and I just wrote, 'I regret that I didn't eat some grass after the match to keep something from this in my body forever'," said Tuchel.

On the unity his players showed in that match, Tuchel pointed to their reaction to Jordan Henderson falling and breaking his arm in the post-match celebrations.

"If you needed any proof, any proof for what it meant to these players and how they were with each other, it was the moment when Jordan fell over and broke his arm," said Tuchel.

Image: Jordan Henderson receives treatment after suffering an injury in the post-game celebrations following England's win against Mexico

"Within a second, the players were there, every single player was there, stopping the celebrations, building a shield, protecting Jordan and not going nowhere in full empathy. It was just so special."

The film will be released on Wednesday September 16 exclusively on the England app.

The build-up to the Mexico game had been dominated by talk of the altitude of the Azteca stadium but also the potential for weather delays, which proved founded with kick-off pushed back.

But Tuchel says a calm came over the group when they trained together in Mexico before the match and meditation and manifestation helped them to achieve the victory.

"In the middle of Mexico City and we arrived and it's an oasis, it's so peaceful, it's an unbelievable pitch and it is so calm, it is so peaceful that it did something to the players," said Tuchel.

"They came out from the gym straight out on the pitch, they were having phone calls, walking around, it was such a peaceful energy.

"So we came up with this line of 'silence is powerful', that we enjoy the silence, we're in a home country, we will play against the whole nation, the whole nation will be against us, the stadium, it's almost impossible to win in the stadium, no one has ever done it before in a World Cup match.

"So let's enjoy the silence, the power of the silence. We even had five minutes on the match day of meditation and manifestation of the last whistle."

Image: Tuchel speaks to players during a hydration break

The FA are currently undergoing a review of England's World Cup campaign but Tuchel says the experience has bonded him and the group together and he is "excited" about what comes next.

England face world champions Spain in the Nations League in the upcoming international break with the 2028 Euros the next major tournament. Tuchel reckons preparing for that tournament will be easier than the planning which was required for the 2026 World Cup.

"It created a huge bond to these players, it feels like they are my players now. This is the beauty of it," said Tuchel.

"When you have a manager and then you have success and you have painful moments together, but you have so much time together and then you create a natural bond.

England's upcoming fixtures England vs Spain - Nations League, September 26

Czech Republic vs England - Nations League, September 29

Croatia vs England - Nations League, October 3

England vs Czech Republic - Nations League, October 6

"I'm happy to see them, I'm happy to challenge them, happy to push them and very proud to be a part of them.

"I'm very excited. I'm excited to work with these players. I'm excited to have new, young players that we can bring into camp and that they can learn.

"We've got another step closer and I think we're there.

"It's very difficult to prepare a World Cup in the US, but it's possible to prepare for a Euros and be prepared in Nations League tier one.

"The target is to have another 10 matches. We had 10 matches in the US, eight wins, one draw, one painful loss, but that is something to build on.

"We have all the right to hold our heads high and go with courage and positivity into the next challenges.

"We have four matches in the Nations League coming up and that's where the focus is."

Tuchel on Harry Kane going to another level

Image: Harry Kane celebrates scoring for England at the World Cup

"Just so easy. He's always there, he's always in training, he always wants to train. The level to which he got himself now, since he's at Bayern Munich.

"The level of commitment and training, how he arrived in prep camp, how he arrived in the qualification matches, the speech after the October camp, and he straight away stood up in the dressing room and said, 'guys, we will keep on going in November, this is what we do'.

"He found another level in his game, but also as a personality, and how he shows up for training, how he drives training standards is one of a kind. The finishing is out of control good."

On Jude Bellingham living up to his full potential

Image: Jude Bellingham celebrates as England go on to beat Erling Haaland's Norway at the World Cup

"He was one of the players of the tournament, not only for us, but of the whole tournament.

"He lived up to his full potential, you could just see what a competitor, what a machine he is, and he just thrives on the pressure. He just loves these moments, he loves these stages, it brings out the very best.

"He came with an amazing mindset into camp, with the best physical preparation. He came fresh, he came hungry, hungry for football, hungry for minutes into camp. He took his place and decided every single match for us."

On the England fans and their 'special' connection with the team

Image: England players join fans for a rendition of Wonderwall after beating DR Congo

"They lived up to the high expectations.

"Everyone told me, 'wait until the tournament starts, we will have the best fans, we will be right on top, it will be amazing, the amount of people…' and it was just like that from the first moment.

"They just felt this team. I believe that fans have a sense, maybe they cannot name it, someone will say, 'yeah, they give everything, they're sweating, after the whistle goes, they have to sit down because they're so tired'. For everyone it's maybe different, they feel it, they could sense it, that this team is together and this team means it.

"That's what made the connection so strong. That was not artificial. That was very special."

Sports.title: DP World Tour unveils big changes to 2027 schedule
Sports.content:
The DP World Tour has announced a new date for the 2027 BMW PGA Championship, as it unveiled a series of big schedule changes for next year's calendar.

The tour also confirmed the return of three national opens, a significant step in its plans to grow, with DP World Tour CEO Guy Kinnings confirming the series will now host 17 national opens across the 2027 season.

After a seven-year absence, the Hong Kong Open will return to the DP World Tour calendar, and the Deutsche Bank Singapore Open has also been added back to the schedule.

Meanwhile, the tour has also confirmed the Open de Portugal | Cascais-Lisboa will return to the calendar.

The DP World Tour has also made a series of adjustments to its Closing Swing and Back 9, with the 2027 Ryder Cup to take place at Adare Manor between September 17 and 19.

The BMW PGA Championship will now be pushed back to September 23-26, a week later than its usual spot in the second week of the month to accommodate the biennial tournament.

The Amgen Irish Open, which was held in the first week of September in 2026, will be played at The K Club between July 1-4.

"As Golf's Global Tour, we are proud to provide this unique platform for our members to showcase their talents as they compete to put their own name alongside some of the iconic champions of our sport. Sports.title: Why Coventry, Tottenham and Aston Villa should not panic about their slow starts
Sports.content:
That optimism we feel at the start of a new season can be intoxicating. Whatever happened last season, there has been a whole summer to correct things. New signings, possibly a new manager, and new possibilities. What could go wrong? Oh, everything. Terrific. We’re only in mid-September, but that early optimism has melted away and been replaced by anxiety for some fans.

Coventry had every reason to look forward to the season, their first in the Premier League since 2001. They were coming off the back of a title-winning campaign in the Championship and were riding the crest of a wave. Now, though, they have fallen off their surfboard and are frantically trying to keep their heads above water as the ferocity of the top flight becomes increasingly apparent.

They are the only Premier League team without a point after four games and they are yet to even score a goal. In fairness, two of their games have been away to the two strongest sides in the league, Arsenal and Manchester City. Coventry were pretty impressive in the latter of those matches, too, and probably deserved something from it.

However, a 1-0 defeat at home to fellow promoted side Hull and a 5-0 thrashing at the hands of Brighton on Sunday have brought stark realisation that the Premier League is a tricky business. Taiwo Awoniyi’s red card in the second half against Brighton did not help, but they were already 2-0 down by then. When Lewis Dunk is bending efforts into the top corner from 30 yards, you know it isn’t going to be your day.

Coventry are the eighth promoted team to lose their first four games of a Premier League season. Only one avoided relegation: Southampton in 2012-13.

Looking at all the teams that have lost their first four game in a Premier League campaign, it is a little more comforting. Eighteen did that before Coventry and eight of them stayed up, the most recent of which was Everton in 2024-25.

We are not here to rub it in, though. We are here to try to provide hope. Somewhere in our sea of Premier League records, surely, we can find something to cheer up struggling teams?

For Coventry, look no further than Crystal Palace from the 2017-18 season. Under the management of Frank de Boer, they did not score or win a single point in their first five games. The Dutchman was sacked and replaced by Roy Hodgson, but the run did not quite end there. Palace went seven games without a goal or point.

Hodgson ultimately turned things around with Palace not only avoiding relegation, but remarkably finishing 11th. We are not suggesting Coventry sack their own Frank, by the way. He has surely earned enough goodwill after getting them into the top flight in the first place. Also, coaxing the 79-year-old Hodgson out of retirement could be tricky (but probably not impossible knowing him).

The other joint-longest run at the start of a Premier League season without a point belongs to Portsmouth, who failed to win their first seven in 2009-10. They did score three times in that run, but, unlike Palace, failed to improve much during the campaign. Pompey finished bottom on 19 points. They were deducted nine points for going into administration, but would have still finished bottom even without that.

Norwich lost their first six in the 2021-22 season and finished bottom on 22 points, while a further three teams have lost their first five in the Premier League: Southampton in 1998-99, Sunderland in 2005-06, and Wolves last season. Saints stayed up, but Sunderland and Wolves both disappeared to the Championship after finishing 20th.

Coventry are not the only team struggling. Things were supposed to be different for Tottenham. After back-to-back 17th-place finishes in the Premier League, Roberto De Zerbi kept them up by the skin of their teeth last season and the club backed him in the transfer window this summer. However, four games into the new campaign and, like Coventry, they are yet to score. They do at least have two points to their name after 0-0 draws against Nottingham Forest and Everton, but that familiar sinking feeling is already dousing pre-season optimism for Tottenham.

It is the first time in the club’s history they have failed to score in their first four league games of a campaign and, as mentioned, only that 2017-18 Palace side have endured a longer start to a Premier League season without scoring (seven games).

It has been 407 minutes since Spurs last scored in the Premier League and the first time they have failed to score in four successive Premier League matches since September 2006.

Apart from Spurs and Coventry this season, there have been five previous examples of teams failing to score in their first four Premier League games. As well as the aforementioned Palace campaign, there was Sheffield Wednesday in 1994-95, Newcastle in 2005-06, Swansea in 2011-12, and Aston Villa last season. Crucially, none of them were relegated with the lowest any of them finished 13th (Sheffield Wednesday).

That should provide plenty of hope for Spurs. Villa did not score until the fifth game last year, but went on to have a stellar campaign, finishing fourth and winning the Europa League. That said, their squad was badly hit by sales in the summer. Perhaps unsurprisingly, they have started slowly, one point from their first four games after a goalless draw at Hull. Defeats to Brighton, Arsenal and Forest have left them in the relegation zone, with a point fewer than they had this time last season.

It is the fourth time Villa have started a Premier League season without winning any of their first four games, after 1992-93, 1997-98, and 2025-26. At least they have scored, though, with Alysson’s equaliser against Forest on Saturday their first in the league. Again, though, Villa can use their marked improvement after this point last season as optimism fuel.

Fulham’s slow start was given a boost on Saturday with a well-earned draw at Liverpool, their first point of the season. Though they remain in the bottom three, they can build on that performance and silence those who had started to doubt them after opening with three defeats to Chelsea, Sunderland and Palace.

It’s four games down, 34 to go. Coventry will want their first points as soon as possible, while something as simple as scoring a goal could unlock Tottenham’s potential. There is plenty of time to restore positive vibes and have a great time between now and the end of May. Perhaps the teams who should be worried do not even know it yet.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: Lewis Koumas on playing ‘the Liverpool way’, showing hunger and hopes for the future
Sports.content:
With a man of the match award in one hand and his phone in the other, Lewis Koumas made a very important call before stopping to speak to the media inside Anfield on Wednesday night. What it means to represent your boyhood club, and to shine for it, was apparent for all to see.

“That was my mum,” said the Liverpool forward, still beaming from the award that Cody Gakpo handed to him following the 3-1 Carabao Cup third round win over Tottenham. “She was here tonight with my nan, my granddad and my sister. They were all in the box. I rang them straight away to show them the trophy and they were buzzing.”

What it takes to impress Andoni Iraola and function effectively in the Basque coach’s front line was also apparent from Koumas’s performance against Spurs. The Liverpool head coach had aimed a pre-match dig at more decorated, expensive names when calling for better pressing and tenacity from his forwards in light of Saturday’s flat draw with Fulham. Koumas was not part of that conversation but as he worked himself to a standstill against Roberto De Zerbi’s defence, creating space and opportunities for others to exploit, it seemed the 20-year-old had taken Iraola’s comments to heart as well as on board.

“The energy he shows is contagious,” Iraola said afterwards. “I’m very happy for him. He does it in training every day. He is very clear what he needs to do, what the team needs.”

Koumas, who celebrates his 21st birthday on Saturday, the day before Liverpool travel to Iraola’s former club Bournemouth, took the compliment in his humble, studious stride. “I think how I play is ultimately the Liverpool way,” he responded. “We’ve always been a club where players have to give absolutely everything on the pitch. We’re bringing that back now and the crowd are loving it. A lot of it is about what I do off the ball. The gaffer has shown trust to me that I can carry out his plans in terms of how we want to play tactically. I was happy to do that for him. It gives me so much motivation the fact he’s putting me in for a game like this. I want to kick on now.”

Iraola placed trust in the Chester-born forward within weeks of his arrival this summer, informing Liverpool’s then sporting director, Richard Hughes, that he wanted Koumas in the first team squad and not sent out on loan again. Having impressed on Liverpool’s pre-season tour of the US, Koumas, the son of former Tranmere and West Bromwich Albion playmaker Jason, has made his first appearances in the Premier League and Champions League this season as a substitute and now has a first man of the match award at senior level.

Could he have imagined that at the start of pre-season? “No, I would have woken up!” the Wales international says. “I would have thought I was dreaming. It’s crazy. But I’m just really happy and very grateful for the opportunities I’ve been given. You never know when your last time on the pitch for Liverpool is going to be. I just try to leave everything out there every time.”

View image in fullscreen Lewis Koumas came close to scoring in the first half against Spurs at Anfield. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

Koumas has been capped 12 times for Wales but has had to bide his time to break through at club level. The forward, who can also operate on the wing, was given his first Liverpool start by Jürgen Klopp over two years ago and marked his full debut with a goal in a 3-0 FA Cup fifth round win over Southampton. He did not feature for his boyhood team again until Iraola arrived, spending the 2024-25 campaign on loan at Stoke, the first half of 2025-26 on loan to Birmingham and the remainder of that season on loan to Hull.

“I never showed a weak mentality about how the future would look for me at Liverpool,” insists Koumas, who cites Michael Owen and Gareth Bale as childhood inspirations. “I always had the drive that I would get here. The reason for going out on loan was to prepare for this moment. A lot of hunger can be lost in the game with how things go. But for me coming through the pre-academy and right through the academy, my hunger has always been there. My hunger comes from representing Liverpool Football Club, wanting to give everything for the best club in the world.”

Sports.title: Xhaka promises ‘fire’ from Sunderland on long-awaited return to Europe
Sports.content:
When Sunderland last played European football, club directors viewed it as a useful means of raising the cash necessary to fund floodlight upgrades at Roker Park necessitated by England’s widespread adoption of colour television.

Back in the autumn of 1973 a lighting system compatible with the demands of broadcasting in black and white was proving increasingly outdated and Sunderland responded by doubling admission prices for the second leg of their opening European Cup Winners’ Cup tie against Vasas of Budapest. Coming at a moment when miners and railway workers were engaged in long-running industrial action and north-easterners’ finances were duly tight, it dictated that a disappointing crowd of under 23,000 turned out to watch Dennis Tueart’s penalty secure a 3-0 aggregate win.

Fifty-three years on, Wearside’s financial outlook is once again uncertain as the gig economy makes security a stranger for many and the cost of living spirals, but a near 49,000-capacity crowd is still expected at the Stadium of Light on Wednesday night.

Sunderland’s opening Europa League match against AZ Alkmaar will be televised across much of the world in HD but if Granit Xhaka has his way, viewers may need to adjust their brightness controls.

“The stadium will be on fire,” says Sunderland’s captain, who at Arsenal and Bayer Leverkusen played in two Europa League finals, losing twice. “And I want to see our players on fire, on and off the ball. I’ve always been a dreamer and, for me, it’s a big, big dream to reach another European final and to get it with this club.”

View image in fullscreen Regis Le Bris has come a long way since he was an academy coach at Lorient. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Ed Sykes/Apl/Sportsphoto

This opportunity is one of the reasons why the 33-year-old Switzerland midfielder resisted overtures from his old friend Xabi Alonso to join Chelsea this summer. Four months ago, after Sunderland, coincidentally, beat Chelsea at the Stadium of Light to secure a seventh-place finish in the Premier League and only the second European adventure in their history, Xhaka grabbed a microphone and declared: “This is just the beginning; we want more.”

Now Régis Le Bris’s side are balancing the notoriously tricky demands of a second top-tier season following promotion with the glamour of a competition that in December will transport them to San Siro and a fixture that has forced Newcastle fans to retire an oft-repeated and much-adored chant declaring: “You’ll never see a Mackem in Milan.”

T-shirts emblazoned with the jubilant message “Mackem in Milan” are fast becoming a staple of Sunderland supporters’ wardrobes but first they want to see their team overcome a free-scoring AZ side who have won five and drawn one of their opening Eredivisie matches. Xhaka may well find himself up against Kees Smit, a 20-year-old widely regarded as among Europe’s most promising young midfielders.

Back in 1973-74 Sunderland were European underdogs, a Second Division team who found themselves unexpectedly engaged in continental combat, thanks to a famous FA Cup final triumph against Leeds. But Le Bris’s class of 2026-27 do not want to be seen as almost accidental tourists.

“It’s a privilege to be here,” says Sunderland’s French manager. “I’m proud but we’ve earned it, the players worked very hard last season. Now we have a good opportunity and it’s important to go all in.

“We want to be strong in both the Premier League and Europe. The players are looking forward to facing AZ; they’re excited. They want to be involved in this competition.”

If Le Bris and his playmaker Enzo Le Fée have travelled a long way since the moment 14 years ago when Sunderland’s manager, then a lowly academy coach in Brittany at Lorient, began working with the 12-year-old Le Fée, so, too, has that pair’s adopted home.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Five years ago Luke O’Nien was playing for Sunderland in League One, facing teams such as Accrington Stanley and Fleetwood. On Wednesday night he will be part of Le Bris’s matchday squad, offering living, breathing proof of the club’s astonishing rebirth under the transformative majority ownership of Kyril Louis-Dreyfus.

View image in fullscreen The captain, Bobby Kerr, is held aloft by his teammates after the 1973 FA Cup final victory over Leeds that took Sunderland into Europe. Photograph: PA

Whereas 53 years ago the Cup Winners’ Cup campaign coincided with the break-up of Bob Stokoe’s Wembley heroes of 1973 and concluded with a narrow aggregate defeat at the hands of Sunderland’s second opponents, Sporting, Louis-Dreyfus intends this to be the first of many European adventures. Certainly Le Bris’s squad seem much better prepared than those members of the Roker Park board who, as the club historian, Rob Mason, details in his excellent Sunderland AFC: The Definitive History, were victims of pickpocketing on that trip to Lisbon.

If it helps that Nordi Mukiele, Reinildo, Omar Alderete, Noah Sadiki, Le Fée, Brian Brobbey and Xhaka constitute a raft of players with previous European experience, the captain is confident the collective mindset is attuned correctly. “To succeed in Europe you need energy in the dressing room,” says Xhaka. “And that is what we have. The first step I took in the dressing room last season, I had a very good feeling. I could smell that it was special.

“So the energy, the mindset is there. If you don’t have this desire, this hunger, this mentality to compete every single day, forget about this level. But this team has it and, game by game, this team will show it. You need luck but I’m very positive and optimistic that we can go very far in this competition.

“The energy, the connectivity, the togetherness in our dressing room is amazing. I’m grateful that I’m here.”

Sports.title: Watching Cavan Sullivan, excitement is tempered by memories of hypetrains past
Sports.content:
The trouble with trying not to hype up Cavan Sullivan is that he keeps on doing cool stuff. Like this past weekend, when he scampers along on a Philadelphia Union breakaway, loses his man by stopping so suddenly it’s as if he’s pulled a ripcord, back-heels the cutback behind his standing leg, watches it slowly kiss off the far post and in, and celebrated the goal by bowing and doffing an imaginary top hat to the crowd.

Like when he doubles the score by setting up an attack and finishing it himself with a left-footed lash through the goalkeeper’s legs form an acute angle. Like when he fashions yet another goal by holding up the play and then suddenly springs a teammate up the right flank.

And that’s just this past weekend.

It’s hard not to get worked up when an American, two weeks and a day before his 17th birthday, almost matches Lionel Messi for goal involvements in Major League Soccer and the Leagues Cup since the World Cup. When he powers an entire team of grown men to a 10-game unbeaten run. When he breaks Freddy Adu’s record as the youngest Major League Soccer debutant by 13 days, at 14 years and 293 days old. When he has netted six goals and five assists in his last eight matches. When he appears to be on the eve of his first United States men’s national team call-up.

When his swagger and flair are vindicated by the advanced metrics, which suggest that he has already compiled the best MLS season ever by a teenager, outdoing Alphonso Davies. That he is, in fact, the league’s second-best American player right now.

What makes Cavan Sullivan so tantalizing is that he isn’t theoretical.

And yet we wince.

We have been down this road before. That way madness lies, let me shun that – so warned King Lear.

As an American soccer community, we have developed a reflexive recoil against the Godding up of yet another prodigy. Still, it’s hard to resist, even though we know better. From the experience of Bobby Convey, and Jamar Beasley, and John O’Brien, and Jozy Altidore, and Juan Agudelo, and Brek Shea, and Julian Green, and Gedion Zelalem. They had skills and bodies and brains we could dream on, which we never managed to resist.

Did you even remember Green and Zelalem? Green is 31 and presently without a club; Zelalem, now 29, plays for New Mexico United. Both were promised to us as potentially first American male superstar when they emerged from the Bayern Munich and Arsenal academies, respectively. But then, all the men on that list, and so many more, were supposed to be that. None of them were.

We’ve been doing this since the 1970s, when it was decided that Kyle Rote Jr, son of the gridiron football hero, would put soccer on the map. He did indeed become famous, but much less for what he did on a soccer field than for thrice winning the popular gameshow Superstars – wherein top players from different sports competed in a series of athletic events. He led the North American Soccer League in scoring as a rookie and then tailed off, taking a “sabbatical” to lead a hunger relief mission to Cambodia in 1980 and never playing soccer again.

They weren’t all failures. Several had solid professional careers. Altidore had a highly productive spell on the United States men’s national team – he is still its third all-time leading scorer, behind Landon Donovan and Clint Dempsey. His club resume, however, amounts to two good seasons in the Netherlands and half a dozen strong campaigns in Major League Soccer, after he had been discarded by five different European clubs.

There’s still no telling, exactly, what the now-23-year-old Gio Reyna might or might not become. His body hasn’t cooperated, breaking down again and again, and neither has he managed to muster the consistency to become a regular and productive starter on a European club (that may change this season with Strasbourg). He’s bounced around, largely anonymously, briefly resurfacing for World Cups. It feels like a long time ago now, when he was 17 and fit seamlessly into Borussia Dortmund’s attacking diamond with Erling Haaland, Jude Bellingham and Jadon Sancho.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Of all the chosen ones, only Christian Pulisic has really panned out something like we had hoped. He has, however, never really been the focal point in the attack of any of his three European clubs. And he’s developed an odd penchant for falling out of favor after two or three seasons, tumbling down the depth chart at Dortmund and then Chelsea and now Milan. Under new manager Ruben Amorim, Pulisic, the author of 52 goals and assists over the last three Serie A campaigns – albeit notably fewer of them in the 2025-26 season – has been benched and has appeared just once in the Italian league.

And all of them toiled under the looming specter of Adu. More than two decades on from Freddymania, his name is still invoked as a cautionary tale. He works as a personal skills coach now, and has done since last playing professionally five years ago.

So we proceed carefully, taking great pains not to make the same mistakes again.

The thing is, Sullivan has already scored more goals in two-thirds of an MLS campaign than Adu did in his highest-scoring season, his rookie year with DC United in 2004. And the league is a hell of a lot harder to score in these days. It’s better set up to handle transcendent talent, too.

Unlike most of the others, there are real numbers there. Real performances. Real highlight clips, captured at the senior level against credible opposition. Manchester City certainly think he’s real, long ago arranging for his transfer when he turns 18. It’s all there, other than the size of Sullivan himself. That may prove problematic. But then he wouldn’t be the first undersized superstar.

And yet.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

Sports.title: When did football fans first start wearing replica kits? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“When did fans wearing replica kits become a thing?” asks Alex Ecob. “Older footage shows people in regular clothes and a few scarves/flags in the team colours. What kickstarted the trend? Did one club get there first?”

As the question suggests, this is a not a straightforward answer. Buckle up folks, as we veer wildly from copyright acts to academia, via multiple reports of unofficial kits, DIY jobs, cup-final special editions, youth strips, sew-on jobs and the like. But if we are to draw a line in the sand, and declare one date or one jersey as the first official, adult replica kit to be sold by a club to the general public (or at least those close enough to the club shop), then we probably have to give the gong to Leeds United in 1973, although only children’s sizes were produced initially.

“The first replica kit was produced by Admiral for Leeds United in 1973-74,” emails Chai from Atlanta. “History has it that Leeds’ manager, Don Revie, and Admiral owner, Bert Patrick, had a chance meeting at a cafe. There they agreed on Admiral paying Leeds £7,000 to wear a redesigned kit with the brand’s logo visible on their shirt and shorts. Patrick also secured the copyright to produce full replica kits for children, which sold for around £5.

“Following Leeds’ success, by the 1977-78 season, 84 out of the 92 clubs in the English Football League featured a prominent manufacturer’s logo and replica kits for kids. In Scotland that year, Umbro was selling Rangers and Celtic and Adidas were selling Aberdeen and Dundee United replica shirts. In Germany, Adidas had a monopoly on the Bundesliga. However they did not sell replica shirts of each club. Instead they sold plain shirts in the various clubs’ colours and kids were expected to sew on the club’s badge themselves to make it look official. If adults wanted to show their support, they were expected to buy the club’s tracksuit in which the players warmed up before the match. The first replica shirt for adults was Admiral’s World Cup 1982 England shirt.”

View image in fullscreen Everton’s Bob Latchford poses with a young boy wearing replica kit during an Umbro advertising photo shoot before the 1978-79 season. Photograph: Harry Ormesher/Popperfoto/Getty Images

The Revie/Patrick/cafe story has been verified by Admiral themselves, here. “Revie, ever pragmatic and ahead of his time, agreed in principle – with one condition,” reveals the company. “The home kit, with its pristine all-white ensemble inspired by Real Madrid, was sacrosanct and not up for discussion. But the away strip and training gear? Those were open to reinvention. A handshake sealed what would become one of the most influential deals in football history. Admiral immediately set to work, with the goal of launching the new away kit by Christmas. The result was a bold and modern design: a vivid yellow shirt with striking blue and white taping down the sleeves – a stylistic innovation never before seen on a football kit. The Admiral logo sat prominently on the chest, alongside Leeds United’s iconic “smiley” crest – a badge introduced by Revie as part of his wider effort to foster a family-friendly, nationally adored image for the club.”

One possible reason why clubs and brands hadn’t explored selling replica kits earlier in the UK was the 1968 Design Copyright Act, which ensured that only a certain brand could produce a particular design once it had been officially registered. Before that point, it was the wild west.

“This article suggests the first replicas were Umbro youthsets (for children) – or Umbrosets – in 1959, with Manchester United as the featured team, albeit unofficially,” highlights Nick Williamson. Early Umbrosets were endorsed by United manager Matt Busby, but by 1964 he had been replaced on the packaging by his young striker Denis Law, who seemed to endorse not only the replica kits of United and Scotland but “also eight other leading English clubs, three Scottish clubs and the international kit of England”.

The article continues: “Football clubs themselves were not a primary, nor even an especially proactive part of the marketing process of these kits, though some, such as Manchester City, did stock replicas in their club shops and promote sales through their match programme.” But it seems that we cannot truly say that these were replica kits, akin to the shirts worn by the players, but rather unofficial garms that were occasionally and sporadically endorsed or stocked by players, managers and clubs.

Paul Haynes flags this academic research by Christopher Stride, Nick Catley and Joe Headland, who scanned crowd photos from the 1960s but could not find evidence of replica shirts being worn as matchday apparel by either adult or child fans until the mid 1970s, and then only by male fans at cup finals.

View image in fullscreen There were flat caps, shirts, ties and jumpers aplenty on the terraces in the 1960s, but no replica shirts. Photograph: PA Photos

“A photo of Newcastle supporters at the 1974 FA Cup final depicts small numbers dressed in (unbranded) replica shirts,” the research reads. “Admiral-manufactured teamwear can also be spotted on adult Manchester United fans at the 1979 final, though in both cases the tightness of the sleeves hints at large youth sizes. Likewise a handful of Liverpool fans at their European Cup finals of 1977 and 1978 wore replica shirts, and the Scotland fans invading Trafalgar Square prior to the 1977 England v Scotland international also featured replica-clad revellers.”

View image in fullscreen A smattering of replica shirts were spotted amongst the Liverpool fans on the terraces of Rome at the 1977 European Cup final. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

We’ll end with a lovely personal tale from Jon Keen, which highlights how slowly some clubs were to catch on to the trend. “In Autumn 1979 I had the bright idea of getting myself a shirt as worn by the Reading FC team that year,” he emails. “The logistics were horrendous, as it seems no one had ever thought of doing that before. I had to order it individually through the local shop that supplied the football club themselves, the wonderful old-school Blake’s Sports Outfitters. They then had to order this, as a one-off, from the manufacturers, Bukta, and I didn’t actually receive the shirt until the following June, when the season was well and truly over! I loved that shirt, I wish I still had it, although no way it’d fit me now!”

Can you find any earlier official replica kits, or from further afield than the UK? Mail us with your answers.

Costly red cards, part II

Last week, we featured some of football’s most damaging red cards, dismissals that acted as the catalyst for a side’s demise, and Chris Lewis has a new suggestion. “Surely Fabio Cannavaro’s sending off in the 2010 Europa League tie versus Fulham merits inclusion?” he emails. “I appreciate the question may have been intended for over 90 minutes, but this turned a two-legged tie on its head for one of the best nights I’ve ever experienced as a Fulham supporter.

“Juventus were 3-1 up from the home leg in Turin, and scored early at Craven Cottage to go 4-1 up on aggregate with an away goal. Although we equalised, the game was finely balanced until World Cup winners Cannavaro made a rash challenge on goal-bound Zoltan Gera, resulting in a red card. After that, we ran riot in a famous night on the River Thames, scoring three more goals – including a sublime chip from Clint Dempsey (during a brief conversation at a ‘meet the players’ event, the American told me he’d intended a cross to the back post) – to settle the tie 5-4 in our favour.”

Matthew Hague offers an unusual example where a red card actually helped. “Barnsley were 1-0 down to Doncaster in 2008,” he writes. “Darren Moore was sent off in the second half and Barnsley scored four to win 4-1. Even the Doncaster manager commented that it was a catalyst for the game to change.”

View image in fullscreen Zoltan Gera of Fulham celebrates with some acrobatics. Photograph: Andrew Winning/Reuters

Knowledge archive

“Barcelona’s MSN have 56, 46 and 48 international goals – has any lineup in history had three players with 50 international goals to their name?” wondered Ben Janeson back in 2016.

“The short answer is no,” emails Chris Goodall. “This is easy to check as there have only been 49 members of the international 50 Goal Club, the majority of whom played for the likes of Thailand and Iraq. If we allow future members of the 50 Goal Club to count, then we have a winner: Ferenc Puskas, Sandor Kocsis and Lajos Tichy all played together for Budapest Honved in the mid-50s, though Puskas had long since defected to Real Madrid and Spain by the time Tichy made it to his half century.

“Then there’s the strange Inter squad of 2000-01, where three players who subsequently scored 50 international goals were kept out of the first team by two players who didn’t. Early in the season Marco Tardelli replaced Marcelo Lippi as manager and installed Álvaro Recoba as Christian Vieri’s strike partner. Hakan Sukur (51 goals for Turkey) was dropped to the bench, Robbie Keane (68 goals for the Republic of Ireland) was loaned out to Leeds, and Ronaldo (62 goals for Brazil) never made it out of the treatment room.”

Update: It should also be noted that the Barcelona trident of Lionel Messi, Samuel Eto’o and Thierry Henry all surpassed 50 international goals but not during the years they played together in Catalonia (2007-09). Messi didn’t reach his half century until 2016, Eto’o in 2011 and Henry in September 2009 (two months after Eto’o left for Inter).

Can you help?

“Jamie Spencer, 17, made his first-ever first-team appearance in a competitive match, for Huddersfield Town at Doncaster on 9 September in the prestigious EFL Trophy,” emails Richard Askham. “He came on as a substitute in the 66th minute and scored with his second touch of the ball, one to control it and the second to score. Has anyone ever scored with their very first touch, which is the only way to better young Spencer’s achievement?”

“Players from 21 different nationalities featured in the starting lineups of Manchester United and Sabah in their Champions League meeting,” notes Sajad 401. “But which match holds the record for the highest number of different nationalities represented in a European football match?”

View image in fullscreen Sabah’s Joy-Lance Mickels, a Rwanda international, is marshalled by Manchester United’s Argentina defender Lisandro Martínez. Photograph: Roger Evans/Action Plus/Shutterstock

“There still hasn’t been a 0-0 draw in Serie A this season, after four rounds of matches,” writes Stephen Hogg. “Is this getting near a record yet?”

“Watford had a starting XI comprised of 11 different nationalities against Preston earlier this month,” starts Peter Skilton. “Not only that, but of the five substitutes used, four were also unique nationalities, giving 15 different countries represented. My question is twofold; firstly has any team completed the full set with 16 different nationalities from the starting 11 and used subs (or more if the competition allows for more than five subs), and secondly, what is the lowest level where 11 different countries have made up a starting XI?”

“If Tottenham fail to score a goal against Aston Villa this weekend it means that they will go from May to at least October without finding the back of the net in a league match (due to the irritating international break coming up),” teases Steven Pye. “In terms of teams firing blanks in the league, what is the longest dry spell both in terms of days and actual game time?”

Sports.title: Max Dowman doubles up for Arsenal’s back-ups to beat Ipswich in Carabao Cup
Sports.content:
The bad news for everyone else is that Arsenal’s next generation is already here. Two mesmerising goals and an assist in a man-of-the-match display from Max Dowman underlined why the 16-year-old has been compared to a certain Lionel Messi by his manager, Mikel Arteta, as Ipswich were swatted aside with ease. Almost as impressive was the performance of the 17-year-old Marli Salmon, who oozed class in central defence on only the second senior start of his career.

Ipswich won here the last time these two sides met in this competition, in 2011, but were beaten 3-0 in the second leg of the semi-final at the Emirates before Arsenal infam­ously lost to Birmingham in the final. ­Fifteen years on, Gary O’Neil’s heavily rotated side stood no chance against last year’s runners up after Dowman’s brilliant opening goal. Noni Madueke and the stand-in skipper Mikel Merino were also on target as Arsenal made it seven wins out of seven to start the new campaign. Having finally ended their long wait for silverware in style, this team are hungry for more and know they can now rely on one of the most exciting talents ever to have emerged from their Hale End academy.

“He can deliver those actions effortlessly. That’s his biggest quality,” said Arteta of the delightful shimmy that preceded Dowman’s first goal. “It’s a joy to have him. But what we have to do is look after him. He’s 16 years old, you don’t see that in this league. In other leagues in Europe, that’s a totally different context. We really need to make sure every time we throw him in, he’s in the right context with the right ­preparation. That’s what we are ­trying to do.”

Both managers made their prior­ities clear as there were a combined 19 changes from their sides’ wins in the Premier League at the weekend. After a summer of heavy spending, many of those who helped Ipswich bounce straight back from the Championship last season were given an opportunity to stake a claim but largely failed to do so. “It’s the most extreme test that you can face,” admitted O’Neil. “Every time we made a mistake we were punished.”

Dowman’s most recent first-team appearance was in the final game of last season when Arsenal were crowned champions, and he has since completed his GCSEs before spending a week in New York during the World Cup where he rubbed shoulders with Paul Pogba.

Arteta said beforehand he would have “earn his minutes” like anyone else and it only took seven of them for Dowman to seize his opportunity. Ipswich’s fans were taunting their Arsenal counterparts about never being crowned European champions when he muscled Santiago Núñez off the ball on the halfway line and set off towards the penalty area. The imposing figure of Cédric Kipré – all 6ft 3in of him – was all that stood in Dowman’s way but he went past the Ivory Coast defender in a flurry of feet before cooly dispatching a shot into the corner and performing a Thierry Henry knee slide for good measure.

Quick Guide Roundup: Bass and Jones Peterborough's shootout heroes Show Peterborough moved into the fourth round of the Carabao Cup for the first time since 2009 thanks to a 7-6 penalty shootout victory over Barnsley that followed a thrilling 3-3 draw between the two League One sides. Barnsley were handed the lead after 61 seconds when a clearance by the Peterborough goalkeeper, Alex Bass, was charged down by Cameron McGeehan, with the Tykes captain nodding in after the ball had come off the bar. Peterborough equalised in the 19th minute when Lucca Mendonca’s cross was pushed out by the Barnsley goalkeeper, Kieran Flavell, as far as Harry Leonard, who prodded in. The hosts then completed the turnaround after 27 minutes when Harley Mills’ free-kick was headed in by the unmarked Danny Ormerod. But the Tykes were level five minutes before half-time when Reyes Cleary beat Mendonca with ease down the left before placing his shot into the bottom corner. The visitors looked to have won it when Cleary bent in his second in the 74th minute, but Ormerod sent the tie to penalties with by heading in Mills’ cross with just two minutes remaining. After 12 successful spot-kicks, a tame effort from Barnsley’s Luke Alker was saved by Bass, giving Harrison Jones the chance to send the hosts through, which he dispatched. Brentford emerged from a tense finish against Reading to book their place in the Carabao Cup fourth round with a 2-1 victory. Callum Wilson and Fabio Carvalho were on target in the first half as the Premier League club showed a clinical touch against League One opposition, who produced a number of chances but lacked the firepower to finish them off. Paudie O’Connor eventually pulled one back to revive Reading’s challenge and Brentford could not rest easy in the remaining 18 minutes, although the substitute Igor Thiago was among those who should have killed the match off. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Ipswich’s mission got even harder when Madueke hammered in after Bruno Guimarães and Merino had combined to set him up after Dowman had started the press. Barely a quarter of an hour had been played. To their credit, the hosts rallied and it needed a clearance off the line from Salmon to deny Zian Flemming. Not to be outdone by Dowman, Salmon – who signed his professional contact when he turned 17 last month having also played in the Champions League and FA Cup last season – set out on a slaloming run just before half-time after calmly turning his way out of trouble under pressure from Flemming, drawing a round of applause from the Arsenal bench.

View image in fullscreen The former Arsenal player Chuba Akpom scores Ipswich’s second goal. Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty Images

Ipswich’s hopes of mounting a comeback were extinguished within two minutes of the restart when Dowman struck again. Martín Zubimendi’s pass found him on the edge of the six-yard box and the finish was caressed into the far corner. Merino then curled home off the post from Dowman’s touch to put the result beyond any doubt, although the biggest roar of the evening came when Ipswich hit back through Anis Mehmeti after he was set up by the substitute Jack Clarke.

Including Myles Lewis-Skelly – a relative veteran these days at 19 and surely in line for an England recall this week after an excellent start to the season – Arsenal had four teenagers on the pitch at the end after the 18-year-old Theo Julienne came on at right-back. Even Ipswich had a Hale End grad­uate in their ranks by then as Chuba Akpom grabbed another consolation in injury time via a deflection. But, not for the last time one suspects, it was Dowman’s name that was on everyone’s lips at the end.

Sports.title: Iranian football returns in the shadow of war and with row over last league title
Sports.content:
Just three months ago, Iran was one of the biggest stories in football as Team Melli arrived at the World Cup to try to play in the US, a country that had been bombing and firing missiles at Tehran and other targets. A disallowed goal and a last-minute effort that hit the bar in the final group game against Egypt confirmed Iran’s group-stage exit – to the delight of some US officials – by the narrowest of margins. It also signalled the abrupt end of international attention.

This week there was a return, however, to international action as Esteghlal and Tractor SC started out in the AFC Champions League Elite. It comes after the Persian Gulf League kicked off in mid-August, almost six months after it was postponed at the end of February, and subsequently abandoned as the war continued.

“The most important impact of the war on Iranian football was the prolonged suspension of competition,” the Esteghlal head coach, Sohrab Bakhtiarizadeh, says. “For months, we were deprived of club football, and not only were the players and teams unable to train, but the fans also had nothing to talk about, engage in banter over, and so on. It was sad that football was suspended for such a long period and it will certainly weaken the sport and its passionate supporters.”

Esteghlal were especially blue as the Tehran giants were top of the league when it stopped with 22 games of the 30 played, two points clear of Tractor. It soon became clear that the season was never going to take place meaning that the 10-time winners feel they should be given number 11. “Esteghlal should be declared the champions of the previous season,” Bakhtiarizadeh says. “Being at the top of the table is a suitable criterion for determining the most successful team in a tournament at any given time. This is also what Esteghlal fans want.”

A decision is to be made soon. The majority of the other clubs seem to be against such a presentation, especially those owned by industrial companies such as the steel-backed pair Sepahan FC and Foolad, which have suffered during the war. Whatever happens, Esteghlal have started pretty well in the new campaign.

As has the league in general. There had been talk in the buildup that the games would be behind closed doors but most matches have had fans, with some decent crowds. At the Tehran derby between Persepolis and Esteghlal, the biggest game in Iran (and many would argue the biggest in Asia), 50,000 fans were in the second city of Isfahan. The usual home of both teams, the capital’s renowned Azadi Stadium, is unavailable, not because of bombs and missile damage, though the wider sports complex has been hit, but because of continuing repairs. The money spent has become a hot topic and it seems nothing is ever simple in Iranian football even during times of relative peace.

Esteghlal may not have got the trophy yet but are representing the country in the AFC Champions League Elite and started with an impressive 3-0 win against the Qatari powerhouse Al-Sadd on Monday. It was even more impressive that the home game took place in the southern Iraqi city of Basra. Iranian clubs are accustomed to playing home games away.

View image in fullscreen Iran’s Mehdi Taremi takes on Egypt’s Mohamed Salah in the group-stage game that confirmed their exit from the World Cup.

Photograph: Troy Wayrynen/Imagn Images/Reuters

“Being deprived of home advantage has been one of the biggest problems that Iranian football has faced in recent years,” Bakhtiarizadeh says. “In every situation, this opportunity has been taken away from Iranian clubs. Nevertheless, it makes us happy to host Al-Sadd in Basra, close to Iran … with the presence of some of our supporters who live in southern Iran.” The 8,000 fans did their best to create a Tehran-like atmosphere in the massive Basra International Stadium.

Given that relations between Iran and the United Arab Emirates are not exactly cordial these days, Tractor may have been relieved that there were just 1,300 in attendance in Dubai as they lost 1-0 against Shabab Al-Ahli. However, given the AFC has, for some reason, followed Uefa’s big league-style group stage, there is a lot of time to overcome a poor start.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

At least Saudi Arabian clubs were avoided, useful on and off the pitch. Even before 2023, when Riyadh and Jeddah sides started spending big, Iranian clubs were unable to compete. Years of international sanctions have had huge economic effects and football – closely connected to the state – has not escaped. Salaries have stagnated, facilities are often neglected and training camps, overseas friendlies and all the rest are harder to arrange here than in most other countries.

But it is not just Iran. No one in Asia can come close to matching the $200m (£148m) plus paid by Al-Hilal alone in the summer for Ollie Watkins, Gabriel Martinelli and Crysencio Summerville. Saudi Arabia (which unbelievably has hosted the Champions League from the quarter-finals onwards for the past two editions, an arrangement that was recently extended to 2029) and Japan have five representatives each in the 32-team tournament. Iran, a leading Asian power, has two.

The Champions League is not a level playing field, then, in many ways, but Bakhtiarizadeh is hopeful that his team, Asian champions in 1970 and 1991, can compete. “It is currently impossible for any team in Asia to match the Saudi spending power,” the former Iran international defender says.

“Nevertheless, I still believe that football is a game in which, over 90 minutes, you may be able to overcome this financial gap through effort, determination and teamwork. Competing against Asian teams is certainly difficult, especially since we have entered the competition without having participated in the summer transfer market but Esteghlal’s history compels us to try.”

Sports.title: Lionel Messi called up by Argentina to make farewell ⁠appearance in friendly
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi has been called up by Argentina to make a farewell ⁠appearance in a home friendly in October following his international retirement, the Argentinian football association (AFA) has confirmed.

“We invited ⁠the best player in ⁠the world ​to play, the icon of our selection, our captain Lionel Andrés Messi, to have a deserved farewell on 6 October, here in Argentina,” the AFA president, Claudio Tapia, said on social media.

Argentina will play three home friendlies during the 21 September to 6 October Fifa international window, their first matches since the World Cup.

They will take on ​Benin in Buenos Aires’ Monumental ‌Stadium on 6 October, ‌where Messi, who announced his retirement from international football last month, has been invited ‌to play his farewell match.

Quick Guide Rodríguez retires from international football Show Colombia midfielder James Rodríguez retired from international football on ⁠Tuesday, having won 131 caps and inspired his country to the 2014 ⁠World Cup ⁠quarter-finals. “Thank ​you for every match, every joy, every tear and every dream we ⁠shared. Defending the colours of the Colombia national team was one of the ⁠greatest honours of my life,” Rodríguez said in ​a video posted ‌on social media. The ‌35-year-old, who made his senior debut in 2011 ‌and often captained Colombia, scored 31 goals and represented his country at three World Cups and four Copa América tournaments. Rodríguez rose to global prominence at the 2014 World Cup in ‌Brazil, scoring six goals to win the Golden Boot as Colombia reached the ​quarter-finals. His volley against Uruguay in the last 16 earned him Fifa’s Puskas Award for the best goal of the year. He signed for Colombian ⁠side Atlético Nacional last week on a deal ​running ​until next June after ​leaving Major League Soccer club Minnesota ​United. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Argentina will also face Bolivia at Córdoba’s Mario Kempes Stadium on 30 September before moving to Buenos Aires to host Burkina Faso on 3 October. The Bolivia match will be played with capacity reduced by 50% as part of Fifa’s sanctions relating to incidents during this year’s ‌World Cup.

“Footballers Messi, [Rodrigo] De Paul and [Giovani] Lo Celso will be in attendance to take part in the final friendly on 6 October. ​Meanwhile, the names of the players called up from the local league will be announced on Friday,” the AFA said in a statement announcing the squad.
