World.title: Mwamba Demands Independent Probe Into Police Officer’s Death at ZP Headquarters
World.content:
Tonse-Pamodzi spokesperson disputes police account that Assistant Superintendent Daniel Banda took his own life, calling it “a suspected murder being presented as suicide”

Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance spokesperson Emmanuel Mwamba has demanded an independent and transparent investigation into the death of a 53-year-old police officer at Zambia Police Service headquarters in Lusaka, disputing the official account that he shot himself. Police say Assistant Superintendent Daniel Banda, attached to the Ballistics Unit, locked himself in his office at around 17:00 hours on 14 September while armed with an AK-47 and a pistol, and threatened to take his own life. Police assistant public relations officer Timothy Malumo said negotiators engaged him for almost four hours before he discharged the firearm and shot himself in the head shortly after 20:45 hours. His body was taken to the University Teaching Hospital mortuary to await a post-mortem.

Mwamba rejected that account, saying the circumstances were extremely worrying because Banda may have died during interrogation rather than by his own hand, and that police were attempting to portray a suspected killing as a suicide. He said Banda was the officer expected to sign off on an exchange of fire and the discovery of a weapons cache during the military raid on the residence of NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile on 14 August, a raid in which former Cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally shot. Sources told journalists Banda was being questioned by senior police officers at the time of his death, naming Criminal Investigations Department commissioner Maxwell Timba Mudenda along with officers Boyd Kayelu, Harrington Akushanga and Innocent Makukwani.

“These prejudicial and extra-judicial killings have sadly continued.”

Mwamba called on police to give the public a full and credible account of what happened. Police say investigations have been instituted and further details will be released in due course. The case adds to a string of contested deaths and detentions since the 14 August raid that have drawn concern from civil society groups and foreign governments over due process in Zambia’s security response to the post-election crackdown.

World.title: M’membe Challenges Constitutional Basis of Paramount Chief Petition for Chief Mukuni
World.content:
Socialist Party leader says title being sought for Chief Mukuni is a colonial invention the courts have already stripped from the President’s hands, while the title of Chief Mukuni Paramount Chief remains contentious.

Socialist Party president Fred M’membe has challenged the constitutional basis of a petition before the Constitutional Court seeking to have Chief Mukuni reclassified as a Paramount Chief, arguing the title itself has no roots in Leya tradition but was invented by colonial administrators in 1936. He emphasized that the debate over the Chief Mukuni Paramount Chief title reflects broader issues of tradition versus colonial imposition.

M’membe traced the modern ranking of Zambian chiefs to the Native Authorities Ordinance No. 9 and the Barotse Native Authorities Ordinance No. 25, both passed in 1936, which graded traditional leaders into Paramount Chiefs, senior chiefs, chiefs and sub-chiefs as an instrument of indirect colonial rule. He said Zambian communities had kings, councils and courts long before that date, and that what the colonial government created was not traditional leadership but a ranking system layered on top of it.

The ongoing discourse around Chief Mukuni Paramount Chief raises critical questions about the recognition and authenticity of traditional titles in contemporary Zambia.

He argued the 2016 constitutional amendments, particularly Article 165, deliberately stripped the state of any power to confer or withdraw chieftaincy titles, a position reinforced by a December 2019 Constitutional Court judgment that struck out sections three to seven of the Chiefs Act after a challenge by Chief Mwene Mutondo Mulubisha of the Nkoya people. On that basis, M’membe said, neither the President nor Parliament currently holds any lawful power to create a Paramount Chief, and a petition invoking Article 165 to achieve exactly what that clause was written to prevent risks reviving a colonial mechanism through the courts instead of government notice.

He raised concern, without alleging any deal, that Chief Mukuni’s reported endorsement of President Hakainde Hichilema’s re-election could create the appearance that any elevation granted by the same administration had been politically rewarded. M’membe warned that opening the door to state-graded titles would invite similar petitions from the Lamba, Lunda, Kaonde, Luvale, Nkoya, Namwanga, Tonga and Mambwe communities, tying up the courts in tribal ranking disputes “in a country still bleeding from August.”

His underlying argument is not that traditional leaders have too much influence but too little: he wants power shared with chiefs, religious leaders and community figures in actual governance and economic decision-making, rather than through titles handed down from State House. He linked the erosion of traditional authority to poverty, noting that Muchinga, Western, Northern, Luapula and Eastern provinces, all areas of historically strong chieftaincy, are also Zambia’s five poorest by the Living Conditions Monitoring Survey.

World.title: Zambia woos investors in critical minerals
World.content:
Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Permanent Secretary Hapenga Kabeta says government has created a conducive environment to attract investment in the country’s mineral resources.

Dr Kabeta said Zambia has undertaken reforms in the mining sector aimed at strengthening investor confidence and promoting sustainable growth and value creation.

He was speaking in a speech read on his behalf by Ministry of Mines Director of Human Resource and Administration Anthony Chilenga during the opening of the two-day Africa Critical Minerals Conference 2026.

The conference has been organised by the Shanghai Metals Market (SMM) in collaboration with the Zambia Development Agency (ZDA).

Dr Kabeta said government has established the Minerals Regulation Commission to regulate mining activities in the country.

He added that Zambia has set a target of producing three million metric tonnes of copper annually by 2031, describing the target as a significant opportunity for investors.

“The National Copper Production Strategy identifies investments in exploration, mining, processing and supporting supply chains to achieve this objective,” Dr Kabeta said.

Meanwhile, ZDA Director General Albert Halwampa said Zambia has continued to improve its investment environment to attract investors.

Mr Halwampa said Zambia and other countries should work together to create value from copper cathodes, which he said would contribute to accelerating the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

He said more than 500 Chinese companies have established operations in Zambia, which he cited as an indication of the country’s conducive investment environment.

“As a country, as we make the investment landscape friendly, other countries should be free to invest in the country,” Mr Halwampa said.

And Shanghai Metals Market organiser Adam Fan said mining remains a cornerstone of national economies.

Mr Fan added that Africa’s mining sector is poised for high-quality growth.

World.title: Lavushimanda reports no Anthrax cases in Livestock
World.content:
The Department of Fisheries and Livestock in Lavushimanda District of Muchinga Province says it has not recorded any cases of anthrax in livestock.

Lavushimanda District Livestock and Fisheries Coordinator Abia Siwiti said the district has been conducting annual mass livestock vaccination campaigns to prevent outbreaks of diseases, following anthrax cases recorded in Muchinga Province in 2023.

Speaking in an interview with the media after a stakeholders’ meeting, Mr Siwiti said the department has embarked on a vaccination exercise targeting more than 5,000 livestock following an anthrax outbreak recorded in Mpika and Shiwang’andu districts.

He said government has provided the district with 6,000 doses of anthrax vaccine for livestock.

“For Lavushimanda, no cases have been reported yet in the livestock sector,” Mr Siwiti said.

He added that sensitisation activities would also be conducted in communities to raise awareness about the anthrax outbreak and the livestock vaccination exercise.

Meanwhile, Lavushimanda District Public Health Officer Jackson Daka said government has put in place measures, including the Incident Management System (IMS), One Health meetings and Rapid Response Teams (RRTs), to enhance public awareness and response to the outbreak at provincial and district levels.

Mr Daka said the Ministry of Health has also collected human and animal samples in Mpika, which have been sent to Lusaka for testing.

“On planning and coordination, they have done IMS and RRTs,” he said.

Mr Daka thanked government, through the Zambia National Public Health Institute (ZNPHI), for facilitating the meeting and bringing stakeholders together to discuss the anthrax outbreak affecting the province.

He said the meeting was important because Mpika is a neighbouring district and is close to Lavushimanda, making the district vulnerable to the spread of the disease.

“It was very important for Lavushimanda to hold this meeting so that we can come up with ways to educate the community,” Mr Daka said.

Mr Daka added that the meeting would help stakeholders conduct sensitisation activities to ensure communities remain alert and take preventive measures against the disease.

Anthrax is a zoonotic and highly infectious disease that can be transmitted through contact with infected animals or consumption of contaminated meat.

World.title: Chiefs back Grow Zambia Agenda
World.content:
Traditional leaders in Kazungula District have pledged to support President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda by contributing to the 10,10,5,3,3,1,1,1 trajectory.

Chief Sekute and Chief Mukuni of Kazungula District in Southern Province said government’s target of producing 10 million metric tonnes of maize for both local and international markets requires the full participation of chiefdoms.

The traditional leaders were speaking when Southern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Gift Monde paid courtesy calls on them at their respective palaces.

The traditional leaders also commended government for its quick response in establishing Food Reserve Agency (FRA) satellite depots to ease the transportation of maize by farmers to marketing points.

Chief Sekute said his chiefdom was ready to contribute to the agenda, adding that farmers were now motivated to increase production following the establishment of a satellite depot in the chiefdom.

“As a chiefdom, we have not had satellite depots for many years, and this was challenging because our farmers had to travel long distances to sell their produce to FRA,” Chief Sekute said.

He commended government for responding to the challenges faced by farmers by bringing the depots closer to them.

And Chief Mukuni thanked government for coming to the aid of farmers by reducing the distances they have to travel to sell their produce.

“We appreciate government for coming through for our farmers. This has been their cry for a long time,” Chief Mukuni said.

Meanwhile, Southern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Gift Monde assured the traditional leaders of government’s commitment to securing maize stocks ahead of the anticipated El Niño conditions.

Mr Monde said government was aware of the challenges farmers in the two chiefdoms had been facing, hence the decision to establish depots within their catchment areas.

“We are aware that farmers want to sell their produce, but let us also be mindful of the El Niño in case we experience a drought,” Mr Monde said.

Mr Monde advised farmers to reserve part of their maize for household consumption in view of the anticipated El Niño conditions.

Stakeholders in Chama District of Eastern Province have expressed satisfaction with the ongoing verification of ballot papers and account forms used during the August 13, 2026 General Elections.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) in Kaoma District has commenced the verification of Ballot Paper Account Forms for the National Assembly and local government elections held during the August 13, 2026 General Election.

The two-day exercise is aimed at auditing and reconciling all ballot papers received, issued, used, unused and spoilt during the elections to ensure accountability and accuracy in the management of election materials.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 16, 2026
World.content:
press review

U.S. Imposes Visa Restrictions Over South Africa

The United States has announced visa restrictions against people it accuses of discriminating against South Africa's white minority. This has further escalated tensions between Washington and Pretoria. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the restrictions would target people involved in what the US describes as race-based discrimination, inciting violence or enabling land confiscation without compensation. No individuals were named. South Africa has repeatedly rejected US claims of discrimination and white persecution, saying its land reform policies are aimed at addressing inequalities created under apartheid and do not allow arbitrary seizure of property. The US embassy in Pretoria said the visa measures were the first in a series of possible escalatory steps. South Africa has sought to ease tensions through diplomatic engagement.

DR Congo Protests Tshisekedi Constitutional Plans

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Police in the Democratic Republic of Congo used tear gas and arrested protesters as demonstrations were held in several cities against President Felix Tshisekedi's plans to change the constitution. Opposition parties have united under the C64 coalition to oppose the proposed changes, which they say could allow Tshisekedi to seek a third term. Clashes broke out between opposition and pro-government supporters in Kinshasa, while police dispersed demonstrations that had been banned by local authorities. Protests were also reported in Lubumbashi and Mbandaka, where activists defied bans and were dispersed by security forces. Opposition figures accused authorities of making arbitrary arrests, while police said they were maintaining public order. The constitutional changes come as the country continues to face conflict in the east, including fighting involving the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group. The opposition has also rejected Tshisekedi's offer of national dialogue, accusing him of using it to strengthen his position.

South African President Vows Justice As More Women's Bodies Found in Kempton Park

South African police are investigating the deaths of eight women whose bodies have been found at different locations in Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg, since July. Several of the women were found naked or partially clothed, with some showing signs of possible sexual violence, raising concerns that the cases could be connected. Police have not confirmed that a serial killer is responsible but are investigating whether one person or a group may be behind the deaths. One suspect remains in custody following the discovery of the first body. The latest deaths have prompted warnings for women in the area to avoid walking or jogging alone, particularly in isolated locations. President Cyril Ramaphosa has ordered police to prioritise the investigations, while Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said the deaths must not be in vain. The killings have intensified concerns over South Africa's persistent gender-based violence, with authorities yet to establish whether the cases are linked.

Algeria Faces Pressure Over Death Penalty Expansion

Amnesty International is urging Algeria to abandon plans to expand the use of the death penalty following deadly wildfires that devastated parts of the country. President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has ordered changes to the Penal Code to allow the death penalty for people convicted of deliberately starting or instigating fires, and has indicated that it could also be extended to child abduction and abuse. Algeria has not executed since 1993, although courts continue to impose death sentences. Amnesty said that the wildfire response should focus on prevention, emergency preparedness and independent investigations into all factors that contributed to the deaths, rather than expanding capital punishment. The organisation also raised concerns over the use of terrorism-related charges carrying the death penalty against people accused of involvement in the fires. It said Algeria should ensure fair trials and accountability while taking into account the role of climate change and weaknesses in disaster preparedness.

Boko Haram Rejects Nigeria Ceasefire Claims in New Video

Boko Haram has denied reports that it reached a ceasefire agreement with the Nigerian government, dismissing the claims as false. In a video, the group's Sharia judge, Mallam Abdulrahman, said its leadership had not agreed to any truce, although he acknowledged that reconciliation was possible under Islamic principles. He accused the Nigerian government of misleading the public and urged fighters not to be discouraged by reports of a ceasefire. The denial follows reports that the government had secretly reached an agreement with a faction led by Bakura Doro, allegedly linked to negotiations for the release of more than 300 civilians abducted in Borno State in March. The reports claimed the agreement had been in place since June and involved a ransom payment, which the government has denied. Nigerian officials have not confirmed the existence of a ceasefire, with the presidency directing questions to the National Security Adviser or Defence Ministry.

Close 

WHO Reports Active Mpox Transmission in 11 African Nations

The World Health Organization said that 11 African countries recorded active mpox transmission during the six weeks to 16 August 2026, reporting 1,153 confirmed cases and seven deaths. Madagascar recorded the highest number with 785 cases, followed by Angola with 184, Kenya with 94, the Democratic Republic of Congo with 41 and Cameroon with 28. WHO said weekly confirmed cases have remained relatively stable at around 200. However, reporting delays and reduced surveillance mean the figures could be underestimated. The figures form part of a wider outbreak that has affected 35 African countries since January 2025. More than 52,000 confirmed cases and 238 deaths were recorded on the continent by 16 August 2026. Madagascar remains the main concern, with WHO describing its outbreak as the largest globally and in Africa since December 2025. Despite Africa CDC ending its continental public health emergency declaration in January, WHO said mpox remains a significant health concern and has extended its standing recommendations through August 2027.

World.title: South Africa: Suspect Sought as Police Probe Ekurhuleni Murders - South African News Briefs - September 16, 2026
World.content:
press review

Police Pursue Person of Interest in Ekurhuleni Murders

Police said that they are pursuing a person of interest in connection with the deaths of eight women in Ekurhuleni, reports EWN. Police have not disclosed the individual's identity or gender, and they have not confirmed which cases the person may be linked to. The women have been found since July, with several discovered half-naked and bruised. Investigators are examining whether the deaths are connected but have cautioned against concluding that a single person or group is responsible for all eight cases. A separate suspect arrested after the first body was found remains in custody.

Madlanga Commission to Hear Vetting Expert



The Madlanga Commission is set to hear evidence from an international vetting expert as it investigates allegations of criminal infiltration within law enforcement agencies, reports SABC News. The expert will testify about the processes used to assess the integrity and suitability of people appointed to law enforcement positions. The evidence could shed light on whether existing vetting systems effectively identify candidates suitable for senior roles, amid testimony on the conduct and integrity of senior law enforcement officials.

SASSA Grant System Faces Scrutiny Over Bank Checks

The South African Social Security Agency's automated verification system for the R370 Social Relief of Distress grant is reportedly causing problems for some applicants because bank transactions can be interpreted as income, according to Wits University legal expert Busisiwe Kamolane-Kgadima. The system checks applicants’ information against government and banking records to determine whether they exceed the income threshold. She said such checks are necessary to prevent people from receiving benefits they do not qualify for. She raised concerns about the heavy reliance on an automated process, which may not account for the nature or source of individual bank transactions.

World.title: Rwanda: Rwanda Eyes Nuclear Tech to Improve Agriculture
World.content:
The governement is exploring the use of nuclear and isotopic techniques to improve agricultural productivity, food safety and resilience to climate change, Minister of State for Infrastructure Armand Zingiro has said.

He was speaking during the 70th Regular Session of the IAEA General Conference in Vienna, Austria, which is taking place from September 14 to 18.

ALSO READ: Inside Rwanda's nuclear development ambitions



"In agriculture and food security, Rwanda recognises the significant potential of nuclear and isotopic techniques to improve agricultural productivity, food safety, nutrition and climate resilience," said Zingiro, who led the Rwandan delegation attending the conference.

Nuclear technology is used in agriculture primarily through radiation and isotope techniques to improve crop yields, control pests, manage natural resources, and ensure food safety.

"Rwanda has therefore expressed its interest in participating in the Atoms4Food initiative, jointly supported by the IAEA and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations."

The initiative supports countries in using nuclear and other technologies to improve agricultural and livestock productivity, manage natural resources, reduce food losses, improve food safety and nutrition, and strengthen resilience to climate change.

Zingiro said Rwanda plans to work with the IAEA and FAO to assess its national priorities and capacities and develop a programme tailored to the country's needs.

He said the cooperation would support the country's efforts to strengthen food security, improve agricultural productivity and food safety, reduce post-harvest losses and build climate-resilient food systems.

ALSO READ: Nuclear energy: Why Rwanda is opting for small modular reactors

The interest in agricultural applications comes as Rwanda continues to develop its wider nuclear science and technology programme, including plans for nuclear power and a research reactor.

In March, Rwanda hosted an IAEA Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review (INIR) mission, which assessed the country's progress in developing the infrastructure needed for the safe, secure and sustainable introduction of nuclear power.

The review provided recommendations for the next stage of the programme, including finalising a comprehensive report to support national decision-making on the introduction of nuclear power, completing the review of national legislation, and further developing and adopting policies and strategies for the nuclear power programme.

"Following the INIR mission, Rwanda has already developed an Integrated Work Plan for the implementation of the INIR recommendations, which provides a coordinated framework for addressing the identified areas and strengthening Rwanda's readiness in line with the IAEA Milestones Approach," Zingiro said.

He said the government would continue working with the IAEA to implement and monitor the work plan.

Alongside the nuclear power programme, Rwanda is preparing to develop a research reactor as part of the planned Centre for Nuclear Science and Technology.

The country hosted an IAEA Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review for Research Reactors (INIR-RR) mission in July to assess its preparedness for developing the facility.

The mission provided recommendations on the institutional, technical and human capacity needed to support the project.

Close 

He said Rwanda was also focused on developing the human and institutional capacity needed to sustain its nuclear programme through specialised training, education, knowledge management and international partnerships.

The government is pursuing nuclear applications in other sectors, including healthcare, where it is working to strengthen cancer diagnosis and treatment through radiopharmaceutical production and Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging.

"Rwanda further reaffirms its commitment to nuclear safety, nuclear security, safeguards and radiation protection as fundamental pillars of its national nuclear programme," he said.

The government, he added, would continue working with the IAEA and other partners to ensure that nuclear activities are carried out in line with international obligations and standards.

World.title: Mali: One Man's Quest to End Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) in Mali
World.content:
United Nations — After years of defending FGM as a cultural practice, Sidi Haidara came to a realization: No tradition should come at the expense of a girl's health, rights, or future.

In Mali, an estimated nine out of ten women and girls have undergone female genital mutilation (FGM). And for years, Sidi Haidara, a father and recognized leader in his community, believed the practice was simply part of life.

Like many people in his community in central Mali, he saw it as a tradition passed down through generations - one that should be preserved.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Today, he walks from village to village with a very different message: No tradition should come at the expense of a girl's health, rights, or future.

His story goes beyond one man's personal transformation. Across parts of West and Central Africa, FGM remains deeply rooted - with Mali having one of the highest rates in the region and no laws that specifically criminalize the practice. Even recently, some men in Mali have launched an all-male pro-FGM campaign on the grounds of protecting tradition.

In places where social norms are deeply entrenched, change often begins with trusted voices from within the community - voices like Haidara's.

After spending years defending female genital mutilation, Sidi Haidara now leads community dialogues in Mopti, Mali, encouraging families to protect girls' rights and abandon the practice. Credit: UN Women/Dieneba Deme

How UN Women and partners are shifting mindsets and empowering new anti-FGM advocates in Mali

"I used to believe that this practice was part of our traditions and needed to be preserved", says Haidara.

Nothing suggested that he would one day become one of the people advocating for its abandonment.

His perspective began to change after taking part in training sessions, workshops, and community dialogues organized through the Men and Boys as Agents of Change project, implemented by UN Women with financial support from the Government of Germany.

As he listened to different experiences and learned about the consequences of FGM, he began questioning his beliefs - beliefs he had never challenged before. He also came to understand that lasting change cannot simply be imposed - it grows through dialogue, trust, and community ownership.

"UN Women's trainings - with the support of Germany - transformed my understanding of female genital mutilation. I learned about the physical, psychological, and social consequences that this practice imposes on girls."

How to end FGM in Mali: Begin with listening, questioning, and conversing

"Today, I regularly organize awareness-raising sessions with families, religious leaders, young people, and women", he explains.

Rather than telling people what to think, he encourages conversations about what it means to protect girls and challenges long-held beliefs through dialogue.

Little by little, those conversations are making a difference. "I can see change: more parents are asking questions, several families are abandoning female genital mutilation, and discussions about protecting girls have become more open."

"I am convinced that protecting girls today means investing in the future of our entire community."

People can change - and so can social norms

Haidara's journey is part of a broader movement taking place across the regions of Mopti and Gao in Mali.

With support from the Government of Germany, UN Women works alongside religious and traditional leaders, women, young people, and men like Haidara who are committed to community-driven initiatives that prevent violence against women and girls and challenge harmful social norms.

To date, 50 community initiatives have been implemented across the two regions, while eight community-dialogue platforms provide spaces for people to discuss girls' rights, their protection, and ways to prevent gender-based violence.

Close 

For Haidara, abandoning a harmful practice is about more than leaving a tradition behind. It is about giving girls the opportunity to grow up safely, stay in school, and shape their own futures.

His journey shows that some of the most meaningful changes happen when those who once upheld harmful social norms become the people helping to transform them.

Haidara knows traditions do not change overnight. But every conversation creates an opportunity for reflection. Every family that chooses to protect its daughters helps write a different future from the one that generations before them inherited.

In Mopti and Gao, these conversations are showing that lasting change does not necessarily begin with a new law or policy. More often, it begins when communities themselves decide to imagine a different future for their girls.

Source: UNFPA

IPS UN Bureau

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Ebola Outbreak Slows in Parts of DR Congo but Crisis Remains Severe
World.content:
Ebola infections are slowing in parts of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo four months into the outbreak, but cases are climbing fast in North Kivu and the World Health Organization (WHO) says it is too early to declare that the epidemic has peaked.

Since the outbreak was officially declared on 15 May, 7,258 cases have been confirmed, including 3,510 deaths, while 1,726 people have recovered. The virus has now reached seven provinces.

Congolese Health Minister Samuel Kamba said on Saturday that the epidemic had passed its peak, pointing to a gradual slowdown in transmission since mid-August. Daily infections have fallen from around 120 new cases to nearly 80.

There are also signs of improvement in Ituri province, the epicentre of the outbreak, which accounts for 78 percent of confirmed cases. Three health zones - Adja, Kambala and Mahagi - have gone 41 days without recording a new case, health officials at the African Union said.



But the WHO has stopped short of declaring that the outbreak has peaked, warning that improvements in some areas mask sharply different trends elsewhere.

Ebola deaths in DR Congo top 3,000 as WHO says vaccine trials imminent

Progress but no peak yet

"Trends at the national level do not reflect trends at the provincial or local level," Olivier le Polain, head of the WHO's epidemiology and analysis unit, told reporters in Geneva.

Asked on Tuesday whether the outbreak had reached a turning point, le Polain remained cautious.

"It's too early to confidently say we have passed a peak."

Ebola is spreading at an "exponential" rate in North Kivu, particularly in the city of Butembo, the WHO said. The province accounted for around 45 percent of all cases reported last week.

South Ubangi became the seventh province affected after a case was detected there last week, far from the epicentre.

The new case shows the risk of the epidemic spreading to other parts of the country as large numbers of people move around, the WHO said.

Another 5,000 health workers are needed to tackle the epidemic, the organisation estimated last week.

Several treatments and vaccines are being tested against the Bundibugyo Ebola virus behind the current outbreak, for which no approved vaccine or treatment currently exists.

DRC school year begins amid Ebola, strikes and conflict

Close 

A months-long fight

Efforts to curb Ebola in eastern DR Congo are beginning to show results, UN officials said on Tuesday, but they stressed that the epidemic remains severe and will take months to bring under control.

"It remains a deadly and a massive epidemic," UN special Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis told reporters in Geneva.

"There are some areas of progress, but nonetheless, in other areas, we continue to see growth in cases."

World.title: South Africa: Ekurhuleni Under Lockdown - Police Launch Manhunt in Kempton Park After Eighth Murder Victim Found
World.content:
The bodies of eight women have been discovered in Ekurhuleni between July and September, prompting an intensive police investigation. Authorities are urging the public to come forward with useful information and avoid speculation.

The SA Police Service (SAPS) is planning to "lock down" Kempton Park and surrounding locales in the coming weeks as an assembled specialist team works to find the killer or killers of eight women whose bodies have recently been discovered in the area.

Speaking to the media on Tuesday night, acting Police Minister Professor Firoz Cachalia gave a briefing on the investigation hours after another woman's body was discovered behind Club 69 in KwaThema, Springs, Ekurhuleni. The body was that of an unidentified woman in her thirties, found naked and in a state of decomposition.

High-level response

Cachalia said a multidisciplinary team with the necessary expertise had been assembled to investigate the killings.

"The team is in place, and I can give you the assurance, based on past experience, that when it comes to such situations, the South African Police Service has the experience, the high-level expertise, to investigate cases of this kind.

"I also give you the assurance that the political leadership has a responsibility, which we will shoulder, to work with our law enforcement agencies, to ensure that the investigation continues until we get clarity, a result that the families deserve and our people expect," said Cachalia....

World.title: Trump's AI race with China could become the biggest mistake of our time
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

In less than two weeks, President Donald Trump will welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington. Trump says AI will be a major topic of their September 24 talks and insists America must stay ahead of China. But the race has acquired a second, more dangerous dimension: some of the people building the world’s most powerful AI systems now warn they are advancing faster than humans can safely control them.

Jacob Coxon, a researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from Anthropic last week with a warning: Competition among frontier labs is driving ever more powerful systems forward before researchers know how to keep them reliably under human control. Coxon told WIRED that colleagues described the next year or two as "crunch time for humanity."

Days later, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei went further. In an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," he argued the industry must deliberately slow how fast it increases model capabilities so safeguards can catch up. "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote, proposing independent evaluators embedded inside frontier labs, coordinated safety standards among democratic nations, and eventually international arrangements covering the most dangerous capabilities. He did not call for halting AI development.

What began as an Anthropic warning quickly became a rare convergence among rivals. OpenAI’s Sam Altman endorsed Amodei’s call for independent evaluators. Elon Musk responded simply, "Dario is right." Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis backed the same direction, while Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that superintelligence that does not help humanity and does not remain under human control is not worth pursuing.

AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST

None of this proves AI is about to destroy humanity, and some of the alarm deserves skepticism. Anthropic is reportedly preparing an IPO that could value the company at nearly $2 trillion. That raises a fair question: Is some of this rhetoric also advertising the extraordinary power, and therefore potential value, of its technology? Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has accused parts of the industry of stoking cybersecurity fears while preparing products to address them. The incentives deserve scrutiny. But Altman’s decision to delay OpenAI’s IPO until 2027 over safety concerns cuts against the claim that this is merely financial theater.

The first AI Cold War question was who would build the most powerful systems. The harder question is whether either side can remain in control of what it builds.

But America cannot consider these warnings in a vacuum. China changes the calculation. In earlier Fox News columns, I have warned against regulating America into technological defeat, copying Beijing’s surveillance model, or treating this as merely a race between chatbots. As I argue in my book, "The New AI Cold War," the competition spans chips, energy, data centers, cyber operations, military power, scientific discovery, and global influence.

TRUMP SAYS CHINESE PRESIDENT XI JINPING WILL VISIT US ON SEPT 24

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent captured the strategic bind bluntly: "We can’t pause. You can’t, because the Chinese won’t pause." Trump has now stated the competing imperative just as plainly. Asked Sunday whether AI development should slow, Trump dismissed the warnings as exaggerated, saying unnamed critics were hyping things that won’t happen. "We’re leading China in AI," he said. "Whoever wins AI wins." He said Washington could still add guardrails.

Bessent’s concern is understandable; the administration is pursuing both speed and safeguards. Trump’s Genesis Mission links federal scientific data and supercomputing to AI research across more than 15 agencies. His June national security directive accelerates AI adoption while requiring systems to remain "robust, steerable, controllable" and subject to human accountability. A separate executive order provides for voluntary pre-release federal cybersecurity evaluation of frontier models.

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL

Congress still lacks a comprehensive statutory framework, but the disagreement has become more explicit. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., rejected an emergency moratorium, warning that if lawmakers rush to regulate, China will close the gap.

Former White House AI adviser David Sacks made the sharper free-market argument: Laboratories that want to slow down can do so themselves. They should not use Washington to force smaller competitors to apply the same brakes.

REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES

Other lawmakers are proposing approaches ranging from bans on superintelligence to narrower requirements that developers test and disclose catastrophic risks. Washington broadly agrees that something consequential is happening. It does not agree on what to do about it.

Then there is China. On Sept. 8, U.S. cyber and law enforcement officials accused Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of distilling American AI technology "at an industrial scale." Beijing rejected the accusations and called distillation a common industry technique. That dispute exposes the danger of unilateral American restraint. Washington can regulate American laboratories; it cannot order Beijing to accept identical limits.

CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE

Beijing made that point explicit this week. Responding Monday to Amodei’s proposal, China’s Foreign Ministry denounced what it called fearmongering and warned that confrontation would disrupt global AI governance. Washington wants China to cooperate on slowing the most dangerous capabilities while restricting Beijing’s access to the chips and model capabilities that could close the gap.

Amodei himself recognizes this: Slowing democratic AI development beyond the American lead could let Chinese Communist Party-linked projects move ahead and create new dangers.

AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY

Yet an unrestricted race creates a different danger. Every laboratory races because its rivals race. Every nation accelerates because it fears falling behind. That is the classic security dilemma I have warned about in "The New AI Cold War". Actions one side takes to increase its security can drive the other side to accelerate, leaving both less secure.

The Sept. 24 summit arrives at that moment. Reuters reported preparations for U.S.-China AI safety discussions covering AI-directed cyberattacks and incident information-sharing, though the White House said no separate meeting had been formally scheduled. The choices range from racing ahead to stopping outright. Between them lie more practical options: safety requirements triggered by dangerous capabilities, independent evaluations, and narrow agreements governing catastrophic uses.

And any agreement faces a brutal problem: verification. Nuclear arms control dealt with warheads, missiles and enrichment plants that leave physical signatures; frontier AI resides largely in software, model weights and computing infrastructure. Amodei acknowledges that limited agreements on clearly dangerous applications may be more realistic than a comprehensive pause, while more ambitious restrictions become progressively harder to verify.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That is the defining paradox of the new AI Cold War. America cannot afford to let China dominate artificial intelligence, but competition does not make technological risk disappear. Trump says whoever wins AI wins. Amodei, Altman, Musk and other industry leaders warn that winning the race will mean little if the winner cannot control what it builds. Beijing, meanwhile, says it supports AI cooperation while rejecting an American strategy designed to preserve the U.S. technological advantage.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

That leaves Trump and Xi with a harder problem than simply deciding who gets there first. The first AI Cold War question was who would build the most powerful systems. The harder question is whether either side can remain in control of what it builds. With Xi coming to Washington on Sept. 24, that is no longer merely an engineering problem. It is a problem of national strategy.

World.title: Rare cancer cases strike in California community as families demand answers
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A cluster of rare cancer diagnoses has sparked concern and prompted environmental testing in Ladera Ranch, California, although state health officials say no specific cause has been identified.

At least six children in the area have been diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma, according to federal officials and local reporting.

This exceptionally rare cancer, which forms in the bone or nearby soft tissue, primarily occurs in adolescents and young adults, per the National Cancer Institute.

WOMAN LOSES BEST FRIEND TO OVARIAN CANCER, THEN RECEIVES SAME DEVASTATING DIAGNOSIS MONTHS LATER

"Knowing that this is a very rare cancer diagnosis amplifies the concerns," Dr. Janet Yoon, a pediatric oncologist and sarcoma specialist at City of Hope in Los Angeles, told Fox News Digital. "Anytime you hear of cases in a geographic location, it does raise some concerns ... I can completely understand why further investigation is being done."

Following the March 2026 death of 17-year-old Brody Matteson from complications of treatment for Ewing sarcoma, more families began speaking publicly about rare cancer diagnoses in the community, according to local reports.

Community seeks answers

Some residents – including Matteson's father, Dustin Matteson – have suggested the illnesses could be linked to the community's use of herbicides and pesticides, which prompted calls for a broader environmental investigation.

"We don't have a clear line of evidence for pesticides, but it is one of the things that concerns us," Matteson said to NBC Los Angeles in July.

ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND

In 2024, prompted by residents’ concerns, the California Department of Public Health conducted a county-level review in an attempt to determine whether pesticide use in the community could have played a role in the development of certain cancer types.

"That analysis did not find an unusual pattern at the county level, but the data available at the time was​ limited," the CDPH stated on its website.

The agency is now conducting a second review of cancer incidence data for the Ladera Ranch area.

"CDPH currently estimates the assessment will be completed in fall 2026, although the timeline may change based on the scope and complexity of the review and any additional information that may need to be evaluated," the agency stated.

"At this time, our colleagues at CalEPA (California Environmental Protection Agency) and its boards, departments and offices have not identified any immediate environmental hazards."

"We don't have a clear line of evidence for pesticides, but it is one of the things that concerns us."

The CDPH stated that it is not yet known whether diagnoses of Ewing sarcoma and other cancer types are higher than expected in the Ladera Ranch community – or whether environmental factors can increase the risk.

In July 2026, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli asked the Environmental Protection Agency to investigate possible environmental factors that could have contributed to multiple pediatric cancer cases.

Over the summer, hundreds of residents gathered at community meetings. At the same time, Ladera Ranch Maintenance Corporation (LARMAC) – the master homeowners association (HOA) for the planned community of Ladera Ranch in Orange County – temporarily paused its use of certain landscape chemicals and formed an advisory committee to review its landscaping practices.

As the investigation has continued, some residents have also publicly reported diagnoses of other cancers, including glioblastoma, although the current state review has not established whether those cases are related.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

On Sept. 14, California State Fullerton researchers began collecting soil and water samples from local parks as part of the environmental investigation.

Jennifer Piazza, Ph.D., professor in the Department of Public Health at Cal State Fullerton, assembled the team of researchers to help address the environmental concerns stemming from the pediatric cancer cases.

"Environmental sampling is the first step of our larger, ongoing scientific investigation," she told Fox News Digital. "We are collecting soil and water samples across Ladera Ranch. They are being analyzed for heavy metals, such as arsenic and lead, as well as pesticides."

The team expects to have results by the end of the year, Piazza said.

"I also want to emphasize that whatever we find does not imply causality in terms of the pediatric cancer cases in Ladera Ranch," she added.

CLICK HERE TO 

LARMAC released a statement to People Magazine, extending its "heartfelt compassion to the families who have been affected by these devastating illnesses."

"LARMAC takes these concerns seriously. We are aware that public health agencies are reviewing available information, and we will continue to cooperate with those efforts and follow guidance provided by the appropriate health and regulatory authorities."

"It's pain that persists. It's pain that wakes them up from their sleep. It's pain that limits their daily activities."

"At this time, we are not aware of any determination by those agencies identifying a specific environmental cause or linking the Association’s landscape management practices to these illnesses," the statement read.

The organization also noted that it has reduced the use of synthetic pesticides and switched to organic pesticides.

What to know about Ewing sarcoma

"With Ewing sarcoma, there is no confirmed genetic or environmental cause that we know of," Yoon told Fox News Digital.

"We have not found any confirmed genetic or environmental factor that increases the likelihood of developing Ewing sarcoma."

Some studies have linked occupational or high-level exposure to certain pesticides with an increased risk of several cancers, although the evidence varies by chemical and cancer type, according to the American Cancer Society.

No known lifestyle-related or environmental cause of Ewing sarcoma has been identified, the ACS states.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The disease most often presents as persistent pain rather than a typical sports injury or growing pain, according to Yoon.

"It's pain that persists. It's pain that wakes them up from their sleep. It's pain that limits their daily activities."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The doctor called cancer the "great masquerader" in children due to its rarity. "Growing pains are much more common than cancer," she added.

Yoon encouraged families to seek medical evaluation if pain is persistent, worsening or interfering with normal activities. Specialized cancer centers with sarcoma expertise can help ensure an accurate diagnosis, she advised.

World.title: Coffee lovers have a new No. 1 city and it's not Portland or Seattle
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The country's best city for coffee lovers is not Seattle, Portland or even New York, according to a new report.

Best known for its area theme parks, Orlando, Florida, has been brewing up a new attraction as America's top destination for coffee lovers, a WalletHub analysis found.

The City Beautiful took the No. 1 spot in WalletHub's ranking of the 100 largest U.S. cities, edging out Portland, Oregon, which fell from first place last year to No. 2.

COFFEE LOVERS CAN TAKE HEART: UP TO 5 CUPS A DAY APPEARS SAFE FOR MOST ADULTS, EXPERTS SAY

Miami ranked No. 3, followed by Long Beach, California, at No. 4 and Seattle, the birthplace of Starbucks, at No. 5.

The results offer a new definition of what makes a great coffee city today. While coffee is a daily habit for 66% of Americans, according to the National Coffee Association, coffee drinkers are increasingly looking for affordable, reliable, highly rated shops that have free Wi-Fi instead of trendy cafés.

Coffee shops increasingly serve as workspaces and social hubs for tourists, students and remote workers, WalletHub analyst Chip Lupo, based in South Carolina, told Fox News Digital.

AMERICA'S BEST FOOD CITIES RANKED BY EXPERT, WITH CHOICES THAT COULD INFURIATE LOCALS

Lupo said Orlando's tourism-driven economy means visitors often need a reliable place to charge their phones, connect to free Wi-Fi and save money where they can.

"People want to have a coffee, they may want to go in and scroll for a little while before they hit Disney World, so they want to make the rest of the experience as affordable as they can to spend more of their money on the tourist attraction," Lupo said.

Orlando is also home to the University of Central Florida, he added.

"There's a lot of broke college kids out there, and they're already spending the little money they have on coffee, so they don't want to have to pay for the Wi-Fi also," Lupo explained.

LOOKING FOR BETTER COFFEE? HUNDREDS OF CHEFS AND SOMMELIERS SAY THESE ARE THE WORLD'S BEST

Cities that attract young adults and college students also ranked highly, including Pittsburgh at No. 9 and Austin, Texas, at No. 10. Pittsburgh's growing med-tech and tech sectors have helped draw young professionals to the city, Lupo said.

Lupo was most surprised that this year's ranking included three Florida cities in its top 10. Tampa landed at No. 6.

"You have three cities in Florida — hot, muggy, warm weather pretty much year-round — and also you have Long Beach, a Southern California city," he said, adding that they could be opting for an iced coffee.

CLICK HERE TO 

"Maybe that's how a lot of folks start off their day, drinking a cold iced coffee first thing in the morning."

Of the 100 cities WalletHub examined, it measured "coffee friendliness," including the price of packaged coffee and cappuccinos, household coffee spending, the share of residents with coffee makers and the number of coffee shops per capita.

The personal finance company also weighed the availability of affordable coffee shops that have at least 4.5-star reviews, free Wi-Fi, coffee and tea manufacturers, doughnut shops and local interest based on Google searches.

In cities such as New York, rising coffee prices and pressure on small, independent shops may help explain why the Big Apple landed at No. 44, Lupo said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

The ranking also underscores how a daily coffee habit affects the wallet.

Households in the most coffee-crazy cities can spend up to $327 a year on the beverage, while frequent espresso and cappuccino drinkers may save by preparing drinks at home, WalletHub found.

Lupo noted that several lower-ranked cities, including Laredo, Texas; Toledo, Ohio; Detroit; Memphis, Tennessee; and Lubbock, Texas, are places where residents may have less room in their budgets for coffee purchases.

"When grocery costs are at a premium, usually one of the first places you'll cut back [is] things like coffee," he said.

Buying a coffee or espresso machine for home can "pretty much pay for itself in the first couple of months," Lupo added.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As for the year ahead, Lupo said he will be watching to see if Portland can reclaim its top spot.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think they're going to try to make some changes to put themselves back in that No. 1 spot," he said.

They also receive information on how to appeal the fine. If they choose not to appeal, the fine is withheld from their next game check.

If a player protests a ruling, he schedules a hearing with the NFL, and his case is assigned to one of the league’s current appeals officers.

World.title: Saudi Arabia accuses Houthis of attacking Mecca, warns holy city is a ‘red line’
World.content:
Saudi Arabia has accused the Iran-backed Houthi rebels of attempting to attack Islam’s holiest city, declaring Mecca a “red line” in the escalating conflict.

The kingdom’s claim drew condemnation from across the Middle East, but no immediate sign of military support as fears grew of a return to all-out war between the key U.S. ally and the Yemeni rebels.

The Houthis swiftly denied targeting Mecca, saying their operations had targeted Saudi oil facilities and military bases, “far removed” from the sacred site of the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad. They accused Saudi Arabia of spreading “fabrications and lies.”

The Houthis’ rapid ground advance in Yemen and aerial attacks on Saudi Arabia have shut down a crucial oil pipeline, threatened energy supplies through a second major shipping route and left the kingdom struggling to respond.

The mounting hostilities have threatened to open a second front in the Iran war, with oil and gas prices rising. President Donald Trump has so far offered no sign of any U.S. plans to intervene in this new theater.

The United States on Wednesday upgraded its travel advisory to Saudi Arabia to Level 3 amid the escalating conflict, warning Americans to “reconsider travel” to the kingdom and banning government employees from travel near the Yemen border.

Saudi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said Wednesday that the country’s air defense forces had intercepted the drone south of Mecca just before 7 p.m. local time Tuesday (12 p.m. ET), according to a statement.

He emphasized that the security of the holy city and of pilgrims was a “red line,” warning there would be no hesitation to take “necessary and deterrent measures” against the Houthis, the statement said.

Mecca is known as the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad, with millions of Muslims from around the world making the pilgrimage to the holy city each year.

“While the Houthis and Saudi Arabia trade barbs over whether the target was Mecca or not,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at New America, a think tank based in Washington, D.C., who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region, “what is clear is you’re seeing a real demonstration of the Houthis’ continued strategic depth.”

He added: “The fact that they were able to strike this deep in Saudi Arabia is really a signal toward their capacity, if not future intentions.”

The Iran-backed rebels have ramped up attacks on cities across the kingdom after also capturing a key Red Sea port city and island in their bid to gain control of the crucial Bab el Mandeb strait.

Oil prices have soared over fears that the Houthis could shut down the waterway, which has been a crucial transit route for Saudi Arabian oil exports with the Strait of Hormuz largely closed by Iran since the U.S. and Israel launched their war in late February.

The international benchmark, Brent crude, was at around $108 per barrel early Wednesday. The nationwide average cost of diesel fuel hit another all-time high of $6.31.

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the alleged Mecca attack as a “dastardly and heinous” act.

Sharif, who recently agreed a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, did not directly mention the Houthis in his statement, but reiterated Pakistan’s general support for the kingdom.

The U.S. conducted a deadly bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, but has shown little appetite for another.

Trump said over the weekend that the Houthis had called his administration and said they “don’t want to fight with us.” Speaking with reporters during a visit to Dublin on Saturday, he said he also spoke with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and maintained that everything would “work out fine and dandy” in the region.

The Houthis and the opposing coalition backing the internationally-supported Yemeni government have been fighting a civil war since 2014, with no clear resolution despite a truce agreed years ago.

The United Nations Security Council met Tuesday in an emergency session to discuss the rising violence in Yemen, the region’s poorest country, with member countries urging de-escalation.

The U.N. warned that the ongoing clashes between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebels have displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September.

World.title: Apple’s record night and Colbert’s Emmys wins highlight TV in transition
World.content:
Some of the biggest laughs of the night came from the mini-monologue John Mulaney delivered as he presented the category of outstanding lead actor in a drama. “This award is for the guys, just men being men,” Mulaney said. “Finally, something for the fellas.” The award itself wasn’t a surprise — front-runner Noah Wyle of “The Pitt” took it home. But Mulaney’s bit, including a joke that earned a bleep from NBC censors, had the audience in the room roaring and people at home wondering how long until he finally hosts a major awards show. (Mulaney did host the Film Academy’s Governors Awards in 2024, but that show isn’t televised.)

The era of Apple

New Apple CEO John Ternus attended the Emmys, and he had lots to celebrate besides the $2,000 foldable iPhone he showed off on the red carpet. For the first time since it launched in 2019, Apple TV collected more Emmys than any other outlet.

Including its wins at last weekend’s two Emmy nights, Apple took home 28 trophies total this year, with a record 14 for freshman comedy “Widow’s Bay” and six for “Pluribus.” HBO came in second with 21, with “DTF St. Louis” collecting seven and “The Pitt” six. Netflix followed in third with 16, winning three each for “Love on the Spectrum” and “Beef.”

Matthew Rhys accepts the award for lead actor in a comedy series for Apple TV's "Widow's Bay." Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images

Quiet reflection over fiery politics

If you were betting on Colbert to riff on President Donald Trump and the Federal Communications Commission or open up about the events leading up to his late-night program’s cancellation, you were out of luck. He kept his acceptance speech focused squarely on his gratitude for his 11-year run at CBS, his writing staff and his wife.

In general, the Emmys were light on topical humor or references to current events such as the Iran war, AI or the looming Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger.

Sally Field did sneak in a subtle line that some interpreted as an anti-merger dig as she accepted an Emmy for her performance in the Netflix movie “Remarkably Bright Creatures.” “We’re the arts,” Field said. “We matter. Our voices matter. Our diversity, our unique storytelling matters. We can’t let those voices be silenced or compromised or merged.”

Instead of fiery political commentary, this year’s ceremony leaned more reflective, with earnest meditations from Hargitay and “Pluribus” creator Vince Gilligan on TV’s power to unite a divided country.

The winner of one of the night’s marquee categories trained his attention on TV’s important role in troubled times. “Yes, we are entertainers. We make you laugh, we make you cry, occasionally we make you look away in disgust,” R. Scott Gemmill, the creator of “The Pitt,” said in his acceptance speech for best drama series. “But when I look around this room, I see something more important than the awards and the ratings. I see a whole community that is still trying to do the right thing.”

Serious notes

In a year filled with losses in the entertainment industry, the telecast included sorrowful tributes to the late Rob Reiner, Catherine O’Hara and sitcom giant James Burrows. Reba McEntire sang Dolly Parton’s “Appalachian Memories” just a few weeks after Parton’s death, and Noah Kahan performed “Bridge Over Troubled Water” during the In Memoriam montage.

But the longest ovation of the night came for a performer who has defied the odds to remain in the business: Michael J. Fox, accepting the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award from his wheelchair. Fox shared that he kept his Parkinson’s diagnosis secret for a long time and wondered whether audiences would still laugh at his jokes if they knew he was sick. Ultimately, he said, “I understood that accepting Parkinson’s didn’t mean I had to surrender to it.”

Julianna Margulies presents Michael J. Fox with the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award. Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

The two Emmys personas

For years, Jack Nicholson appeared in the front row at the Oscars, the picture of cool detachment and old Hollywood charm. “Shrinking” nominee Harrison Ford seems to be stepping into that role at the Emmys as the guy everyone else seems to want to get next to, who really himself just wants to get home.

Harrison Ford shares a laugh with Jason Segel. Jordan Strauss / Invision for the Television Academy / AP

In contrast Monday night was enthusiastic “Widow’s Bay” creator Katie Dippold, who didn’t even try to contain her glee at her show’s many awards. During her acceptance speech for writing, Dippold declared: “I promise all of you that no one will ever step foot in my home without seeing this thing [her Emmy]. I’m sorry, this is going to become my entire personality now.”

World.title: U.S. accuses Russia of plot to kill a prominent dissident in Washington
World.content:
The Kremlin orchestrated a murder-for-hire plot against a prominent Russian dissident in Washington, D.C., this summer, the Department of Justice has said, as it unsealed charges against five people it alleged were part of a “global assassination network” aimed at causing “destruction and mayhem around the world.”

The five people charged are still at large, the DOJ said in the indictment unsealed late Tuesday, describing the wider operation being run by Russian intelligence as “brazen, aggressive, and far-reaching.”

The FBI said it had disrupted the plot, although officials did not detail how.

Since at least 2024, the network is alleged to have paid Americans and foreigners to spy on targets, “carry out targeted killings,” and “commit acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that are aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine,” the DOJ said.

Asked for a response to the allegations by NBC News, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a daily briefing call with reporters that “until we have heard or seen any reasonable evidence and arguments based on at least something tangible, we do not consider it necessary to comment on this news.”

Russia has for decades been accused by Western governments of carrying out attempted and successful killings abroad. Despite substantial evidence, it has always denied these allegations.

The indictment did not name the intended victim in Washington. The DOJ lists the defendants as Yuri Khrameev, known as “Colonel Yuri,” 63, and his son Kirill Khrameev, 27, both of Russia; Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, known as “Viking,” both 35 and Cuban nationals; and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, of Venezuela.

The indictment describes Durruthy as “an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia,” where it says Suarez and Castro also reside.

All face a conspiracy to finance terrorism charge. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro face an additional charge of conspiracy to commit murder for hire.

Yuri Khrameev is alleged to be a former Russian intelligence colonel, while his son is an officer in Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB.

Prosecutors allege the network recruited a Venezuelan citizen living in Brooklyn this summer, promising him between $1,000 and $1,500 to photograph and film two locations associated with the Washington target.

The man carried out the surveillance but declined an offer from Suarez and Castro of $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target himself, prosecutors said. The alleged recruiters asked whether he knew somebody who would.

Suarez also offered substantial sums of money to other people in the U.S. to finish the job, the indictment said.

Messages quoted in the indictment show the conspirators allegedly referring to murder as “construction.” Surveillance instructions included putting the man’s phone into airplane mode and filming while passing the house.

Suarez allegedly said he also had people in Mexico who could carry out the killing, but they were delayed.

A second alleged plot involved a dissident believed to be living in Lithuania who the network accused of making derogatory statements about Russia.

In that case, a U.S. citizen was promised $200 to photograph the target’s address in 2025, then offered around $25,000 to kill him, prosecutors said. When he refused, Yuri Khrameev allegedly offered a “simpler job” — setting fire to a warehouse or attacking an electricity substation.

The purpose, Khrameev allegedly said, was to target “all the countries that are helping Ukraine.”

Durruthy, meanwhile, is accused of coordinating logistics for attacks in Prague in June 2024 and Lithuania that September.

Lithuanian authorities had publicly named Durruthy as wanted in January in a case involving attempts to burn military equipment intended for Ukraine, according to Lithuanian broadcaster LRT.

“These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit U.S. citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.

“Actions like these represent a gross violation of our sovereignty and a threat to our national security.”

James C. Barnacle Jr., head of New York’s FBI office, said the agency “disrupted this operation through relentless work and rock-solid partnership.”

World.title: Alleged discrimination vs. White people prompts new U.S. sanctions on South Africa
World.content:
The Trump administration has announced that it will impose travel bans on officials it claims are responsible for discrimination against White people and other minority groups in South Africa.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday he would revoke U.S. visas or reject visa applications from foreign nationals found to be responsible for, or complicit in, enacting or enforcing laws and policies that allow uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination and the incitement of violence against minority ethnic and racial groups in South Africa.

"The United States will not allow such behavior to go unchecked," Rubio said in a statement. "These actions directly undermine peace, economic stability, and the rule of law, and they are incompatible with the pillars of America's foreign policy."

The South African government has strongly rejected U.S. allegations of discrimination against whites, calling the claims made by the administration since President Trump returned to office last year baseless and a result of misinformation.

South Africa's foreign ministry said Wednesday that it had "noted with concern" the new U.S. visa restrictions, adding that the U.S. announcement aligned with "the mischaracterization of South Africa's domestic policies by fringe groups," according to the Reuters news agency.

Rubio didn't identify any officials who would be targeted with the travel restrictions, though a lobby group for minority White people in South Africa has previously called for the U.S. to sanction officials of the African National Congress party, the party of South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and the largest in South Africa's Parliament.

It's the latest move by the Trump administration to sanction South Africa over its claims that white people, and especially the Afrikaner group, are being discriminated against by their Black-led government. Afrikaners are descended from mainly Dutch and French colonial settlers who first came to South Africa in the 17th century. They were at the heart of South Africa's previous apartheid system of racial segregation.

There are approximately 4.5 million White people in South Africa's population of 62 million, which also includes White people with British or other heritage.

The U.S. has cited a contentious South African law that allows the expropriation of unused private land without compensation in some circumstances, affirmative action policies that advance opportunities for Black people and others, and a small number of violent crimes against White farmers as evidence of a larger anti-White stance in South Africa.

The Trump administration has also strongly criticized South Africa's move to accuse U.S. ally Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza in a highly emotive case in the United Nations' top court. Israel vehemently denies that allegation.

The U.S. has enforced a series of other sanctions against South Africa during Mr. Trump's second term for purported anti-White and anti-American policies. They include barring South African officials from meetings of the Group of 20 economic bloc this year in the U.S., and phasing out aid for South Africa's HIV treatment program.

The U.S. has also launched a refugee program for Afrikaners and other White people, claiming baselessly that they are victims of a humanitarian emergency in South Africa.

The State Department argued that Afrikaners faced "escalating hostility," including critical statements by politicians and a December raid by South African authorities on a U.S. refugee processing center. At the time, South African officials said they had arrested Kenyans who were working at the center illegally, but the U.S. condemned the raid.

The U.S. says the sanctions are because South Africa hasn't changed its policies.

"This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America's firm resolve in this matter," the official U.S. Ambassador to South Africa account posted on X on Wednesday, referring to Rubio's visa announcement.

Rubio said on social media that "As [Mr. Trump] has made clear, the South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority."

World.title: Charlie Kirk's family blames Utah officials for failing to prevent his murder
World.content:
Charlie Kirk's family blamed Utah officials for failing to prevent the conservative activist's assassination at a state university, in a wrongful death notice announced Wednesday that presages a possible lawsuit.

Attorneys for the family said Kirk's death resulted from a string of "reckless decisions" by officials at Utah Valley University that left him exposed to a rooftop sniper, who fired a fatal shot from more than 400 feet away on Sept. 10, 2025. The university has faced harsh criticism for a lack of key safety measures on the day of the shooting.

Kirk, 31, had been debating students in an outdoor courtyard surrounded by tall buildings and with several thousand people in attendance. An Associated Press review following the shooting showed the campus in Orem did not use several public safety practices that have become standard safeguards at events around the country.

Campus police staffing was far below recommended levels for a school of that size. They also did not fly a drone to monitor rooftops or coordinate with local law enforcement to secure the event attended by about 3,000 people. There were no bag checks or metal detectors.

"The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," Kirk family attorney D. Loren Washburn wrote in the notice to state and university officials.

The document, dated Sept. 9, a day before the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, is a required step under state law before his family can file a formal claim or lawsuit. It names the university and its then-president, Astrid Tuminez; the campus police department and its chief, Jeffrey Long; and the state of Utah.

In a statement to CBS News on Wednesday, the university said: "We are aware of the notice of claim. UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes. Our focus remains on supporting our campus community."

The Utah Attorney General's Office said it does not comment on potential litigation.

Attorneys for Kirk's family alleged additional lapses by officials, including not conducting an adequate risk assessment before approving the event, failing to establish a secure perimeter and having no first responders immediately available, resulting in Kirk being taken to a nearby hospital in a private vehicle rather than an ambulance after he was shot.

"Situation that rendered Mr. Kirk helpless"

"Tragically, the UVU Parties took none of these safety measures - steps only they had the authority to take - resulting in a situation that rendered Mr. Kirk helpless before his assassin," Washburn wrote.

Long said after the shooting that six of his officers staffed the event and coordinated with Kirk's eight-person private security team. The school said it was expanding its police force following the shooting.

Utah resident Tyler Robinson turned himself in a day after Kirk's killing. Prosecutors say he told his romantic partner that he "had enough of his (Kirk's) hatred." The state of Utah argued Robinson targeted Kirk because of his political beliefs, and knowing that children were present and would witness the shooting.

Robinson is charged with aggravated murder, making him eligible for the death penalty if convicted. A judge on Sept. 1 ordered the case to proceed toward trial. A date has not yet been set.

Prosecutors during a preliminary hearing in July presented what they characterized as overwhelming evidence against Robinson. That includes surveillance video of Robinson on the campus, DNA tests linking him to a rifle found near the assassination site and a handwritten note he allegedly left for his romantic partner that read, "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it."

Kirk's parents, Robert and Kathryn Kirk, and widow, Erika Kirk, attended the hearings.

State law allows heirs or personal representatives of people who die to file lawsuits seeking damages if the death was caused by a wrongful act or negligence. The notice from Kirk's family did not specify what damages they may seek.

Kirk and the organization he co-founded, Turning Point USA, galvanized the conservative youth vote to help President Trump win a second term. At a Presidential Medal of Freedom award ceremony on what would have been Kirk's 32nd birthday, Mr. Trump credited the political activist with helping him win a greater share of the under-30 vote in the most recent presidential race.

Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, said during his memorial service that she forgives Robinson.

At a December CBS News town hall, Erika Kirk was asked if she had any words for the accused killer.

"Nothing. I have nothing to say to you. Nothing," she said.

She added that there's a difference between forgiving someone and still wanting justice. "We serve a just God, and I rest easy in knowing that. He's sovereign, but he's just. And so let the Lord handle that."

World.title: Aly Raisman on Listening to Your Body and Advocating for Yourself
World.content: Aly Raisman on Listening to Your Body and Advocating for Yourself Olympic Gold Medalist Aly Raisman joins Norah for a vulnerable discussion about giving yourself grace and why she no longer feels guilty for resting her body when she needs to. Raisman has become an outspoken voice on mental health and the importance of advocating for yourself. The two discuss how so many women struggle to get the care they deserve and why it's important to talk about issues that are often considered taboo, from painful periods to IUDs.

World.title: How Olympian Aly Raisman learned to advocate for her own health
World.content:
Aly Raisman has competed at the highest levels as an Olympic gymnast, often pushing her body to the limits.

A decade since she last competed, Raisman has been learning to take care of her body after years of overtraining and anxiety.

"My body completely just gave up on me," she said on the latest episode of "Healthful."

Now, Raisman is advocating for women, not just athletes, to prioritize taking care of themselves and speaking up for their needs even when they feel ignored.

The importance of listening to your body
