World.title: Polls show Argentine distrust of Milei's shift on the Falklands
World.content:
Polls show Argentine distrust of Milei's shift on the Falklands

14th Monday, September 2026 - 22:06 UTC Full article

Photo: Nicolás Aguilera/AFP

Two private Argentine pollsters released findings this week pointing to an adverse reception of President Javier Milei's shift on the Falklands, even though the sovereignty claim commands broad consensus in Argentine society.

The consultancy Analogías, which surveyed views of the national government between September 5 and 8, reported that 61% of respondents expressed distrust of the president's new position: 49.8% said they did not believe him at all and 11.2% believed him little. The firm did not publish technical details such as sample size or margin of error.

Monitor Digital, which analyzed 89,900 mentions of the government on social media, ranked the Islands as the second axis of the official digital conversation, clustered around terms such as sovereignty, measures, the United Kingdom and the United States. Its director, Diego Corbalán, told Perfil the volume did not translate into support: “In some way the government managed to place the issue, but it is not clear that all of it works to its benefit.”

The same study played down the reach of the matter beyond political circles. Across nearly a thousand Google trends recorded in the week after the September 3 televised address, the cluster associated with the Islands appeared only at 27th place, with some 50,000 searches, and the foreign policy category accounted for 0.8% of the total, far below sports and entertainment.

The sequence began with that address, in which Milei asserted sovereignty over the archipelago and announced measures against oil development. The following day the government confirmed sanctions against individuals and companies linked to that activity, and this week it is preparing to send Congress a National Sovereignty Defense bill.

The announcements followed the World Cup episode in July, when National Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva endorsed a ban on flags and shirts referring to the Islands during the semifinal between Argentina and England. The players themselves defied the measure by displaying a banner at the end of the match, and the episode led to the suspension of debate on the land ownership bill in the Senate.

On Sunday the government distributed to the press an institutional video by Santiago Oria, director of audiovisual production at the Presidency, combining statements by Milei, remarks by U.S. President Donald Trump on a possible review of Washington's neutral position, and footage of the match against England, set to terrace music. Milei and La Libertad Avanza figures shared the piece.

Corbalán criticized the strategy in political terms: in adopting it, he said, the libertarians “embrace the whole Kirchnerist populist mode,” which he described as chauvinism.

Islanders confirmed their status as a British Overseas Territory in the 2013 referendum, with 99.8% of the vote.

World.title: Is Mexico’s soccer league a monopoly? Antitrust officials are looking to find out
World.content:
The National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has unilaterally opened an investigation into Liga MX, Mexico’s top professional soccer league and a massive cultural touchstone that captures the country’s passion for the sport.

An internal CNA document says the investigation aims to identify “the possible commission of relative monopolistic practices in the market of ‘affiliation, organization and access’ to professional federated football competitions in Mexico, as well as similar or related services.”

⚽ ¿Cómo investigamos el funcionamiento de un mercado?

José Manuel Haro Zepeda, titular de nuestra Autoridad Investigadora, explicó en @MVSNoticias las herramientas con las que contamos para analizar la organización y acceso a competiciones de fútbol profesional en México. pic.twitter.com/r2qgofrR9M — Comisión Nacional Antimonopolio (@AntimonopolioMX) September 15, 2026

In short, the CNA wants to know if a small group is violating the Federal Law of Economic Competition by unfairly controlling who can join, who can compete and how tournaments are organized, to the exclusion of other interested parties.

“After analyzing the events that occurred in recent months, the Investigating Authority determined that it has sufficient evidence to formally open an investigation on its own initiative for possible monopolistic practices in the professional soccer market in Mexico,” the CNA said in a public report.

The recent events referred to are likely related to a Liga MX decision in July to scrap promotion/relegation between the top-flight Mexican soccer league and the second-tier Liga Expansión. Liga MX also announced the end to payouts to the second-tier sides.

Promotion and relegation were scrapped in 2020 to insulate the clubs from the financial impacts of lost revenue during the enforced lockdown ordered due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed the decision, even filing a suit with the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which ruled that the 2026-27 campaign was the earliest point at which promotion/relegation ought to be reinstituted.

Critics have also identified the league’s policy regarding possession of television broadcasting rights by teams as a monopolistic practice.

The commission has sought to make clear that there are no defendants identified as yet and it hasn’t been determined exactly who will be investigated. Instead, the probe will simply review whether competition law is being followed.

The investigation can last up to 120 business days, but can be extended up to three times longer if necessary. During that time, the CNA can request documents, visit offices, summon people to testify and conduct inspections.

If guilt is determined, the Liga MX and its member teams could face a penalty of up to 10% of their annual income and would be required to correct any monopolistic practices detected.

With reports from ESPN, El Economista, El Universal and SportCa

World.title: Should you be worried about the presence of brain-eating amoeba in Yucatán water bodies?
World.content:
A man died of Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) in a Mérida hospital last week, most likely from contact with the brain-eating amoeba Naegleria fowleri, the Yucatán Health Services (SSY) reported on Monday.

The SSY confirmed the presence of N. fowleri in an artificial lake at the La Isla shopping center in Mérida, where the 34-year-old man worked as a water sports instructor.

FAMILIARES DESPIDEN A CARLOS, INSTRUCTOR QUE F4LL3C10 POR AMEBA COME CEREBROS#Video | Familiares y amigos despidieron con tristeza a Carlos, el joven instructor de wakeboard de 33 años que perdió la v1d4 tras contraer una agresiva infección por la ameba ‘Naegleria fowleri’ en… pic.twitter.com/f57zIqs8Ly — Yucatán Ahora (@yucatanahora) September 15, 2026

“It is a serious and extremely rare disease; this is the first case registered in Yucatán,” the SSY said in a statement.

The microorganism is most commonly found in stagnant, warm waters between 35°C and 46°C. It enters the body when contaminated water is forcefully inhaled through the nose, although it can also occur while swimming, diving or submerging one’s head in lakes, rivers or poorly chlorinated swimming pools.

PAM is not transmitted from person to person and is not acquired by drinking contaminated water, the SSY emphasized.

People living in the Yucatán capital have expressed concern about the water quality in nearby cenotes, where swimming is common. However, experts suggest that natural freshwater bodies are cooler, at between 24°C and 26°C, making the presence of N. fowleri far less likely.

The development of microorganisms in pools can be avoided through chlorination and pH management, and in larger water bodies through adequate water movement, which promotes aeration. Regular cleaning and maintenance can also help avoid the accumulation of sediment, organic matter, algae and biofilms in stagnant water, conditions that attract N. fowleri.

The first symptoms of PAM are usually severe headache, fever, nausea and vomiting. According to initial reports, the victim presented with severe symptoms of central nervous system infection and was taken to a hospital in the city, where he died.

Health authorities ordered the temporary closure of the water feature at La Isla while samples were tested at the Hidalgo State Public Health Laboratory, which confirmed the presence of N. fowleri. Meanwhile, cleaning efforts and technical inspections were carried out at the site.

Epidemiological investigators are conducting interviews to locate other individuals who may have come into contact with the water.

The SSY said it plans to investigate the companies responsible for water quality and lake maintenance for their compliance with Mexican rules and regulations.

“Anyone who has violated health regulations will be sanctioned,” the SSY stressed.

According to the SSY statement, once the responsible company demonstrates through laboratory tests that the lake water is suitable for recreational use in accordance with legal standards, a new verification and sampling of the water will be conducted and a decision will be made on whether to lift the temporary closure.

With reports from Reportur, La Jornada and Diario de Yucatán

World.title: 139 US troops cleared to enter Mexico for joint training in Chihuahua
World.content:
More than 100 U.S. soldiers will travel to Mexico this month to participate in joint training exercises with Mexican military personnel in the northern state of Chihuahua.

The federal Senate on Monday granted President Claudia Sheinbaum the authority to allow the entry into Mexico of 139 U.S. Army troops, who are scheduled to land at the Santa Gertrudis Air Force Base south of Chihuahua city this Sunday.

The granting of that authority comes amid security-related tension in the Mexico-U.S. relationship.

Among the causes of that tension are the CIA’s alleged participation in a drug lab raid in Chihuahua in April without the knowledge or authorization of the Mexican government; U.S. prosecutors’ drug-trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya and other current and former officials; and suggestions from Trump administration officials that the U.S. could take unilateral action against Mexican drug cartels on Mexican soil.

While each of those developments has drawn the ire of Sheinbaum, the president remains committed to cooperating with the Trump administration on security on the proviso that Mexican sovereignty and territorial integrity are respected. One example of that cooperation is a joint anti-drone operation that is currently taking place on the border between Tijuana and San Diego.

U.S. soldiers have previously traveled to Mexico to undertake joint training exercises with Mexican personnel. However, the U.S. contingent set to arrive in Chihuahua on Sunday is larger than previous ones that have come to Mexico.

Here’s everything you need to know about the upcoming military collaboration on Mexican soil.

Where will the joint training exercises take place?

The joint training exercises will take place at the Centro Nacional de Adiestramiento (National Training Center), located in Santa Gertrudis in the municipality of Saucillo, Chihuahua. The CNA is the Mexican military’s largest training facility.

Among the simulated combat exercises U.S. and Mexican military personnel will conduct are the destruction of sniper positions; the seizure of an airfield; an air assault; the destruction of a fuel-supply point; and the capture and extraction of a target using live fire.

The U.S. soldiers will stay at the CNA during their time in Mexico.

What is the objective of the training exercises?

The Senate said in a statement that the aim of the joint training exercises is to “strengthen operational capabilities between the United States and Mexican Armed Forces through the planning and execution of military operations under the principles of respect, sovereignty and territorial integrity; shared responsibility; mutual trust; and collaboration without subordination.

The Senate said that the joint training “will not only have a positive impact on strengthening individual and collective preparedness, but will also contribute to the improvement of bilateral military cooperation mechanisms.”

How long will the US soldiers remain in Mexico?

The U.S. troops will arrive in Chihuahua on a U.S. Air Force plane on Sept. 20 and return to the United States on Sept. 30. Therefore, the soldiers will be in Mexico for a total of 11 days.

The Senate noted that the U.S. troops will enter Mexico “with weapons.”

Which division of the US army to the soldiers belong to?

The 139 soldiers coming to Mexico belong to the 101st Airborne Division of the U.S. Army. The division, known as the “Screaming Eagles,” is the only air assault division of the United States Army. It is based at Fort Campbell, Kentucky.

With reports from La Silla Rota, El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Tehran’s Azadi Tower bears Mexican flag in first-ever Independence Day tribute
World.content:
For the first time, Iran lit one of its most recognizable landmarks in the green, white and red of the Mexican flag, turning Tehran’s Azadi Tower into a striking Independence Day tribute Tuesday night.

The Azadi Tower illumination marked the 216th anniversary of the Grito de Dolores — the 1810 call by priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla that launched Mexico’s war for independence from Spain.

La emblemática Torre Azadi, símbolo de Teherán, se iluminó con los colores de la bandera mexicana para conmemorar el 216° aniversario de la Independencia de México. La Embajada de Irán en México destacó el acto como un gesto de amistad entre ambos pueblos. Más en La Jornada:… pic.twitter.com/tfgRRj5ddy — La Jornada (@lajornadaonline) September 15, 2026

“Today, Mexico is not in Mexico. It is in the heart of Iran,” the Iranian Embassy in Mexico posted Sept. 15 with a video of the glowing monument.

The display marked the first time Iran has illuminated a monument in honor of Mexico, according to the newspaper El Universal.

Those colors, however, are not inherently unusual at Azadi Tower, since green, white and red are also Iran’s national colors. For example, on Feb. 10, 2024, it was lit up in that way for the 45th anniversary of the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Speaking to HispanTV from Tehran, Mexican Ambassador Guillermo Puente Ordorica called the lighting “a great gesture of friendship” that Mexicans will cherish.

Built in 1971, the 45-meter Azadi Tower was originally called Shahyad Tower, then renamed Azadi (Persian for “freedom”) after the 1979 revolution. The tower and its surrounding square are often the site of major public gatherings.

Beyond Iran, Mexican communities and diplomats marked Día de la Independencia across several continents.

In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani was grand marshal Sunday at a Mexican Independence Day parade in Brooklyn, wearing a tricolor sash and carrying a Mexican flag. He said he was proud to be the first New York City mayor to march in the parade with “a community that has fostered cultural pride for generations.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani (@nycmayor)

Mamdani’s remarks came just days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance criticized a protester carrying a Mexican flag at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, calling him an “idiot” and telling him, “If you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.”

Elsewhere, Mexico’s ambassador to the United Kingdom, Alejandro Gertz Manero, led a Grito ceremony in London, where festivities included music, food, dance and other traditions.

In Madrid, the Mexican Embassy hosted a public Grito in Chamberí Square, followed by folk ballet, mariachi and a circus performance.

Mexican celebrations were also reported in Krakow, Rome, Vienna, Beijing, Seoul, Barcelona, Budapest and Kansas City.

With reports from El Universal, La Jornada and Madrid Gazette

World.title: New US-Mexico water agreement means reduced allotments but a heathier Colorado River
World.content:
A long-running dispute between Mexico and the United States over Colorado River water-sharing has been resolved — at least for the next two years — with Mexico getting significantly less water as a result.

The U.S. is also receiving less water as part of a joint effort to mitigate ongoing drought conditions and low reservoir levels in the Colorado River basin.

In fact, under the new agreement, formally called Minute 334 and finalized by the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC) on Sept. 2, Mexico’s 16.7% (250,000 acre-feet) annual reduction of its previous typical water allocation is equivalent to water-use reductions imposed on U.S. Lower Basin states (Arizona, California and Nevada).

The agreement also implements a strategy to manage the salinity of Colorado River water as it reaches Mexico. Consultations regarding possible further cuts are contemplated for 2028 if conditions worsen.

Minute 334 was signed by Mexican IBWC Commissioner Adriana Reséndez and her U.S. counterpart, Chad McIntosh, with the participation of Mexican IBWC Secretary Manuel Morales. The U.S. Department of the Interior confirmed the approval of both governments.

“This Minute makes sure water is shared fairly among our users and protects the health of the Colorado River during these difficult times,” McIntosh said in a news release. “Both countries deserve a lot of credit for agreeing to these water reductions and other measures.”

Reséndez insisted on proportionality between the two countries, defending Mexico’s position even as it has struggled to meet its obligations in the original 1944 treaty.

When the most recent five-year cycle of that treaty came to an end on Oct. 24 last year, Mexico still owed 865,136 acre-feet of water, though the terms of the treaty grant Mexico five years to catch up.

The reduction agreed to in Minute 334 is equivalent to one-sixth of Mexico’s annual allocation established in the treaty, about 1.85 billion cubic meters.

The two nations also agreed to cooperate on managing the Colorado River Delta in Mexico, which has been transformed from a lush 2-million-acre wetland into a mostly dry salt flat due to decades of intensive upstream dam construction and water diversions.

With reports from El Universal, WaterWorld and The Colorado Sun

World.title: MND Local: WTA Tennis, an international film fest and more events in Guadalajara
World.content:
Late September in Guadalajara brings an action-packed calendar. Upcoming events include a World Migrant Day celebration benefiting a local nonprofit organization, an international film festival and the 2026 Guadalajara Open, an important stop on the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) professional tour.

Top female tennis players to compete at the Guadalajara Open this week

Following hard on the heels of the U.S. Open in New York City, Zapopan welcomes a select group of the WTA’s brightest stars to the Guadalajara Open this week.

The annual event, played at the Panamerican Tennis Center in Parque Metropolitano, attracts a diverse group of top female tennis players from around the globe. The field will compete in singles and doubles for a US $1.2 million purse and a top singles prize of US $185,500.

Confirmed players for this year’s event include world number 11 Marta Kostyuk of Ukraine and world number 14 and defending champion Iva Jovic of the United States.

Kostyuk returns to Mexico as one of the hottest players on the WTA tour during the 2026 season, having reached the semifinals of Wimbledon and Roland Garros, in addition to claiming two titles on clay last spring. She last competed at the Guadalajara Open in 2023, where she reached the second round.

Latin American tennis will also be well represented, with Colombian veteran Camila Osorio and Mexican No. 1 Renata Zarazúa scheduled to compete.

For details, visit the tournament website.

Dates: Sept. 13-19, 2026.

Sept. 13-19, 2026. Location: Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco.

Centro Panamericano de Tenis, Zapopan, Jalisco. Cost: Individual tickets start at 866 pesos, not including fees. Tournament packages are available on Boletomovil.

Aeroméxico to launch nonstop service from Guadalajara to Paris in 2027

Savoring the perfect pain au chocolat is about to get a little easier for Francophile Tapatíos. Starting April 13, 2027, the city will have its second direct European flight route, as Aeroméxico launches nonstop service between Guadalajara’s Miguel Hidalgo International Airport (GDL) and Paris-Charles de Gaulle (CDG).

The route will run three times per week on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays, departing Guadalajara at 1:55 p.m. and arriving in Paris at 9:25 a.m. the following day. Return flights will operate on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays, departing Paris at 11:40 a.m. and arriving in Guadalajara at 4:10 p.m. the same day.

“Adding Guadalajara–Paris … strengthens our network, offers customers more travel options and further consolidates our position as the leading airline between Mexico and Europe,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeroméxico, told Aviacionline last week.

Celebrate World Migrant Day with the Rhizome Center

Later this month, Guadalajara residents will have the opportunity to celebrate World Migrant Day at a community celebration featuring local food, culture and a social cause.

Hosted by The Rhizome Center, this year’s festival, “Many Journeys. One Community,” is both a fundraiser and an opportunity to raise awareness about the organization’s work. During the event, guests can sample food from 15 migrant kitchens, enjoy live French, Cuban and Syrian music, listen to storytelling, and meet artists sharing their craft and culture.

The Rhizome Center was founded in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term, with a mission to provide direct support to deportees and refugees sent to Mexico.

Since his return to office, the need has grown. Many deportees arrive with no resources or documentation to regularize their status in Mexico. Filling that void, the organization provides legal aid, crisis assistance, counseling and other services.

Run by executive director and founder Tran Dang, The Rhizome Center derived its name from plant rhizomes — the underground roots that provide essential nutrients — symbolizing humanity’s resilience and interconnectedness across borders.

For more information about The Rhizome Center for Migrants and details on how to support the cause, visit the group’s Instagram account. Donations are accepted via PayPal and Zelle.

Date: Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Saturday, Sept. 27, from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. Location: Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara.

Casa Zuno, Avenida Unión 2226, Colonia Americana, Guadalajara. Cost: General admission is 375 pesos. VIP tickets are 500 pesos per person and guarantee a seat.

The MUBI film fest lands in Guadalajara next weekend

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MUBI México (@mubimexico)

Global distributor, producer and streaming service MUBI recently added film festivals to its portfolio and announced a Guadalajara edition from Sept. 18-20. The festival will screen independent feature films and shorts, alongside filmmaker Q&As, workshops, installations and DJ sets.

Anticipated films on the schedule include:

“Her Private Hell” by Nicolas Winding Refn

“Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?” by Garth Jennings

“Hope: The First Impact” by Na Hong-jin

“Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” by Jane Schoenbrun

“Rose” by Markus Schleinzer

For moviegoers seeking nostalgia, Ridley Scott’s 1991 feminist classic “Thelma & Louise,” starring Susan Sarandon, Geena Davis and Brad Pitt, is also on the schedule.

For full program details, visit Mubi Mexico’s website. In addition to Guadalajara, MUBI Fest 2026 made stops in Mexico City, São Paulo, Bogotá and Buenos Aires this year.

Dates: Sept. 18-20.

Sept. 18-20. Location: FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan.

FICG Cineteca, Av. Perif. Pte. Manuel Gómez Morin 1695, Rinconada de la Azalea, Belenes Norte, Zapopan. Cost: Tickets available on the MUBI website.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Mexico City-area airports to halt takeoffs and landings for 4 hours tomorrow
World.content:
Takeoffs and landings at the Mexico City International Airport (AICM) will be suspended for four hours on Wednesday, Sept. 16, to ensure that military aircraft can operate safely in the capital’s airspace while the annual Independence Day parade takes place below.

The Mexican Navy, which operates the AICM, announced the suspension in a statement.

El AICM suspenderá operaciones aéreas por desfile del 16 de septiembre. ➡️ https://t.co/T6iEPTFtOa @aeropuertos_GAM pic.twitter.com/wJK8Khf3YB — Aeropuerto Internacional Benito Juárez CDMX (@AICM_mx) September 14, 2026

“To ensure the safety of the military air maneuvers that will be carried out to commemorate the 216th anniversary of the start of Mexico’s independence, and as directed by the aviation authority, the Mexico City Benito Juárez International Airport (AICM) will suspend aircraft takeoffs and landings on September 16 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.,” the navy said.

“According to NOTAMs [Notices to Airmen] A8260/26 and B1724/26, … issued by the Federal Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC) and disseminated through the Mexican Airspace Navigation Services (SENEAM), the airport will be closed to all types of flights during the specified hours.”

The Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA) in México state will also suspend takeoffs and landings between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. Wednesday. Military aircraft that will conduct flyovers as part of the Independence Day festivities will take off from the Santa Lucía Air Force Base, which adjoins AIFA.

The navy advised air passengers who have a flight scheduled for Wednesday to ask their airlines about the status of their flights as “this event will result in some adjustments to scheduled times.”

The Independence Day parade is scheduled to begin at 10 a.m. Wednesday with a flyover of nearly 100 Air Force and National Guard airplanes and helicopters above the Zócalo, Mexico City’s central square — including F-5 fighters performing a fleur-de-lis maneuver.

The ground procession will start near the Zócalo, pass the Palacio de Bellas Artes (Palace of Fine Arts), continue along Juárez Avenue and Paseo de la Reforma, and end at the Campo Marte military complex near Chapultepec Park.

World.title: Following a higher soda tax, is a salty foods tax coming next?
World.content:
Lawmakers from Mexico’s ruling party Morena, the Workers’ Party (PT) and the Green Party (PVEM) have submitted a congressional proposal to apply a Special Tax on Production and Services (IEPS) to certain processed foods with excessive sodium content, such as cured meats, instant soups, sauces and dressings.

The initiative seeks to expand a tax strategy that has been applied since the 1980s to products considered harmful to health, such as sugary drinks, tobacco and high-calorie foods.

The bill’s proponents estimate that a tax on products with high sodium levels could generate approximately 12 billion pesos (US $116.6 million) in additional federal revenue, while helping reduce the prevalence of diseases associated with excessive salt consumption.

The focus would be on processed products exceeding technical criteria for sodium content, particularly front-of-package warning labels under NOM-051, which indicate “Excess Sodium.” This means that the potential measure would not penalize the domestic use of salt, nor would it, in principle, indiscriminately cover all salty foods.

The initiative follows growing concerns regarding average sodium intake in Mexico.

According to the NGO El Poder del Consumidor (The Power of the Consumer), the Mexican adult population consumes an average of 3.3 grams of sodium per day, far exceeding the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendation, which advises against exceeding 2 grams daily. Excess sodium consumption is related to cardiovascular diseases – the leading cause of death in Mexico – and hypertension.

Meeting the WHO’s target of a 30% reduction in sodium intake by 2030 could save an estimated 7 million lives globally and annually prevent approximately 5% of deaths in Mexico from cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease and stomach cancer.

Dr. Jorge Vargas, a researcher at El Poder del Consumidor, told the news outlet Infobae that “the fact that Mexico is finally considering a sodium tax is positive news,” but cautioned that the technical design would be a decisive factor in determining whether the tax alters consumption habits and drives companies to reduce the salt content of their products. He also urged lawmakers to review the results observed in other countries before voting on the initiative.

The proposal follows a recent IEPS increase targeting domestic sugar consumption, which, according to the government’s 2027 budget proposal, is forecast to bring in over 76.92 billion pesos ($4.5 billion) next year from soft drinks alone.

With reports from El Universal and El Financiero

World.title: Guyana’s Unemployment Falls to 6.2% as Food Prices Climb
World.content:
GUYANA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Guyana’s unemployment rate fell to 6.2%, its 2026 Mid-Year Report says.

— How big The government counts more than 156,000 new jobs created since 2020.

— The catch Food prices rose 6.7% in the same first half of 2026.

— What it means Guyana’s labour force has grown 47.8% since early 2020, official data show.

— Who it affects Employers report a shortage of skilled workers, not a shortage of jobs.

— What’s not known The report does not break down which industries created the new jobs.

Stabroek Market in Georgetown, Guyana’s capital and commercial hub. (Photo: "Stabroek Market Georgetown Guyana" by John Cray, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.) (Photo, internet reproduction)

Guyana’s government says its economy has produced over 156,000 new jobs since 2020, even as food prices climb faster than overall inflation.

Guyana’s unemployment rate has fallen to 6.2%, according to the government’s 2026 Mid-Year Report. The Ministry of Finance report, posted on 15 September 2026, also credits the economy with more than 156,000 new jobs since 2020.

A Report Rio Times Had Been Waiting For

Guyana’s Ministry of Finance publishes a Mid-Year Report most years, covering January through June. Rio Times noted on 15 September that this year’s edition had not yet appeared.

President Irfaan Ali had already cited preliminary growth numbers by then.

The report is now posted on the ministry’s website. It fills in labour-market and price detail the government did not have ready when it first announced its headline growth figure.

The Jobs and Unemployment Numbers

Unemployment stands at 6.2%, the report says. Guyana’s labour force has grown 47.8% since the first quarter of 2020, according to the same report.

Officials count over 156,000 new jobs created since 2020. A Finance Ministry statement in July 2026 had put a similar tally at “over 104,000” jobs added over six years.

The new, higher figure reflects further hiring since that July statement.

A Familiar Growth Story, Confirmed

The same Mid-Year Report puts real GDP growth at 33.3% for the first half of 2026. That matches what President Ali announced at a press conference, as Rio Times reported this week.

Non-oil growth ran at 10.1% over the same period, the report confirms. This article focuses on the labour-market and price detail that first report did not cover.

The Other Side of the Ledger

Consumer prices rose 4.4% between the end of 2025 and the end of June 2026, the report says. Food prices climbed faster, up 6.7%, and made up most of that overall increase.

The 12-month inflation rate eased slightly, to 4% in June 2026 from 4.2% a year earlier. Prices are still rising, in other words, just not accelerating as fast as before.

Where Skilled Labour Is Scarce

The report says labour demand has outpaced the supply of workers with technical and professional skills. The government expects that gap to persist in the near term.

That is a different problem from unemployment. Guyana appears to have enough jobs; it may not yet have enough trained workers to fill the more specialized ones.

The Relief Already in Place

The government has leaned on direct cash support to offset rising costs. It paid a G$100,000 grant to every adult Guyanese, worth about US$477 at the September 2026 rate of roughly G$209.5 per US dollar.

That grant alone totalled G$42.5 billion, or about US$203 million, by mid-year.

It also raised the Old Age Pension from G$41,000 to G$46,000 a month (about US$196 to US$220). Public Assistance rose from G$22,000 to G$25,000 (about US$105 to US$119), Guyana Chronicle reported on 15 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

The report does not break the new jobs down by sector. It is not clear how many are linked to oil, construction or services.

It is also unclear whether the 6.2% figure uses the same methodology as the 6.8% rate the government cited for 2024. Rio Times could not confirm the exact comparison base behind the 6.2% number from the material available at publication.

What This Means for Guyanese Households and Newcomers

A falling unemployment rate and a tight market for skilled labour point the same direction. Workers with technical training have more leverage than they did a few years ago.

For foreign professionals considering Guyana, that skills gap can mean real openings, particularly in construction, engineering and energy-linked services. For lower-income households, food prices climbing faster than overall inflation matters more than any headline jobs number.

The government’s cash grants and pension increases are aimed directly at that second group. Whether they keep pace with food prices over the rest of 2026 is the open question.

What Comes Next

Guyana’s Bureau of Statistics is expected to keep publishing detailed data through the rest of the year. Whether the 156,000-job figure holds up under closer scrutiny remains to be seen.

That scrutiny will shape how ordinary Guyanese experience an economy still growing faster than almost any other in the world.

More: Guyana news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Guyana’s unemployment rate?

6.2%, according to the government’s 2026 Mid-Year Report, posted on 15 September 2026.

How many jobs has Guyana created?

The government counts more than 156,000 new jobs since 2020. The labour force has grown 47.8% since early 2020.

Are prices rising in Guyana too?

Yes. Consumer prices rose 4.4% in the first half of 2026. Food prices rose faster, up 6.7%, the same report says.

Is this the same report behind Guyana’s 33.3% growth figure?

Yes. Both come from the government’s 2026 Mid-Year Report, which also confirmed the growth rate President Ali announced earlier in September.

Sources: Guyana Ministry of Finance (Mid-Year Report 2026), Guyana Chronicle, HGPTV, Rio Times prior reporting. https://finance.gov.gy/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Mid-Year-Report-2026.pdf https://finance.gov.gy/mid-year-reports/ https://guyanachronicle.com/2026/09/15/massive-relief-package-cushions-effects-of-rising-prices/ https://www.hgptv.com/food-prices-up-6-7-govt-report-reveals-cost-of-living-pressure/ https://www.riotimesonline.com/guyana-economy-grew-33-3-in-first-half-of-2026-ali-says/

World.title: Bladex Grants Panama a Record US$1 Billion Loan
World.content:
PANAMA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Bladex agreed to lend Panama’s government up to US$1 billion.

— How big It is the largest single loan the trade bank has ever structured.

— What it’s for Panama will use the money for general budget spending, Bladex said.

— The catch Neither side has disclosed the interest rate or the repayment schedule.

— Why it matters Panama lost its investment-grade rating from Fitch back in 2024.

— What comes next Panama’s fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.78% of GDP through July 2026.

Panama’s government has borrowed up to US$1 billion from Bladex. It is the biggest single deal the regional trade bank has ever made.

Bladex has agreed to lend the government of Panama up to US$1 billion. The Panama-based trade bank announced the deal on 15 September 2026, calling it the largest single loan it has ever structured.

What Was Announced

Bladex, formally the Banco Latinoamericano de Comercio Exterior, said it structured a senior loan for Panama’s Ministry of Economy and Finance. The facility is worth up to US$1 billion.

A senior loan gives its holder priority for repayment ahead of other creditors.

Samuel Canineu, Bladex’s Executive Vice President of Business, called the deal significant. “This transaction reflects Bladex’s ability to structure large-scale financial solutions for sovereign and institutional clients across the region,” he said.

Who Is Bladex

Bladex is a multilateral trade bank founded in Panama in 1979 to finance foreign trade across Latin America. It became the first Latin American bank listed on the New York Stock Exchange, in 1992.

The bank mainly finances trade for companies and governments across the region. Standard & Poor’s upgraded Bladex’s own rating to BBB+ in June 2026, a notch above where Fitch currently rates Panama’s sovereign debt.

What the Money Is For

Panama’s government will use the loan for “general budgetary purposes,” according to Bladex. The announcement did not name a specific project or spending line.

Panama’s Ministry of Economy and Finance helped structure the deal. Neither Bladex nor the ministry named an individual minister or signatory in the statements Rio Times reviewed.

What Wasn’t Disclosed

Bladex did not publish the loan’s interest rate, its final drawn amount, or its repayment period. Those terms often surface later, if at all, for a private bank loan rather than a public bond.

It is also not yet clear whether other banks will join the facility, or whether Bladex is lending the full amount alone. Rio Times found no confirmation either way as of publication.

Why Panama Is Borrowing Now

Panama has lost ground with credit rating agencies over the past two years. Fitch downgraded Panama to BB+, below investment grade, back in March 2024.

Moody’s still rates Panama at Baa3, its lowest investment-grade level, but with a negative outlook in place since late 2024. Moody’s has said it intends to resolve that outlook before the end of 2026, Rio Times reported previously.

Panama’s non-financial public sector deficit ran at 2.78% of GDP for January through July 2026. That is an improvement on 3.27% in the same period of 2025, though it remains a real shortfall.

Borrowing from a range of lenders, rather than relying only on bond markets, is one way governments manage that kind of pressure.

Part of a Wider Financing Push

Panama refinanced a Eurobond due in 2031, worth about US$3.3 billion, earlier this year, Rio Times reported in July 2026. The Bladex loan adds a separate, additional source of financing on top of that.

Bladex framed the new loan as a way to help Panama “diversify its sources of financing.” That phrase points to the same underlying pressure: fewer easy options in bond markets while rating agencies stay cautious.

What It Means for Investors and Residents

For most people in Panama, this loan changes little day to day. A government financing deal does not directly move wages, taxes or public services in the short term.

For investors watching Panama’s debt, it is one more data point on how the government is funding its deficit. A wider mix of lenders can support market confidence. It does not, by itself, close the deficit or lift the country’s ratings.

What Comes Next

Moody’s has said it will resolve Panama’s negative outlook before the end of 2026. Analysts will also watch whether Panama returns to bond markets again this year, or leans further on bank loans like this one.

More: Panama news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Bladex lend Panama?

Up to US$1 billion, in what Bladex called its largest single loan to date, announced on 15 September 2026.

What will Panama use the loan for?

Bladex said the funds would support Panama’s general state budget, without naming a specific project.

Why is Panama borrowing from Bladex instead of only the bond market?

Panama has faced ratings pressure, including a Fitch downgrade to BB+ in 2024 and a negative Moody’s outlook. It is diversifying its financing sources in response.

What is Bladex?

Bladex, the Banco Latinoamericano de Comercio Exterior, is a Panama-based trade bank founded in 1979. It became the first Latin American bank listed on the NYSE.

World.title: Bolivia Warns of State of Siege If Blockades Return
World.content:
BOLIVIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Bolivia’s government says it may declare a state of siege if road blockades return.

— The bigger step Officials just extended the country’s separate state of exception for 90 more days.

— Why now The last 90-day period included 53 days of blockades, a government spokesman said.

— What it means A state of siege would let the government use troops and curfews to reopen roads.

— The catch No state of siege is in force yet, and Congress has not approved the extension.

— Who it affects Diesel subsidy cuts have already drawn threats of new blockades from some sectors.

Bolivia’s government says it is ready to go further than its current state of emergency if road blockades come back.

Bolivia’s government said this week it could declare a state of siege. That would be a stronger emergency power than the state of exception already in force. Presidential spokesman José Luis Gálvez made the warning on 15 September 2026.

What Gálvez Said

“If necessary, we will declare a state of siege,” Gálvez told reporters in La Paz. “We will use constitutional force, and we will use the military.”

He said the government would only take that step if blockades or attacks on public order return. Gálvez added that “the threats remain in force,” pointing to unrest tied to this month’s diesel-subsidy changes.

Two Levels of Emergency Power

Bolivia’s Constitution allows four kinds of state of exception. A state of siege is the most severe of the four, meant for serious internal unrest.

The government is not using it yet. It has only extended the milder state of exception, in force since 20 June 2026 under Supreme Decree 5636.

That decree lets police and soldiers work together and limits movement and gatherings in affected zones. A state of siege would go further, allowing wider military deployment and curfews, nationwide or in specific regions.

Article 140 of Bolivia’s Constitution requires Congress to review any state of siege within 72 hours. The same 72-hour rule applies to the extension request now before lawmakers.

A Second 90 Days

Bolivia’s cabinet approved a decree on 14 September 2026 to extend the state of exception by 90 more days. The existing decree was due to expire on 18 September.

Gálvez said the previous 90-day period included 53 days of road blockades. He called the extension necessary to keep hospitals, food and fuel supplies moving.

The Plurinational Legislative Assembly still has to approve the extension. Some lawmakers outside the governing coalition have questioned whether it remains necessary.

What Sparked the Latest Warning

Bolivia has cut diesel subsidies this year as part of a wider fiscal correction, including Decree 5676 in late August. That decision has proven unpopular in several regions.

Sectors in Santa Cruz and Cochabamba have since announced plans for marches and blockades against the diesel decree, Bolivian outlets reported. The government cites those threats as the reason it wants to keep stronger emergency powers in reserve.

What Happened Earlier This Year

Farmers, transport unions and other groups blocked highways for weeks in May and June 2026. Infobae reported at least five deaths tied to the unrest by early June.

Bolivian outlets estimated losses at close to US$978 million after roughly a month of blockades, citing government and industry figures. Bolivia is landlocked, so blocked highways can empty a city’s shelves within days.

What Is Not Known

It is not yet confirmed whether the assembly will approve the full 90-day extension, or a shorter one. No formal state-of-siege decree has been drafted or published as of this writing.

It is also not clear which specific groups the government considers the biggest threat. Gálvez did not name them in his 15 September remarks.

A Government Under Political Pressure

President Rodrigo Paz took office in November 2025, ending nearly twenty years of government led by Evo Morales’s political movement. Morales faces two arrest warrants and has not appeared in public to answer them.

He has called the current government “agonizing” over its handling of fuel subsidies.

Some of the government’s critics have suggested the state-of-siege warning is more political signaling than an imminent order. Rio Times could not independently confirm that reading, and the government has not addressed it directly.

What This Means for Residents and Businesses

For now, daily life in Bolivia runs under the existing state of exception, not a state of siege. Travel and commerce continue normally outside any active blockade.

A state of siege, if it comes, would most likely target specific roads or regions rather than the whole country at once. Past emergency decrees have exempted food, fuel and medical transport from restrictions.

Business owners and residents in blockade-prone areas such as Cochabamba and Santa Cruz have the most reason to watch this closely. Travelers moving between Bolivian cities by road should expect delays if new blockades appear.

What Comes Next

Bolivia’s Legislative Assembly is expected to take up the 90-day extension in the coming days. Whether new blockades actually materialize over the diesel decree will likely decide if the state-of-siege warning becomes more than talk.

More: Bolivia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a state of siege in Bolivia?

It is the most severe of four types of state of exception under Bolivia’s Constitution. It allows wider military deployment and curfews during serious internal unrest.

Has Bolivia actually declared a state of siege?

No. As of 15 September 2026, the government said it would only do so if blockades return. None was in force at that time.

Why is Bolivia extending its state of exception?

The government says a previous 90-day period included 53 days of road blockades. It wants emergency powers in place as diesel-subsidy cuts fuel new protest threats.

What triggered the latest tension?

Diesel subsidy cuts under Decree 5676 have led some sectors in Santa Cruz and Cochabamba to threaten new marches and blockades.

World.title: Cost of Living Oaxaca 2026 — What a Newcomer Really Pays in Mexico’s Highland Capital
World.content:
MEXICO · COST OF LIVING

Rent in the historic centre runs to double the rent a few streets out. The cost of living Oaxaca asks of a newcomer starts with that one choice.

Vendors and shoppers among stalls of produce at the Tlacolula market in Oaxaca, Mexico

Key facts What this is — Oaxaca City is the capital of Oaxaca state, in the southern highlands of Mexico. What it costs — A one-bedroom in the historic centre ran 5,000 to 7,000 pesos a month in 2026 (about US$290 to US$410). Why it stays cheap — Food comes from markets, a bus costs 10 pesos (about US$0.58), and the cool climate needs no air conditioning. The catch — Local wages are low, and rents across the city rose 6 percent in a single year. What moves the price — The Guelaguetza festival every July lifts hotel rates by 30 to 60 percent across the city. What comes next — A stronger peso means dollar earners now get less for the same money than they did in 2024.

A one-bedroom in Oaxaca City’s historic centre was listed at 5,000 to 7,000 pesos in April 2026 (about US$290 to US$410). The cost of living Oaxaca sets for a newcomer starts at that address and spreads outward from there.

Two rents in one valley

Oaxaca City sells housing at two prices, and they sit ten minutes apart. The line runs roughly where the colonial grid ends.

CuantoMeCuesta, a Mexican cost-of-living site, priced a central one-bedroom at 5,000 to 7,000 pesos in April 2026 (about US$290 to US$410). For Jalatlaco, the cobbled barrio east of the centre, it gave 5,500 to 8,000 pesos (about US$320 to US$466).

Xochimilco, an older neighbourhood north of the centre, came in at 4,000 to 5,500 pesos (about US$233 to US$320). The peripheral colonias were cheaper again, at 3,000 to 4,000 pesos (about US$175 to US$233).

GoOaxaca, a local English-language guide, put the whole local market at 3,000 to 12,000 pesos in August 2026 (about US$175 to US$700). A colonial house in the centre ran 10,000 to 20,000 pesos and upward (about US$583 to US$1,165).

Furniture and included bills move the number again. A furnished one-bedroom near the Soledad church was advertised at 15,000 pesos in August 2025 (about US$874), water and power included.

Read across those lists and the pattern is plain. The same flat costs roughly twice as much inside the tourist grid as outside it.

What a week of food costs

Oaxaca eats from its markets, and the markets set the floor. A kilo of tortillas cost 24.50 pesos in the city in 2026 (about US$1.43).

The federal economy ministry’s own price monitor carried that number on 14 September 2026. El Imparcial, a Mexican daily, published the same 24.50 pesos in April (about US$1.43).

The comida corrida, a set lunch with soup and a main course, ran 80 to 120 pesos (about US$4.70 to US$7). Street food sat below that in August 2026, at 50 to 100 pesos (about US$2.90 to US$5.80).

Sitting down in a restaurant is where the gap opens. A main dish in a mid-range place ran 150 to 250 pesos (about US$8.70 to US$14.60).

Numbeo, a crowd-sourced price database, put an inexpensive restaurant meal in Oaxaca at 165 pesos (about US$9.60). Its readings for the city stop in late 2025, and nobody has published a fresher local series.

A household that shops in the Central de Abastos and cooks at home spends a fraction of what a restaurant habit costs. That one choice separates the two budgets more than any other.

The month the city changes its price

Every July, Oaxaca fills for the Guelaguetza, the state’s festival of regional dance and dress. Hotel rooms respond first.

Budget guesthouses ran 400 to 900 pesos a night in 2026 (about US$23 to US$52). Mid-range boutique hotels ran 1,500 to 3,500 pesos (about US$87 to US$204).

One 2026 travel guide put the Guelaguetza premium at 30 to 60 percent above the ordinary rate. Another recorded budget rooms at US$80 to US$120 a night in late July, against about US$30 in October.

A resident on a twelve-month lease steps outside that cycle entirely. A newcomer who arrives in July and rents by the month pays the festival price for a home.

No agency publishes a Guelaguetza index for long-term rents. The hotel rate is the only public signal of how far July moves the city.

Ten pesos across town

Getting around Oaxaca City is the cheapest line in the budget. A standard city bus charged 10 pesos in August 2026 (about US$0.58).

The BinniBus, the city’s newer service, charged 8 pesos (about US$0.47). A taxi inside the historic centre ran 70 to 100 pesos (about US$4.10 to US$5.80).

Livingcost.net, a cost comparison site, put a single local fare at 9.18 pesos in August 2026 (about US$0.53). The two readings describe the same short ride.

The centre is walkable, and many newcomers never buy a car. That saving shows up as a blank line rather than as a bill.

The open-air Guelaguetza auditorium above Oaxaca city

Power, gas and a fibre line

Oaxaca City stands high in a dry inland valley, at somewhere between 1,555 and 1,597 metres above the sea. Nights are cool, and almost nobody installs air conditioning.

That single fact keeps the electricity bill small, which is not true of Mexico’s coasts. Cooking gas is the bigger line, and a 20-kilo bottle cost 400 pesos in August 2026 (about US$23).

Home internet ran 350 to 600 pesos a month (about US$20 to US$35). Livingcost.net put a typical plan at 529 pesos (about US$31).

Water and rubbish collection are billed modestly and rarely decide a budget. The building and the landlord matter more than the tariff does.

Doctors are cheap, insurance is the open question

A private consultation with a doctor in Oaxaca ran 500 to 1,000 pesos in August 2026 (about US$29 to US$58). Paying cash for routine care is ordinary here, and uncomplicated.

The city has a cluster of small private hospitals rather than one large one. Hospital Reforma stands on Reforma street in the centre, and Clinica Hospital Florencia in Jalatlaco.

Others, among them Medica 2002 and Clinica Hospital Betesda, sit in the Colonia Reforma district. All are private, and all bill the patient directly.

The insurance side is where a budget goes blurry. Mexico’s social security institute has not published a 2026 voluntary premium for a foreign resident.

Private policies are quoted one at a time, by age and by medical history. The quote a fifty-year-old receives says nothing about what a thirty-year-old will pay.

The wage underneath the rent

Every price above sits on top of a local wage. Mexico’s general daily minimum wage rose 13 percent on 1 January 2026, to 315.04 pesos a day (about US$18.36).

Thirty days at that rate come to 9,451 pesos (about US$551). A central one-bedroom at 7,000 pesos (about US$408) takes most of that away.

That arithmetic is why gentrification is an open argument in Oaxaca. Researchers cited by Mexico News Daily in 2022 linked foreign residents in Xochimilco and Jalatlaco to rising rents and food prices.

One studio they traced went from 1,000 pesos in 2001 to 20,000 pesos in 2021 (about US$58 to US$1,165). Those pesos bought less each year, so the raw jump overstates the real rise.

More recently the movement has been steadier. Data from Propiedades.com, reported in June 2025, showed Oaxaca rents up 6 percent over the year.

Six percent a year is a market drifting, not a market running. It is also faster than a minimum wage earner’s life improves.

La Santa Cecilia live — the Grammy-winning Los Angeles band plays Mexico City’s Teatro Metropólitan on September 12, 2026

What the lease and the visa demand

Behind the rent sits the residency rule. Mexico ties temporary residency to a monthly income test, indexed to a national accounting unit rather than to a fixed sum.

Immigration advisers put the 2026 threshold near 79,800 pesos a month over six months (about US$4,650). Each consulate applies it with its own conversion, so the figure quoted differs from city to city.

That income test has nothing to do with what Oaxaca actually costs. It only decides who is allowed to find out.

Many newcomers arrive on a tourist permit and rent month to month at first. They pay the short-term price while they learn the long-term one.

Frugal, comfortable and the space between

Two published 2026 estimates bracket the answer. SnapCostOfLiving put a single person’s monthly spending in Oaxaca City at about US$965.

GoOaxaca put comfortable living for one person at US$800 to US$1,400 a month. It called US$1,000 workable for someone cooking at home and renting outside the centre.

The frugal version is a bus fare, a market basket and an outer colonia. The comfortable version is a centre address, restaurants several nights a week and taxis after dark.

Nothing forces a newcomer to pick one end of that scale. Most settle in between, and the settling point is decided by the lease rather than by the groceries.

Where the price is heading

Oaxaca’s direction of travel is upward, but gently. A 6 percent annual rent rise is well short of a market pulling away from local incomes.

The state drew more than four million visitors between January and August 2025, on its tourism ministry’s count. Every year like that adds pressure to the centre.

The peso itself is the quiet variable. Every dollar figure here uses a rate of 17.16 pesos to the dollar, read on 16 September 2026.

That peso is stronger than it was two years ago, so a dollar earner gets less Oaxaca for the same money. The rent did not have to move at all for that to happen.

The number worth watching is not the rent in the centre. It is the rent two streets beyond it, where the city decides what it still costs to be from here.

More: Mexico news in English

Sources: CuantoMeCuesta, GoOaxaca, SNIIM (Mexican Secretariat of Economy), El Imparcial, Numbeo, Livingcost.net, SnapCostOfLiving, Mexico News Daily, Propiedades.com via Vallarta Daily, Sectur Oaxaca, Bloomberg Tax. https://cuantomecuesta.com/mx/costo-vida-oaxaca/ and https://gooaxaca.com/cost-of-living-in-oaxaca/ and http://www.economia-sniim.gob.mx/TortillaMesPorDia.asp and https://www.elimparcial.com/mexico/2026/04/15/de-15-a-33-pesos-el-kilo-asi-cambia-el-precio-de-la-tortilla-en-mexico-con-el-norte-entre-las-zonas-mas-caras-del-pais/ and https://www.numbeo.com/cost-of-living/in/Oaxaca-Mexico and https://www.livingcost.net/mexico/oaxaca-de-juarez and https://snapcostofliving.com/cost-of-living/oaxaca and https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/changes-in-oaxaca-brought-by-foreigners/ and https://www.vallartadaily.com/mexico-news/south/oaxaca/oaxaca-city/gentrification-is-being-blamed-for-annual-rent-prices-rising-6-7-in-oaxaca-and-merida/ and https://theoaxacapost.com/2025/09/28/more-than-4-million-people-visited-oaxaca-from-january-to-august-2025-sectur-oaxaca/

World.title: Ecuador Imposes New Curfew in Four Coastal Provinces
World.content:

Get the brief

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Key Facts —

What happened Ecuador’s government ordered a new nighttime curfew starting September 17.

—

Where Guayas, Manabí, Los Ríos and El Oro provinces, from midnight to 5 a.m., through September 30.

—

The catch Interior Minister John Reimberg says no special travel passes will be issued this time.

—

Context It is Ecuador’s third curfew of 2026, layered on a state of exception covering ten provinces.

—

Who it affects Residents of the four coastal provinces face nightly movement limits for two weeks.

—

What comes next The curfew arrives days after President Noboa removed his air force commander.

A community police surveillance post in Guayaquil, one of the four provinces under the new curfew. (Photo: Freddy eduardo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0) (Photo, internet reproduction)

A New Curfew for Ecuador’s Coast

Ecuador will impose a nighttime curfew across four provinces starting Thursday, September 17. Interior Minister John Reimberg announced the measure on September 11, according to Primicias and Infobae.

The curfew runs from midnight to 5 a.m. daily through September 30. It covers Guayas, Manabí, Los Ríos and El Oro, four provinces along Ecuador’s Pacific coast.

Which Provinces, What Hours

Guayas is home to Guayaquil, Ecuador’s largest city and a hub of drug-trafficking violence. Manabí, Los Ríos and El Oro have also seen recurring gang activity this year.

During curfew hours, only a short list of people may circulate. That includes healthcare workers, emergency responders, and prosecutors or lawyers attending urgent hearings.

Journalists may also move during the curfew, but only when accompanied by security forces. Everyone else must stay off the streets until 5 a.m.

No Exceptions This Time

Reimberg said the government will not issue salvoconductos this time around. Those special passes had let residents bypass earlier curfews under limited conditions.

He told Primicias there would be “no type of safe-conduct” for this round of restrictions. That marks a tougher line than Ecuador’s earlier curfews this year.

Reimberg said the curfew targets groups trying to “sow fear and challenge the authority of the State.”

He asked residents for patience despite the disruption. Past curfews this year have drawn similar appeals from Ecuadorian officials.

Part of a Broader Security Offensive

This is Ecuador’s third curfew of 2026. President Daniel Noboa’s government imposed similar nighttime restrictions in March and again in April.

Each earlier curfew followed roughly the same pattern. A spike in gang violence led to a presidential decree, then a temporary nighttime lockdown in the affected province.

Noboa has made the anti-crime crackdown a central plank of his presidency. He took office in late 2023 promising to confront Ecuador’s cartels directly.

Why Ecuador Keeps Declaring Curfews

Ecuador’s homicide rate hit 50.9 per 100,000 people in 2025, according to InsightCrime’s annual round-up. That was a 31 percent jump from 2024 and a record high for the country.

InsightCrime linked the surge to fighting between the Choneros gang and its rival, Los Lobos. The clashes escalated after the 2025 arrest of Choneros leader Adolfo Macías Villamar, known as “Fito.”

Prison riots added to the toll last year. InsightCrime counted at least 75 deaths across four separate riots inside Ecuadorian prisons in 2025.

The State of Exception Behind It

The new curfew sits inside a wider state of exception that Noboa renewed on August 14, 2026. That decree covers ten provinces and three cantons, according to Infobae.

A state of exception lets Ecuador’s government deploy the armed forces alongside police. It can also suspend some constitutional rights for a limited period.

The curfew itself needs no separate legal basis once a state of exception is active. It is simply one tool available to security forces during the emergency.

A Tense Month for Noboa’s Government

The curfew announcement came one day after Noboa dismissed his air force commander. Lieutenant General Mauricio Xavier Salazar Machuca was removed on September 10 via Executive Decree 496, Rio Times reported.

Salazar had reportedly sought written legal guidelines for United States military flights at Ecuador’s Taura air base. The government gave no public reason for his removal.

The two events are not officially connected. Together, they show a government moving fast on security and defense matters this month.

Economic Backdrop

The security crackdown unfolds against a steadier economic picture. Ecuador’s central bank raised its 2026 growth forecast to 2.5 percent in April, up from earlier estimates.

The International Monetary Fund projected similar growth of about 2.0 percent for the year in a March estimate. Dollarization has kept inflation below 3 percent, well under the regional average.

What Happens Next

The curfew is due to lift on September 30, unless officials extend it again. Ecuador’s earlier 2026 curfews were sometimes renewed once their initial deadlines passed.

Security forces plan to increase patrols in Guayaquil and the three other provinces during restricted hours. Tourism and nightlife businesses are likely to feel the sharpest impact.

Residents and rights groups will also watch how strictly the no-exemptions rule gets enforced. Ecuadorian courts have previously reviewed curfew measures for their scope and duration.

Ecuador’s earlier 2026 curfews hit at least 120,000 businesses, Expreso reported in May, citing economist Juan Sebastián Naranjo. He estimated losses of US$16 million to US$32 million from those restrictions.

Bars and discos lost up to 80 percent of sales on curfew days, Naranjo found. Container and logistics operations also reported sales declines of up to 40 percent.

Background: Ecuador Has Imposed a Nighttime Curfew Across Four Coastal Provinces.

World.title: What to Do in Rio in September 2026: the First Semana de Arte and Nine Free Things
World.content:
What to Do in Rio in Late September 2026: MIMO, Zélia Duncan, Angra and Twenty Free Things

=====

Rio de Janeiro · Culture

The first Semana de Arte do Rio runs to the 27th, MIMO takes the Circo Voador for free on the weekend, the harp festival gives twenty-three concerts for nothing, and Zélia Duncan, Angra and Marcelo D2 play the big rooms. Here is the rest of September, day by day.

RIO DE JANEIRO — There is a great deal to do in Rio in September, and very little of it is written down anywhere in English. This guide is the monthly selection for people who live here rather than visit: what is on, where, when, what it costs, and why it might be worth crossing the city for. Most of the entries below are free.

Rock in Rio is over. What remains of the month is better distributed and cheaper: until the 27th, the first Semana de Arte do Rio pulls more than ten festivals under a single banner, with twenty-three free harp concerts inside it; on the weekend of 19 and 20 September the MIMO festival takes over the Circo Voador for nothing, and two Brasileirão home games land in São Januário and the Maracanã. After that the month belongs to Zélia Duncan, Angra, Marcelo D2 and the orchestras. Plan accordingly.

Also running now

Nicole Musafir’s Pra Quem Não Me Conhece opens at the Casa de Cultura Laura Alvim. (Photo: Elisa Maciel)
