11 to 27 September, Fridays and Saturdays 8pm, Sundays 7pm A Pequena Prisão Teatro Laura Alvim, Casa de Cultura Laura Alvim, Av. Vieira Souto 176, Ipanema · R$30–60 · 60 minutes · 16+ Nine performances only, after more than forty at the Teatro Poeira. Vino Fragoso plays over thirty characters in the first stage adaptation of Igor Mendes’s book on the Brazilian prison system. In Portuguese, and physical enough to follow without it.

9 to 24 September, Wednesdays and Thursdays, 7pm Nicole Musafir — Pra Quem Não Me Conhece Casa de Cultura Laura Alvim, Ipanema · Price from the venue This is a short run of a one-woman show. Musafir built it out of the diaries she has kept since she was six. Blocked creatively for years, she went through the box and put what she found on stage; pianist Ceci Nery accompanies, with musical direction by Leo Valor. In Portuguese, and personal enough to reward the effort if you can follow it.

Photo: Divulgação

11 to 27 September, opening 11 September at 8pm 19º Niterói em Cena — International Theatre Festival Theatro Municipal de Niterói and venues across the city · Free Paulo Betti opens with his monologue Autobiografia Autorizada. What follows is free for seventeen days: companies from Angola, Georgia, Senegal, Mexico, Colombia, Paraguay and Peru, plus street theatre on the Praça João Saldanha. The street programme — clowning, acrobatics, the Peruvian Inka Clown Show — needs no language at all. Twenty minutes on the ferry from Praça Quinze.

16 to 27 September: the first Semana de Arte do Rio

16 to 27 September Semana de Arte do Rio — first edition Museums, cultural centres, theatres and galleries across the city · Varies; much of it free More than ten festivals come under one banner for the first time. In addition, there are exhibitions, street interventions and events in both public and private venues. Part of the Centro Cultural Justiça Federal programme falls inside it. If you have one week of Rio in September to give to the city’s art scene, make it this one.

Wednesday 17 and Friday 19 September, 8pm Carmem — Cia. de Dança Thiago Soares Teatro Multiplan, VillageMall, Av. das Américas 3900, Barra da Tijuca · From R$110, through Sympla Thiago Soares went from hip-hop in São Gonçalo to Principal at the Royal Ballet, and now runs his own company here. His Bizet is pulled towards Latin America and mixes classical technique with urban and contemporary vocabulary. Sasha De Sola, principal at San Francisco Ballet, dances both nights in her Brazilian debut — the run was consolidated from four dates to these two, and tickets for the cancelled performances remain valid through Sympla. Dance, so the language question does not arise.

Wednesday 16 September, 12.30pm and 5pm RioHarpFestival opens — Walter Morato, and a harp-and-guitar duo Museu Nacional de Belas Artes, Av. Rio Branco 199, Centro; then Associação Comercial, Rua da Candelária 9 · Free The Argentine harpist Walter Morato opens the Latin American edition at the national fine-arts museum at 12.30pm. At 5pm the Paraguayan sisters Rosalía and Gabriela López play harp and guitar at the Commercial Association. Two free concerts in two buildings most visitors never get inside.

Thursday 17 September, 12.30pm XXI RioHarpFestival — Walter Morato at the Museu da Justiça Museu da Justiça, Rua Dom Manuel 29, Centro · Free The Argentine harpist plays the old jury room of the Tribunal do Júri, a courtroom turned museum that is rarely open for anything else. A hundred and twenty seats, and no ticket. Thursday 17 September, 6pm XXI RioHarpFestival — Luis Castro Centro Cultural Justiça Federal, Av. Rio Branco 241, Centro · Free The Venezuelan harpist plays the Latin American leg of the harp festival. Free, an hour long, and in the middle of the working city — the easiest good concert to walk into during Rio in September.

Friday 18 September, 12.30pm and 6pm Navy wind sextet, then the Camerata do Uerê at the Palácio Tiradentes Espaço Cultural da Marinha, Praça XV; then Palácio Tiradentes, Rua Primeiro de Março · Free The Marine Corps symphonic band sends a wind sextet to the naval cultural centre at midday, with the Brazilian harpist Giovana Sanches. In the evening the Camerata do Uerê, made up of young musicians from the Maré favela complex, plays the old chamber of deputies with the Chilean harpist Christian Rodrigues.

Saturday 19 and Sunday 20 September, 1pm and 3pm Harp weekend at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro · Free The National Symphonic Band plays the ground-floor rotunda on the Saturday and an orchestra of ukuleles takes it on the Sunday, each with a guest harpist. Upstairs at 3pm on both days, Nicolas Almada and Letícia Rodriguez sing Uruguayan candombe and milonga. Turn up and walk in.

Saturday 19 September Feira das Yabás at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Centro · Free entry; food paid A samba circle with Marquinhos de Oswaldo Cruz alongside the cooking that gives the fair its name — feijoada, angu à baiana, roast meat. The Feira das Yabás is normally a Madureira institution; catching it in Centro is the easy version.

Wednesday 16 September, 6pm Diogo Nogueira opens the Semana de Arte with the Petrobras Symphony Praça dos Arcos, Arcos da Lapa, Centro · Free The official opening concert of the first Semana de Arte do Rio: the city’s reigning samba singer in front of the Orquestra Petrobras Sinfônica under the Lapa arches. Free, open-air, and the biggest single crowd-puller of the fortnight.

Thursday 17 September, 6.30pm BNegão sings Dorival Caymmi at the Museum of Tomorrow Museu do Amanhã, Praça Mauá, Centro · Free The Carioca rapper takes on the Caymmi songbook as part of Rio Ocean Week, on the museum’s outdoor esplanade. Caymmi wrote about the sea; the setting does half the work.

Friday 18 September, from 4pm Próxima Parada Samba: Mart’nália at the Capanema Palácio Gustavo Capanema, Rua da Imprensa 16, Centro · Free The former Ministry of Education — arguably the finest modernist building in the Americas — opens its forecourt for the samba strand of the Próxima Parada festival: Mart’nália on the Friday, a Beth Carvalho roda on the Saturday afternoon, and the Terreiro de Mangueira on the Sunday. The building alone justifies the bus ride; the music is free.

Friday 18 September, 7pm Fafá de Belém at the Arcos da Lapa Praça dos Arcos, Lapa · Free The Pará singer headlines the free Amir Haddad festival strand under the arches, with carimbó from Baque Mulher and the Festa Xêpa DJs afterwards. The praça fills; arrive before seven.

Saturday 19 September, 2pm Project Aquarius: Leci Brandão, Emicida and the Brazilian Symphony Orchestra Praça Mauá, Centro · Free The Orquestra Sinfônica Brasileira, conducted by Carlos Prazeres, meets rap and samba head-on: Emicida and Leci Brandão in front of the museum district, open-air, free. The most Rio concert of the month.

Saturday 19 September, 8pm MIMO Rio, night one: Tiken Jah Fakoly, Fernanda Abreu Circo Voador, Lapa · Free (advance ticket) The travelling world-music festival opens its free Rio edition with Malian reggae heavyweight Tiken Jah Fakoly and Rio’s own Fernanda Abreu, plus the Cape Verdean-Portuguese rapper Capicua and DJ Reborn.

Sunday 20 September, 6pm MIMO Rio, night two: Tinariwen, Capicua & Emicida Circo Voador, Lapa · Free (advance ticket) Tuareg guitar legends Tinariwen headline the second night, with the Capicua–Emicida meeting and the pianist Bianca Gismonti. Tickets are released in advance and go; the same programme would cost real money anywhere else.

Saturday 19 September, 8.30pm · Sunday 20 September, 6.30pm Brasileirão in Rio: Vasco at São Januário, Flamengo at the Maracanã Estádio São Januário (Vasco x Coritiba); Maracanã (Flamengo x RB Bragantino) · Tickets from the clubs and the usual outlets Two home games close the league’s 28th round: Vasco host Coritiba in the tight, old-school ground on Saturday night, and Flamengo, still chasing the leaders, take on RB Bragantino at the Maracanã on Sunday. Ninety minutes of Brazilian football culture without a festival wristband.

Monday 21 to Friday 25 September, 12.30pm and 3pm Harp at lunchtime: five weekdays at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Rua Primeiro de Março 66, third-floor auditorium, Centro; and the Liceu Literário Português, Rua Almirante Barroso 118, on the 22nd · Free The quiet middle of the festival, and the easiest thing on this list to walk into on a working day. Nicolas Almada and Letícia Rodriguez sing Uruguayan candombe and milonga on the 21st, 23rd and 24th; Rafael Deboleto plays on the 21st and, at the Liceu, on the 22nd; Alessandro Aguiar pairs harp and Japanese koto with a French horn on the 23rd; the Paraguayan Júlio César Villaalta takes the 24th and 25th, and the Venezuelan Luis Castro the 25th. A hundred and six seats, sung in Spanish or not sung at all. Tuesday 22 September, 6pm Madrigal Cruz Lopes at Santa Cruz dos Militares Igreja Santa Cruz dos Militares, Rua Primeiro de Março, Centro · Free Choral music under José Machado in an eighteenth-century garrison church, with the Venezuelan harpist Jesús Suárez as guest. The building is worth the walk on its own.

24 to 27 September Mostra Violas Brasileiras: Da Raiz ao Contemporâneo Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Centro · Free Curated by Ivan Viela. The viola caipira is the instrument most foreigners never hear in Rio, because it belongs to the interior. Four days to correct that.

Saturday 26 and Sunday 27 September, 1pm and 3pm The RioHarpFestival closes at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Rua Primeiro de Março 66, ground-floor rotunda and third-floor auditorium, Centro · Free Harold Emert’s Camerata Viva Música takes the rotunda on the Saturday with the Venezuelan harpist Luis Castro. On the Sunday a bagpipe band closes the Latin American edition at 1pm — gaitas de foles under Maestro J. Paulo, which is not a sentence anyone expects to read about Rio — and Castro plays the last recital upstairs at 3pm with the Japanese musician Michinari Usuda.

Late September

Thursday 17 September, 7pm · Friday 18 September, 7pm Quarteto Kalimera plays Nosferatu live Sala Cecília Meireles, Rua da Lapa 47, Lapa · R$20 (half price) The 1922 Murnau silent screened with a live score by a Rio quartet, in the best-sounding room in Lapa. Cinema-with-orchestra for the price of a cinema ticket.

Friday 18 September, 7pm Angra — “Holy Land” turns 30 Vivo Rio, Av. Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo · From R$75 (half price) Rio’s own power-metal band plays its 1993 concept album end to end with a full production. Loud, local, and ten minutes from most hotel districts.

Friday 18 September, from 7pm Dia do Cliente at Bar Bukowski Bar Bukowski, Rua Álvaro Ramos 270, Botafogo · R$39.90 at the door (a drink included before 10pm); guest-list entry free from 1am The Botafogo rock bar marks Cliente’s Day with the self-deprecating festa “Vocês nem sempre têm razão”: rock and pop across two floors, karaoke with prizes, a 2000s cover band, and a raffle that makes one customer “the owner’s friend” for the night — queue-jump, DJ requests and a R$500 tab included. Guest list via the bar’s Instagram.

Friday 18 September, 8pm Thaís Fraga — Mais de 30 Anos de Bossa n’ Jazz Vinícius Show, Ipanema · Price from the venue Bossa nova, samba-jazz and jazz standards in the bar named for the poet, from a singer with three decades of that repertoire behind her. The trio includes Amaro Junior, Emílio Santiago’s historic drummer, brought up from São Paulo for the run.

Sunday 20 September, 3pm Jorge Aragão at the Renascença Clube Renascença Clube, Rua Barão de São Francisco 54, Andaraí · R$50 (half price) The great Andaraí samba composer in the club where samba de raíz still runs the Sunday afternoon. Cheap food, cold beer, no stage tricks.

Malize performs Baile da Saudade at the Teatro Firjan SESI Centro on the 23rd. (Photo: Thaís Monteiro)

Wednesday 23 September Malize — Baile da Saudade, live with band Teatro Firjan SESI Centro · Price from the venue The 27-year-old singer and producer from Rio’s Zona Norte performs the first single from his debut album. Alongside it, the venue screens the video that won backing from the Mosaico Rio 2026 fund. Both form part of the Mostra Firjan SESI. MPB as a foundation with everything else layered on top.

Monday 21 September, 7pm Canto pela Democracia: Cordão do Boitatá, with Geraldo Azevedo, Sandra de Sá and Diogo Nogueira Teatro Riachuelo, Rua do Passeio 40, Cinelândia · R$40 advance The travelling democracy festival lands at the Riachuelo with a bill that reads like an MPB family tree: Geraldo Azevedo, Sandra de Sá, Diogo Nogueira and Moysés Marques around the Cordão do Boitatá collective.

Monday 21 September, 8pm Lauren Jauregui Teatro Clara Nunes, Shopping da Gávea, Gávea · From R$150 (half price) The week’s biggest international pop booking: the former Fifth Harmony singer’s first Rio solo date, in an intimate theatre above the Gávea shopping centre.

Tuesday 22 September, 6.30pm Mariana Aydar at the Theatro João Caetano Praça Tiradentes, Centro · R$2.50 (half price) Not a typo: the municipal theatre’s pricing policy puts one of Brazil’s smartest MPB singers within reach of a bus fare. The building, from 1813, is the oldest working theatre in the city.

Tuesday 22 September, 8pm Cida Moreira Teatro Ipanema, Rua Prudente de Morais 824, Ipanema · R$50 (half price) The deep-voiced interpreter of the Brazilian songbook in the pocket theatre two blocks from the beach.

Wednesday 23 September, 8pm Teresa Cristina at the Teatro Riachuelo Rua do Passeio 40, Cinelândia · From R$50 (half price) The sambista’s sambista in the plush reopened theatre on the boulevard. If you only know the name from records, the live timing is the revelation.

Thursday 24 September, 8pm Aguidavi do Jêje, with Chico César, Gilsons and Pretinho da Serrinha Circo Voador, Lapa · R$70 (half price) The Tocantins singer-songwriter’s biggest Rio date yet, with guests spanning generations: Chico César, the Gilsons, Pretinho da Serrinha and Carlinhos 7 Cordas.

Thursday 24 September, 8pm Marcelo D2 at Rio Gastronomia Jockey Club Brasileiro, Rua Jardim Botânico 1003, Gávea · R$40 (half price) The rapper closes a week of food-and-music programming at the Jockey Club’s food festival, with the Botafogo and Corcovado views thrown in. Eat first; he goes on at eight.

Friday 25 September, 7pm Zélia Duncan at Vivo Rio Av. Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo · From R$60 (half price) The singer in full band at the Flamengo park auditorium — the month’s biggest room dedicated to Brazilian song.

Friday 25 September, 8pm Cachorro Grande and Vanguart at the Circo Voador Lapa · R$70 (half price) A Porto Alegre rock double bill: Cachorro Grande’s retro-groove with Vanguart’s psychedelia, in the Lapa tent on a Friday.

Friday 25 September, 8.30pm Baile Charme de Madureira at the Capanema Palácio Gustavo Capanema, Rua da Imprensa 16, Centro · Free Twelve years of the charm baile that put Madureira’s black-music scene on the national map, played free in the Capanema forecourt as part of the Próxima Parada festival.

Saturday 26 September, 7.30pm Petrobras Symphony honours Moacir Santos, then Hamilton de Holanda Praça dos Arcos, Arcos da Lapa · Free The Orquestra Petrobras Sinfônica plays the great composer-arranger’s orchestral music with Fabiana Cozza and Marcos Sacramento, and Hamilton de Holanda’s trio closes the night. Free, under the arches.

Saturday 26 September, 8pm Ave Sangria, Papangu and Zepelim at the Circo Voador Lapa · R$80 (half price) Pernambuco psych-rock from the 1970s — Ave Sangria, reformed and on form — with Recife’s current experimentalists Papangu. The month’s best double bill for guitar music.

Sunday 27 September, 4pm Festival Solar: a tribute to Ney Matogrosso Praça dos Arcos, Arcos da Lapa · Free Juliana Linhares, Linn da Quebrada, MC Tha, Tássia Reis and Xênia França take on the maestro’s repertoire — the most interesting free bill of the closing weekend, and the last big day of the Semana de Arte.

Until 4 December The Jazz Room: a Sinatra and Armstrong tribute Teatro Rival Petrobras, Rua Álvaro Alvim 33, Cinelândia · From R$100 The Rival’s long-running tribute evening — the American songbook with a live band in the Art Deco theatre off Cinelândia. The reliable option when nothing else on this list fits the night.

Saturday 26 September Seal — 30 years Qualistage, Barra da Tijuca · Price from the venue The thirtieth-anniversary tour. A large, comfortable room and a set of songs most people in it will know by heart.

Saturday 26 September, 6pm Tribute to Luiz Carlos de Moura Castro — Palácio São Clemente Portuguese Consulate, Rua São Clemente 424, Botafogo · Free Martin Almeida at the piano, with Jesús Suárez on harp, in a posthumous tribute to the pianist who was a long-standing partner of the series. The consulate residence opens for it, which is reason enough to go.

Tuesday 29 September, 6pm Recorders and voices at the Forte de Copacabana Museu do Exército, Forte de Copacabana, Praça Cel. Eugênio Franco 1, Posto 6 · Free The recorder ensemble Fino Som and the vocal group Vozes Encanto play international classics, directed by Nelma Pataro. The fort sits on the rocks at the end of Copacabana beach and the view alone carries the evening.

Wednesday 30 September, 12.30pm Mignone, 40 anos de saudade — the month closes at the CCBB Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Rua Primeiro de Março 66, 4th floor, Centro · Free Five pianists mark forty years since the death of Francisco Mignone, one of the central figures of Brazilian concert music, with video testimony from the composer between the pieces. A good last free hour of Rio in September.

Opera and orchestras in Rio in September

September Festival Oficina da Ópera Theatro Municipal, Cinelândia, Centro · Price from the box office The Municipal’s September strand brings Mascagni’s Cavalleria Rusticana and Donizetti’s Il Campanello. The building alone justifies the ticket; it was modelled on the Paris Opera and finished in 1909.

16 to 20 September Festival Rio Cello Churches and halls across Centro — Igreja de Santa Cruz dos Militares, the Sala Mário Tavares by the Theatro Municipal, BNDES · Free Five days of cello recitals within a fifteen-minute walk of Cinelândia: the Salles Geiger duo on the 16th, Gilson Peranzzetta with Mauro Senise and David Chew on the 18th, Victor Biglione with the Rice Cello Ensemble at BNDES on the 19th, and the Lindarte Plano Quartet at the Municipal’s annexe on the 20th. All free.

Through September 21st RioHarpFestival and Música no Museu Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil and partner venues · Mostly free Twenty-three harp concerts run from 16 to 27 September inside the Semana de Arte, all of them free — at the CCBB, tickets are handed out at the box office from 9am on the day. They sit alongside the Música no Museu series, which is in its twenty-ninth year and puts classical music into museums, palaces and churches at no charge. The September dates are listed individually above: the CCBB on the 9th and the 30th, the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes on the 16th, the Palácio Tiradentes on the 18th, the Palácio São Clemente on the 26th and the Forte de Copacabana on the 29th. One of the best-value things in the city and almost unknown to new arrivals.

Free all month in Rio in September

Until 12 October Vik Muniz — season extended Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Centro · Free Brazil’s most internationally recognised living visual artist, in the show that has been held over. If you see one exhibition this month, this is the one to see.

2 September to 16 November Amazônicas — Poéticas Femininas Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Centro · Free Sissa Aneleh curates work by women from the North of Brazil. The reading is decolonial, and it foregrounds Afro-indigenous ancestry. Furthermore, the show uses virtual and augmented-reality elements.

September African Cinema showcase Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil cinemas, Centro · Free or low cost Ten features and six contemporary shorts. Given how little African cinema reaches Brazilian screens, this is the rare chance.

Until late September Coleção Ingá: Brasil Plural — final weeks Centro Cultural Justiça Federal, Centro · Free Around 200 works come from the Museu de História e Artes do Estado. Among them are Di Cavalcanti, Portinari, Goeldi and Mestre Guarany. The CCJF’s September programme also runs open-air cinema, short-film and Spanish-cinema seasons, choral concerts, flamenco, choro and indigenous music, literary workshops and two theatre productions — nearly all of it free.

Until 10 October, Tuesday to Saturday, midday to 7pm Inefável Presença — nine painters from one Tijuca studio Centro Cultural dos Correios, R. Visc. de Itaboraí 20, Centro · Free Nine artists have shared a studio in Tijuca for seven years. Ayla de Oliveira curates the show, and also exhibits in it. The group formed around a life-drawing class at the UFRJ fine arts school in 2017 and kept meeting on Monday evenings. Figurative painting, unfashionable for a while, now finding buyers.

Planning your Rio in September

Where we have not printed a ticket price, the organisers did not publish one — check with the venue before you travel. Programmes at the CCBB, the Theatro Municipal and the CCJF change during Rio in September, so confirm on the day.

This guide to Rio in September runs monthly, and returns in October. If you run a venue, a gallery or a production in Rio and would like to be considered, write to the newsroom with the date, the time, the address and the ticket price. Those four things are what get an event into the list.

More on living here: our Rio de Janeiro coverage and Expats in Brazil.

World.title: Argentina’s Navy Uncovers Payroll Fraud Inside Its Own Ranks
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Key Facts —

What happened Argentina’s Navy filed a fraud complaint against its own payroll office on September 15.

—

The scheme Staff allegedly padded travel and per-diem payments for personnel abroad, then split the excess.

—

How many Reports put the number of personnel involved at up to 50.

—

The money About 1.6 billion pesos (roughly US$1.05 million, official rate, September 15, 2026) is said to be involved.

—

The court The case has gone to Federal Court No. 2 at the Comodoro Py courthouse.

—

The catch It is at least the third defense-sector graft case to surface in Argentina this year.

The Edificio Libertad, Navy headquarters on Comodoro Py avenue, where the fraud complaint was filed (Photo, internet reproduction).

A Fraud Uncovered From Within

Argentina’s Navy has asked federal prosecutors to investigate its own payroll department. The institution filed the complaint itself on September 15.

The case centers on the office that liquidates salaries and travel allowances for Navy personnel. Internal reviewers found discrepancies serious enough to trigger a criminal referral rather than a purely administrative one.

The accounting department’s own chief brought the irregularities to a federal court. That step, rather than handling the matter quietly in-house, is what turned an internal audit finding into a criminal case.

How The Scheme Allegedly Worked

Investigators say staff falsified receipts tied to personnel traveling abroad. Per-diem and travel-allowance payments were inflated beyond what those trips actually cost.

In some cases, the payments reportedly kept flowing even after the traveler had returned to Argentina. Payments to people who had already left the Navy were also allegedly kept active.

Those involved are said to have split the diverted funds roughly evenly. Beneficiaries allegedly returned part of each padded payment to whoever had processed it.

The two sides would then divide those returned proceeds between them. That structure is what investigators describe as an organized scheme rather than scattered individual errors.

The Numbers Behind The Case

Local outlets reporting on the complaint put the number of implicated personnel as high as 50. Estimates of the total diverted funds cluster around 1.6 billion pesos.

At the official exchange rate of roughly ARS 1,530 per dollar on September 15, 2026, that is about US$1.05 million. Some accounts put the figure closer to 1.5 billion pesos, or roughly US$980,000 at the same rate.

One report describes the scheme as running since 2022. If accurate, that would mean the alleged fraud continued undetected, or unreported, for several years before this month’s complaint.

Neither figure, 1.5 billion or 1.6 billion pesos, has been confirmed by a court ruling. Both are drawn from early reporting on the complaint rather than an official Navy tally.

Where The Case Goes Now

The complaint has been assigned to Federal Court No. 2. That court sits within the Comodoro Py complex in Buenos Aires, home to Argentina’s highest-profile corruption cases.

The Navy says an internal administrative investigation is also underway, separate from the criminal case. Officials have described a policy of “zero tolerance” for the conduct described in the complaint.

A judge must now decide whether to open a formal criminal investigation. That step would allow prosecutors to subpoena records and question personnel under oath.

No individual has been publicly charged in connection with the case as of this writing. Any prosecution would likely take months to move from a criminal complaint to formal charges.

Argentine federal cases of this size often take years to reach trial. The Comodoro Py courts are already handling a heavy docket of corruption and financial-crime cases.

Not The Only Defense Scandal This Year

The payroll case lands amid a string of other controversies touching Argentina’s defense establishment in 2026. A state workers’ union has separately accused Defense Minister Luis Petri of misusing funds tied to a defense research institute.

That case involves a private company that rented parking space at a military research facility during a music festival. The union alleges the promised research funding from that arrangement never materialized.

Hundreds of vehicles reportedly parked overnight at the site for several days, generating tens of millions of pesos for the operator. The union says only a fraction of that money was ever meant for the institute’s own research budget.

A separate investigation is also examining a multibillion-peso loan the armed forces’ social security institute made under scrutiny from prosecutors. Taken together, the cases point to a defense sector facing unusually heavy financial scrutiny this year.

Even the Air Force has faced its own procurement controversy in 2026. A Clarín investigation earlier this year found the Air Force paid roughly double the market price for a used aircraft.

None of those earlier cases is directly linked to this month’s Navy complaint. Together, though, they have put Defense Minister Luis Petri’s ministry under sustained pressure for most of the year.

What It Means

For the Navy, the timing is awkward. The institution is already managing tight budgets and personnel reductions across Argentina’s armed forces.

A retired admiral warned in August that low salaries were already pushing experienced officers toward early retirement. A payroll fraud case inside the office that processes those same salaries only sharpens that complaint.

A payroll fraud case adds pressure even when the Navy itself reported it. The institution still has to show it can manage its own resources responsibly.

How prosecutors and military authorities handle the case matters beyond the Navy. It could shape public trust in the broader defense budget for months to come.

World.title: Brazil Polls Show Tight Governor Races in Pará and Alagoas
World.content:

Get the brief

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

Key Facts —

What happened New polls this month show tight governor races in both Pará and Alagoas.

—

Pará Real Time has Hana Ghassan at 37 percent and Dr. Daniel at 35 percent, a technical tie.

—

Alagoas, poll one AtlasIntel puts JHC ahead of Renan Filho, 49.3 percent to 46.4 percent.

—

Alagoas, poll two Days later, Real Time flips the order: Renan Filho 46 percent, JHC 43 percent.

—

Approval Alagoas Governor Paulo Dantas, who backs Renan Filho, holds 61 percent approval.

—

The catch Both Alagoas polls sit inside their own margins of error, so neither race is settled.

Pará Governor Helder Barbalho, whose administration looms over the state’s tight 2026 governor’s race (Photo, internet reproduction).

RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. Two States, Two Close Races

Brazil’s state elections run alongside the October 4 presidential vote. New polling this month shows just how unsettled two of those state races remain.

Pollsters surveyed voters in Pará and Alagoas in the first two weeks of September. Both states now show contests too close to call outright.

Neither race has an incumbent seeking re-election. Pará’s Helder Barbalho is term-limited after two consecutive terms.

Alagoas’s Paulo Dantas, by contrast, chose not to run. He has said publicly he will seek no office at all in 2026.

Pará: A Technical Tie At The Top

Real Time Big Data surveyed 1,600 Pará voters from September 3 to 7. It found Hana Ghassan of the MDB at 37 percent and Podemos candidate Daniel at 35 percent.

With a margin of error of 2 points, the race sits within reach for either candidate. Araceli of the PSol trailed with 5 percent, while 8 percent said they would cast a blank or null vote.

Another 14 percent of respondents declined to answer at all. That undecided share is large enough on its own to swing the outcome once the campaign enters its final weeks.

In a simulated runoff, Real Time put Ghassan ahead of Daniel, 40 percent to 36 percent. That gap is still inside the poll’s own margin of error.

A Second Pollster Agrees It’s Close

An earlier Quaest poll, conducted August 25 to 28, told a similar story. It had Daniel at 28 percent and Ghassan at 27 percent, also a statistical tie.

Quaest’s simulated runoff showed the two candidates dead even, at 36 percent apiece. Different pollsters, different topline numbers, but the same basic picture: Pará’s governor race is up for grabs.

The same Quaest survey found Pará’s Senate race far more settled. Term-limited Governor Helder Barbalho is running for Senate instead, and he led with 23 percent.

Delegado Éder Mauro followed at 14 percent, with Zequinha Marinho at 11 percent. No other Senate candidate cracked double digits in that same poll.

Alagoas: Two Polls, Two Frontrunners

Alagoas offers a messier picture. AtlasIntel surveyed 1,208 voters from September 4 to 9.

It found JHC of the PSDB leading Renan Filho of the MDB. The margin was 49.3 percent against 46.4 percent.

In AtlasIntel’s runoff simulation, JHC extended that edge slightly, to 49.9 percent against 46.7 percent. With a 3-point margin of error, the race was effectively tied either way.

Then, days later, a different pollster flipped the script. Real Time Big Data surveyed 1,600 Alagoas voters from September 10 to 14.

That poll found Renan Filho ahead instead, 46 percent to 43 percent for JHC. The lead changed hands depending on which firm was asking.

Why The Two Polls Disagree

Pollsters use different turnout models and question wording, which can shift results by several points. Both firms’ Alagoas numbers technically fall within striking distance of each other once margins of error are applied.

What is not in dispute is Governor Paulo Dantas’s own standing. Real Time found his approval rating at 61 percent, against 35 percent disapproval and 4 percent with no opinion.

A more detailed breakdown found 40 percent rating his government as excellent or good. Another 29 percent called it average, and 30 percent rated it negatively.

The two questions measure slightly different things: general approval versus a graded performance review. Together, they still point to a governor most Alagoas voters view favorably.

The Dantas Factor

Dantas is not on the ballot himself, but he is far from a bystander. He is actively campaigning for Renan Filho, his political ally, according to the Real Time report.

A popular incumbent’s endorsement can matter more in a tight race than in a lopsided one. If Alagoas stays this close through October, Dantas’s 61 percent approval rating could end up being the deciding factor.

JHC, for his part, is running as the change candidate against an administration voters largely still like. That is a harder pitch to make when approval numbers are this high.

What Comes Next

Both states vote for governor on the same day as Brazil’s presidential first round, October 4. A runoff, if needed, would follow later that month.

With multiple pollsters now active in both states, expect the numbers to keep moving. Neither Pará nor Alagoas looks like a race anyone can call with confidence yet.

Both contests will also be shaped by whatever happens at the top of the ticket. A strong national showing for either major coalition could pull undecided state voters along with it.

Even so, governors’ races in Brazil rarely move in perfect lockstep with the presidential contest overhead. Local dynamics, and the size of each state’s undecided vote, will likely decide both outcomes.
