World.title: Saxophone Still Getting Louder For Jimmy Rojas: 3 years for boutique burglary; Still facing charges for breaking police cameras
World.content:
Saxophone Still Getting Louder For Jimmy Rojas: 3 years for boutique burglary; Still facing charges for breaking police cameras

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize City resident Jimmy Estuardo Rojas has been sentenced to three years in prison after changing his plea to guilty for burglarizing a Mahogany Street boutique where police reportedly caught him inside with bags packed with merchandise.

Rojas appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, September 15, where he changed his original not-guilty plea and admitted to burglarizing Jay’z Pick & Wear Boutique at the corner of Mahogany and Jasmine streets.

The Magistrate sentenced Rojas to three years imprisonment, effective Tuesday.

The burglary occurred in the early morning hours of September 22, 2025. Police responding to a report of a burglary in progress arrived at the business and, with the owner present, entered the building believing the intruder was still inside.

According to the facts of the case, officers found Rojas inside the boutique along with several bags containing items taken from the business.

Investigators later determined that entry had allegedly been gained by damaging wooden boards at the rear of the building.

Rojas initially pleaded not guilty after being charged, but reversed that plea nearly a year later. The conviction is his first for burglary, although he has had previous encounters with the criminal justice system.

He still has another burglary charge pending in connection with the March 2026 break-in at the security booth of Saint Luke Methodist Primary School. Police alleged surveillance footage captured Rojas during that incident. He pleaded not guilty and was denied bail.

Rojas is also before the court on damage-to-property charges after police alleged that surveillance cameras and related equipment valued at almost $49,000 were damaged at two locations in the Saint Martin de Porres area in August. He has pleaded not guilty to those allegations.

Those matters remain pending before the court and are separate from Tuesday’s burglary conviction.

World.title: Mexican businessman fined for illegal entry into Belize; US$10,500 undeclared cash now under scrutiny
World.content:
Mexican businessman fined for illegal entry into Belize; US$10,500 undeclared cash now under scrutiny

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Mexican businessman who pleaded guilty to an immigration offence on Tuesday remains in police custody after authorities discovered he was carrying US$10,500 in cash which he allegedly failed to declare upon entering Belize.

Rafael Moran Gama, 40, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to failing to present a visitor’s permit on demand to an Immigration Officer.

Gama was fined $1,000 plus $5 cost of court, payable forthwith, in default six months imprisonment. When informed of the default sentence, Gama reportedly expressed concern about being sent to prison.

His problems, however, did not end with the immigration charge.

According to Immigration personnel present at court, police have custody of US$10,500 found among Gama’s belongings and he is expected to be interviewed by personnel from the Belize Tax Service Department regarding the money and why it was not declared when he entered the country.

At the Central Bank’s fixed buying rate of US$1 to BZ$2, the cash amounts to approximately BZ$21,000. Official Financial Intelligence Unit guidance states that Belize increased its traveller cash-declaration threshold in 2016 from BZ$10,000 to BZ$20,000, with declarations to be made to Customs officers when entering or leaving the country.

That means Gama was carrying approximately BZ$1,000 above the declaration threshold. Carrying more than BZ$20,000 is not itself prohibited, but the amount must be declared to Customs. The FIU has identified failure to declare funds at or above the threshold as an offence under Belize’s customs framework.

Gama told the Chief Magistrate that he travelled by taxi from Mexico to the Corozal Free Zone, where he later accepted a ride from a taxi bearing Belizean licence plates into Belize City.

He claimed that when they reached the Belize side of the border he was sleepy and handed his passport to the taxi driver, but could not say whether the driver ever presented it to Immigration authorities.

Gama was later encountered during a police operation in Belize City at around 8:00 a.m. and detained. During the processing of his belongings, authorities recorded the US$10,500 in his possession.

He was escorted back to the Queen Street Police Station following his arraignment pending the financial interview.

Gama told the court the seized cash is all the money he currently has available and that he needs access to it to pay his $1,005 court fine.

Once the immigration fine and the outstanding matter concerning the cash are resolved, authorities are expected to arrange for Gama to be returned to Mexico.

No charge relating to the US$10,500 had been announced as of Tuesday afternoon.

World.title: Extortion case against Immigration Officer Monique Escalante discontinued after High Court rejects hearsay evidence
World.content:
Extortion case against Immigration Officer Monique Escalante discontinued after High Court rejects hearsay evidence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The extortion case against interdicted Immigration Officer Monique Meisha Escalante has been discontinued after the prosecution was unable to secure the testimony of the Jamaican national who accused her of taking US$3,000 at the Philip Goldson International Airport.

Escalante, 34, appeared before High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Tuesday, where the Director of Public Prosecutions’ Office entered a nolle prosequi after the court refused to admit a statement from virtual complainant Jahnoi Shaun-Dhee Richards as hearsay evidence.

The matter had been proceeding through a voir dire—a hearing to determine the admissibility of evidence—because Richards could not be located to testify.

The Crown called four witnesses in an attempt to establish the circumstances surrounding Richards’ statement and his absence from Belize. Prosecutors told the court that repeated telephone calls to Richards went unanswered, an email received no response, and attempts to contact him through social media were also unsuccessful.

At the close of the Crown’s evidence, Escalante’s attorney, Leslie Hamilton, made a no-case submission, arguing that prosecutors had failed to establish the legal basis necessary to admit Richards’ statement in his absence. Justice Pilgrim upheld the defence submission and declined to admit the statement.

With its principal witness unavailable and his statement excluded, the Crown entered the nolle prosequi, discontinuing the prosecution. Escalante was subsequently discharged from the extortion charge. The outcome is not an acquittal, however, and the prosecution could potentially bring the matter again if Richards becomes available and the necessary evidence can be presented.

Escalante was originally charged in March 2024 after Richards, then 27, alleged that while entering Belize through the PGIA on March 15, 2024, he was instructed to place money inside his passport and eventually handed over US$3,000. Public reporting at the time stated that airport surveillance footage was reviewed during the investigation and that several other immigration officers were detained and questioned before being released.

Escalante pleaded not guilty after being arraigned and was granted $8,000 bail with conditions, including surrendering her travel documents, reporting weekly to police and having no contact with Richards.

Richards reportedly left Belize following his stay, and despite efforts by prosecutors to locate him, he did not appear to give evidence in the High Court proceedings.

Escalante left court Tuesday with documentation confirming that the prosecution had been discontinued, bringing the case against her to an end for now.

World.title: Briceño says Guatemala billboards are tourism ads, not political messaging
World.content:
Briceño says Guatemala billboards are tourism ads, not political messaging

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Prime Minister John Briceño says the controversial Guatemala billboards appearing across Belize City should be viewed as tourism promotion, even though he acknowledged that their wording may be “a bit misleading.”

The Prime Minister was responding to growing public criticism of the s, which feature Guatemalan scenery alongside the message encouraging people to visit and return.

Briceño said his understanding is that the billboards are part of a standard campaign promoting Guatemala as a travel destination.

His comments come after Opposition Leader Tracy Taegar Panton demanded that the billboards be removed immediately, describing them as a political provocation and an affront to Belize’s sovereignty and national identity.

The controversy has gained added attention because it comes only days after renewed tensions in the Sarstoon and as Belize marks its 45th anniversary of Independence.

Briceño, however, did not adopt that interpretation.

Instead, he sought to separate the s from the territorial dispute, saying that while the wording may raise questions, he understands the intention behind them to be tourism related.

The matter has also raised questions over the approval process for billboards within Belize City, where s generally require municipal approval.

For now, the Prime Minister’s position is clear: the message may not have been perfectly framed, but he does not view the campaign itself as a political challenge to Belize.

World.title: Laguna Rio offers lagoonfront living in San Pedro with residences from US$169,000
World.content:
Laguna Rio offers lagoonfront living in San Pedro with residences from US$169,000

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A new residential development on Ambergris Caye is offering buyers an opportunity to own a private lagoonfront residence while remaining just minutes from the heart of San Pedro Town.

Laguna Rio, a Blue Ocean Belize development, features waterfront residences designed around open spaces, natural light, coastal materials and outdoor living. Resale prices currently start at US$169,000.

The residential community sits on the lagoon side of Ambergris Caye and combines access to the water with proximity to some of San Pedro’s most important services and attractions.

According to the development information, the Boca del Rio Bridge is approximately three minutes away, Central Park is five minutes away, Ambergris Hope Hospital is seven minutes away, John Greif II Airport is eight minutes away and the San Pedro International Ferry Terminal is approximately 10 minutes away.

One available configuration, Studio A, offers approximately 646 square feet, with one bedroom, one bathroom, a full sized kitchen, living area, laundry closet and verandah.

Laguna Rio is designed for both full time island living and buyers looking for a second home or real estate investment in Belize.

Another major feature is direct seller financing through Blue Ocean Belize.

Financing options include plans starting with 30 percent down, while other structures offer lower fixed interest rates or longer repayment periods. Final terms and availability are subject to confirmation by Blue Ocean Belize.

Interested buyers can contact Blue Ocean Belize at +501 636 5752, toll free at +1 800 928 6890, or email [email protected].

World.title: Man who likes to play with guns and little girls given no jail-time once again as psychiatrists insist he has ‘the mind of an 8-year-old’
World.content:
Man who likes to play with guns and little girls given no jail-time once again as psychiatrists insist he has ‘the mind of an 8-year-old’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-two-year-old Mark Stephen Godoy Jr. has avoided an immediate prison sentence after pleading guilty to two counts of unlawful sexual intercourse with a 14-year-old girl, with High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim instead imposing three years’ probation after considering Godoy’s significant intellectual disability.

Godoy admitted to having sexual intercourse with the girl on two occasions in March 2024, when he was 20 years old and she was 14.

Justice Pilgrim initially assessed the offences at a five-year starting point under the sentencing guidelines, finding the harm to the victim to be high and noting significant psychological effects. The provisional sentence was later reduced after the court considered the absence of violence, coercion or grooming, as well as Godoy’s guilty pleas, lack of previous convictions, remorse, family support and intellectual impairment.

The court ultimately found special circumstances justifying a departure from an immediate custodial sentence and placed Godoy under the supervision of a Community Rehabilitation Officer for three years. He must report as directed, comply with reasonable instructions and notify the supervising officer of any change of residence.

Public reporting on Monday’s ruling similarly said Justice Pilgrim considered imprisonment disproportionate in light of Godoy’s permanent intellectual limitations and warned that the probation order was not simply a “slap on the wrist.” A breach or new criminal offending could return him to the High Court for sentencing.

The case followed months of litigation over whether Godoy was legally competent to face the charges. Crown Counsel Kirk Brown, representing the Director of Public Prosecutions, fiercely contested the defence position and argued that although Godoy had intellectual limitations, he could understand the charges and participate in the proceedings with appropriate assistance.

Two psychiatric reports had identified intellectual impairments, with evidence before the court placing some aspects of Godoy’s functioning around the developmental level of an eight-year-old. The medical experts considered him unfit to stand trial, but Justice Pilgrim ruled in June that the legal test was different from the clinical assessment. He found that Godoy could understand the proceedings, make a plea, instruct counsel and give evidence if questions and concepts were simplified.

Godoy subsequently pleaded guilty to the two USI counts on July 29.

According to the facts, Godoy began communicating with the girl through Facebook Messenger and Instagram sometime after February 14, 2024. He allegedly told her he was 20 and she told him she was 14.

They later met on March 1 and again on March 5, 2024, and had sexual intercourse on both occasions.

The court’s decision comes months after a separate Magistrate’s Court matter in which firearm and ammunition charges against Godoy were struck out after he was also found incompetent to stand trial in that proceeding.

World.title: Father of newborn twins fined $105 after pleading guilty to possessing 0.2 grams of crack cocaine
World.content:
Father of newborn twins fined $105 after pleading guilty to possessing 0.2 grams of crack cocaine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 54-year-old security guard and father of recently born twins pleaded guilty Monday to possessing 0.2 grams of crack cocaine after police allegedly found the drug in his pocket during a stop and search.

George Clinton Sanchez of Zacaranda Street appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on one count of possession of a controlled drug.

Police say Sanchez was on Marigold Lane in the Saint Martin de Porres area at around 9:50 a.m. on Sunday, September 13, when officers stopped and searched him.

During the search, police allegedly found two small pieces of a white substance suspected to be crack cocaine inside Sanchez’s left pants pocket. The substance was later weighed at 0.2 grams.

Sanchez pleaded guilty and became emotional while addressing the court, explaining that he is the father of newborn twins and asking the Senior Magistrate for leniency.

As a first-time offender, he was fined $100 plus $5 cost of court, bringing his total penalty to $105.

World.title: One week after being charged for knife, Basil Willis remanded for allegedly trafficking crack
World.content:
One week after being charged for knife, Basil Willis remanded for allegedly trafficking crack

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Less than a week after being fined for carrying a four-inch knife in public during prohibited hours, 58-year-old Basil Earl Willis is back before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court — this time accused of possessing crack cocaine with intent to supply.

Willis, a car washer of Black Orchid Street, was arraigned on three charges: possession of 5.4 grams of crack cocaine with intent to supply, possession of 20 grams of marijuana, and resisting lawful arrest.

The charges reportedly stem from a police operation on Marigold Lane on Sunday, September 13.

Willis pleaded not guilty to all three counts.

The prosecution objected to bail, citing the seriousness of the drug-trafficking allegation, Willis’ criminal history and the prevalence of illegal drugs in the community.

Willis told the court he was not a flight risk and promised to attend every court date.

Despite the objection, the Senior Magistrate granted him bail of $2,000 plus one surety in the same amount. His bail is subject to a condition that he not be arrested and charged with another offence while the case is pending.

Willis is due back in court on October 28.

The new allegations come only days after Willis pleaded guilty to possession of an article with a blade. Police said he was riding a bicycle along Mahogany Street at about 4:50 a.m. on September 4 when officers found a four-inch knife tucked into his waistband.

During that case, Willis reportedly told police, “I always have my knife on me because yuh neva know.” He was fined $150 plus $5 cost of court and given until October 30 to pay.

Willis has pleaded not guilty to the latest charges, and the allegations against him have not yet been proven in court.

World.title: Family services shake-up
World.content:
The Ministry of Education has severed ties with the heads of two of its primary family services agencies — the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) and the National Parenting Support Commission (NPSC) — reportedly to undertake a major shift in their operations, the Jamaica Observer has learnt.

As part of that shake-up, chief executive officer of the CPFSA Laurette Adams-Thomas, who took the helm of the agency in October 2023, will demit office next month.

In a brief response to the Observer, Adams-Thomas said her contract expires on October 1, 2026 and she was “officially notified on July 23, 2026” that it would “not be renewed”.

The CPFSA is an executive agency which was formed from the merger of the Child Development Agency (CDA) and the Office of Children’s Registry (OCR). Adams-Thomas, an educator and social worker, took over its leadership following an eight-year stint as general manager of the largest infirmary in the Caribbean — Jamaica’s Golden Age Home — where she had oversight responsibly for protection and welfare services for more than 450 indigent people from the parishes of Kingston and St Andrew. Prior to assuming that position, she was interim executive director/registrar at the OCR, where her focus was centred on ensuring that an effective system was maintained to facilitate the confidential receipt, assessment, and referral of reports of known or suspected cases of child abuse.

She holds a master’s degree in business administration, bachelor of science in human resource management, and a number of certifications in leadership, corporate governance and strategic planning.

In the meantime, the Observer was reliably informed on Monday that NPSC CEO Kaysia Kerr “is no longer with” the entity. Efforts to get an official response from Kerr were unsuccessful. A pre-recorded message on her personal mobile phone directed all callers with queries related to the commission to contact the education ministry or the commission itself.

A source with knowledge of the development said the ministry had decided to disengage with Kerr due to a breakdown in relations.

She took the helm of the commission in 2017, succeeding Dr Patrece Charles. In an interview with the

Observer at the time, Kerr said she hoped to craft and design programmes for parents and children of all 13 categories of disabilities, move the organisation out of eastern Jamaica to serve other parishes, take some of the programmes internationally, and get the unit to a stage where it generates income.

The former NPSC head has a solid background in education and has completed studies in business and professional management at Nova Southeastern University, along with a first degree in special education and a master’s in administration and supervision from Western Carolina University.

The commission coordinates a wide range of services for parents and also delivers programmes that build parenting skills and promote parental involvement in education.

The Government of Jamaica mandated the establishment of the NPSC in response to the 2004 task force report on the status of education in Jamaica.

The NPSC began operating in January 2013.

World.title: Global aviation squeeze
World.content:
Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose says Jamaica needs more airline seats to meet strong demand as carriers face aircraft shortages and higher fuel costs amid the impact of the war in the Middle East.

Addressing the media during the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) forum in Ocho Rios on Tuesday, Rose said Jamaica’s immediate challenge is not a lack of demand, but having enough airline seats to bring visitors to the island.

“The immediate thing that we do need is more seats into the destination. The good news is, and I really want this to land, the good news is the airlines know this. The airlines are preparing because they don’t want to leave business on the table. The airlines know that the demand is there. The airlines are preparing to put in additional flights,” he said.

His comments come as Jamaica’s tourism industry continues its recovery following last year’s Hurricane Melissa, with hotel capacity gradually returning and airlines looking to adjust their schedules accordingly.

Rose said the global aviation industry is itself under pressure, making it difficult for airlines to simply add capacity whenever demand rises. He pointed to higher fuel costs linked to developments in the Middle East, as well as problems affecting aircraft engines, servicing and maintenance.

“As you all know, there are global pressures now on the aviation space. What’s happening out there in the Middle East has really impacted oil prices, which impacts fuel prices. In the best of days, the margins are exceedingly thin for airlines. You’re going to add this increase in jet fuel, it puts additional pressure on the industry,” he explained.

“Along with that, there is a shortage of aircraft because of issues to do with the engines, which I won’t really bore you all with. There are some service and maintenance things that are going on, which means a lot of aircraft have been pulled out of service,” he added.

The result, he said, is that Jamaica cannot depend on unlimited airline capacity, even as demand remains strong

“Airlines across the world don’t have infinite aircraft. That means that seats are not infinite. When the seats are full, the seats are full. Because of the demand that we have been generating for Jamaica, the vast majority of the flights into Jamaica are full,” he added.

Still, Rose said the outlook for airlift is positive, with airlines preparing to increase service as more hotel rooms become available.

He said airlines are also preparing to return to the flight schedules that existed before Hurricane Melissa, although they first have to resolve their own aircraft availability issues and factor in Jamaica’s accommodation capacity.

World.title: KINGSTON BOOKSHOP’S $1-B EXPANSION
World.content:
Kingston Bookshop’s new distribution centre on Lyndhurst Road in St Andrew.

Kingston Bookshop has pumped approximately $1 billion into a new distribution centre on Lyndhurst Road in St Andrew as its wholesale business takes a larger share of sales.

The company told the Jamaica Observer that business-to-business (B2B) sales now account for approximately 25 per cent of revenue, up from just under 20 per cent about four years ago as it widens the range of products supplied to schools, bookstores, pharmacies, offices, and other businesses across Jamaica.

That growth had begun to stretch an operation that was still being run from three separate warehouse properties on King Street in downtown Kingston.

The new Lyndhurst Road facility, which became operational in May 2025, brings warehousing, purchasing, and business-to-business sales together in one location and gives Kingston Bookshop significantly more room to handle stock.

Director of Strategy and Innovation Shauna Fuller Clarke said the company had reached the point where its old warehouse arrangement no longer matched the scale of the wholesale business.

“As that side of the business grew, so did our warehousing and operational requirements. At one point we were operating from three separate warehouse locations, so the decision to develop the Lyndhurst Road facility was a strategic one,” Fuller Clarke told the Business Observer.

“It allowed us to consolidate our warehousing, B2B sales, and purchasing operations in one location, creating a more efficient operation and, importantly, enabling us to provide better service to our customers.”

The approximately 42,000-square-foot facility includes a 39,000-square-foot warehouse and another 3,000 square feet for the company’s B2B sales and purchasing teams.

Kingston Bookshop previously operated with about 34,000 square feet of warehouse space across 72, 74, and 80 King Street.

The gain at Lyndhurst Road, however, is larger than the difference in floor space suggests.

Fuller Clarke said the height of the building and the racking system allow the company to make far greater use of vertical storage, taking usable capacity to the equivalent of approximately 50,000 square feet.

“The investment was, therefore, about much more than simply adding square footage. It was about creating the infrastructure to operate more efficiently, improve inventory management, and better support our retail and B2B customers,” she said.

The expansion comes more than three decades after Kingston Bookshop first moved into wholesale distribution. The company said that business began with stationery in the 1990s and later expanded into textbooks, general books, games, and technology products. It has recently added sports gear and equipment, particularly for schools.

That widening product range has helped Kingston Bookshop deepen its relationship with existing wholesale customers rather than relying only on traditional book sales.

“As our customers seek to diversify their own product offerings, we have been able to respond by supplying more of what they need rather than limiting our B2B operation to traditional books and stationery,” Fuller Clarke said.

The company now supplies customers in all parishes through its own delivery fleet.

New plan for former warehouses

The move to Lyndhurst Road is also changing how Kingston Bookshop uses its downtown real estate.

The company has already vacated 72 King Street, which was leased, while an expansion of its retail footprint at the 74 King Street head office is under active consideration.

That leaves the other warehouse property, at 80 King Street — one of its busiest retail stores — as the likely candidate for a mix of Kingston Bookshop operations and commercial rental space similar to what the company has adopted in Portmore, St Catherine, with the Script Cafe. The location is particularly significant given its position along one of downtown Kingston’s main retail corridors, where a large volume of shopping activity is concentrated.

“One option under active consideration is expanding our retail footprint at 74 King Street, while another property may incorporate a mix of Kingston Bookshop operations and commercial rental space, similar to the mixed-use approach we have successfully adopted at our 31 East Plaza location in Portmore,” she said.

The possible expansion downtown comes after Kingston Bookshop closed its Boulevard location earlier this year, but Fuller Clarke said that decision should not be read as a pullback from physical retail.

She told the Business Observer that stores remain Kingston Bookshop’s largest sales channel, even as wholesale contributes more and online purchasing continues to grow.

“The two decisions should not be viewed as Kingston Bookshop moving away from physical retail. They reflect our ongoing assessment of how and where we deploy our resources across the business,” she said.

“Our physical stores remain our largest sales channel, while B2B now represents approximately 25 per cent of sales and continues to grow. We are also steadily seeing increased purchasing through our e-commerce platform.”

Kingston Bookshop is continuing to invest across those three areas, but Fuller Clarke said expansion will be driven by where the company sees a commercial case rather than simply adding more locations.

“Our focus is not expansion simply for the sake of adding locations. We are looking at how we can strengthen the business across our retail, B2B, and digital channels while improving the customer experience and the efficiency of our operations,” she said.

That investment is being made at a time when one of Kingston Bookshop’s most important retail periods has produced little growth.

Fuller Clarke disclosed that revenue from the company’s stores during the 2026 back-to-school period was broadly similar to 2025 and, after accounting for inflation, the company considers sales relatively flat year on year.

The company continues to see strong demand for early childhood and primary-level material, including supplementary resources for Primary Exit Profile preparation, but purchasing at the secondary level has become more selective.

Parents have access to the Government’s textbook rental programme, second-hand books, online resources, and are increasingly deciding which items must be bought immediately and which can wait.

“Given the cost of preparing children for school, particularly for households with more than one child, parents are understandably making very deliberate choices about what they purchase,” Fuller Clarke said.

According to the company, workbooks and other books considered essential tend to be purchased first, while stationery and other supplies are sometimes bought later.

The company is also reporting a rise in parents choosing to pay for purchases in instalments.

“We have also seen more parents taking advantage of our lay-away programme, which allows them to make a deposit and pay towards their purchases over time,” Fuller Clarke said. “That provides families with another way of managing the cost of back-to-school preparation without having to meet the entire expense at once.”

The investment at Lyndhurst Road also leaves Kingston Bookshop with additional capacity that could eventually support more business outside Jamaica as well.

The company has previously supplied special orders to customers in smaller Caribbean islands, although Jamaica remains its main wholesale market.

Fuller Clarke reasoned that while the new facility puts Kingston Bookshop in a better position to pursue opportunities elsewhere in the region, the cost of distribution will determine how aggressively it moves.

“The cost of moving stock across the Caribbean can be significant, so both demand and logistics are important considerations in determining where and how we expand. We, therefore, see the Caribbean as an area of opportunity, but one where expansion has to be driven by sustainable demand and commercially viable distribution arrangements,” she said.

World.title: Visual Vibe takes screens off-grid with solar partnership
World.content:
A Visual Vibe outdoor screen at Mandela Park in Half-Way-Tree, St Andrew.

Digital advertising company Visual Vibe Limited is moving to take its entire network of outdoor screens off the national grid as it seeks to halve energy costs and eliminate outage-related downtime.

Following a recent partnership with Florida-based renewables firm Rush Hour Engineering, the Kintyre Holdings (JA) Limited subsidiary is getting ready to install solar power across its network of outdoor advertising screens.

Kintyre Holdings founder, chairman, and CEO, Tyrone Wilson, who also heads Visual Vibe, said the plan is to have every screen in the network — existing and new — powered by solar energy.

Visual Vibe currently operates 14 outdoor digital signs, for which energy costs now averages about $24 million annually, but the company will be adding another 15 screens shortly, which Wilson said could push annual electricity costs to as much as $60 million as the network expands.

The solar roll-out is, however, expected to reduce those costs by at least 50 per cent, bringing yearly energy expenditure to about $30 million.

“Electricity cost has long been one of the digital advertising business’s largest single monthly expenses, and with the war pushing up gas prices, we don’t see that easing anytime soon. So we had no other choice than to tap into solar,” Wilson told the Jamaica Observer.

“If we can cut our electricity bill by about 50 to 60 per cent, that would lift Visual Vibe’s profits enough so that we can keep funding growth from our own cash flow instead of seeking outside investment,” he further said to the Business Observer.

Stressing the need to have more efficient systems, Wilson said the new partnership also allows Visual Vibe to offer greater reliability to its clients during periods of disruption.

“Reliability is the currency of advertising. When a brand invests in our network, their campaign must be on screen every single time — and rising energy costs and grid outages have been a real challenge for our entire industry, and so this partnership with Rush Hour Engineering aims to solve those issues permanently “ Wilson said.

“By taking our screens off-grid, we are eliminating downtime completely while protecting our advertisers’ investment, as we also build the kind of resilient, sustainable media infrastructure that Jamaica deserves. It is a multimillion-dollar commitment to our clients and to the environment,” he added.

The solar programme forms a part of broader upgrades and expansion of Visual Vibe’s network and coincides with the company’s latest quest to deploy its newest high-resolution screens to flagship sites and premium locations along some of the city’s busiest corridor.

Phase one of the solar installation is scheduled to begin this week in the new Kingston area before being rolled out across the wider network.

Visual Vibe was acquired by Kintyre (trading then as iCreate) about three years ago for more than $500 million. Since then, the company has continued to expand its digital advertising operations, which now account for a substantial portion of group revenue.

In addition to its outdoor signs, Visual Vibe operates more than 50 indoor screens. Through a multichannel model combining outdoor billboards, indoor screens, and mobile formats, the company seeks to give advertisers multiple ways of reaching their target audiences.

Rush Hour Engineering President and CEO Edwin Xiao, commenting on the partnership, said the project demonstrates the potential for renewable energy to transform commercial infrastructure.

“We are proud to partner with Visual Vibe on a project of this scale,” Xiao said.

“Powering Jamaica’s largest digital advertising network entirely with solar energy demonstrates what renewable technology can do for the country’s commercial infrastructure. This partnership sets a new standard for how media assets are powered across the region.”

Rush Hour Engineering is a provider of engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) services for residential and commercial projects. In addition to solar systems, its capabilities include electric vehicle chargers; LED lighting; and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) design.

The Florida-based company, as a Tesla-certified partner, also provides energy-efficiency and renewable-energy solutions aimed at reducing electricity costs and carbon emissions.

As Kintyre doubles down on opportunities arising from the shift towards renewable energy, the Jamaica Stock Exchange-listed holding company earlier this year announced, through a separate partnership with Rush Hour Engineering, plans to strategically enter the EV market as it also positions to capitalise on developments in the transport sector.

“Renewable energy is the future, and we’re investing in it. It has been on our radar for a very long time, but we are now actively tapping into its potential,” Wilson said.

World.title: Raheem Sterling pleads guilty to dangerous driving after Lamborghini crash
World.content:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - AUGUST 02: Raheem Sterling #17 of Chelsea FC looks on during the pre-season friendly match Borussia Dortmund at Soldier Field on August 2, 2023 in Chicago, Illinois. Justin Casterline/Getty Images/AFPJustin Casterline / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP

LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP) — Footballer Raheem Sterling pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving after he crashed his Lamborghini on a motorway in May.

The 31-year-old also admitted possession of six nitrous oxide canisters for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen for analysis when he appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court, about 50 miles southwest of London.

Sterling, who attended court wearing a black suit jacket, black trousers, black shoes and a dark top, was arrested after crashing on the M3 on the morning of May 28.

Police said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.

READ: Raheem Sterling arrested for suspected drug-driving

The winger won 82 England caps, the last of which came at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

Sterling made his senior debut at Liverpool before joining Manchester City in 2015, winning four Premier League titles and other silverware at the Etihad.

He left for Chelsea in 2022 but subsequently fell out of favour and spent the 2024/25 season on loan at Arsenal.

Sterling joined Feyenoord on a short-term deal in February, playing eight times in the Eredivisie.

World.title: JAMAICA gets Disney boost
World.content:
Disney Cruine Line’s Disney Destiny will make its inaugural call on Jamaica next month.

OCHO RIOS, St Ann — Jamaica’s tourism industry is set to receive a big boost on October 13 when one of Disney Cruise Line’s top modern vessels, Disney Destiny, makes its inaugural call at Falmouth’s historic cruise port bringing just under 2,800 passengers to the island.

The announcement was made by Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose during Monday’s opening of the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) at Moon Palace Jamaica in Ocho Rios.

The arrival of Disney Destiny adds to the growing roster of Disney Cruise Line vessels calling on Jamaica, alongside ships operated by Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Princess Cruises, and Virgin Voyages.

From January to July this year, according to data shared by Rose, Jamaica recorded 234 cruise calls and 736,372 passengers. Montego Bay, Falmouth and Ocho Rios accounted for most visits, while four ships also called at Port Antonio and Kingston.

Rose pointed out that the cruise industry remains an important partner, particularly in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa — which hit sections of Jamaica last October — and reminded that it could provide a pathway to attracting visitors for longer stays.

“It’s often said you can come down, get a little taste of Jamaica on the cruise ship, then we can convert them, or they go back home and say that was too much of a teaser, and they come back,” he said.

The JTB official said cruise visitors are encouraged to venture beyond established resort centres, particularly towards Kingston and Port Antonio, to experience a wider range of the Jamaican product.

Reacting to news of Disney Destiny’s impending visit, Chukka Caribbean Adventures deputy executive chairman and Jamaica Tourist Board member John Byles pointed to the benefit it will bring to local artisans and attractions. According to Byles, Disney passengers tend to leave the ship and spend on Jamaican tourism experiences.

He welcomed the impending Disney Destiny call, describing it as a sign of the company’s growing trust in Jamaica.

“It is always very heartening to see the confidence that a brand like Disney continues to show for the Jamaica product and Jamaica destination,” Byles told buyers and suppliers attending the first day of JAPEX, a staple on the tourism calendar.

The trade show is being held under the theme ’Jamaica Reimagined’. Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) President O’Brian Heron used his address to stress that Jamaica’s recovery from Hurricane Melissa must lead to a stronger and more adaptable tourism industry.

“Resilience is not simply about recovering, It is truly about what comes next,” he said.

He noted that changing travellers, technology and artificial intelligence were reshaping how people discover and experience destinations, requiring Jamaica to embrace innovation without sacrificing its authenticity.

The JHTA head said Jamaica’s strongest differentiator remains its people, pointing to the warmth of the welcome, culture, creativity, music, spirit, and food.

Officially declaring the trade show open during an address delivered virtually, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett stressed the importance of adapting to shifts in the global tourism marketplace, strengthening competitiveness and building resilience while safeguarding the characteristics that make Jamaica distinctive.

“An event like JAPEX is never just a trade show. Last year, JAPEX facilitated an estimated US$100 million in contracts and business negotiations. Behind that figure are real hotels, real workers, real families, and real communities. That is precisely why, in fact, we do this,” Bartlett said.

World.title: Veteran journalist Balford Henry passes
World.content:
HENRY... his quiet and composed demeanour belied his sharp wit, keen sense of discernment, hard work, and professional integrity that have been the hallmark of his more than four decades as a top print reporter

THE local media fraternity has lost one of its calmest and most easy-going veterans, Balford George Henry, who died on Monday after a brief illness.

He was 74.

Henry’s quiet and composed demeanour belied his sharp wit, keen sense of discernment, hard work, and professional integrity that have been the hallmark of his more than four decades as a top print reporter.

Henry served both national newspapers, The Gleaner and the Jamaica Observer, in several capacities. He also served as consulting editor at the Jamaica Information Service (JIS) and worked at

New York Daily News, WLIB Radio in New York as a correspondent.

Henry was also editor of Reggae Times in the 1990s and reporter for the Overseas Gleaner (North America Edition) in New York during the 90s.

In a 2011 interview with JIS the unflappable Henry said he simply loves to write, and responded to the call to the fourth Estate during the summer of 1971, while a sixth former at Wolmer’s Boys’ School in Kingston.

“At that time, The Gleaner advertised for trainee journalists. I was among scores of young people from across Jamaica who sat the initiative tests, coincidently held at Wolmer’s Boys’ School auditorium. Fortunately, I was among the handful of successful candidates,” he recalled.

At that time, The Gleaner was the only institutionalised daily newspaper in the country and, in the absence of a school of journalism in Jamaica and indeed, the wider region, the North Street facility prided itself as the nursery and training ground for print reporters.

“I was exposed to the veterans of the craft, people like Ken Allen, Calvin Bowen, LK Southerland, and Editor-in-Chief Theodore Sealy. Barbara Gloudon, in particular, discovered very early in my career that I enjoyed writing features, and encouraged and nurtured my efforts,” said Henry in the JIS interview.

He recalled that the training period was tough, with the late Fitzroy Nation “being the only other member of my group to survive that ordeal”.

Henry further honed his skills as a Commonwealth Press Union (CPU) Fellow, London, 1977; earned a journalism diploma as a Thomson Foundation scholar in Cardiff, Wales, 1977; and was one of 12 journalists from around the world chosen by the World Press Institute (WPI) for a fellowship at Macalester College, St Paul, Minnesota, in 1983.

Early in his career Henry reported on sittings of the then Kingston and St Andrew Corporation (KSAC), as well as major social and cultural activities and events.

Later, as a veteran labour relations reporter, he covered industrial relations issues including major strikes and disputes during the volatile 1970s.

The recipient of a number of professional awards, Henry had also been the winner of the Press Association of Jamaica (PAJ) Honorary Award for a series on the social and economic problems facing Jamaican youth in Britain’s inner cities, based on his own experience while living in that country in 1977.

He had also won the PAJ Best Story award for his coverage of the funeral of the late reggae icon Bob Marley in 1981; as well as the PAJ’s first Cultural Story Award for the feature entitled: ‘Fall of a Superstar’, on the rise and fall of Jamaican reggae singer Junior Byles.

In 2011 Henry was conferred with the Order of Distinction (Officer Class) for distinguished service to journalism.

Reacting to his passing, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness expressed sadness and said he remembers Henry as a committed journalist who understood the responsibility that comes with telling Jamaica’s story.

“His work reflected a deep knowledge of our politics, our people and the issues affecting our country,” Holness said in a post on Instagram.

“His passing is a loss to Jamaica’s media fraternity and to the many people who knew and worked with him over the years. I extend my heartfelt condolence to his family, friends, colleagues and the wider journalism community,” the prime minister said.

Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Minister Olivia Grange also expressed sadness at Henry’s passing, describing him as “a first-rate journalist” who was committed to his craft.

Grange said Henry was an “outstanding writer and questioner whose easy-going demeanour belied the penetrating nature of his questions”.

“I had great respect for Balford. He was always professional in his interactions and in his journalistic pursuits. He was sharp, he was keen, he could be tough, but he was always fair,” Grange said, and offered condolence to his family and colleagues.

Journalist Wilton Dyer, who was already at The Gleaner when a very young Henry arrived in 1971, remembers “a very quiet, contemplative man” who brought a “very dilligent, single-minded approach” to journalism.

“He was very efficient and driven,” Dyer said, recalling that Henry quickly developed a “mastery of labour relations and parliamentary reporting”.

Dyer also recalled that Henry was steeped in Jamaican music and also produced a record of his own called Bits of Paper.

By the mid-1970s Henry was among the leading Jamaican entertainment writers, said Dyer.

Fellow veteran journalist Garfield Myers remembered Henry as a workaholic.

“He was one of those who, when I went to The Gleaner in July 1973, had been there for a couple of years — very young man, a couple of years older than me — and he was one of those who showed me the way,” said Myers, a former Observer sports editor who still writes for the newspaper from St Elizabeth.

He said that Henry became very adept at labour relations and trade union coverage, which was a very important beat back in those days.

“Over time he graduated to Parliament and became one of the better parliamentary reporters, and mastered that beat. He was a very good reporter. Some journalists graduate to become editors but Balford was a reporter par excellence. Trying to make him into something else wouldn’t work,” Myers said.

Observer Executive Editor, Publications Vernon Davidson also commented on Henry’s mastery of parliamentary reporting, noting that he often returned from a long day of covering the legislature with stories missed by some of his colleagues.

“We could always depend on Balford to deliver, regardless of how long the sittings were, as he had an exceptional eye for detail and the type of patience required to cover Parliament,” said Davidson who also worked with Henry at The Gleaner in the early 1980s.

“Bally also provided excellent coverage of politics and would be our point reporter during the annual budget debates,” said Davidson who recalled that Henry joined the Observer in November 2003, left for JIS in 2009, and returned to the newspaper in 2012.

“He was a quiet fountain of knowledge and we are poorer for his passing. We extend our deepest condolence to his family, friends and colleagues,” Davidson said.

Henry is survived by his widow Claudia Stockhausen-Henry and was the father of two sons and two daughters.

World.title: Music in her bones
World.content:
Reggae songstress Sevana strikes a pose during an intimate gathering on Friday evening to celebrate her latest single, Jeans an’ Marina.Karl McLarty

If one were to choose a word to describe Sevana, multi-talented would certainly be in the running.

The Jamaican creative has spent years moving between worlds, so much so that when things appear quiet on one front, chances are something else is unfolding behind the scenes.

And if her recent absence from the musical spotlight left anyone wondering where she had been, Sevana has a simple explanation.

“When we’re quiet one place, we’re working in the next,” she said.

On Friday, the singer welcomed specially invited guests into an intimate, house party-style gathering at Cherry Drive Estates for the release of her newest single, Jeans an’ Marina.

The relaxed setting was fitting for a song inspired not by glamour or exclusivity, but by Sevana’s memories of community, simplicity, and the kind of Jamaican togetherness that requires little more than good company, music, and somewhere to gather.

It also marked Sevana’s re-emergence into a space she insists she never truly left.

“I was working on a lot of acting projects while you weren’t actively hearing from me on the entertainment scene, but I was still making a lot of music,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Sevana has been acting since 2017, but in recent years has deliberately positioned herself “a little deeper into that world”.

Her growing résumé includes an appearance in the Robert Nesta Marley biopic Bob Marley: One Love, while she is also featured in UK series Possession, now streaming on Sky TV, in which she plays an escaped revolutionary woman. She has also landed her first starring role in a feature film, Threads of Us, which she said is currently touring the United States.

“I have different projects that I’m pushing at the moment,” she explained.

But for all the creative lanes she has been exploring, there remains one that feels particularly like home.

“Music is my first love, and it is the thing that has continued to save me time and time again,” Sevana shared. “It’s not something I can let go. It’s in my bones, it’s in my blood and I love it. I will never stop.”

Her return, then, is perhaps less of a comeback and more of a refocusing. Sevana said she resisted the urge to release material simply for the sake of remaining visible, choosing instead to build a catalogue she genuinely believed in.

“Navigating the entertainment industry, it takes a lot out of you, especially if you’re trying to do multiple things at once,” she said. “I was really committed to putting together a body of work that I could be really proud of once I hit the ground running again.”

She wanted, she explained, to feel excitement about everything she eventually shared. “So I wasn’t in a rush to push any singles or anything until now.”

That patience has brought her to Jeans an’ Marina, a record whose roots stretch far beyond the studio and all the way back to Sevana’s childhood in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland.

The inspiration was partly sparked by what she witnessed following last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

Even amid the sombre mood that engulfed sections of the country, Sevana found herself reflecting on the way Jamaicans instinctively pulled together.

“That’s the vibe I was going for on this single. I wanted it to feel like a coming together,” she said.

But the feeling was familiar. Growing up in Savanna-la-Mar, Friday nights offered Sevana an early lesson in what community could look like when stripped of pretence.

“Every Friday night the community would gather in the square under the street light to just hang out,” she recalled. “We’d play dominoes, ludo, listen to music, buss a one beer and just relax.”

There was no dress code. No pressure to manufacture an image for the evening. Nobody needed an elaborate outfit or an exclusive invitation.

“It never felt like pressure to get all dolled up or anything like that. You could wear weh yuh have, and everybody had jeans and merina. You would put it on and just come out and have fun,” she said.

It is that uncomplicated sense of belonging that Sevana has attempted to bottle in the new single.

“The idea back then was for the community to come together and heal each other, and that’s what this song is about — being unified and arite,” she said.

The singer then went on to share that Jeans an’ Marina is not a standalone return to music. It is the opening note of what she hopes will be a sustained new chapter with her next single expected at the end of September. Sevana then plans to release new music every month heading into 2027, tracks that may eventually culminate in something much bigger.

World.title: Russian drone found off Poland’s coast carried explosive warhead, prosecutor says
World.content:
Investigators have not officially established where or when the drone was launched, where it entered the sea or what mission it was carrying out.

According to the Operational Command’s spokesperson, Lt Col Jacek Goryszewski, the most likely explanation is that the drone drifted from international waters to Poland's territorial waters.

The incident comes amid mounting tensions between Russia and European countries. On Tuesday, NATO jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, and a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish military helicopter.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Sunday that “the coming weeks and months will be a period of very intense Russian activity,” adding that “the escalation of the Russian Federation's actions is becoming a fact, and examples of this are getting closer and closer to our border.”

World.title: Hague court sentences Kosovo ex-president Thaçi to 25 years in prison for war crimes
World.content:
The charges of crimes against humanity were dropped, while Krasniqi was sentenced to 25 years, Selimi to 13 years and Veseli to 18 years for the other offenses.

According to the judgment, the court found that the prosecution had failed to prove the existence of widespread and systematic attacks against civilians, a key element for crimes against humanity.

Following the ruling, Thaçi’s brother Gani told the media that the family is convinced of his innocence and “we are waiting for the appeal.”

In a social media post, Krasniqi’s daughter Gresa called the ruling an “unjust, political, racist, and criminal” decision and claimed that many individuals responsible for war crimes against Kosovo Albanians remain free in Serbia today.



Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama called the ruling a “shame.” Meanwhile, scuffles broke out at The Hague between supporters assembled to hear the verdict and Dutch police.



Thaçi was indicted in November 2020 and resigned as president in the same month to face the proceedings. He has remained in detention in The Hague since then. “I expect to be acquitted of every charge,” Thaci said in a recent interview in August. The other defendants have all denied the charges against them.

Kosovo Albanians gather during a rally in Pristina on September 16, 2026 on the day of the war crimes verdict in the trial held in The Hague of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi. | Elvis Barukcic/AFP via Getty Images

Thaçi also faces a separate trial later this month over alleged witness intimidation.

The 1998-1999 Kosovo war took place between the KLA and Serbian forces, who carried out a systematic campaign of ethnic cleansing, displacing over 1 million Kosovo Albanians, killing about 11,000, and injuring many thousands more.

World.title: 12 takeaways from von der Leyen’s State of the Union
World.content:
1. Canada could become the EU’s first “associate member”

The biggest surprise came when von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member.”

Speaking directly to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was sitting in the Parliament hemicycle, von der Leyen proposed an ambitious, far-reaching new alliance spanning tech, defense, energy, critical minerals, AI, the Arctic and more.

In a message that could have been addressed directly to U.S. President Donald Trump, von der Leyen said: “This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength.”

While it remains to be seen whether EU member countries are on board with so-called associate membership — a model, it should be noted, that does not currently exist — the proposal is a striking signal of how badly Brussels wants to deepen ties with Ottawa.

2. Europe might finally get a security council

The idea of a European security executive body has been floated in various forms for years, but has taken on fresh urgency against the backdrop of Trump undermining the transatlantic security relationship and Russia’s war against Ukraine spilling over into the bloc.

Von der Leyen injected new life into the discussion by calling to create a European Security Council, saying it would bring together the EU and like-minded countries, including the United Kingdom, Canada, Ukraine and Norway (notably, there was no mention of the U.S.) to discuss and manage threats.

World.title: EU capitals caught off guard as von der Leyen announces ‘associate membership’ for Canada
World.content:
But the message wrong-footed national capitals, which were never asked to sign off on the idea before the speech, said three diplomats, granted anonymity to speak freely. Granting membership to the EU is a responsibility of the European Council, and no model for associate membership exists.

"Nobody really knows what it means," said one of the envoys, who has been involved in talks with the Commission about relations with Canada in recent days. "Member states have tried to manage expectations. There are only warm feelings for Ottawa, but we need to know what the details are."

A second diplomat put it more bluntly, predicting that while Canada could be given an equivalent of the EU's Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Areas deal — a market access arrangement offered to Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine — there is little mandate for other economic or political integration. "Member states will not agree on anything else," the diplomat said.

A third diplomat added that any associate membership status would require changes to the EU’s fundamental treaties — which is “impossible” due to a lack of support.

Among the potential issues that would come up if they considered going beyond that, according to the diplomats, are thorny questions around Ottawa's Made in Canada preference, which could fly in the face of single market rules; Canada's steel industry, which rivals Europe's own; taxation on the EU's car exports and its rules limiting imports of European alcohol; and its differing guidance on genetically modified produce.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has previously suggested "associate membership" as a way for closer alignment with Ukraine, although the idea was rejected by Kyiv and failed to win the support of other leaders.

World.title: JD Vance: US cannot be ‘subservient’ to Israel on Middle East policy
World.content:
The Trump administration and Israel launched an attack on Iran on Feb. 28 — sparking an ongoing war in the Middle East, which has driven up energy prices and stifled marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital chokepoint for the transport of fuel.

The Israeli parliament hailed U.S. President Donald Trump last year, for America’s role in releasing hostages held by Palestinian militants in Gaza. On March 5, Defense Minister Israel Katz thanked Trump for his “great support for Israel” and said cooperation between Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was “changing regional and global history.”

That optimism masks an increasingly complicated relationship. In June, Vance warned Israel that it had few friends left and should think carefully before alienating Washington.

The U.S. vice president already angered parts of Israel’s diplomatic community — as well as the pro-Israel Republican establishment. His defense in June of a ceasefire agreement with Iran rattled Israeli officials and damaged his standing with some pro-Israel Republican donors.

In Tuesday’s remarks, he also praised Trump for being willing to break with Netanyahu when American and Israeli interests diverged.

“Donald Trump is the one president of the last 40 years who’s been willing to say ‘You know what, yeah Bibi’s a good partner, but also Bibi and I have a different opinion on this,’ or ‘Bibi’s wrong about this,’ or maybe ‘Bibi’s right about this from the perspective of Israel, but the American people need us to go in a different direction,’” he said.

Vance also compared the relationship with Israel to Washington’s European alliances, saying U.S. policy should not be “subservient to NATO” either.

World.title: Turkey sees Greece’s militarization of Aegean Islands as ‘threat’
World.content:
“The militarization of the islands that have a demilitarized status constitutes a threat for us … We invite our neighbor and ally to implement its obligations that derive from international treaties in a more mature manner, in the spirit of the alliance,” Fidan said. “Greece must not add another provocation to the numerous security challenges our region faces.”

Despite being NATO allies, Greece and Turkey have been at odds for decades over a number of bilateral squabbles, including quarrels over maritime boundaries, overlapping claims to their continental shelves and the long-running Cyprus dispute.

Tensions between Athens and Ankara have seen a recent uptick, particularly following a recent strengthening of ties between Greece and Israel, which Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan sees as a bid to “encircle” his country.

Earlier this month, Greece delivered a formal complaint to Ankara over Turkey’s declaration of “national” marine parks, which Athens considers “invalid and lacking legal effect” as they extend into areas outside Turkish jurisdiction and within the Greek continental shelf.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis raised the issue in a meeting with European Council President António Costa in Athens.

“My country is a peaceful country that poses no threat to anyone. However, it will not accept instructions from anyone on how to strengthen its defense capabilities,” Mitsotakis said.

World.title: UK to make ‘doxxing’ a criminal offense
World.content:
Nandy said the companies disclosed inconsistent approaches to removing names and addresses of people shared online — and accused Elon Musk’s X of “contempt” for failing to send a representative to the meeting. X did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

More broadly, Nandy said the U.K. government would be “moving at pace to make sure that we keep people safe and we clean up our online space, which has been left to the private sector to police for far too long.”

“Our government intends to be more interventionist in this area,” she said.

In a separate interview on Wednesday, Nandy said the government wanted to see regulator Ofcom enforcing the Online Safety Act “more robustly and more quickly.”

A review of Ofcom’s resources and enforcement powers is ongoing, with the regulator set to soon take on additional responsibilities to enforce a social media ban for under-16s.

“We’ve been more active than any other regulator in the world when it comes to enforcing online safety law,” an Ofcom spokesperson said.

“In the first 18 months of the Online Safety Act coming into force, we've investigated more than 100 platforms, and issued fines totaling more than £7 million against 11 providers,” they added.

This article has been updated to include comments from an Ofcom spokesperson.

World.title: Ukraine ready for energy ceasefire but Russia is yet to agree, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Kyiv is ready for an energy ceasefire with Moscow, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, adding that Russia has yet to make the same commitment.

 

In an interview with CBS, Zelenskyy said US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility during their recent visit to Kyiv. He said Ukraine agreed, on condition that Russia also stops all attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure**.**

“We never attack first. Our tactic is to respond where we can because Putin doesn’t respect and won’t even think of negotiating with weaklings,” Zelenskyy said.

“When Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were here, they proposed thinking about refineries and other energy. I told them we are ready for an energy ceasefire, but you need to know what that means for Ukraine.”

Zelenskyy stressed that an energy ceasefire would have to cover different types of infrastructure: Russian oil and gas facilities targeted by Kyiv, and the electricity and gas infrastructure Moscow has repeatedly struck in Ukraine**.**

“For Putin, energy is selling oil and gas. For us, energy is having electricity and gas supplies for our people,” Zelenskyy said.

“My message was, if the Russians are ready for an energy ceasefire, it means no strikes of any kind with any type of weapon on energy.”

A worker leaves the damaged gas station after a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. AP Photo

But Moscow is yet to change its tactic. Right after Donald Trump announced the energy truce, the Kremlin-affiliated outlets presented it as a one-way measure, claiming Kyiv will stop its long-range strikes. There was no word regarding Moscow not attacking Ukraine.

The Kremlin has described the proposal as a “very good idea,” but has also linked the wider energy issue to safe commercial shipping, particularly for oil tankers, and the lifting of sanctions on Russia.

Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries and other oil infrastructure, saying that energy revenues help finance Moscow’s ongoing all-out war.

Russia meanwhile has repeatedly attacked Ukraine’s electricity and gas infrastructure, leaving the country and millions of Ukrainians particularly vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of war.

World.title: Von der Leyen describes ‘horror’ at Mladić funeral but holds off on Serbia measures
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday that she was "horrified by the images" of covincted war criminal Ratko Mladić's funeral in Belgrade earlier this month, but stopped short of announcing any punitive measures against Serbia.

 

"The glorification of war criminals simply has no place in the European Union," von der Leyen said during her annual State of the European Union speech. She refrained from directly criticising Serbia despite calls for firmer action from the bloc.

Mladić, known as the "Butcher of Bosnia", died in August while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during the Bosnian War in the 1990s.

His body was flown to Belgrade on a state plane, greeted by an honour guard by the Serbian military and various security forces, and commemorated by the public broadcaster and the Serbian Orthodox Church. His coffin was wrapped in a Serbian flag.

Officials in Belgrade had previously denied that he would be given a funeral with state honours.

The images prompted outrage across Europe, with Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković criticising the EU's muted response.

The Commission helmed by von der Leyen had been pushing to advance Serbia's bid to become an EU member by unlocking Cluster 3 talks on economic growth.

But EU capitals blocked the move, citing persistent concerns over democratic backsliding – even after the Venice Commission said Belgrade had implemented most of its recommendations on judicial reforms.

Diplomats have told Euronews that the funeral given to Mladić has effectively put Serbia's accession push on hold, with one saying that "anyone even considering opening Cluster 3 will think twice".

Henrik Dahl, a Danish lawmaker for the European People's Party (EPP), told Euronews on Tuesday that "Serbia has put themselves in the back of the waiting line (to join the EU) because they gave a state funeral to a war criminal".

Several EU lawmakers have also questioned the affiliation of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party to the EPP, the centre-right political family to which von der Leyen belongs.

The EU's enlargement chief, Marta Kos, postponed her planned visit to Belgrade in response to the funeral, prompting speculation that von der Leyen could announce similar repercussions.

The Commission chief is widely expected to tour Western Balkan candidate countries including Serbia this autumn, but the executive has refrained from confirming whether the programme for the visit is yet confirmed.

World.title: No word from Riyadh on oil delivery cancellations as scale of disruption remains unclear
World.content:
Saudi Arabia has not commented on reports that it has cancelled or delayed crude oil shipments to European refiners following last week's drone strikes on its East-West pipeline, as the scale of the disruption to European deliveries remains unclear.

 

Energy pricing agency Argus reported on Tuesday that at least three European refiners had cargoes scheduled for late September cancelled or postponed, in some cases until November, citing unnamed market sources.

Saudi Arabia's energy ministry announced a precautionary shutdown last Friday after drone attacks on the pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions the previous day.

Saudi and Iraqi authorities said the drones came from Iraq. The ministry said technical teams were checking the pipeline, but did not say when pumping would restart.

The pipeline carries crude from Saudi Arabia’s eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

From Yanbu, tankers heading to Europe sail north towards the Suez Canal. Egypt’s SUMED pipeline provides another route for crude to reach the Mediterranean from the Red Sea.

Oil stored at export terminals can keep cargoes moving during a shutdown. How long those stocks last depends on the amount available and how quickly pipeline deliveries resume.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Tuesday that the pipeline interruption would be “measured in days”.

Saudi Arabia’s state-controlled oil company Aramco did not respond to Euronews’ request for comment at the time of publication.

Bab el-Mandeb in Houthi crosshairs

The Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday that it had intercepted a Houthi drone south of Mecca the previous evening. The Houthis denied targeting the city.

Last week, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis took control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea after seizing the port of Mokha and nearby islands from Yemen's Saudi-supported internationally recognised government.

Bab el-Mandeb lies south of Yanbu, on the direct route to Asia. Europe-bound tankers sailing north from Yanbu do not pass through it, but the strait is a key passage for trade between Europe and Asia.

Qatar warned on Tuesday that losing access to Bab el-Mandeb would worsen the disruption already affecting shipping through Hormuz.

Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of media and communication at Qatar’s foreign ministry, told a briefing in Doha that this would be “catastrophic for the entire world," calling for international efforts to keep the waterway open.

Meanwhile, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi discussed the security of regional shipping routes in Cairo on Tuesday.

El-Sisi said Saudi and Gulf security formed part of Egypt's national security, expressing support for Saudi measures to protect the kingdom and calling for a political settlement in Yemen.

World.title: Air pollution exposure linked to higher risk of suicide and suicidal thoughts, study finds
World.content:
Exposure to polluted air may increase the risk of suicidal ideation and death by suicide both in the short and long term, highlighting the influence of environmental factors on people’s health.

 

A new analysis, published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health, found evidence that short-term exposure to small particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), as well as long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and PM2.5, increases the risk of death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal ideation.

Researchers analysed more than 40 studies examining different types of air, noise, light and water pollution, and their relationship with death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal thoughts.

Over 720,000 people die by suicide globally every year. In the European Union, more than 48,000 people died as a result of intentional self-harm in 2023, according to the latest Eurostat data.

“While there is no one single cause for suicide, reasons have been described as multifaceted and include several individual and biological factors in addition to wider cultural and social factors,” the authors wrote.

These findings contribute to a broader understanding of the role environmental exposures play in suicide risk, the authors noted. Yet, the environmental risks remain not fully understood, they noted.

How does the environment influence health?

The analysis points to possible mechanisms connecting air pollution and suicide. For example, air and water pollution have been linked to neurological effects, including chronic inflammation and neurotoxicity, which can harm brain function and influence mood and stress resilience.

Traffic and other sources of environmental noise and light pollution have also been linked to higher stress levels via circadian rhythm disruption.

“The main contribution of the study is not to demonstrate that pollution is a causal factor in suicidal behaviour, but rather to remind us that psychological suffering always occurs within a particular context,” said Susana Al-Halabí, a psychology professor at the University of Oviedo in Spain, who did not participate in the study.

She added that pollutants can also be a maker of more vulnerable social environments, such as neighbourhoods with poorer living conditions, lower environmental quality, more everyday stress or higher levels of inequality.

According to the authors, further research should investigate the cumulative effect of these environmental exposures to better understand their role in shaping suicide risk.

“These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts,” they wrote.

If you are contemplating suicide and need to talk, please reach out to Befrienders Worldwide, an international organisation with helplines in 32 countries. Visit befrienders.org to find the telephone number for your location.

World.title: 'Lack of focus': Charles Michel slams von der Leyen for 'very slow' progress
World.content:
The European Commission President is "very slow" to make the necessary decisions on the current challenges facing the European Union (EU), Charles Michel, who headed the European Council during von der Leyen's first term as Commission chief from 2019 to 2024, said.

 

His comments came ahead of von der Leyen's highly anticipated annual State of the European Union address before the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday, in which she outlined her vision and priorities for the coming year.

Michel, however, was focused on her failure to fulfil the promises made in previous years.

"I'm observing that, today, the EU is facing complicated challenges because there are more and more conflicts; there is a war on European soil, and we are in a difficult position in terms of competition with China and the United States," Michel told Euronews' flagship morning programme Europe Today.

"We should focus on the core issues, and the core issue is not about communication; it's not about more initiatives. The Commission over the last years launched 400 initiatives. But where are the deliveries? Where is the improvement? When I meet entrepreneurs, they are disappointed because they don't feel a sense of urgency."

Over-regulation makes EU weaker

Michel argued that when it comes to strengthening the EU's competitiveness, identified by Michel as the top priority facing the bloc today, there is a deadlock.

"There is a question, a very simple question: 'Is the EU a better place to invest? Is the EU a better place to innovate?' We've seen a lot of regulations, over-regulation," he said.

Michel went on to say that there has been no significant progress when it comes to, for example, the capital markets union - essentially a single market for capital across the EU identified as a key pillar for strengthening competitiveness.

"It makes us weaker, too weak in the current context." While conceding this is not entirely von der Leyen's fault, he did emphasise that "she has a responsibility," adding that "there is no doubt that she is very slow in making her decisions. I have the impression there is a lack of focus on what matters."

The Commission chief addressed this matter in her speech on Wednesday, arguing that, with the EU single market and "world-class industry and services," the bloc has the foundations to compete and scale alongside major global powers such as China and the US, but that it is still too fragmented.

Von der Leyen argued the Commission is delivering on this front. "We now have the political agreement on the One Europe, One Market Roadmap. And together, by the end of next year, we can and must complete this historic overhaul of the Single Market."

'Blindly following US'

According to Michel, von der Leyen's approach to dealing with the US under Donald Trump's presidency has also put Europe's security at risk. She was criticised by MEPs, among others, for the so-called "Turnberry Agreement", the EU-US trade deal agreed to last summer, which some saw as lopsided.
