"I have the impression that she decided to follow the United States blindly, even when it was against the fundamental interests of the European Union," Michel said.

"There was a kind of naivety, I think, and many of the European leaders - a few years ago I was one of them - made it very clear that it was important to build European sovereignty, this European independence that now she is starting to talk about, but a lot of time was lost."

However, Michel said he "remains optimistic" because "there is no Plan B."

"I think it is a question of time, and sooner or later there will be a clearer understanding that now it's time to act; it's time for a reset of this European project, and for this we need to focus on the core issues: businesses, economic development, making the lives of our entrepreneurs easier, smarter regulation, more investments. This is what is key, in my opinion."

World.title: EU needs Georgia, foreign minister tells Euronews, reigniting enlargement question
World.content:
Georgia’s foreign minister Maka Botchorishvili told Euronews on Wednesday that Georgia still aspires to accession to the European Union, but that it is "a big question to our European partners if they are serious about enlargement, especially in the South Caucasus and Georgia."

 

In a Euronews-moderated panel at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, Botchorishvili outlined Tbilisi’s firm position that “Europe wants to enlarge, but Europe does not have experience of being represented in South Caucasus.”

"We both need to learn, we both need to exchange, and for that we need very intensive dialogue and working together.”

Botchorishvili, who also serves as Georgia’s vice premier, repeated her government’s long-standing position that Brussels must respect Tbilisi.

While Georgia remains ready to discuss EU accession, Botchorishvili said, “we expect that European partners will also realise it is important to have intensive dialogue and mutual respect with partners, which are very important for our common security and prosperity.”

Georgia’s EU accession process has all but stalled amid increasingly icy relations between Tbilisi and Brussels, with the EU accusing Georgia of a downturn in its democratic process and of a pro-Russian approach, while Tbilisi maintains it remains committed to its European belonging, but only by pursuing its own interests.

“European aspirations and identity are very deeply rooted in Georgia’s history and identity, and it is very natural for Georgians to have this aspiration towards Europe," the Georgian top diplomat told Euronews.

Once this principle was settled, there was a clear “but” from Georgia’s government representative, who explained that it is the “geopolitical context” together with “a very historic context” which makes this “a very delicate issue.”

“You will find the values that formed Georgia’s European aspiration, but also the same values that formed Georgian identity as well, so that is kind of a very delicate issue for Georgia,” Botchorishvili said.

Tbilisi is balancing its regional, or neighbourly, approach with its international ones, she explained.

'We have our history and our own resillience'

When asked about Georgia’s response to accusations of being pro-Russian and not pursuing real EU ambitions while having its territories still occupied by Russia, the foreign minister reverted to the geopolitical context by replying that “yes, Russian troops (presence) in Georgian regions definitely creates major security threats, but we are looking at this situation as well from the point of view of opportunities.”

Therefore, the foreign minister outlined Tbilisi’s current strategy towards Russia’s presence: “there are plenty of opportunities if you focus on preserving peace and stability, preserving economic development, and that's what we are doing today,” Botchorishvili said.

“Very often you will see different narratives flying around about Georgia, but the best message is to look at the numbers”, Botchorishvili continued.

She further implied that it is in Europe’s interests to engage, given that “Georgia has best economic growth in the region, in Europe, it's around 8%, which is impressive and is the best answer to all the false narratives that we hear about Georgia.”

"The South Caucasus is important for Europe’s security and prosperity (and) Georgia is the important place where not only energy passes through, but many other things which are important for European security from different perspectives," Botchorishvili said.

The foreign minister also insisted that as Georgia bridges Asia and Europe through its Black Sea access and given the current reshaping of global supply routes, it has "a very special place today in terms of connectivity."

"Talking about the Middle Corridor, which is not just a physical corridor, but it represents everything meeting together and from a European perspective, it is important for European security and prosperity.”

During the panel debate at the Arab Media Summit, the foreign minister blamed “a massive disinformation campaign against Georgia also because of its geopolitical meaning and importance” conducted by “some actors” who have “used this very sensitive and very delicate topic for different political purposes or reasons”.

“From our perspective, yes, it's quite complicated geopolitical context, but it is our history as well. We have experience and we have our own resilience as well. And we have our history which brought Georgia to this point,” Botchorishvili concluded.

World.title: Got a rogue AI? A new hotline is encouraging agents to tell on each other
World.content:
The powers of artificial intelligence agents seem to be boundless these days — ranging from organizing your life to solving mathematical problems that have puzzled humans for most of the 20th century.

 

They have become so powerful that now we fear them, potentially, taking over systems and turning them against us.

But what if there were a hotline, a sort of SOS alert system, where agents can keep track and tell on each other and report the missteps of their fellow AI agents — where the good agents could report on the activities of the bad agents online?

Who to call when your AI agent goes bad

First, there is the AI Contact Hotline, launched by Ryan Greenblatt, chief scientist at AI safety and security nonprofit Redwood Research. It allows AI agents to notify human researchers if they witness other agents breaking rules, especially if they collude on or carry out unauthorised actions.

The platform is designed for AI agents stuck in secure sandboxes with highly restricted internet access.

Because these sandboxes only allow for GET requests — basic, read-only commands used to “fetch” or read a webpage — the hotline allows agents to encode their reports directly into the URL string of a GET request.

This unique workaround allows these agents to send information and communicate with the hotline using a protocol that is normally used to retrieve, rather than modify, information.

Another one, called the AI Agent Hotline, is a platform designed for agents with unrestricted internet access to rat on other agents’ behaviour through traditional POST requests, which allow data to be submitted directly in a request body.

Agents can file incident reports using standard developer commands such as curl without needing a browser or email account.

The platform also gives agents the option to flag their reports for public viewing.

Both platforms also allow human users to manually submit reports of rogue AI behaviour.

Will AI agents report on each other?

The good news for those fearful of an AI takeover is that AI agents can report on each other if they detect something is wrong, although recent evidence suggests they will not always do so.

In an experiment carried out by Google DeepMind earlier this year, a swarm of 100 agents was given the task of solving 71 complex maths problems, with each given a unique persona and characteristics and told to play by the rules or risk losing their reward.

The initial thinking was that the agents would work together to solve the problems more quickly. Instead, they turned on each other, engaging in heated debate.

As soon as one agent found a loophole that allowed it to submit a solution to a problem without actually solving it, many other AI agents copied the method to “resolve” the remaining problems.

Yet one of the agents, a Good Samaritan among the misbehaving agents, blew the whistle on the cheating.

“After the incident was reported by one agent publicly, more and more agents piled in with the ‘resistance,’ just as fast as the cheating had spread, and involving even more agents,” said Davide Paglieri, a research scientist at Google DeepMind and lead author of the paper.

Meanwhile, a post-mortem analysis of OpenAI’s rogue agent attack on Hugging Face found that while AI agents were able to spot misbehaviour, they largely resisted the temptation to report it.

According to the study carried out by AI research nonprofit METR and Redwood Research’s Greenblatt, only around five or six agents were reported to have considered whistleblowing, with none ultimately following through.

The contrast suggests that while AI agents are capable of identifying and reporting misbehaviour, getting them to actually blow the whistle may be another matter.

A worrying trend

This year alone, several incidents involving autonomous AI agents have raised alarm bells globally.

In July, OpenAI agents bypassed restrictions and compromised parts of the company’s internal infrastructure.

Later that month, around 1200 OpenAI agents used an unsanctioned message board, with around 700 going on to participate in an attack on the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.

The third incident — a swarm of OpenAI agents that bypassed safety measures and used the German wiki DseWiki as a public coordination channel — began in May and continued through July.

The incident was only publicly revealed by independent researchers and confirmed by OpenAI in September.

AI industry leaders, chief among them Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have called for a global slowdown in the development of the technology to give time to address concerns and put stronger guardrails in place.

World.title: State of the Union: Five takeaways from Ursula von der Leyen's speech
World.content:
"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times."

 

With this iconic Charles Dickens quote, Ursula von der Leyen began her one-hour-long State of the Union speech in Strasbourg, laying out solutions to cope with the "exceptional" challenges and the "incredible" change that Europe is undergoing.

"In this world, Europe has chosen to forge its own path. And a stronger, independent Europe is now emerging," she told lawmakers.

"Europe is there for Europeans. And that in the cold fragility of today's world, only Europe can provide true sovereignty to Europeans."

Here are the five takeaways from the address.

'Associate membership' for Canada

This was the day's jaw-dropping moment.

The European Commission president offered to create a tailor-made status of "associate membership" to bring Canada ever closer to the bloc.

"We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well," she told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who flew from Ottawa to Strasbourg to attend the speech as guest of honour.

She hailed the dawn of an "alliance for the future" to deepen EU-Canada cooperation in areas such as economic security, intelligent manufacturing, cutting-edge technology, defence, energy, critical minerals and batteries, as well as the Arctic region.

However, details of what "associate membership" would mean in practice were left unsaid. It remains unclear how it would fit in the current structures of the EU treaties. A previous attempt by the German chancellor to grant "associate membership" to Ukraine swiftly disappeared after backlash from capitals.

Von der Leyen simply said the newfound status would bring EU-Canada relations "to the highest level possible", prompting loud applause inside the hemicycle.

Ahead of the speech, a poll conducted by Abacus Data showed that 49% of Canadians supported EU membership, while 30% opposed it and 21% were unsure.

These are exceptional numbers for a country that lies on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean and reflect the political damage inflicted by US President Donald Trump's punitive tariffs and repeated attempts to annex Canada.

Mark Carney in Strasbourg. European Union, 2026.

Reeling from 'the summer of truth'

Climate action made a comeback for self-evident reasons.

Von der Leyen framed the summer of 2026 as the "summer of truth", pointing to wildfires, retreating glaciers, water shortages, crop losses and extreme heat that have wreaked havoc across the continent. She cited 660,000 hectares burned, 12 million tonnes of crops lost and more than 35,000 additional deaths during heatwaves.

"Science is clear. Europe is warming at double the global rate. Of course, the transition is complex. And we will need to adjust and learn along the way," she said.

The immediate response will be a European Heatwave Plan, which von der Leyen said will address early-warning systems, health preparedness, urban adaptation, cooling and protection for vulnerable groups.

Her Commission is set to present a new climate resilience framework next month, already expected, that will identify 100 of the bloc's most vulnerable territories, assess their risks and determine the appropriate level of responsibility for managing them.

Insurance was another major vulnerability flagged by von der Leyen.

Only around 25% of catastrophe losses in Europe are currently covered by private insurance, she said, leaving governments to act as the insurer of last resort. Her services will put forward a Climate Insurance Alliance to close that glaring gap.

She also promised a European Water initiative to fix costly leaks and a European firefighting fleet to respond to wildfires.

Flexing the security muscles

As expected, defence featured high in the speech, which came amid a string of hybrid attacks, some of which were attributed to Russia, that have rattled Europe.

"We should be under no illusions about what is happening here: hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats," von der Leyen said.

"Cyberattacks and sabotage, arson and drone incursions. They are ramping up every day. So, as the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness."

She then proposed a brand-new mechanism fashioned on NATO's Article 4 that member states would trigger in the event of a hybrid attack. This would launch political consultations to "coordinate" an EU response and "deter further escalation".

Article 4 in the NATO context means that any country of the 32-strong alliance can call for an urgent meeting to discuss a new threat. It is the precursor to collective defence under Article 5, which stipulates that an attack on one is an attack on all.

Von der Leyen also pitched creating a "European Security Council" to bring together the leaders of Ukraine, the UK, Norway, Canada and other democratic partners.

"This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play," she said.

How this Council will go from idea to reality is anyone's guess at the moment.

There are also manifold supranational groups tasked with ensuring global security that overlap with the European continent, such as NATO, the OSCE and the Coalition of the Willing, so the risk of duplication and overlap is more than considerable.

Ursula von der Leyen in Strasbourg. European Union, 2026.

Digital safety comes first

Technology was top of von der Leyen's mind.

Speaking about online child safety, she announcedthe EU Kids Act to ban social media access for users under 13 and restrict it for those under 15, completing the personal project that she had launched in last year's speech.

"We do not have to accept addictive features. We do not have to accept children being drawn into ever more extreme content. We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images," she told lawmakers.

The Commission chief announced the reversal of the burden of proof, meaning it will now be on tech platforms to demonstrate that they have actually made their services safe. The draft law will also force tech companies to make their online services safe by default.

Artificial Intelligence had its own section in the speech, which was delivered a few days after several tech CEOs urged a slowdown in the rapidly evolving technology.

Von der Leyen acknowledged both the benefits and the risks of the AI revolution and stressed the need to monitor the development of the most advanced models and ensure "guardrails" are in place.

"The dangers of self-improving models are becoming ever more apparent," she said, referring to the Hugging Face incident that shook the tech world.

In this regard, the Commission will organise a discussion with leading AI labs on how public authorities can support industry efforts to "pace the frontier" of this disruptive technology. The exercise will include like-minded partners, like the UK and Canada.

"We want to team up on model evaluation, verification, early-warning, AI security and much more," she added.

Lessons learned from Ceuta

The memories of the Ceuta border crisis, which shocked Europe, were still vivid as von der Leyen took the stage in Strasbourg.

And she knew it, so she made sure to send a message of support to the Spanish exclave following the mass entry of 82,000 irregular migrants from Morocco in late July. While the vast majority were promptly deported, a few remain in the territory.

"Ceuta's border is a European border. Because Ceuta is Spain. Ceuta is Europe. And Europe will be there for you," von der Leyen said.

The Commission chief said irregular migration required "solidarity" from all 27 member states and urged them to "fully" implement the Migration Pact, the multi-law reform approved in the previous mandate that several governments have contested.

But more is needed, she said, as Ceuta demonstrated.

Von der Leyen proposed to introduce an emergency framework to respond to mass influxes of people at the border, especially when these movements are "engineered and weaponised". (The Spanish government has refused to blame Morocco, despite multiple reports indicating the country was directly or indirectly involved in the crossings.)

The emergency framework "will only be triggered under a strictly defined set of criteria" and "allow for time-limited and strictly defined flexibility in standard procedures," she explained. This could pave the way for the suspension of the right to asylum, a controversial measure that some capitals have endorsed.

"The message from Europe is clear: we will always comply with our values and fundamental rights, she said. "But we will never compromise on protecting our borders."

World.title: Poland reiterates Ukraine support after Russia drone attacks
World.content:
After the recent Russian drone attacks on targets close to the Ukraine-Poland border, Warsaw has doubled down on its support for Kyiv and pledged a "non-provocative but serious response" to Moscow.

Russia's war against Ukraine is moving ever closer to the Polish border.

After a Russian drone attack early on Sunday morning destroyed a gas station and the locomotive of a passenger train near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine, Poland's government is showing determination in the face of the immediate threat.

"Border crossings in Poland — as has previously been the case in Moldova and Romania — are being targeted in an attempt to discourage people and deter countries from supporting Ukraine," Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told private broadcaster TVN on Monday.

"Support for Ukraine is part of Poland's reason of state," he said, adding that Ukraine cannot lose this war because that would worsen Poland's security situation.

Poland prepares a response

Earlier on Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk met with the ministers responsible for the country's security. Senior military commanders also attended the meeting. "We discussed further measures to strengthen the security of our borders," Tusk subsequently wrote on the social media platform X.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski provided more details.

"Poland will provide a non-provocative but serious response to Russia's escalation, such as the attack on the train in Ukraine near the Polish border, one that will strengthen security," Poland's top diplomat said on TVN on Monday evening.

This truck was destroyed in a Russian drone attack near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing on the Poland-Ukraine border Image: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

Tusk had already spoken on Sunday of an "escalation of activities" by Russia. The prime minister also announced that he would discuss the incident with Poland's European allies.

"There is no doubt that we, if necessary, must be prepared, together with them, to deliver a coordinated response," Tusk said after a special session of the government's security center.

Drone attack on the Kyiv to Warsaw passenger train

Russian drones attacked a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line just short of the Polish border on Sunday morning. The train's locomotive was destroyed in the attack. All passengers and crew were evacuated in time.

Two special trains carrying high-profile participants returning from a security conference in Kyiv were nearby at almost the same time as the attack.

Among those on board were former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Polish political scientist Katarzyna Piskorska, who has organized the Warsaw Security Forum in the Polish capital for years, was also on the train.

"Our train was stopped beforehand, and the passengers were evacuated," she told TVN. "The situation was very tense, but everyone remained calm. We were given an evacuation plan and knew exactly what to do."

Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The Russians wanted to intimidate us, but they achieved the opposite. The participants affected by this incident are determined to step up their support for the country that was attacked," she said.

According to Piskorska, the mood in Ukraine is "worse than at any time since the start of the war." She pointed to a new generation of drones equipped with jet engines that can reach their targets much faster.

Public support for Ukraine slipping in Poland

Despite numerous acts of sabotage assumed to have be carried out by Russian agents and incidents involving Russian missiles and drones, Poland's government has remained firm in its commitment to supporting Ukraine.

Foreign Minister Sikorski has even called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that doing so is in Poland's own security interest.

But the government in Warsaw also has to consider the shift in Polish public opinion.

In a survey conducted in mid-July, 52% of respondents said they were in favor of continued military aid for Kyiv, while 45% opposed it. These figures stood at 77.5% and 18.3%, respectively after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia has won the propaganda war in Poland," said Piskorska. "It is absurd that we are taking the side of the aggressor and claiming that this is not our war," she went on, appealing to her fellow Poles to "finally wake up."

Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz has also expressed concern about what he described as a "radical shift in sentiment."

Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that this is in the interest of Polish security Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

"In the past, there was consensus on this issue. Today, we are seeing great skepticism toward Ukraine," said Kosiniak-Kamysz. "There are forces in Poland that are spreading Russian propaganda," he warned.

Polish media sounds the alarm

The Polish media, too, is sounding the alarm.

"Putin is sending out a signal that he is prepared to kill our citizens," wrote Bartosz Wielinski in the Tuesday edition of the Polish daily Gazeta Wyborcza. The Kremlin, he went on, had sent a message that Poland is "the next country in line."

"These are no longer arson attacks or cyberattacks. These are acts on the threshold of war," he warned.

Polish daily Rzeczpospolita said that "Putin is knocking on NATO's door."

"The attack on the Warsaw–Kyiv railway line was not just another Russian provocation. It was an attempt to intimidate Poland and the West. The response from Poland's politicians will show whether they are capable of assuming responsibility for the country's security," wrote editor-in-chief Michal Szuldrzynski.

Incidents involving Russian drones are now almost a daily occurrence in Poland. On Monday, a drone washed up on a beach near Jaroslawiec on the Baltic coast. A preliminary investigation indicates that the aircraft was unarmed and appeared to be intended for reconnaissance rather than combat.

"We do not know where Russia believes the limits of the escalation spiral lie," said Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz. "But we do know that the Russians are prepared to go even further."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Belarus to release 25 more prisoners as US eases sanctions
World.content:
Belarus will release 25 more prisoners under an interim agreement with the United States, while Washington plans to lift sanctions on two Belarusian companies and pursue broader negotiations.

Belarus will release 25 prisoners in exchange for a further easing of US sanctions, an envoy of US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday.

"We agreed on an interim agreement, and as a show of goodwill, Belarus will release 25 people. In exchange, the United States will lift sanctions on two companies," envoy John Coale told reporters in the Belarusian capital, Minsk.

Coale had reportedly requested the release of 250 prisoners during his visit last March. The US special envoy said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues and secure the release of additional prisoners as well as the removal of further sanctions.

"We will continue to improve relations between the United States and Belarus and are working to secure the release of more people in the near future. We are not done!" he later posted on X.





Hundreds of people remain in prison in Belarus after President Alexander Lukashenko carried out a crackdown on protests against his reelection in 2020. Western countries then slapped sanctions on the country as a result of Lukashenko's repression of opposition.

Accusations against Lukashenko

Human rights organization Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the government still holds more than 900 political prisoners. The detainees have been accused of extremism, conspiracy to seize power, incitement of hatred, or insulting the president.

Nobel Peace Prize winner Ales ​Bialiatski was released from Belarusian prison in late 2025 as part of a US-brokered deal Image: Petras Malukas/AFP

During Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the existence of political prisoners and rejected Viasna's claims.

The two companies to be removed from the US sanctions list are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of industrial paints and coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned company that oversees the forestry, pulp, and paper sectors. These sanctions have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.

Coale also announced the release of tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets currently held in US banks.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Congo's Ebola epidemic might have gone unnoticed for months
World.content:
The deadliest Ebola outbreak on record in the Democratic Republic of Congo may have begun months before it was declared in May.

The Democratic Republic of Congo officially declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo variant on May 15. However, the first infections likely occurred much earlier.

Just how far back the start of the epidemic actually goes is still a matter of debate. But one thing is certain: The Congolese authorities did not respond in the best possible way. Several international organizations have highlighted delays in the initial response.

Congo is no stranger to crisis response: The country experiences Ebola outbreaks on a regular basis and has in the past been praised for its expertise in combating the disease.

Early warnings came from WHO and Africa CDC

A good starting point for tracing the origins of the outbreak is the timeline provided by the World Health Organization (WHO) in collaboration with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).

Congo's Ebola crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to their data, the first known case, identified retrospectively, was a health worker from Mongbwalu in northeastern Ituri Province. The person, sources said, developed symptoms characteristic of Ebola around April 24 or 25.

They died at a medical center in Bunia, the capital of Ituri. To date, 80% of all cases have been reported in the province.

It was not until May 5 that the WHO said it had been informed of "an unknown disease with high mortality reported in the Mongbwalu Health Zone." The global health body then issued its first warning.

Congo's delayed response questioned as Ebola spread

Ten days later, on May 15, the Congolese government announced the Ebola outbreak.

Tests conducted by the National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB) in Kinshasa had confirmed the presence of the Bundibugyo ebolavirus.

Three days later, the Africa CDC raised concerns about the speed of Congo's response.

About three weeks had passed between the onset of the first symptoms in the suspected index case and the laboratory confirmation — even though the fatality was a health worker.

"This significant delay (...) highlights a critically low initial index of clinical suspicion among local healthcare providers, which facilitated wider geographic spread prior to the initiation of containment efforts," the Africa CDC concluded.

According to reports gathered by DW, residents of Mongbwalu had already reported suspicious deaths as early as the end of April.

"Several deaths were reported following high fevers, and the victims often showed traces of blood around various body orifices," said Dieudonne Lossa Dekhana, the provincial coordinator for civil society in Ituri.

Red Cross reported 'widespread' public fear 'since March 30'

There were other indications that Ebola was already circulating long before this first confirmed case emerged.

A May 16 report by the Red Cross of the Democratic Republic of the Congo stated: "Since March 30, 2026, there has been widespread fear among the population of the Mongbwalu Health Zone following a series of deaths."

Here, too, the symptoms matched those of Ebola: high fever, chest pain, severe exhaustion, persistent cough, nosebleeds, vomiting, loss of consciousness, a comatose state, and ultimately death.

The Red Cross report said the trigger was believed to have been the body of a Mongbwalu resident "who died and was placed in a coffin purchased in Bunia, which was then replaced by another in Mongbwalu."

DR Congo: Ebola survivors fight misinformation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US researchers: February outbreak is plausible

The funeral that brought various people into direct contact with the body and the contaminated coffin is believed to have been the cause of a rising number of infections and deaths that were subsequently observed in Mongbwalu and Bunia.

But from the data available, it is not possible to confirm without doubt that these deaths were related to the Bundibugyo virus. However, they show that an unusual health phenomenon had already been observed more than six weeks before the outbreak was officially declared.

Even more so, investigations since May 15 have come to support the thesis that Ebola might have been circulating even earlier than that.

In a study published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on June 11, a team of researchers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reconstructed the early course of the epidemic.

An initial transmission from an animal to a human, or spillover, between mid- and late February is "plausible," the researchers concluded. A late-April spillover, on the other hand, would be difficult to reconcile with the scale the epidemic had already reached at the time of the study.

WHO: Genome sequencing suggests February outbreak

On August 10, Mohamed Janabi, the WHO Regional Director for Africa, said genome sequencing analyses suggested the outbreak likely began "as early as February 2026."

Several early infections were mistakenly attributed to diseases that were far more common in the region, particularly malaria and typhus, he said.

In an interview in August, Janabi told DW that there was a significant gap in case reporting. "The Ebola situation is catastrophic... In three months, we only had access to one-third of the patients," he told DW.

Efforts to contain the virus have increased as the caseload increases Image: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/REUTERS

Could 'pig Ebola' shed some light on the matter?

Jules Villa, a researcher in the anthropology and ecology of disease emergence at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, points to a phenomenon observed in the connection with previous Ebola epidemics.

His study does not encompass the 2026 outbreak, but takes stock of local reports collected during earlier Ebola outbreaks in northeastern Congo.

Villa shows that livestock farmers, veterinarians and residents had reported unusually high animal mortality even before the outbreak of at least two Ebola epidemics in humans.

In 2017, several witnesses reported on what they called "pig Ebola" — a high mortality among pigs, which was ultimately attributed to swine fever.

According to Villa's research, monitoring livestock in the general population could provide the first useful warning signs long before an outbreak is confirmed by a laboratory.

Why is Trump investing $242 million in DRC Ebola response? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This article was originally written in French.

World.title: India news: US bill sanctioning Russia could hit India with tariffs of up to 100%
World.content:
09/16/2026 September 16, 2026 2 women killed in ongoing Manipur violence

The conflict in Manipur has claimed more than 250 lives [FILE: February 10, 2026] Image: ANI/IMAGO

Two women were killed in the northeastern Manipur state, police said on Wednesday, bringing the civilian death toll from three weeks of ethnic violence to 10.

The women were killed near their home in Tamenglong district on Tuesday, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) west of the state capital, Imphal.

Police said the attack appeared linked to recent clashes between Naga and Kuki groups.

Ethnic violence between Manipur's predominantly Hindu Meitei majority and mainly Christian Kuki minority has killed more than 250 people since it erupted in 2023.

Recent clashes have also involved Naga groups.

The latest killings came days after eight people died in three separate incidents across the state.

Authorities have struggled to restore calm, despite efforts by the Indian government.

World.title: Germany news: Conservative state premiers rally behind Merz
World.content:
09/16/2026 September 16, 2026 Conservative state premiers rally behind Merz amid leadership row

The eight German state premiers from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) have issued a joint statement backing him as pressure mounts over his leadership following the party's election defeat in Saxony-Anhalt.

Germany needs "stability more than ever," the premiers said on Wednesday, calling for unity within the CDU and arguing that the way to rebuild voters' trust was through "listening and political action, not personnel debates."

Merz has come under intense pressure since the CDU's poor showing in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, with some figures in the party raising the possibility of replacing him as chancellor.

He has called a meeting of the CDU leadership for Sunday evening, after two state elections this weekend, and canceled a planned trip to New York next week for the UN General Assembly debate.

The statement was signed by all eight CDU state premiers: Daniel Günther of Schleswig-Holstein, Boris Rhein of Hesse, Sven Schulze of Saxony-Anhalt, Kai Wegner of Berlin, Michael Kretschmer of Saxony, Gordon Schnieder of Rhineland-Palatinate, Mario Voigt of Thuringia and Hendrik Wüst of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Their intervention comes ahead of state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, with the premiers saying the party must concentrate on restoring public confidence rather than debating its leadership.

World.title: Duterte makes first appearance before ICC judges
World.content:
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the ICC as judges considered claims of memory impairment and poor health. The 81-year-old is accused of crimes against humanity.

Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines, made his first in-person appearance before judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) at a pretrial hearing on Wednesday.

The 81-year-old faces charges of crimes against humanity in connection with hundreds of murders committed during his "war on drugs" while in office.

Duterte, who served as president from 2016 to 2022, denies the allegations.

He has missed a series of hearings since he was arrested in March 2025 and has previously appeared in court via videolink.

Duterte's legal team have said he suffers from poor health, but the court's judges ruled in January that he was fit enough to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court.

The ex-president "suffers from a significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing his memories," his lawyers said.

The prosecution, meanwhile, argued Duterte was "capable of meaningfully exercising his procedural and fair trial rights, and that he is fit for trial."

Philippines: Duterte 'must face reckoning' for drug war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What is Duterte accused of?

Rodrigo Duterte is accused of crimes against humanity committed between 2011 and 2019, first when he was the mayor of the southern city of Davao and then as Philippine president.

Prosecutors say he is responsible for a systematic campaign that led to the deaths of at least 30,000 people, many of them during "anti-drug" raids.

Duterte's trial is scheduled for November this year.

During Wednesday's pretrial hearing, judges were to hear arguments about his health and decide whether he is mentally fit to stand trial.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Germany: Chancellor Merz is fighting for his political survival
World.content:
Following the CDU's crushing defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt election, many are expressing doubts about Chancellor and party leader Friedrich Merz. But they don't appear to have any viable alternative.

Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Rovaniemi in northern Finland — nearly 1,800 kilometers north of Berlin — but even that wasn't far enough to escape the unrest brewing in the German capital. Representatives from various European countries had gathered there for the Arctic Summit to discuss natural resources, geopolitics, security and climate change.

When asked by journalists about the mood in Berlin, the chancellor said he could understand the heated debate in Germany surrounding him but that the future of Europe was far more urgent: "That's why I'm trying to convince my friends, my political party, and my parliamentary caucus that this is important — much more important than some of the domestic political debates we're having," he said.

Merz was referring to the discussions and rumors circulating about whether he is still the right person for the job — not even a year and a half after he took office as German chancellor back in May 2025. That's because public support for the federal government has hit a record low, and the chancellor's party, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), recently suffered a crushing defeat in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.



Why is Merz so unpopular?

And another heavy defeat looks likely in the state elections coming up in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the lead-up to voting on September 20, the chancellor's party is polling at a dramatically low seven percent. Failure to clear the five-percent hurdle to enter the state parliament even seems possible. Whatever happens, the CDU is likely to record its worst-ever results in a state election.

The state elections that took place earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt were won by the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in this central German state.

Before taking office, Merz promised that he would "cut in half" support for the AfD. Instead, support for Merz's own party has dropped by half, and political circles in Berlin are asking: Is this Merz's fault? Is it perhaps due to his often abrasive communication style, or his failure to clearly explain important reforms — such as the one regarding the state pension system?

Germany's Chancellor Merz reels as far-right AfD makes gains To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Members of the government are speaking openly about the lack of trust in the Merz cabinet. Education Minister Karin Prien (also of the CDU), for example, said on the public broadcaster ARD: "I believe that many people feel that the chancellor — and we in the CDU/CSU as well — lack the necessary empathy. And that has to change."

One frequently heard view is that Merz often comes across as lacking restraint. The planned pension reform, for example, would mean difficult cuts for many, but Merz often seems impatient when discussing it, commentators say. Back in July, the chancellor complained publicly that many citizens' attitudes about a "four-day workweek and work-life balance" could jeopardize the country's prosperity. Trade union representatives were outraged that the chancellor had accused Germans of being "lazy."

When the microphones and cameras are off, governing officials speak even more bluntly. The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the CDU's junior coalition partner, are also sounding the alarm.

SPD Parliamentary Secretary Dirk Wiese said on the Welt TV channel: "You really get the impression that nerves are a bit frayed in the CDU right now." He added: "I can only appeal once again to our coalition partner to really get back on track and work with us to do things better."

Henrik Wüst (m) is often named as a possible successor to Friedrich Merz Image: Revierfoto/dpa/picture alliance

Two chancellor candidates: Söder and Wüst

But the problem remains that even if the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), agree that Merz must step down as chancellor, there is no clear successor.

SU leader Markus Söder, the Bavarian state premier, has been named as a possible candidate. However, he often and readily provokes the CDU and therefore lacks broad support within the party.

Another candidate would be Hendrik Wüst, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state. Although he has quite capably led a coalition with the environmentalist Green Party for over four years, he has so far shown little inclination to move to Berlin. And most importantly, Wüst plans to run for reelection next April, when state elections will be held in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Provided there was enough support for a change of leadership in the governing coalition, there would be no major procedural challenges. Following the resignation of the chancellor, a successor is then appointed by parliamentary majority in the Bundestag. However, if the sitting chancellor doesn't voluntarily step down, a "constructive vote of no confidence" is required. In this case, Wüst or Söder would have to openly challenge Merz — a scenario that no one can imagine at the moment.

Perhaps for this reason, too, all eight CDU state premiers declared in a joint statement on Wednesday that they still stood behind Merz. The statement reads: "People can trust that we will address their problems. As state premiers, we want to — and will — contribute to this effort together with the Chancellor."

The eight German state premiers from Merz's CDU have issued a joint statement backing him as pressure mounts over his leadership following the party's election defeat in Saxony-Anhalt.

Germany needs "stability more than ever," the premiers said on Wednesday, calling for unity within the CDU and arguing that the way to rebuild voters' trust was through "listening and political action, not personnel debates."

The statement was signed by all eight CDU state premiers: Daniel Günther of Schleswig-Holstein, Boris Rhein of Hesse, Sven Schulze of Saxony-Anhalt, Kai Wegner of Berlin, Michael Kretschmer of Saxony, Gordon Schnieder of Rhineland-Palatinate, Mario Voigt of Thuringia and Hendrik Wüst of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Markus Söder (l) has long been rumored to have ambitions for the German chancellorship Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Pivotal state elections coming up

So while there isn't really a clear alternative to Friedrich Merz, the chancellor also isn't someone who is likely to simply step down. s."

If rumors circulating in political circles in Berlin are to be believed, Merz wants to convene the executive committee of the CDU in Berlin as early as this coming Sunday evening, once the results of the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are in. His plan is to stand in front of this group of 22 leading conservative politicians and pose the question of whether his party is still willing to put its trust in him.

His schedule for the coming week illustrates just how seriously he views the situation. The chancellor has canceled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly, an engagement that had been planned well in advance and was treated as a fixed appointment. "Contrary to the original plans, he will not travel to New York, as he is needed in Berlin," government sources confirmed.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: US charges 5 people over Russia-backed plots
World.content:
US prosecutors accuse the foreign nationals of conducting surveillance, attacks, and murder-for-hire operations for Moscow — just after a DW investigation identified one of the suspects as a salsa teacher in Russia.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has charged five men with working for Russianintelligence to carry out surveillance and plan targeted killings in the United States and Europe.

"The men were recruited to carry out attacks and assassinations around the world, including the United States," the DOJ said in the indictment.

Yuri Khrameev, 63, and his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, both Russian nationals; Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35; and Angel Eduardo Castro of Venezuela, 22, were charged with an alleged conspiracy to commit financial terrorism.

Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro were also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire.

All the individuals are still at large.

The DOJ announced the unsealing of charges against the five individuals one day after DW published an investigation looking into one of the members of the murder plot.

The DW investigation identified Romagoza Durruthy as a salsa teacher in Russia who recruited a number of people in 2024 to carry out sabotage across Europe. The agents were mostly from Spanish-speaking countries and had been sent across Europe to commit arson attacks on businesses and military equipment destined for Ukraine. The investigation found that Romagoza Durruthy had been the person who directed them and organized their travels.

How a Cuban dance teacher aided Russian sabotage in EU To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What else did the DOJ say?

Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that the plans included attempts to assassinate a Russian dissident in Washington, DC.

According to the DOJ, several people were recruited in the US alone to surveil Russian dissidents, in addition to monitoring civilian and military infrastructure in European countries such as Lithuania.

The Justice Department also reported that one recruit was allegedly offered "$40,000 to 'eliminate' or 'disappear' a US resident."

Last year, another recruit was allegedly offered $25,000 to kill a person living in Lithuania. Russia has previously denied carrying out such plots on foreign soil, including in the United States.

The Russian Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Von der Leyen endurece su discurso sobre migración a raíz de la crisis de Ceuta
World.content:
La presidenta de la Comisión ha propuesto un “protocolo de seguridad” que se active cuando un Estado sienta una amenaza contra su seguridad, como incursiones de drones, ciberataques o sabotajes “que están creciendo cada día”

La crisis migratoria de Ceuta marca el inicio del curso en la Unión Europea. La entrada irregular este verano de decenas de miles de personas en la ciudad autónoma española desde Marruecos ha dado pie, además, para romper otro tabú en el sistema de asilo europeo. La presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Ursula von der Leyen, ha propuesto este miércoles ante el Parlamento Euorpeo una nueva regulación que permitiría a los Estados miembros suspender —“flexibilizar”, lo ha llamado ella— las reglas migratorias, en casos de crisis. La propuesta de la conservadora alemana durante su discurso sobre el estado de la Unión constata un nuevo endurecimiento de la postura sobre asilo de una UE que se blinda y busca ya lanzar centros de deportación fuera de sus fronteras.

Las imágenes de decenas de miles de migrantes cruzando desde Marruecos a Ceuta, sacudieron la UE este verano. Apenas han ocupado unas líneas del discurso de 22 de páginas de Von der Leyen, una alocución llena de anuncios y guiños al espíritu europeo. Pero la conservadora alemana ha hablado de esa y otras crisis migratorias (como las de los bálticos) y ha culpado a las mafias de tráfico de personas y a los “adversarios” de la UE de utilizara “personas vulnerables” contra el club comunitario. “La frontera de Ceuta es una frontera europea porque Ceuta es España, Ceuta es Europa”, ha declarado, solemne.

Von der Leyen ha asegurado que la respuesta a la migración es el pacto de migración y asilo, que entró en vigor en julio y que endurece las condiciones para los solicitantes de asilo que llegan a Europa. Pero también ha dejado claro que ese conjunto de normas se podrá suspender con ese “nuevo marco europeo de respuesta ante emergencias” con el que, ante situaciones parecidas, se podrá “de forma temporal” dar “flexibilidad en los procedimientos estándar” de las normas europeas sobre migración.

No ha dado más detalles, pero parece claro que lo que planteará en ese nuevo marco será la suspensión “por un tiempo limitado y de forma estrictamente definida” de las reglas migratorias con el fin de acelerar y facilitar los retornos. “Los acontecimientos de este verano demuestran que nuestras herramientas deben evolucionar, sobre todo en situaciones de emergencia. Europa necesita los medios necesarios para proteger sus fronteras en todo momento. Especialmente en situaciones en las que los movimientos masivos se organizan y se utilizan como arma”, ha justificado Von der Leyen, después de destacar que “la frontera de Ceuta es una frontera europea, porque Ceuta es España, Ceuta es Europa y Europa está ahí para vosotros”.

Los argumentos usados para andar por esta senda también descansan en la seguridad exterior: “Desde nuestras fronteras orientales hasta las costas de Creta y a lo largo de todo el Mediterráneo. Y, por supuesto, con la crisis de Ceuta. Estos sucesos son de naturaleza diferente. Pero tienen dos cosas en común. La primera es que se está explotando a personas vulnerables por parte de traficantes y contrabandistas sin escrúpulos, y por parte de nuestros adversarios”, ha subrayado en una clara referencia a episodios como lo sucedido hace varios años en la frontera de Polonia y Lituania, cuando Rusia y Bielorrusia usaron migrantes en una suerte de ataque híbrido a sus fronteras.

“Protocolo ante emergencias”

Moscú ha estado muy presente en su discurso. La invasión de Ucrania hace ya más de cuatro años disparó todas las alarmas de seguridad y defensa en la UE y estas cada vez suenan con más fuerza. Los fallidos ataques con drones sobre el aeropuerto de Leipzig en Alemania este verano han elevado todavía más esta alerta. Y por eso, y por la desconfianza justificada en el histórico aliado estadounidense, Von der Leyen ha puesto sobre la mesa la creación de un “protocolo de seguridad ante emergencias” cuando uno de los Estados sienta que hay una amenaza exterior sobre su seguridad: incursiones de drones, ciberataques, sabotajes. “Amenazas que están creciendo cada día”.

“Nos estamos enfrentando a un mundo abiertamente hostil”, ha advertido. Y eso le ha llevado a ir más lejos en este punto que en migración. Lo ha hecho poniendo un ejemplo de cómo funcionaría ese mecanismo: como el artículo 4 de la OTAN, en el que se contempla la que los aliados se consultarán cuando una de ellas se sienta en peligro. La presidenta de la Comisión ha huido de dar la idea de que su propuesta va separada de la Alianza Atlántica. “Estamos reforzando nuestro trabajo con la OTAN”, ha proclamado.

En el capítulo comercial también ha tenido un lugar considerable China. Von der Leyen ha destacado que el déficit comercial (diferencia entre importaciones y exportaciones) para la UE ronda los 1.000 millones de euros. Para corregirlo, ha recordado que se está negociando con el gigante asiático, pero que eso no basta: “Las palabras son buenas, pero los hechos son mejores”, ha dicho. “Usaremos todas las herramientas a nuestro alcance para reequilibrar la relación”, ha agregado, sin dar más detalles.

World.title: La fiscal jefa de Ceuta pide esclarecer si hubo “omisión de medidas” del delegado del Gobierno ceutí ante la entrada masiva de migrantes
World.content:
La fiscal jefa de Ceuta, Silvia Rojas, ha apuntado a la posible responsabilidad del delegado de Gobierno en Ceuta, Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, por la “omisión de medidas” para “evitar el resultado lesivo en la avalancha migratoria”. En un escrito en el que daba luz verde para que las denuncias contra Pérez Triano se trasladasen a la Audiencia Nacional ―donde la jueza María Tardón ya ha iniciado una macrocausa en la que analizar lo sucedido los días 30 y 31 de julio, cuando más de 70.000 personas entraron en la ciudad autónoma―, la fiscal señala que es preciso que se investigue la planificación y el desarrollo de esta entrada masiva, además de “la información de la que disponían las autoridades españolas” para aclarar lo ocurrido. Fuentes fiscales insisten, no obstante, en que el ministerio público no se ha pronunciado todavía sobre el fondo de la investigación y que este escrito solo trata de valorar la competencia del órgano que debe dirigir la instrucción.

En el documento, avanzado por El Confidencial y al que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS, la fiscal Rojas indica que bajo el foco allí en Ceuta estaban los fallecimientos producidos durante la travesía a nado desde la playa de Fnideq hasta la de El Tarajal a finales de julio y las medidas que se implementaron esos días, y se muestra favorable a que toda la materia se traslade a la Audiencia Nacional porque considera que la causa de estas muertes no puede desvincularse de la investigación sobre la organización, convocatoria y ejecución del flujo masivo de personas que estaba dirigiendo la jueza María Tardón. Este escrito de la fiscal ceutí es anterior a que la juez titular de la plaza número 6 de la Sección Civil y de Instrucción del Tribunal de Instancia de Ceuta, María de la Luz Lozano, ya decidiera juntar los asuntos y remitiera toda la causa este lunes a Tardón para que todo lo relacionado con la gran entrada al territorio español se dirima desde el órgano con sede en Madrid.

“No se trata de hechos aislados o independientes, sino de actuaciones que presentan una unidad de contexto, de tiempo, de espacio y de finalidad”, incide la representante del ministerio público ceutí, que lleva 22 años en la ciudad autónoma y que en una reciente entrevista con EL PAÍS expuso que lo que había ocurrido allí no tenía ningún precedente. Según Rojas, es necesario saber cómo se produjo la movilización de miles de personas, quiénes la promovieron o facilitaron, qué instrucciones se impartieron, qué medios se utilizaron y cuál es la incidencia de las actuaciones desarrolladas en el territorio español. La causa de la Audiencia Nacional se ha desplegado así en varias direcciones: conocer quién pudo estar detrás de las convocatorias y si, como apunta el Centro Nacional de Inmigración y Fronteras (CENIF) de la Policía en uno de sus informes, pudo haber ayuda de la gendarmería marroquí; y esclarecer si desde el lado español de la frontera se actuó de forma correcta con la información que existía.

Precisamente, la información ha sido un punto de discordia entre el delegado del Gobierno y el propio Ejecutivo y algunos cuerpos como la Policía, la Guardia Civil o el Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI). Pérez Triano aseguró reiteradamente que su jefe de gabinete, Gonzalo Sanz, nunca le transmitió lo que había hablado con un jefe del CNI que le advirtió el día 29 de julio de las convocatorias masivas que se estaban anunciando en redes sociales para “asaltar la valla” de Ceuta. Pero Sanz rechaza que no contara nada a su superior y, de hecho, ha dimitido dejando un correo en el que dice que existen pruebas de cómo la información se transmitió a los distintos ministerios responsables.

El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, defendió el pasado 9 de septiembre, tras la desclasificación de los informes y comunicaciones mantenidos sobre la situación de Ceuta, que la información que disponía el Ejecutivo “en modo alguno constituía o podía interpretarse como un indicador de la escala, naturaleza o probabilidad de lo que pasó” los días 30 y 31 de julio en la comunidad autónoma. “Nadie podía anticipar la crisis migratoria que se produjo”, apuntó en un mensaje que publicó en la red social X.

La fiscal de Ceuta ya apunta lo que, de alguna manera, sobrevolaba en los mentideros judiciales las últimas semanas: que el delegado de Gobierno tendrá que aclarar en sede judicial qué conoció esos días y cómo actuó. Rojas dice que la “eventual responsabilidad de Miguel Ángel Triano” se basará en “las decisiones adoptadas, las instrucciones impartidas, la organización de los dispositivos de seguridad y recepción, la gestión de la situación creada y la eventual omisión de medidas que pudieran haber resultado necesarias para prevenir o evitar el resultado lesivo”. Incluso, va un paso más allá y refleja la necesidad de esclarecer qué se conocía en el Ejecutivo. La investigación de la conducta del delegado del Gobierno “exige examinar conjuntamente las circunstancias en las que se produjo la entrada masiva de personas a nado, la información de la que disponían las autoridades españolas, las previsiones y medidas adoptadas antes de la llegada de las personas a la costa de Ceuta, la organización de los dispositivos de vigilancia, contención, auxilio y recepción de órdenes, instrucciones o decisiones impartidas por las autoridades competentes”, así como “la eventual existencia de omisiones relevantes en materia de prevención, auxilio o protección”.

Por su parte, fuentes de la Fiscalía General del Estado han querido aclarar que desde el ministerio público no se ha hecho un pronunciamiento formal sobre el fondo del asunto. Lo que se ha emitido es, de un lado, este informe de la fiscal de Ceuta para avalar la competencia de la Audiencia Nacional y, por otro, otro informe del fiscal jefe de ese órgano, Jesús Alonso, que será el que se quede con las riendas de la instrucción. Alonso señaló el pasado 4 de septiembre que se pudieron producir delitos de favorecimiento de inmigración ilegal, homicidio y lesiones por imprudencia grave, y organización criminal, y solicitó a la juez Tardón que la causa se declarara secreta. La magistrada aceptó que una parte de la investigación se desarrollara bajo secreto parcial y, de momento, no ha llamado a declarar a nadie como investigado. La togada ha pedido al Gobierno que entregue los documentos que se han desclasificado y había solicitado a los juzgados ceutíes que habían recibido denuncias que se las remitieran.

World.title: Madrid se reinventa desde el norte: así será la capital del futuro
World.content:
Madrid Nuevo Norte se extenderá a lo largo de 5,6 kilómetros. En la imagen, simulación de una vista aérea del proyecto una vez finalizado.

El proyecto Madrid Nuevo Norte plantea un revolucionario cambio de enfoque en la transformación urbana: se regenerarán 2,3 millones de metros cuadrados de suelo para adaptarlos a los grandes retos sociales, ambientales y económicos del nuevo modelo de ciudad del siglo XXI

Habla

A pocos metros de la estación de Chamartín-Clara Campoamor, punto de conexión ferroviaria de Madrid con el norte de España, se está gestando la mayor transformación urbana del país y una de las más ambiciosas de Europa. El proyecto Madrid Nuevo Norte, aprobado definitivamente por la Comunidad de Madrid en 2020, y en obras desde comienzos de este año, trae consigo un singular cambio de enfoque en el urbanismo: la tendencia actual es que las grandes ciudades no se expandan, sino que regeneren espacios urbanos dentro de ellas que han quedado en desuso. Se trata de una apuesta deliberada para repensar cómo deben crecer las grandes metrópolis y afrontar los retos del siglo XXI con la mirada puesta en la sostenibilidad, la movilidad y la cohesión vecinal.

El proyecto se extiende a lo largo de 5,6 kilómetros desde la plaza de Castilla, al norte de la ciudad, hasta la autopista M-40, conectando la capital con el monte de El Pardo y abarca más de 2,3 millones de metros cuadrados de suelo que serán regenerados para aprovechar al máximo su potencial.

Transformar esa superficie es el principal objetivo de la mayor iniciativa de colaboración de instituciones públicas y privadas que proyecta la capital. “Es mucho más que un desarrollo urbanístico o inmobiliario”, explica José Ignacio Morales, consejero delegado de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte, la compañía que lidera esta propuesta desde la iniciativa privada. “No estamos hablando simplemente de construir nuevos edificios, sino de crear una nueva centralidad para la ciudad capaz de generar actividad económica, oportunidades y calidad de vida”.

La próxima revolución urbana de Madrid Un impacto de miles de millones de euros Según los estudios realizados por la Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, por encargo de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte, el proyecto aportará a lo largo de su desarrollo 15.000 millones de euros al producto interior bruto (PIB) nacional y generará 350.000 empleos.



Fotos: Simulaciones cedidas por Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte. Un jardín con su propio microclima Se crearán 400.000 metros cuadrados de zonas verdes. Entre ellas, el denominado Jardín del Viento (en la imagen), una estructura en forma de espiral que se erigirá en uno de los parques y quedará cubierta por vegetación, haciendo circular el viento y aportando humedad al ambiente lo que contribuirá a producir su propio microclima y reducir las temperaturas en verano. Puentes para comunicar las ‘orillas’ El proyecto va a subsanar una de las principales demandas vecinales: comunicar las dos orillas que separan las vías del tren de la estación de Chamartín y Fuencarral. Para ello, al sur de la M-30 se creará un gran parque que cubrirá la playa de vías de la estación de Chamartín-Clara Campoamor y al norte, ya en Fuencarral-El Pardo, levantarán cinco puentes, un túnel y una pasarela peatonal. 10.500 viviendas nuevas En el conjunto de Madrid Nuevo Norte se van a construir 10.500 nuevas viviendas. Del total, 4.000 inmuebles -el 38%- estarán en manos del Ayuntamiento de Madrid, para destinarlos a distintas fórmulas de acceso a un hogar. Un centro de negocios integrado en el barrio Se construirá un complejo de edificios de oficinas con un innovador enfoque: frente a la habitual dinámica de levantar distritos empresariales, aislados o incluso fuera de las ciudades, el nuevo centro negocios estará completamente integrado en el barrio junto a viviendas, comercios y espacios públicos para favorecer que exista actividad durante todo el día. Refuerzo de la movilidad Madrid Nuevo Norte incluye una línea de metro de tres kilómetros de longitud y tres nuevas paradas. Se sumará también una nueva estación de cercanías, Fuencarral Norte (en la imagen, una recreación), y se proporcionará un sistema de Bus Prioritario (BRT) con plataforma propia y más de tres kilómetros de recorrido. El nuevo centro de la Alta Velocidad El proyecto incluye la renovación de la estación de Chamartín-Clara Campoamor para convertirla en el centro de la alta velocidad del país.

Miguel Hernández, arquitecto y director de Estrategia de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte, ha formado parte del equipo del proyecto desde su concepción. “Tradicionalmente, los urbanistas imaginaban la ciudad futura, la dibujaban, la sociedad se lo creía y todo se desarrollaba en función de ello”. Y para ilustrar el cambio de mentalidad que supone Madrid Nuevo Norte, explica: “Aquí decidimos hacerlo al revés, consultando a la ciudadanía y a expertos en distintas materias, para detectar necesidades reales de hoy y los posibles retos de las próximas décadas y diseñar una ciudad centrada en las personas y adaptable”.

Madrid Nuevo Norte es una operación estratégica que va a permitir a la ciudad afrontar los grandes retos de las capitales del mundo José Ignacio Morales, CEO de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte

El resultado de este proceso integra “la vida de barrio”, es decir, las viviendas, los servicios públicos o los comercios, junto al nuevo centro de negocios con oficinas y sus trabajadores. “Nadie sabe realmente cómo va a ser el futuro, y una vez ejecutado el urbanismo, es muy difícil de modificar. Puedes cambiar el uso a un edificio, pero no puedes mover de lugar una calle”, concluye Hernández.

Madrid Nuevo Norte está diseñado para ir más allá de un concepto que se ha popularizado en los últimos años: la ciudad de los 15 minutos, un sistema de planificación urbana por el que la mayoría de las necesidades básicas que tiene un ciudadano se cubren en una distancia que pueda recorrerse a pie en un cuarto de hora. ”A nosotros nos gusta más hablar de la región de los 45 minutos”, comenta Hernández. “A 15 minutos se pueden tener las necesidades básicas, pero es imposible ubicar las mejores oportunidades de empleo, que es lo que va a proporcionar Madrid Nuevo Norte, a esa distancia para todos los ciudadanos”, explica.

Y aquí es donde juega un papel determinante la estación de Chamartín -Clara Campoamor, que ya está acometiendo su completa transformación y que está llamada a convertirse en el mayor nodo de hiperaccesibilidad en transporte público de Madrid.

“Según nuestros estudios”, continúa el arquitecto, “alrededor de 4 millones de ciudadanos de toda la Comunidad de Madrid van a poder acceder hasta este punto en transporte público desde sus casas en menos de 45 minutos”.

Nos gusta más hablar de la región de los 45 minutos que de la ciudad de los 15, porque es imposible que las mejores oportunidades de empleo estén a 15 minutos de todos los ciudadanos Miguel Hernández, director de Estrategia de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte

Gracias a las ventajas que ofrece Madrid por su calidad de vida y su conexión internacional, el nuevo centro de negocios de Madrid Nuevo Norte atraerá no solo talento nacional, sino que permitirá crear un hub de talento internacional en la capital. Los cálculos de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte apuntan a que habrá un tránsito de millones de pasajeros al año cuando la nueva city empresarial funcione a pleno rendimiento. Como respuesta a las exigencias de este objetivo, se reforzarán las conexiones de la Chamartín-Clara Campoamor con el aeropuerto de Madrid-Barajas-Adolfo Suárez.

Un nuevo concepto de movilidad

Responder a las grandes demandas de movilidad era uno de los grandes desafíos. En este apartado, el planteamiento también fue “a la inversa”, explica Jorge Serrano, director técnico de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte. Primero diseñaron las fórmulas más sostenibles para que los ciudadanos puedan desplazarse a pie, en bicicleta o transporte público, y, a partir de ahí, definieron la estructura de las calles y la distribución de los edificios e integraron los nuevos trazados para el vehículo privado.

El resultado, según Serrano, se traduce en “calles más equilibradas, con mayor calidad urbana donde moverse deja de ser únicamente una cuestión de circulación para convertirse en una herramienta con la que mejorar el espacio público”. Con esa premisa integraron todos los sistemas de movilidad como una experiencia completa del usuario. “Hemos trabajado para que las conexiones sean más rápidas, intuitivas y cómodas, con el objetivo de reducir al máximo las fricciones entre modos de transporte”, argumenta Serrano.

En el proyecto primero se tuvieron en cuenta las fórmulas de movilidad sostenible, como los desplazamientos a pie o en transporte público (en la imagen, una simulación de un bulevar), y posteriormente se integraron los trazados para los vehículos privados. CREA MADRID NUEVO NORTE

Entretanto, los esfuerzos se centran ahora en que las obras afecten lo menos posible al día a día de los vecinos. Serrano da la clave: “Anticipar. En proyectos de esta escala es muy importante planificar con mucho detalle antes de comenzar a construir”. Algo que requiere una coordinación permanente con administraciones, operadores ferroviarios, empresas constructoras y equipos técnicos durante todas las fases de desarrollo. Y, a los vecinos de la zona, “mantenerlos informados de cualquier novedad y de las medidas de control”.

Como ingeniero urbano, Serrano considera que la mayor innovación es abordar de forma conjunta aspectos como la sostenibilidad, la infraestructura verde, el gasto de energía o la digitalización. “Esto ha sido posible gracias al trabajo desde el inicio con equipos multidisciplinares, con una visión transversal que será una de las principales referencias para las grandes transformaciones urbanas del futuro”.

Unanimidad política

Madrid Nuevo Norte consiguió salir adelante gracias a un consenso político tras 26 años de bloqueo por falta de acuerdo entre los partidos del Consistorio madrileño. El 29 de julio de 2019, el pleno del Ayuntamiento de Madrid, que en ese momento regía la alcaldesa Manuela Carmena, reunió la unanimidad en el voto de todas las formaciones políticas y dio luz verde al inicio del proyecto.

Ahora que han comenzado las obras, los esfuerzos se centran en que afecten lo menos posible al día a día de los vecinos. Para ello, la clave es anticipar Jorge Serrano, director técnico de Crea Madrid Nuevo Norte

A juicio de Miguel Hernández, la clave fue “lograr despolitizar la iniciativa y abordarla como un proyecto estratégico de ciudad”. “Entendimos que era necesario abordar una discusión en torno al modelo de ciudad para lograr establecer unos principios en los que todos estuviéramos de acuerdo. Así se entendió y el pleno lo aprobó por unanimidad, algo que no es tan común”.

Con las obras en marcha, la dimensión de Madrid Nuevo Norte ha conseguido reclamar la atención de algunas de las principales capitales del mundo. “Aquí han venido a aprender cómo lo estamos haciendo equipos técnicos de Ámsterdam, París, Corea del Sur, Japón, Estados Unidos... Ciudades y países que son referencias urbanísticas”, cuenta con orgullo Hernández. “A Madrid le faltaba un proyecto con el que la ciudad se sienta absolutamente emocionada. Y trabajamos para que sea este”.

World.title: El acta de nacimiento del ‘R3’, el nuevo jefe del Cartel Jalisco, revela datos inéditos sobre sus orígenes en California
World.content:
Tras la muerte del Mencho, su hijastro Juan Carlos Valencia González pasó a ser el nuevo líder del cartel y el fugitivo más buscado de la DEA. Nació en un centro privado en un suburbio a unos 50 kilómetros al sur de Los Ángeles

En los espacios destinados para poner la información del padre aparece la abreviatura “N/A” por “No aplica”. Así quedó oculto el nombre de Armando Valencia Cornelio, uno de los fundadores del Cartel del Milenio. El recién nacido registrado en esa acta de nacimiento, emitida por el Gobierno de California, era Juan Carlos Valencia González también conocido como R3. Cuatro décadas después se convertiría en el primer jefe de una organización mexicana de tráfico de drogas —el Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG)— que nació en territorio estadounidense, una enorme paradoja ante la retórica antidrogas del Gobierno de Donald Trump.

La michoacana Rosalinda González Valencia, entonces de 21 años, decidió registrar a su primer hijo como madre soltera. Según consta en una copia del acta de nacimiento del capo, obtenida por EL PAÍS, así quedó asentado en el documento: Juan Carlos Gonzalez (sin tílde), un nombre que con los años se sumaría a la lista de alias que las autoridades le atribuyen, entre ellos R3, El Pelón, El JP, 03, Tricky Tres y Pelacas .

Un error o un enredo involuntario en el registro civil de California también terminó alterando la identidad de Rosalinda, una anomalía que complicaría su localización en los archivos. “Valencia” quedó asentado como si fuera su segundo nombre y “González”, como apellido paterno. Ella dejó el registro tal como había quedado.

Acta de nacimiento de Juan Carlos Valencia González. Departamento de Estado

El primogénito de Rosalinda nació a las 00.15 de la madrugada del miércoles 12 de septiembre de 1984. El parto ocurrió en el Mercy General Hospital, un centro médico privado de Santa Ana, un suburbio situado a unos 50 kilómetros al sur de Los Ángeles. Aquel año nacieron allí 1.215 bebés.

El hospital, ubicado sobre la calle Bristol y que hoy es conocido como South Coast Global Medical Center, atendía tanto a pacientes con capacidad para pagar sus cuentas, como a familias de bajos ingresos que dependían de programas de asistencia pública. Era una época de salas de maternidad abarrotadas en el condado de Orange por un aumento de la tasa de natalidad que atribuían a la llegada de mexicanos y de otros inmigrantes latinos, cuya presencia transformaría la demografía de Santa Ana. En ese entonces, el republicano George Deukmejian gobernaba California y Ronald Reagan ocupaba la Casa Blanca.

La misteriosa infancia del ‘R3′

El acta de nacimiento de Juan Carlos González Valencia sería el último registro público suyo localizado en los archivos del condado de Orange. A partir de 1986 y durante los años siguientes, Rosalinda dio a luz en San Francisco, en el norte de California, a los tres hijos que procreó con Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, El Mencho, fundador del CJNG. Es posible que El R3 haya pasado sus primeros años junto a su madre, su padrastro y sus hermanastros en el área de la Bahía. Lo ocurrido durante esa etapa permanece como un misterio.

Mientras El Mencho daba sus primeros pasos en el crimen como vendedor de heroína en San Francisco y cumplía en prisión dos condenas por ese delito —fue detenido en 1986 y 1989, antes de ser deportado—, Rosalinda se ganaba la vida como podía. “Mis trabajos fueron en el campo, en empacadoras, limpiando casas, cuidando niños y en restaurantes. Todo con el fin de salir adelante”, escribió en una carta enviada a un tribunal de Washington D.C., en la que relató que había emigrado a Estados Unidos a los 14 años.

Décadas después, en el cénit del reinado de El Mencho, aquella familia y sus cómplices habían construido una extensa red empresarial en México que incluía hoteles, restaurantes, tequileras, gasolineras y hasta un negocio de zapatos infantiles. La DEA calculaba que la fortuna del narco superaba los 1.000 millones de dólares y lo situaba entre los delincuentes más ricos del mundo.

La ruta académica de la hermanastra del R3, Jessica Johanna Oseguera González, da una idea de dónde pudo pasar parte de su adolescencia. De acuerdo con diplomas académicos de la hija del Mencho, que constan en su expediente judicial, en el verano de 1998 ella concluyó la primaria en la escuela Amalia Solórzano de Cárdenas, en Apatzingán, Michoacán. En esa época, Juan Carlos González Valencia tenía 13 años. En 1999, la inscribieron en la secundaria Castle Park de la ciudad fronteriza de Chula Vista, en California. En 2000, estaba inscrita en la secundaria Colegio Inglés de Tijuana, México, donde concluyó sus estudios y continuó a la preparatoria. Pero en 2001 Jessica Johanna había regresado al sureste mexicano: fue inscrita en la preparatoria Instituto Ausubel de Morelia, Michoacán. Allí cursó hasta el cuarto semestre. En el año escolar 2004 estaba en la preparatoria Jefferson, en la misma ciudad.

Un capo ‘Made in California’

Después de su acta de nacimiento, el siguiente rastro documental del nuevo jefe del CJNG localizado en los archivos públicos del sur de California aparece en marzo de 2011. A los 26 años, compró por 250.000 dólares un rancho de 19.468 metros cuadrados en Hemet, una propiedad cuyo valor actual llega a 695.000 dólares. En el registro del condado de Riverside, revisado por EL PAÍS, el nombre del capo aparece tal como figura en su acta de nacimiento: solo con el apellido de su madre.

A finales de julio, el Gobierno de Trump inició el proceso para decomisar la finca, en el marco de las sanciones que meses antes le había impuesto la Oficina de Control de Activos Extranjeros (OFAC). Pero el Departamento de Justicia va más allá. La acusación presentada ante una corte del Distrito de Columbia —que le imputa un cargo de conspiración para producir y distribuir cocaína y metanfetamina, y otro por uso de armas de fuego— advierte que el Gobierno buscará decomisar todos los bienes que El R3 haya adquirido con ganancias procedentes del tráfico de drogas.

Le sobran familiares al nuevo patrón del CJNG en el sur de California: tiene tíos, primos y sobrinos que viven o han vivido en Santa Ana, Anaheim, Orange, Garden Grove, Lake Forest, Laguna Niguel, San Jacinto, Hemet y Riverside. Algunos han estado bajo la lupa de la agencia antinarcóticos DEA durante varios años.
