World.title: Prague Is Turning a Historic Factory Chimney Into an Observation Deck
World.content:
A glass elevator will carry visitors through the preserved chimney of a former distillery before emerging above its rim to reveal views of the city.

Inside the developing Lihovar district in Smíchov, a historic factory chimney is being transformed into a viewing platform, with visitors set to travel through the structure in a panoramic glass elevator.



The chimney, which stands approximately 50 meters tall, is part of the former Zlíchov distillery. Rather than demolishing the industrial landmark, developers have incorporated it into the redevelopment of the site.

The project is being developed by Trigema, which is building the new Lihovar district on the former distillery grounds.

The elevator itself is one of the project’s most unusual features. Once it reaches the top of the chimney, the cabin will lift a special cap weighing approximately 500 kilograms, allowing it to rise above the chimney’s opening.

The glass cabin will then serve as an observation deck, offering a 360-degree view of Prague.

From industrial site to new Prague district

The Lihovar development is being built on the site of the former Zlíchov distillery in Prague 5. The redevelopment includes new buildings alongside the preservation of selected elements of the original industrial complex.

The factory chimney is among the structures being retained. Another is the historic former brewhouse, which is planned for cultural use.

The opening date for the observation deck has not been announced.

World.title: Riegrovy Sady to Host Goodbye Summer Party With Three Live Acts
World.content:
Summer may be drawing to a close, but the music season at Riegrovy Sady is not over yet.

On Thursday, 17 September, Energy Pub will host the Goodbye Summer Party, organised by Ploom in cooperation with Energy Pub.



The evening will feature a DJ set by Forgen, a performance by Jirka Drtil and a live concert by Renne Dang, following his sold-out show at Forum Karlín.

Tickets cost CZK 100 and the event is open exclusively to guests aged 18 and over.

The last long days and warm evenings of summer will get a musical send-off at Riegrovy Sady. The Goodbye Summer Party is designed for everyone who is not quite ready to say a final goodbye to summer and wants to enjoy one of the last outdoor evenings of the season.

The evening will kick off with a set by DJ Forgen, followed by a performance by musician Jirka Drtil. The main highlight of the evening will be a concert by Renne Dang, Ploom brand ambassador, whose current music blends elements of rap, pop and pop-punk.

His distinctive personal lyrics and energetic guitar-driven sound have already taken him to some of the country’s biggest stages. His recent achievements include a sold-out concert at Forum Karlín.

The Last Party of the Summer

Music will not be the only reason to head to Riegrovy Sady in September. The evening will also feature a dedicated Ploom zone, where adult guests can take a break during the programme and enjoy the atmosphere of one last summer party.

Every ticket holder will also receive a complimentary welcome drink. A food pop-up by Pavel Berky will be part of the event as well.

When: Thursday, 17 September 2026, doors open at 6:00 PM

Where: Energy Pub, Riegrovy Sady 28, Prague 2

Line-up: DJ Forgen, Jirka Drtil, Renne Dang

Tickets: CZK 100, including a welcome drink

Entry: 18+ only

Capacity: Limited

World.title: Fresh from France: Meet Benjamin, the Founder of The French in Prague
World.content:
For the past 12 years, Benjamin has been building a life in Prague – and helping bring a taste of France to the Czech capital.

What began as a business supplying wine to hotels, restaurants and wine bars 10 years ago has gradually grown into The French, a food business focused on bringing French products directly to Prague.

The company started with an e-shop selling mainly wine, pâté, jam, honey and foie gras. But Benjamin soon realized there was something missing: fresh French produce.

“The idea, step by step, was that we were missing fresh products to be able to open a physical shop. That’s how, two years ago, we started importing fresh products.”

Today, The French operates two shops in Prague and imports a wide range of products directly from France, with a focus on freshness and quality while keeping prices accessible.

“It cannot be fresher than what we import.”

From Breakfast to Dinner

Fresh fruit and vegetables have become one of the shop’s main attractions. The products are imported weekly, with a truck leaving France every Tuesday carrying oysters, mussels, cheeses, fish, meat, fruits and vegetables.

“Two days ago it was in the sea and today it’s already in Prague, sitting in our fridge.”

The shop aims to cover the entire day, from breakfast to dinner. Customers can pick up croissants and pain au chocolat in the morning, fresh coffee, and a selection of French products for lunch and dinner.

Among the more distinctive products are French crème fraîche and salted butter. Benjamin points out that the natural colour of the dairy products can change during the year depending on what the cows eat. “If you have the same colour of butter or cream throughout the whole year, it’s because they are not eating grass.”

A New Home in Vinohrady

The company recently expanded with a larger shop in Vinohrady, giving customers access to a wider range of ultra-fresh products imported directly from France, as well as cosmetics from Provence.

The French also supplies restaurants and hotels across Prague with products including butter, cream, cheese, ham, sausages and olives. Much of the range comes directly from the Rungis International Market near Paris, one of the largest food markets in Europe.

The company also works with direct farmers, with some products clearly marked as coming from individual producers. “In Prague, you don’t have any shop that is grouping all of these categories of products.”

Customers can also order through The French’s e-shop at francouzske-speciality.cz and either have their purchases delivered or collect them from a shop.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The French.cz (@the_french_cz)

But Benjamin says the experience is intended to be more personal than a standard supermarket. “We are not a shop where people are just behind the cash desk. We have people going into the shop to explain what we have, recommend what to cook and what to pair.”

The shops also have a weekly tasting calendar, giving customers the chance to try different products and discover new flavours.

French Food for Everyone

Although many customers are French, The French is not specifically aimed at the French community.

The Vinohrady shop attracts a large number of expats, while the company’s Prague 4 location has a much higher proportion of Czech customers. Benjamin says the goal is to serve people living in the neighborhood regardless of nationality. “We are not targeting especially expats or especially French. We are trying to target everyone living in the area who like gastronomy.”

There are, however, some differences in what Czech and French customers look for. Stronger French cheeses, for example, can take some getting used to, while certain French cuts of meat differ from traditional Czech ones.

Some types of fish are also relatively unfamiliar. Red mullet, or rouget, is widely used in French cuisine and high-end restaurants but is less common in Czech kitchens.

Growing Across Prague

The French has ambitious plans for the coming years. After opening its Vinohrady location and another shop in Prague 4, the company is preparing to open another location in Prague 9 in January.

The long-term goal is to operate five or six shops across Prague, with Holešovice, Karlín and Dejvice among the areas being considered.

World.title: Prague Has the Most Unaffordable Rents for Minimum-Wage Earners in the EU
World.content:
Prague has the highest rent-to-minimum-wage ratio among EU capitals, with the average two-bedroom apartment costing 185% of the gross minimum wage.

Prague has become the European Union’s least affordable capital for minimum-wage earners looking to rent a home, according to a new analysis by the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC).



The average monthly rent for a two-bedroom apartment in the Czech capital reaches €1,710, compared with a gross monthly minimum wage of €924. This means rent alone amounts to 185% of the minimum wage.

Lisbon follows in second place, with rent accounting for 168% of the gross minimum wage. Budapest ranks third at 159%, followed by Bratislava at 158%.

Other capitals where average rent exceeds the gross minimum wage include Sofia (154%), Athens (153%), and Riga (151%).

The figures highlight the pressure facing minimum-wage earners in cities where housing costs have risen significantly faster than incomes.

How Prague Compares with Western Europe

Prague’s position is particularly striking when compared with several Western European capitals.

In Paris, average rent accounts for 138% of the gross minimum wage, while the figure stands at 125% in Madrid and 113% in Dublin.

At the other end of the ranking, Brussels is the most affordable capital for minimum-wage earners in the comparison. Average rent there represents 70% of the gross minimum wage. Berlin follows at 76%, while the figure is 85% in Nicosia and 87% in Luxembourg.

Housing Costs Across the EU

According to Eurostat’s latest figures cited in the analysis, housing and utility bills account for 23.6% of household spending across the European Union.

The ETUC has called for stronger collective bargaining, greater consideration of housing costs when setting minimum wages, and increased investment in social housing.

The organisation also noted that rents can be more affordable when measured against national minimum wages rather than those in capital cities. Among the 16 EU countries analysed, the share of the gross minimum wage required for rent ranged from 33% in Poland to 61% in Malta.

World.title: Prague 8 Pirates to Host English-Language Guide to Czech Local Elections
World.content:
EU citizens living in Prague 8 can learn how to vote in the upcoming municipal elections at an event on 17 September.

The Prague 8 branch of the Czech Pirate Party is inviting international residents to an English-language evening explaining how EU citizens can take part in Czech local elections.

The event, titled “Hey, You Can Vote Too!”, will take place on Thursday, 17 September, at 6 PM at Pauza Palmovka in Prague 8.



The evening will offer a practical introduction to the Czech voting system, an overview of the Prague 8 Pirates’ local programme, and an opportunity for international residents to share their views on life in the district.

Organisers say the event is intended to help EU citizens understand their voting rights and discuss what they would like to see improved in Prague 8.

Who Can Vote in Czech Local Elections?

Citizens of other EU Member States can vote in Czech municipal elections if they meet certain conditions.

Voters must:

Be at least 18 years old by the second day of the election.

Have permanent or registered temporary residence in the municipality.

Be entered in the supplement to the permanent electoral register.

EU citizens who are not already registered must apply by 7 October 2026 at 4 PM.

“Many people from other EU countries live in Prague 8, work here, raise their families here and use the same schools, parks, streets and public services as everyone else. Yet many still do not know that they can vote in local elections,” said Martin Štěrba, the Czech Pirate Party’s candidate for mayor of Prague 8.

“We want to explain how it works and hear directly from them what Prague 8 could do better.”

The Czech municipal elections will take place on 9 and 10 October 2026.

Voters in Prague 8 will elect representatives to both the Prague 8 Municipal District Council and the Prague City Assembly.

World.title: Nearly 40 Percent of Young Czechs Experience Financial Stress Every Month
World.content:
Money worries affect almost one in three Czech adults, but younger people are facing a greater burden.

A new survey found that 39 percent of people aged 18 to 26 experience financial anxiety at least once a month, with household income playing a major role in how people feel about their finances.



Financial concerns are common across the Czech Republic. According to a survey conducted by Ipsos for Home Credit, 28 percent of adults experience worries about money at least once a month. Another 35 percent report financial stress several times a year.

Young adults face the greatest pressure

People aged 18 to 26 are the most likely to experience regular financial stress. Nearly four in ten respondents in this age group said they worry about money at least once a month.

Home Credit attributed the pressure partly to the cost of housing and everyday expenses. For young adults trying to establish themselves financially, rising prices in recent years have made it harder to absorb unexpected costs.

An unplanned bill or other expense can therefore create a serious problem, particularly for those who have limited savings.

Household income makes a significant difference

The survey found a clear relationship between household income and financial anxiety.

Among households earning up to CZK 40,000 per month, 41 percent of respondents reported experiencing financial stress. The proportion decreases as household income rises.

People living in households with monthly incomes above CZK 70,000 reported the lowest levels of financial concern.

Age and education also appear to influence how people view their finances. Respondents aged 54 to 65 and university students reported lower levels of stress than some other groups. In both categories, 43 percent said they did not experience financial stress at all.

Financial stress may also affect physical health

The consequences of financial difficulties can extend beyond anxiety and everyday worries.

The material also refers to research published by the American Mayo Clinic in 2025. According to the research cited, long-term financial distress and food insecurity may be associated with poorer cardiovascular health and a higher risk of death.

The findings underline the potential connection between financial security and overall well-being. However, the Czech survey does not establish whether financial stress directly causes health problems.

The survey was conducted by Ipsos in June 2026 among 1,026 people.

World.title: 10 Chinese guest workers and 37 bunk beds found at former restaurant building in Szeged
World.content:
Authorities found 10 Chinese guest workers and 37 metal bunk beds at a former restaurant in Szeged during inspections in late July. Officials subsequently determined that the building, in its current condition, was not suitable for use as accommodation.

Guest workers from China found in a dilapidated restaurant building

The inspections took place between 29 and 31 July at the former Kék Csillag Restaurant on Olajbányász Square. Authorities examined both the property and the foreign nationals present there. The Csongrád-Csanád County Government Office identified several irregularities at the property. There was no fire safety policy, while the operator could not demonstrate that the guest workers had received fire safety training, writes local outled Szegeder.

Several safety problems uncovered

The building had neither an operating fire alarm control panel nor a built-in fire extinguishing system, and no fire extinguisher with a valid inspection was available. Officials also found that the operator could not prove that the kitchen ventilation system and electrical equipment met fire safety requirements, or that LPG cylinders were being stored properly. The property’s large kitchen gas appliances also lacked the required certificates of conformity.

The government office therefore concluded that the building was not currently suitable for accommodation. The operator was warned and instructed to remedy the irregularities. Officials said they had not identified circumstances posing an immediate threat to life, physical safety or property, so a warning was issued rather than a more serious measure.

Immigration proceedings launched

The presence of the 10 Chinese nationals led to a separate procedure by the National Directorate-General for Aliens Policing (OIF). All 10 guest workers had valid Chinese passports and valid Hungarian residence permits authorising them to work in Hungary. However, officials found that they were working at a location and in occupations different from those specified in their residence permits.

The OIF therefore launched immigration proceedings to examine whether their employment was lawful. The authority has not disclosed why the workers were at the former restaurant or whether they were staying there.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

But why were there 37 bunk beds?

The discovery of 37 bunk beds raised questions about whether the former restaurant was being used as guest workers’ accommodation. During its inspection, the local authority counted 37 metal bunk beds in the former dining area. However, officials said it was clear that the beds were not in use and that only their frames remained inside the building.

The municipality nevertheless warned the operator that the property could not be used as a guest workers’ hostel in its current condition. Such accommodation would have to meet legal requirements covering sleeping, washing and toilet facilities, as well as cooking, food storage and dining. Importantly, there was no registered accommodation service at the property.

Municipal records show that the Kék Csillag Restaurant had been registered as a catering establishment since 1997, but there was no record of accommodation services. The operator subsequently announced that the restaurant business would cease and that the property would be rented out. The establishment was later removed from the official register.

In case you missed it: Temu, Shein and AliExpress lose ground in Hungary after new EU customs charge

Was it actually a guest workers’ hostel?

Despite the bunk beds and the presence of the Chinese nationals, there is currently no official confirmation that the building was operating as a workers’ hostel or that the Chinese nationals were staying there. The OIF has not disclosed the purpose of the workers’ presence at the property or whether they had any connection with the bunk beds.

Questions about a possible connection between the property and BYD or its suppliers have also remained unanswered by the Szeged municipality. When journalists visited the site on 7 September, the building’s windows were covered from the inside, making it impossible to establish whether the bunk beds or other accommodation-related equipment were still there.

For now, authorities have established several safety deficiencies and a breach of the conditions attached to the workers’ residence permits. Whether the former restaurant was actually being used to accommodate the workers remains unconfirmed.

World.title: Travel across Hungary for less than EUR 3 during European Mobility Week’s Car-Free Day
World.content:
Hungary is offering special public transport discounts during this year’s European Mobility Week, including free bicycle transport on intercity trains and nationwide travel for just HUF 999 on Car-Free Day.

Free bicycle transport for a week

Dávid Vitézy, Minister for Transport and Investment, announced the measures on Wednesday, saying the aim is to encourage more people to choose public transport as an alternative to travelling by car.

From 16 to 22 September 2026, passengers can transport bicycles free of charge on trains available for intercity travel. Where a bicycle reservation is normally required, passengers will still need to obtain one, but the reservation itself will also be free during the promotional period.

Unlimited travel for less than EUR 3

The main promotion will take place on 22 September, Car-Free Day. Passengers will be able to purchase a special Car-Free Day ticket for HUF 999 (around EUR 2.74), allowing unlimited travel for one day on eligible intercity public transport services across Hungary. The ticket will have the same geographical validity as the Magyarország24 day ticket and will cost HUF 999 through all sales channels.

There is an important limitation, however: the ticket does not cover local public transport, including in cities where county passes are otherwise accepted on local services. Any additional supplements required for a particular journey, such as a seat reservation, must also be purchased separately.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Encouraging alternatives to driving

Vitézy said the measures were introduced to demonstrate that public transport can be a genuine alternative to the car for many journeys. In a Facebook post, he said that it was not enough simply to talk about alternatives to driving; they also needed to be made easier and cheaper to use.

He acknowledged that public transport cannot replace cars for every journey, but said that where trains, buses or bicycles provide a suitable alternative, the government wants more people to try them.

The HUF 999 day ticket is intended to make that particularly simple on Car-Free Day, allowing passengers to explore eligible intercity routes throughout the country for a single day. The promotions form part of Hungary’s participation in European Mobility Week, which runs from 16 to 22 September.

World.title: Volánbusz scandal: what we know about why one of Hungary’s wealthiest was detained
World.content:
Hungary’s long-running Volánbusz investigation has taken a major new turn after authorities brought in billionaire businessman Dániel Jellinek and former state asset manager Norbert Szivek for questioning.

The Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office (KNYF) said investigators carried out searches and seizures at several locations on Tuesday, 15 September, in connection with a suspected bribery case involving passenger transport services and bus procurement at Volánbusz, reaching HUF billions. Four people were questioned as suspects and three were detained. The case centres on transactions dating back to 2015–2018, when more than 600 used buses were allegedly purchased at inflated prices.

HUF 10 billion in suspected damage

According to the National Bureau of Investigation (NNI), the suspected transactions caused around HUF 10 billion (EUR 24.7 million) in financial damage to Volán companies. Investigators are also examining the purchase of a Volán company’s headquarters in Kecskemét, which they allege was overpriced and caused at least HUF 550 million (EUR 1.5 million) in financial damage.

Authorities suspect that money originating from the disputed transactions was subsequently moved through intermediary companies and purported loan agreements. The NNI has said the funds may have been used for property projects, cash withdrawals exceeding HUF 1 billion (EUR 2.74 million) and the purchase of a high-value car.

The investigation has therefore expanded beyond the original Volánbusz purchases. Investigators are attempting to reconstruct a chain of transactions and establish who arranged particular deals, who approved them and who ultimately benefited. Earlier proceedings reportedly examined three main strands: a leasing transaction involving 138 buses, a maintenance contract connected to 250 buses, and the Kecskemét property transaction.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Who are Jellinek and Szivek?

Dániel Jellinek, the head of Indotek Group, is Hungary’s seventh wealthiest businessman, with major interests in property. He has also had business dealings with several prominent figures in Hungary’s business world. One company linked to Jellinek that has appeared in reporting about the case is Barwald Real Estate Ltd.

According to Telex, investigators suspect the company received a loan of around HUF 1.25 billion (EUR 3.4 million) from a person linked to the Volánbusz investigation. Telex reported that the money was subsequently placed in escrow with interest, although this happened after police searches and questioning had begun.

Norbert Szivek is also a significant figure in the Volánbusz case. He was the former chief executive of the Hungarian National Asset Management Company (MNV), which exercised ownership rights over the Volán companies during the period under investigation. His alleged role is therefore being examined in connection with decisions made within the state asset-management structure.

Could the investigation reach further?

The investigation of the Volánbusz scandal has also prompted reports about other prominent figures who have had business or institutional links to people already mentioned in the case. HVG.hu said the investigation could potentially reach figures including businessman István Tiborcz, son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán and former development minister Miklós Seszták.

Tiborcz has had business relationships with both Jellinek and Szivek, while Seszták was the minister responsible for the ministry overseeing the relevant state asset-management structure during part of the period under investigation.

These reports do not mean that either man has been charged with a crime in the Volánbusz case. Their names have emerged in reporting about the wider network surrounding the investigation. HVG has also reported that investigators are interested in whether those being questioned will provide information about other possible participants.

What can possibly come next?

The Volánbusz bribery case has been under investigation for years now, so this operation means a huge step. Jellinek’s Indotek Group has rejected the allegations against its chief executive, saying he has committed no crime and is co-operating fully with the authorities. The company said Jellinek had voluntarily complied with an NNI summons on 10 September and had remained available to investigators.

The authorities now face the task of determining whether the complex series of bus purchases, property transactions, loans and other financial movements amounts to criminal conduct and, if so, who can be held responsible.

It is important to note that being questioned as a suspect or detained does not mean that a person has been convicted or that the allegations have been proven. The investigation remains ongoing, and the precise roles of those involved — as well as whether further people will become suspects — remain to be established.

World.title: New EU housing rules could pave the way for tighter Airbnb restrictions in Budapest
World.content:
The European Commission has proposed new rules aimed at tackling Europe’s housing crisis, giving cities a clearer framework for restricting short-term rentals and investment-driven property use. However, the proposal would not introduce an automatic Airbnb ban. Decisions on restrictions would remain with national governments and local authorities, under strict conditions.

Hungary could be particularly affected in Budapest, as well as in several major university cities, according to an analysis by property website ingatlan.com.

Restrictions would require proof of a housing crisis

The European Commission presented its proposed regulation on affordable housing in early September. The package aims both to give cities struggling with housing affordability more room to act and to encourage the construction of more homes.

Under the proposal, restrictions could only be introduced in specifically identified areas experiencing what would be defined as “housing stress”.

Three conditions would have to be demonstrated at the same time:

the ratio of property prices to incomes is persistently high, with an average home costing at least the equivalent of eight years of average net income;

the situation has deteriorated, with this ratio having increased over the previous ten years; and

housing pressure is not expected to ease over the following three years.

Any restrictions could remain in place for a maximum of five years and would have to be reviewed regularly.

Budapest could be among the areas affected

Based on current official income data and asking prices per square metre, the price of a 60-square-metre flat in Budapest is roughly equivalent to 11–13 years of net income, according to ingatlan.com. The ratio is lower nationwide, while homes in county capitals correspond to around eight to nine years of average earnings.

However, the exact areas covered by any future rules cannot yet be determined. Balogh László, chief economic expert at ingatlan.com, noted that much would depend on the EU methodology and the income levels used for the calculations.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Budapest has already tightened short-term rental rules

Several central Budapest districts have already introduced or considered restrictions on short-term rentals.

In Terézváros (District VI), short-term accommodation has been banned since January. In Józsefváros (District VIII), the number of flats available for short-term rental will be capped at 3.5% of the district’s housing stock from next year, while District I has also been considering tighter regulation.

Data from ingatlan.com suggest that the measures in Terézváros have already had a noticeable effect on the local rental market. Following the introduction of the restrictions, the supply of flats available for long-term rent in the district increased by 34%, while interest in such properties rose by 32%. At the same time, the average monthly rent fell from HUF 300,000 to HUF 280,000.

The figures suggest that restrictions can significantly reshape the local rental market, although they do not solve the wider shortage of housing on their own.

“One of the most important changes could be that EU regulation would create a clearer legal framework for cities seeking to ease housing pressures by restricting short-term rentals or investment-driven property purchases,” Balogh László said.

He added that restrictions alone could not solve the shortage of homes, with more new housing, faster development and greater supply needed to address the wider problem.

Brussels also wants more homes to be built

The EU package therefore places considerable emphasis on increasing housing supply alongside possible restrictions.

The European Commission would encourage faster planning and permitting procedures, brownfield development, the construction of rental housing and student accommodation, the creation of land banks and the use of vacant homes.

There may also be significant untapped potential in Hungary. According to the 2022 census, nearly 572,000 residential properties were classified as unoccupied nationwide, including more than 160,000 in Budapest.

However, ingatlan.com points out that these properties are not necessarily all sitting empty. Some are being used for other purposes, while others are not suitable for habitation or require major renovation. A proportion could nevertheless potentially return to the housing market following investment and refurbishment.

EU funding could support housing programmes

The proposal also has a significant financial component. It envisages mobilising tens of billions of euros through EU and European Investment Bank funding for affordable housing initiatives.

According to ingatlan.com, this could also support some of the housing policy objectives already being pursued in Hungary.

Balogh László said that, from the perspective of the Hungarian housing market, increasing the supply of affordable new homes could prove more significant in the long term than individual restrictions.

Hungary continues to face a shortage of newly built affordable homes, while demand remains strong in well-connected urban areas. A sustained increase in new construction could also help renew the country’s housing stock and improve its energy efficiency.

The proposal is not yet final

The European Commission’s proposal is still at an early stage. It must be approved by both the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union, and the legislative process could take 18 months to two years, according to ingatlan.com. If adopted, the regulation would apply directly in Hungary as well.

World.title: Watch: Dominik Szoboszlai scores stunning Liverpool goal against Tottenham
World.content:
Hungarian international Dominik Szoboszlai produced a spectacular long-range goal as Liverpool defeated Tottenham Hotspur 3-1 at Anfield and advanced to the fourth round of the English League Cup. The midfielder came off the bench before sealing the victory in stoppage time with a strike that left even Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola impressed.

Liverpool took control of the third-round tie through goals from Alexis Mac Allister and Cody Gakpo, while Conor Gallagher pulled one back for Tottenham. Szoboszlai then put the result beyond doubt late in the match, firing home from long range to complete a 3-1 victory.

Dominik Szoboszlai produces a spectacular finish

Szoboszlai entered the game as a substitute with Liverpool already ahead, but still managed to become one of the main talking points of the evening.

With the hosts leading 2-1 in stoppage time, the Hungarian midfielder controlled the bouncing ball with his chest before unleashing a powerful shot from roughly 30 metres. The effort flew beyond the Tottenham goalkeeper and into the net, ending any remaining uncertainty over qualification.

It was another demonstration of one of the most recognisable elements of Szoboszlai’s game. The Hungary captain has built a reputation for his shooting ability from distance, and Liverpool’s coaching staff were quick to acknowledge the quality of his latest effort.

Iraola described Liverpool’s third goal as “world-class” after the match. The coach said that while such a shooting position might appear too far from goal for many players, Szoboszlai is capable of making such attempts look realistic.

If you missed it: Talented Hungarian footballer Patrik Farkas joins Liverpool FC

Liverpool’s much-changed side delivers at Anfield

The result was also significant because Liverpool fielded a heavily rotated team. Iraola made ten changes from the side used in the club’s previous fixture, giving several squad players and youngsters an opportunity at Anfield.

Mac Allister opened the scoring in the first half with an emphatic finish before Gakpo doubled Liverpool’s advantage shortly after the interval. Tottenham responded through Gallagher, whose goal briefly brought the visitors back into contention.

Szoboszlai, introduced during the second half, eventually ensured there would be no late comeback.

Liverpool’s official match report said the Hungarian international “spectacularly” struck the bouncing ball from long range in stoppage time to secure the club’s place in the next round. The home side ultimately progressed with a convincing 3-1 victory.

Mac Allister was also unsurprised by his team-mate’s finish. As quoted by 24.hu, the Argentine midfielder explained that Liverpool’s players regularly practise shooting in training, adding that long-range efforts seem to come naturally to Szoboszlai.

Szoboszlai continues to provide decisive moments for Liverpool

For Hungarian football followers, Szoboszlai’s latest goal offers another high-profile moment in English football. The midfielder remains one of Hungary’s most prominent sporting figures abroad and continues to play an important role in one of the Premier League’s biggest clubs.

Liverpool’s victory sends the Reds into the fourth round of the League Cup, leaving them among the final 16 teams in the competition. The next-round draw is scheduled to take place on Wednesday evening following the remaining third-round matches.

The manner of qualification will also give Iraola encouragement after making extensive changes to his starting XI. For Szoboszlai, meanwhile, a relatively short appearance was enough to produce the defining image of the night: a spectacular long-range strike at Anfield that his own coach labelled world-class.

World.title: Hungary-based energy group secures 25-year deal for massive 500 MW solar project in Africa
World.content:
Hungary-based EnerSynk Group today announced the signing of a 25-year Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with ZESCO Limited for the development of a 500 MW utility-scale solar power project in Zambia’s Copperbelt Province.

The agreement marks a major milestone in the development of the project and reflects EnerSynk Group’s long-term commitment to supporting Zambia’s energy security, economic growth and diversification of its power-generation mix.

The project is planned for development in phases and is expected to supply electricity into Zambia’s national power system.

Jason Temasfieldt, Founder and Executive Chairman of EnerSynk Group, said: “Today represents an important milestone not only for EnerSynk, but for the long-term partnership we want to build with Zambia.

“We have tremendous respect for Zambia, its people and its potential. Our ambition goes beyond developing a single solar project. We want to become a trusted long-term partner — bringing together international capital, technology, expertise and partnerships to help develop the energy infrastructure Zambia needs for its next chapter of economic growth.”

The signing comes as Zambia continues efforts to increase electricity generation, strengthen energy security and attract greater private-sector investment into the power sector.

Zambia Development Agency Director General Albert Halwampa said: “Projects of this nature are important to Zambia’s efforts to expand electricity generation and strengthen energy security. Private-sector investment will be critical to achieving our national energy ambitions, and we welcome investors who are prepared to develop projects that contribute to reliable power supply, economic growth and the diversification of our energy sector.”

If you missed it: Hungarian government announces one of the country’s largest renewable energy investment programmes in decades

Bishop Joshua Banda, EnerSynk Group’s Strategic Advisor in Zambia, said: “This is more than an energy project. It is an investment in Zambia’s future. Reliable electricity supports industry, businesses, families and communities, and we look forward to seeing this project contribute meaningfully to the country’s development.”

The Power Purchase Agreement establishes the commercial framework for the sale of electricity generated by the project to ZESCO over a 25-year period.

EnerSynk Group will now advance the project through its next stages of development, including technical studies, environmental and regulatory processes, project financing and implementation in collaboration with relevant government institutions, stakeholders, investors and technical partners.

“There is still important work ahead,” Temasfieldt added. “But today is an opportunity to recognise how far we have come and to thank ZESCO, the Government of Zambia, the Zambia Development Agency, the Energy Regulation Board, our local partners and everyone who has helped bring the project to this milestone.”

Upon completion, the project is expected to rank among Zambia’s largest utility-scale solar installations and contribute significant new generation capacity to the national electricity system.

The project forms part of EnerSynk Group’s wider strategy to develop reliable, sustainable and scalable energy infrastructure across Africa.

World.title: Another side of Poland: factories, startups and city-building in Lower Silesia
World.content:
In two cities in south-western Poland, we looked at how local leaders are trying to attract multinational companies, strengthen home-grown businesses and create an environment where people want not only to work, but also to live. As part of an eight-member international group of journalists, we visited Wałbrzych and Wrocław on a study tour organised by the Warsaw Enterprise Institute. From a Mercedes plant and a Polish SME to a technology company that started life in a garage, a surprisingly consistent strategy emerged. Hungarian cities and their leaders might also find ideas worth considering here.

The multi-day programme was supported on behalf of the Warsaw Enterprise Institute by Marta Roels and Łukasz Wojdyga. Both work in strongly international fields: Roels is a WEI project coordinator and analyst, while Wojdyga specialises in international academic and research cooperation.

Our first major economic stop was Wałbrzych. One phrase kept returning during the opening presentations: building an ecosystem. In other words, bringing in a factory is not enough. Everything that enables it to operate successfully over the long term has to be built around it. And the right environment can benefit SMEs just as much as the industrial giants next door.

Poland’s industrial zone is no longer only about gigafactories

The presentation of the Wałbrzych Special Economic Zone – WSEZ “Invest-Park” was opened by Marcin Lerner, president of the company’s management board. Katarzyna Prociak, director responsible for investment acquisition and sales, then gave us a closer look at how the zone operates.

According to the figures presented, nearly 450 investors are active in the zone, with total investment worth around PLN 48 billion. Companies operating there are credited with creating approximately 90,000 jobs.

Some of the best-known names include Toyota, Mercedes-Benz and Electrolux, while Mercedes also operates a plant in nearby Jawor. Yet one message was repeatedly stressed during the presentations: the strategy is no longer focused solely on gigafactories. Polish and foreign small and medium-sized companies are also actively targeted.

Investors can also receive tax incentives. What makes the scheme interesting is that the support is not paid out as one large grant. Instead, an eligible company can gradually use the approved amount when paying tax. The level of support depends, among other things, on the size of the company and the investment itself, with a benefit of up to 25 per cent available in the most favourable cases.

Invest-Park also runs a training centre supporting companies already operating in the region, while InvestUp connects startups with established businesses. The thinking behind both programmes is the same: a factory needs suppliers, skilled workers, research capacity and a new generation of companies around it.

Roman Szełemej talks about an entire city, not isolated projects

At Invest-Park, Roman Szełemej, Mayor of Wałbrzych, introduced us to the city. A cardiologist by profession, he has led Wałbrzych since 2011 and was re-elected in 2024 with 71 per cent of the vote. The impression from his presentation was that residents have largely embraced the direction he has set for the city and that development is being treated as a broader community project.

Roman Szełemej, Mayor of Wałbrzych

Perhaps the most striking part of Szełemej’s presentation was that he did not try to sell us one spectacular flagship development. He spoke about housing, transport, healthcare, education and energy supply with the same emphasis as industrial investment.

Wałbrzych, which is celebrating its 600th anniversary, has a population of roughly 100,000. According to the presentation, 66 per cent of its territory is covered by green space and around 750,000 tourists visit annually. One of the city’s priorities is keeping young families there, partly through the construction of new municipal housing.

Szełemej also spoke with particular pride about the expanding role of biomass-based energy. At the same time, Wałbrzych is trying to turn its geography into a competitive advantage: the Czech border is just over 20 kilometres away, while Berlin, Prague and Vienna are all close enough that it makes little sense to view the city’s economic position only in relation to Warsaw.

The city’s concrete investment opportunities were presented by Arkadiusz Grudzień, head of InWałbrzych. The role of the municipal company is essentially to turn broader urban strategy into tangible investment offers.

A large company and an SME: John Cotton and WLV

The afternoon factory visits demonstrated what supporting both large and smaller companies means in practice.

Our first stop was the John Cotton Europe plant. According to Michael Harrington, the group’s managing director, the more than century-old family business now operates in seven countries across three continents and employs around 1,600 people.

Tesco played an important role in bringing the company to Poland, inviting it into Central Europe as a partner. Its next major step will be automation: the company is preparing a new logistics centre where, once a lorry arrives, the movement of goods could eventually be handled entirely by automated systems.

One of the more memorable side topics during the factory visit was pillow replacement. Harrington surprised the group by saying that, from a hygiene perspective, pillows should ideally be replaced every six months. Polish consumers, he said, reportedly keep theirs for around eight and a half years on average. Hungarian households may not necessarily perform much better.

From there, we travelled to the plant of WLV W. Kocoń M. Joński. The Polish SME works with industrial plastics technology, air and gas purification systems, tanks and other specialised industrial solutions.

WLV may be a less recognisable name than Mercedes, but that is precisely why its inclusion in the programme mattered. Poland’s huge number of SMEs collectively provides a major base for employment, production and tax revenues. What is more, some of today’s medium-sized local businesses could become the large Polish manufacturers and brands of the next 10 or 20 years.

After a packed day in Wałbrzych, the programme became somewhat more relaxed: the evening ended with a George Dyer Blues concert at the Vertigo Jazz Club in Wrocław.

Vertigo Jazz Club, Wroclaw, Poland. Photo: Daily News Hungary

The day in Wrocław began with State Secretary Michał Jaros

The following morning, Michał Jaros, state secretary at Poland’s Ministry of Development and Technology, joined us for an informal breakfast. Jaros himself has strong ties to Lower Silesia and, as both a politician and economist, was able to discuss the region from a national economic policy perspective after we had spent the previous day looking at it from factory level.

He currently serves as a state secretary in the Polish government, and our closed-door discussion touched on some of the most important investment issues facing the country.

Wrocław immediately feels like a different world from Wałbrzych. The architectural legacy of the former German city of Breslau remains highly visible, while the modern city around it feels young, energetic and conspicuously international.

Radosław Michalski, director responsible for Wrocław’s city brand, explained this side of the city in more detail. His role is essentially to combine Wrocław’s economic, tourism and cultural strengths into a single, recognisable image.

Alongside him, Magdalena Okulowska, president of the Wrocław Agglomeration Development Agency, or ARAW, presented the investment potential of the wider metropolitan area. ARAW works, among other things, on attracting investors and supporting development projects across the agglomeration.

According to the presentation, one in five Wrocław residents is a foreigner, while around 60,000 foreign students and employees representing more than 120 nationalities live in the city. Wrocław also has 30 international schools and kindergartens.

More than 126,000 students attend 30 higher education institutions, while several hundred research and development units operate across the region. The presence of LG is also worth highlighting, as it has helped create particularly strong business links with South Korea.

Don’t miss it – Looking beyond price per square metre: how Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest’s new-build home markets differ

Wrocław wants to persuade more than investors

Quality of life features surprisingly prominently in Wrocław’s economic strategy. Culture, life along the Oder River and, increasingly, gastronomy all form part of the city’s pitch.

In 2026, 28 Wrocław restaurants were included in the Michelin Guide, six more than the previous year. BABA and MOST each received a Michelin star, three restaurants were awarded Bib Gourmand status, while the others were included among Michelin’s recommended establishments.

We had the opportunity to experience this side of the city ourselves. One evening took us to Przystań & Marina, which is among the Wrocław restaurants recommended by the Michelin Guide. Located on an island directly beside the Oder, the restaurant is highlighted by the guide for its Mediterranean-inspired cooking, use of local ingredients and waterside setting.

Our group worked its way through a multi-course tasting menu, which proved unanimously popular among the eight international journalists. After days of presentations and factory visits, it also offered a chance to understand Wrocław’s much-advertised quality of life through something other than investment statistics.

That matters because Wrocław is clearly not simply trying to sell jobs. The city also wants to convince engineers, researchers, managers and their families arriving with new investors that there are reasons to stay for the long term. International schools, cultural institutions, parks and riverside areas, together with an increasingly Michelin-recognised food scene, all form part of the same strategy.

From laboratory to market

At Wrocław Technology Park, or WPT, we saw the idea of a business ecosystem in physical form.

According to the presentation, more than 200 companies operate on the campus and employ over 2,000 people. The eight-building complex provides around 66,000 square metres of offices, laboratories, research infrastructure, production facilities and warehouse space.

We were also shown a pilot production area where companies can test a process on a small scale before potentially building an entire factory around it. This is particularly important for smaller businesses: a startup does not have to invest millions of euros in its own laboratory before it can begin experimenting with a real product.

A garage startup and the future of digital identity

Our final business stop was Identt, which began as a classic garage startup and now develops digital identity solutions for banks, financial companies and other regulated sectors.

One of the system’s jobs is to verify whether the person on the other side of a camera really is who they claim to be. The same technology can also be used in access-control systems: stealing or borrowing somebody else’s entry card is of limited use if the system also identifies the person holding it.

The next major change could come with the European Digital Identity Wallet. Under the concept, users themselves will be able to control exactly which pieces of information they share from their identity documents, driving licence, diploma or other digital credentials, and with whom.

Poland no longer simply wants to be cheaper

After visiting the two cities, we ended up back where Marcin Lerner and Katarzyna Prociak began in Wałbrzych: with the idea of an ecosystem.

Roman Szełemej and Arkadiusz Grudzień are trying to transform a former industrial city into a place where domestic companies such as WLV have a future alongside Mercedes. In Wrocław, Radosław Michalski and Magdalena Okulowska are working with the tools available to an international city: universities, foreign talent, technology infrastructure, culture, multinational companies and startups.

And that may have been the most interesting lesson of the trip. This part of Poland is no longer trying to compete with Western Europe simply by being cheaper. The aim is to build an environment in which the investment of a foreign industrial giant matters just as much as the local small business that may one day grow into Poland’s next major international brand.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar to meet Pope Leo XIV in private Vatican audience
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar is set to travel to the Vatican on 24 September, where he will be received by Pope Leo XIV in a private audience.

Péter Magyar is about to visit the Vatican very soon

Magyar announced the visit on Facebook, adding that he will subsequently hold talks with Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s Secretary of State and a key figure in its diplomatic and governmental affairs. The meeting will give Magyar an opportunity to discuss issues of interest with the head of the Catholic Church before his talks with one of the Vatican’s most senior officials.

The Pope had a meeting not so long ago with Viktor Orbán

Pope Leo XIV has previously received former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán at the Vatican. Orbán met the pontiff in October last year and was accompanied by his wife, Anikó Lévai, and several members of his family, writes VG.hu.

During that meeting, the two sides discussed bilateral relations and the role of the Catholic Church in Hungarian society. Family policy, the education and future of young people, and the protection of Christian communities living in war zones were also among the topics addressed. Orbán said afterwards that he had asked the Pope to continue supporting Hungary’s efforts to promote peace.

Tisza delegation previously met the Pope

The upcoming meeting will also follow an earlier Vatican encounter involving Magyar’s political movement. In April, Pope Leo XIV received representatives of the European People’s Party at the Vatican, including members of the Tisza Party. Magyar’s private audience therefore means the continuation of the relations between the Vatican and the Tisza politicians.

World.title: Hague Court Convicts Kosovo Liberation Army Leaders of War Crimes
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip



Rexhep Selimi, Hashim Thaci, Jakup Krasniqi, and Kadri Veseli in court on September 16, 2026. Photo: Screenshot/Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

Kosovo’s former head of state Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague on Wednesday for the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed from April 1998 to June 1999 during the Kosovo war.

“In the names of the people of Kosovo, the panel finds you, Hashim Thaci, guilty of arbitrary arrest and detention as a war crime against at least 385 persons; cruel treatment against at least 49; torture as a war crimes against at least 303 persons; murder as a war crimes committed against 96 persons,” presiding judge Charles Smith III announced.

Thaci’s co-defendants Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi were sentenced to 25, 18 and 13 years in prison respectively. All four men were found guilty of bearing responsibility for the crimes while they were senior officials of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA during the war with Serbian forces.

The four men were found not guilty of the crimes against humanity of persecution, imprisonment, other inhumane acts, torture, murder and enforced disappearances because the crimes were committed after the end of the Kosovo war.

Thaci, along with former parliament speakers Veseli and Krasniqi, and former MP Selimi, had all pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Thousands of supporters of the defendants, who had travelled to The Hague for the verdict and listened to the livestream in a public park, erupted in anger when the convictions were announced. There was a brief clash with Dutch police, who prevented them marching towards the court.

The Specialist Chambers found that Thaci, Veseli, Krasniqi and Selimi were part of a joint criminal enterprise that aimed to exert control by targeting perceived opponents of the KLA.

These opponents included people associated with other political or military groups that had not pledged their loyalty to KLA – in particular the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK party – as well as individuals alleged to be associated with the Serbian authorities and members of non-Albanian ethnic groups like Roma people and Serbs.

Hundreds were imprisoned and some killed, according to the verdict. “Some detainees died because of severe beatings from their KLA captors,” judge Smith said.

During the trial, the defence insisted that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have genuine control over lower-ranking fighters. However, judge Smith said the court found that the KLA’s political directorate, which Thaci led, had huge authority over the guerrilla force.

The presiding judge said that the accused worked together with others to set up detention facilities and establish a military police force, intelligence service and special units, and tasked them with carrying out their “criminal plan” to establish their authority in Kosovo. They also “secured impunity for the perpetrators of these crimes as a matter of policy”, the judge added.

The time that the defendants have spent in detention since November 2020 will be counted against their sentences. They have the right to appeal.

This is the highest-level case to be heard at the so-called Kosovo Special Court and has been marred by delays and controversy, as well as a series of protests staged by supporters of the defendants in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague.

Many ethnic Albanians consider the court biased against the KLA’s war against repression by the Serbian authorities.

Delivering the verdict, judge Smith insisted that the case was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army”.

“This case is not concerned with crimes of Serbian army and paramilitaries that undoubtedly committed against the Albanians in Kosovo. This case is not concerned with any claims of self-defence. Instead this case is exclusively concerned if the crimes alleged in the indictment were committed,” he said.

The lengthy trial was marred by accusations of witness-tampering. As a result, Thaci faces judgment in another case for obstruction of justice. Judge Smith lamented that the trial had taken place in “climate of witness intimidation”, saying that some witnesses lied or changed their previous accounts in court, and that some may have been afraid due to concerns for their safety or out of loyalty.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. The court is part of Kosovo’s justice system, but based in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters, who are seen by many in the country as heroic liberators from Serbian oppression.

World.title: Russian Despatch: Moscow Plays Old Cards in Balkan Elections
World.content:
Russia enters autumn in an atmosphere of foreboding. Intensified Ukrainian strikes, a gasoline deficit, and lack of progress on the battlefront are leading more and more people to surmise that the Kremlin is no longer able to wage its war against Ukraine as a distant operation that has little impact on Russian everyday life.

It will only get worse, and soon the regime will demand more sacrifices for its geopolitical adventures.

The date for change looks set for late September, following parliamentary elections.

Though the vote is tightly managed by authorities, the Kremlin still pays lip service to democratic procedures. It avoids taking unpopular steps during the campaign and strives to preserve a semblance of stability at least until after voting day.

World.title: European Parliamentarians Slam Serbia for ‘Disturbing’ Funeral of Ratko Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told a debate in the European Parliament on Tuesday about the glorification of convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic that images from Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade were “profoundly disturbing”.

The debate was held a week after Mladic’s funeral with military honours in Belgrade prompted strong reactions from European institutions and several EU member states.

“It was especially disturbing to see Serbian ministers, state officials and military representatives alongside leaders and politicians from [Bosnia’s Serb-led entity] Republika Srpska, attend the funeral and publicly honour a war criminal,” Kos said.

Serbia is an EU candidate state and Kos said that Belgrade must fulfill its responsibilities. “By applying for EU membership, Serbia committed to our standards, principles, and values,” she said.

“The European Commission has been clear that the glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism is fundamentally incompatible with these values. It has no place in the EU. It has no place in the EU candidate countries,” she added.

Mladic, who died in The Hague while serving a life sentence for genocide and war crimes, was buried at Belgrade’s Topcider Cemetery in Belgrade on September 7. The funeral service was led by Serbian Orthodox Church Patriarch Porfirije, and Serbian government ministers came to pay their respects.

At Tuesday’s debate, several Croatian MEPs slammed the Serbian administration and President Aleksandar Vucic for their role in Mladic’s funeral.

Davor Ivo Stier, MEP for Croatia’s Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, which sits with the European People’s Party, EPP, group said Serbian President Vucic “did not organise a state funeral, but as commander in chief, is responsible for the military honours shown to Mladic”.

“We need to be loud and say clearly that our politics towards Serbia have been mild and ineffective and we need to show and decide that there is no place in Europe for those who glorify Ratko Mladic, and we should not give European funds to those who do not want to distance themselves from [former Yugoslav leader] Slobodan Milosevic’s politics,” Stier added.

Tonino Picula, from the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats group in the European Parliament, said that it is “justified to ask whether the European Union needs to continue negotiating with Serbia while this government is in power”.

Helmut Brandstatter, who sits with Renew Europe, said that the EPP should cut its ties with Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party.

“We cannot tolerate the celebration of a war criminal. A government that glorifies such atrocities can never be part of the European Union,” Brandstatter added.

Brandstatter also highlighted that Serbian society is European and that Serbia should be part of the European Union, but as a democracy.

Commenting on Serbia’s upcoming snap elections, Brandstatter said: “He [Vucic] wants to have a small majority again to get our money – and friendship with Russia, and that cannot happen. The Serbs are welcome here but the authoritarian regime is not part of the European Union.”

World.title: Romanian Sheep Farmers’ Protest Turns Violent in Bucharest
World.content:
A protest by Romanian sheep farmers in front of the government building in Bucharest descended into clashes on Tuesday, with riot police using tear gas as groups of demonstrators broke through security cordons and threw objects at officers.

Around 15 people, including seven gendarmes, required medical assistance after being exposed to tear gas. Four people were detained for violent behaviour.

President Nicusor Dan condemned the incidents. “Attacks and assaults, as well as acts of vandalism, are unacceptable and must be severely punished in accordance with the law,” Dan said. Interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan said he respected all citizens’ legal right to peaceful protest but Tuesday’s events “degenerated into regrettable acts of violence”.

Thousands of sheep farmers from across Romania had gathered to protest the extension of a ban on live sheep exports until the end of the year. The European Commission imposed the measure following outbreaks of Peste des Petits Ruminants, or sheep and goat plague, citing insufficient preventive measures by Romanian authorities.

Crop farmers also joined the protest, angered by reduced drought compensation. Although they had been promised 100 euros for every hectare of affected crops, they will now receive only 19 euros per hectare, which they say is far below the losses caused by the prolonged drought.

World.title: Police in The Hague Brace for Rallies Ahead of Kosovo Trial Verdict
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Supporters of Hashim Thaci and his co-defendants rally in Pristina, September 12, 2026. Photo: EPA/Georgi Licovski .

Ethnic Albanians and supporters of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, are expected to demonstrate in The Hague on Wednesday as Kosovo’s ex-President Hashim Thaci and three other former guerrilla fighters hear their war crimes verdict.

The announcement of demonstrations and of numerous ethnic Albanians travelling to the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague for the verdict has prompted the court and Dutch police in The Hague to take special security measures.

Prior to the verdict, several transitional justice NGOs from Kosovo and Serbia, which are part of the Specialist Chambers’ outreach forum, the Court Information Network, were notified that their scheduled meeting at the court had been cancelled for security reasons.

Sofija Todorovic, director of the Belgrade-based Youth Initiative for Human Rights Serbia, told BIRN that NGOs that were part of the Court Information Network had a meeting planned when the verdict was to be announced in The Hague.

“But we received information from the court that due to the announced demonstrations and the large number of people coming to The Hague for the verdict, basically the circumstances had changed and they could not guarantee that we will not be recognised by someone and will not face some sort of hostility, so they decided to cancel the meeting,” Todorovic said.

Dusan Radakovic, from a North Mitrovica-based civil society organisation, Advocacy Centre for Democratic Culture, ACDC, told BIRN that “the decision to cancel the visit was primarily related to security concerns and the announced large-scale protests, as can also be inferred from the explanation provided in the email informing us about the cancellation. Particular concern was likely related to the protests expected outside the court following the anticipated decision.

“As a lawyer, I considered it a valuable opportunity to directly observe the work of such an important institution at a time when it is dealing with a matter of considerable public significance,” Radakovic said.

A Dutch police spokesperson in The Hague told BIRN: “We do not announce measures taken and we do not comment on threats in general. We know there will be demonstrations and we will be present in the location.”

Angela Griep, the court’s spokesperson, told BIRN that the Kosovo Specialist Chambers was “undertaking all necessary security measures within its authority and responsibilities on 16 September, also taking into account the announced possible protests”.

Thaci, together with former Kosovo parliament Speakers Kadri Veseli and Jakup Krasniqi, and former MP Rexhep Selimi, are accused of committing crimes against humanity – including murder, torture and illegal detention – during the Kosovo conflict in the late 1990s. They have been in detention in The Hague since November 2020 and have all pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers have called for a 45-year prison sentence. Defence lawyers have urged acquittal.

This is the highest-level case held at the so-called Kosovo Special Court and has been marred by delays and controversy.

It has also been accompanied by protests staged by supporters of the defendants in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague. Many ethnic Albanians consider the court biased against the KLA’s war against repression by the Serbian authorities. The trial has been surrounded by accusations of fake news and hate speech, and has even led to witness intimidation charges and convictions.

Radakovic told BIRN that, “although I can understand the security considerations that may have led to the cancellation of the visit, I believe that such a decision, particularly the way it was communicated, and if no further explanation is provided, may further increase mistrust among certain groups of citizens and reinforce perceptions of insufficient transparency on the part of the court”.

Todorovic told BIRN that the cancellation of the NGOs’ visit was “not in general a good message”. While she understood the importance of security measures, especially for the protection of witnesses, she said this level of security measures for the monitoring of civil society organisations was problematic.

“The monitoring visit does not affect the outcome of the verdict whatsoever, it just is part of a dialogue that should be ongoing in general with the people that work on these topics [of transitional justice] and the work of the court reflects the work of dealing with the past that we have on the ground,” she said.

She added that the cancellation “decreases the trust in the overall impact of the work of the court. That is the big issue and it fuels this feeling of uncertainty among many people who are waiting to see the output of the work of the court while waiting for the verdict.”

Rallies have been announced across Kosovo, with family members and supporters announcing they will be waiting for the verdict at Pristina’s main square starting from Tuesday evening.

The US embassy in Pristina issued a demonstration alert for Wednesday, warning that “these demonstrations may cause large crowds, road closures and severe traffic disruptions. It is advised to limit travel to the immediate area of your residence and to avoid travel to your workplace and schools if your route passes through impacted areas, as you may not be able to complete the journey in a timely manner.”

On September 12, thousands of supporters of the defendants also marched through Kosovo’s capital, Pristina.

Prosecutors accuse the four men of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania. Those include more than one hundred murders. The charges cover the period during and just after the Kosovo war in 1998 and 1999.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. As prime minister in 2014, Thaci signed the agreement with the European Union to establish the court.

It is based in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters. Veterans are widely viewed as heroes in Kosovo and the potential for witness intimidation was a serious concern.

During the trial, the prosecution argued that the defendants’ senior roles in the KLA meant they were responsible for subordinates who committed crimes. The defence insisted that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking fighters.

World.title: Albania’s High Court Rules Against Tirana Mayor’s Release
World.content:
Jailed Tirana mayor Erion Veliaj being accompanied to the Constitutional Court in October 2025. Photo: LSA.

Albania’s High Court ruled on Tuesday that Tirana Mayor Erion Veliaj, who is accused of corruption, money laundering and concealment of wealth, should remain in jail after his arrest was challenged in several courts.

Veliaj’s defence has strongly challenged the enforcement measure that has kept him in detention for about a year-and-a-half. After losing an appeal in the Court Against Corruption and Organised Crime of First Instance and Appeals and in the High Court, the case was taken to the Constitutional Court with the argument that the arrest was disproportional.

The Constitutional Court redirected the case to the High Court, which has decided that Veliaj should stay in detention.

The ruling was “an extremely concerning development for the rule of law, legal certainty, fundamental rights, and, above all, for democracy in this country,” his lawyer, Plarent Ndreca, told the media.

Veliaj was arrested in February last year. The Special Prosecution Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, accused him of creating “a complicated scheme” whereby public money was transferred to a group of NGOs “de facto” run by his wife, Ajola Xoxa, using several local businessmen.

His wife faces the same charges. He and his wife both deny the accusations.

Although his trial is ongoing, there have been no significant developments because of repeated delays.

Only a few days before the latest court ruling, on August 28, Veliaj dismissed Tirana’s acting mayor, Anuela Ristani, and his lawyer declared that he would run the city from pre-detention, asking for “practical conditions” to be provided for this.

Many saw this as an attempt to put pressure on the court by portraying his role in the city as too important to be exercised from a jail.

Albanian analyst Andi Bushati said on Tuesday that following the court decision against Veliaj, he should resign.

“The court decided to keep Veliaj in jail. And now the entire strategy devised in recent weeks risks backfiring on him. If the primary concern up to this point was serving the residents, caring for the city, and ensuring the smooth running of Tirana, shouldn’t Veliaj consider resigning for the sake of these very causes?” Bushati wrote on the Lapsi news site.

Veliaj was dismissed by the Municipality Council in September last year after Prime Minister Edi Rama declared that Tirana needed an active mayor.

New elections for Tirana were called and a campaign started – but the Constitutional Court then ruled in November that the way in which Veliaj had been dismissed was unconstitutional. Therefore he remains mayor of the city.

World.title: Autism Centre: 35 Million Euro Zagreb Project Gets Underway After 20+ Years
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – The long awaited Autism Centre is an enormous 35 million euro Zagreb project that is finally getting underway after a long 20+ year wait.

After over 20 years of announcements, the City of Zagreb has finally obtained a building permit for the construction of a new Autism Centre in Oporovec. It will provide modern and adapted conditions for learning, development and professional support for around 200 children, and will bring together programmes that are currently run at multiple locations across Zagreb.

Poslovni reports that the estimated value of the new Autism Centre in Oporovec is around 35 million euros, of which 19.3 million euros will be financed from EU funds through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), while the remaining amount will be secured from the City of Zagreb budget. Once the building permit becomes final, the preparation of project documentation and the public procurement procedure for selecting the contractor will follow. Construction is planned to start in the summer of 2027, with a planned duration of 18 months.

The new school will have 48 classroom departments and educational groups, as well as three preschool education and care groups. Specialised spaces are also planned for music and art therapy, household skills and aquatic therapy with a pool, sports halls and other facilities adapted to the needs of users.

According to the project by the architectural office SODA-ARHITEKTI, the centre will cover more than 9,600 square metres on three floors, with 60 parking spaces, nine of which are designated for people with disabilities. Attention has also been paid to the outdoor landscaping, with a main square featuring a sensory park, fountains and facilities for developing motor skills planned. “This is another of the projects that have been promised in Zagreb for more than twenty years, and now it is finally going into realisation,” said Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević.

Deputy Mayor Danijela Dolenec stressed that the new school will represent a major step forward in the quality of spatial and programmatic conditions for the education and upbringing of children and young people with autism. The Autism Centre currently cares for around 300 users through preschool programmes, primary education, full-day and half-day stay programmes, and organised housing, she said.

Dolenec added that the City of Zagreb continues to invest in the existing capacities of the Autism Centre. A public procurement for the renovation and arrangement of the sports hall in Ljevakovićeva Street, worth 250,000 euros, was recently launched, and around 750,000 euros has been invested in the renovation of the Centre’s existing facilities in recent years.

By the end of the year, the opening of a new Centre space in Juraj Dalmatinac Street is also planned, where early developmental and psychosocial support services will be provided for 40 children, as well as a stay programme for 30 adults with autism spectrum disorders. The City of Zagreb has also stated that 24 new special classroom departments and educational groups have been established in the new school year, increasing existing capacities by almost a quarter.

The number of special classroom departments has grown from 64 back in 2021 to 126 in 2026, while the network of schools implementing these programmes has been expanded to 55 schools across Zagreb, according to the City of Zagreb press release.

World.title: Zadar Mobile Boat Pharmacy is in the Final for the Best EU Project Award
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – The very commendable Zadar mobile pharmacy on a boat is in the final for the Best EU Project Award.

The Zadar project “Mobile Pharmacy – boat for the islands of Zadar County” has secured a place in the final of this year’s competition for the best EU project in the category Contribution to the Local and Regional Community. Morski reports that this very commendable initiative is primarily aimed at introducing a mobile pharmaceutical service in the island area in order to significantly facilitate residents’ access to medicines and professional advice, especially those in more traffic-isolated places.

The competition is organised by the Croatian Association of Counties, the Office of the European Parliament in Croatia and the portal Župan.hr, under the auspices of the Ministry of Regional Development and EU Funds. In strong competition from almost 50 projects submitted from all over Croatia, the expert jury selected a total of 36 finalists, with the Zadar mobile pharmacy competing among the 18 best in its category.

The winners in the readers’ choice category are decided by the public, and public voting officially ran from the 8th to the 15th of September, 2026.
