Chandrababu Naidu and Minister for IT Nara Lokesh were holding talks with global investors to make the State a hub for investment, she said, adding that large industrial investments flowing into the State would create thousands of jobs for local youth. She urged the younger generation to take part responsibly in nation-building and to use their vote to elect leaders who could shape the future of society.

After her speech, the MP took questions from the students and answered them in detail, on higher education, competitive examinations, start-up ideas and jobs in local industries.

G. Ramakrishna Reddy, Chairman of Sri Ramakrishna Educational Institutions, said the ideas of the youth formed the strong foundation for nation-building. ‘Today’s students possess immense talent and a fresh perspective; with the right guidance and support, they can achieve wonders,‘ he said.

College Director G. Hemanth Reddy said: ‘India possesses the largest youth workforce in the world. Our country’s development and economic prosperity depend entirely on the decisions made and the initiative shown by the youth; the power to reshape the course and destiny of future generations lies solely with the youth.‘

World.title: Only Prime Minister’s Office can grant sanction to prosecute IAS officers, Centre tells Madras High Court
World.content:
The Central government on Wednesday (September 16, 2026) informed the Madras High Court that the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) was the competent authority to grant the statutory sanction required to prosecute Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officers in criminal cases.

Appearing before Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, Sushil Kumar Patel, Joint Secretary, Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), said that the files are sent first to the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) for its remarks and then forwarded to the PMO, seeking sanction.

The submission was made in response to a query raised by the court to explain who the competent authority was to sanction prosecution against IAS officers and why it takes a very long time to obtain such sanction before prosecuting bureaucrats in corruption cases.

What is the case about?

Justice Venkatesh had raised the question during the hearing of a case related to the delay in obtaining sanction to prosecute IAS officers K.S. Kandasamy and K. Vijaya Karthikeyan in a ₹98.25-crore corporation tender irregularities case registered primarily against former AIADMK Minister S.P. Velumani.

Arappor Iyakkam, an anti-corruption organisation represented by its managing trustee Jayaram Venkatesan, had filed the case. Its counsel, V. Suresh, told the court that the alleged irregularities in the award of Greater Chennai and Coimbatore municipal corporation contracts had occurred between 2014 and 2018.

The Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) had registered a First Information Report in this regard in 2021 and completed the probe a few years later. On February 12, 2024, then Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly Speaker M. Appavu had granted sanction to prosecute Mr. Velumani.

However, as there was a delay in obtaining sanction to prosecute the two IAS officers, Arappor Iyakkam had moved the High Court with the present petition last year. Following a nudging by the High Court, the Tamil Nadu government forwarded the proposal for grant of sanction to the DoPT.

Explaining the reason for the sanction not having been granted so far, Mr. Patel said that the DoPT had received voluminous documents running to thousands of pages from the State government, and they had to be carefully perused before sending them to the CVC for its remarks.

After receiving the remarks from the CVC, the file would be forwarded to the PMO for obtaining sanction, the officer said. He assured the court that DoPT was according top priority to the issue at hand and that the entire process would be completed within the next two months.

Justice Venkatesh recorded his submissions and adjourned the case filed by Arappor Iyakkam to November 12, 2026. He directed the Joint Secretary to file an affidavit, during the next hearing, explaining the entire process of sanction, from November 2025, until a decision is taken by the PMO.

World.title: Demolish dangerous buildings in Thrissur without delay, Kerala State Human Rights Commission tells city Corporation
World.content:
The Kerala State Human Rights Commission has directed the Thrissur Corporation to expedite the demolition of dilapidated buildings that pose a potential threat to public safety, particularly those not involved in litigation.

Commission member V. Geetha issued the direction after the Corporation informed the commission that steps had been initiated to demolish such unsafe structures. The Corporation Secretary has been asked to submit a detailed status report on the action taken at the commission’s sitting in October 2026.

Notice issued

According to the Corporation’s report, 15 buildings have been identified for immediate demolition. Two have already been pulled down, while demolition work is under way on two others. Six buildings are involved in court cases. Notices have been issued for the demolition of two government buildings, while four buildings have been earmarked for repairs.

The Corporation said the survey of dilapidated buildings was carried out after dividing the city into six sectors.

The report said 14 buildings identified as being in a dangerous condition could be spared demolition if they obtain structural safety certificates. Another 128 buildings can be retained after necessary repairs.

The commission directed the Corporation Secretary to submit details of action taken in compliance with its directions at the October 2026 sitting.

World.title: Madras High Court rejects plea challenging election of DMK whip E.V. Velu from Tiruvannamalai constituency
World.content:
The Madras High Court on Wednesday (September 16, 2026) rejected an election petition filed by Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) candidate Arul Arumugam against the victory of Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) whip and former Minister E.V. Velu from the Tiruvannamalai Assembly constituency this year.

Justice D. Bharatha Chakravarthy allowed two applications filed by Mr. Velu and concurred with the submissions of senior counsel P. Wilson that the election petition must be rejected at the threshold, as the plea does not disclose any cause of action requiring the conduct of a full-fledged trial.

In his first application, the returned candidate had urged the court to strike off from the election petition 57 paragraphs and 32 grounds. In his second application, he had pleaded for rejecting the election petition in toto, as the petitioner had not pleaded any material facts.

Allowing both applications, the judge said: “The complete and careful reading of the election petition discloses only two facts. The election petitioner, being a first-time candidate, had to suffer the one-upmanship of the returned candidate who belonged to the then ruling party. Despite this, the margin of victory was only 2,455 votes. The election petition, however, does not concisely point out any single circumstance that could vitiate the election so as to make out a triable issue.”

Mr. Velu was declared elected from the Tiruvannamalai constituency on securing a total of 88,273 votes as against 85,818 votes garnered by Mr. Arumugam. Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) candidate C. Elumalai had stood third by receiving 34,280 votes.

Four poll pleas rejected so far

As many as 54 election petitions were filed in the Madras High Court after the conduct of the general elections in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry this year. So far, the High Court had rejected four of those election petitions in limine, without undertaking the elaborate process of examining witnesses.

Justice Chakravarthy had already rejected the election petitions filed against the victory of TVK MLA N. Elaiyaraja from the Uthangarai constituency and that of S. Jayakumar, who contested as an All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) candidate in the Perundurai constituency but joined the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam after resigning from his MLA post.

Separately, Justice G.K. Ilanthiraiyan had rejected the election petition filed against the victory of Minister for Revenue and Disaster Management K.A. Sengottaiyan from the Gobichettipalayam constituency.

World.title: EU chief pitches 'associate member' status for Canada
World.content:
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen raised the prospect on Wednesday (September 16, 2026) of Canada becoming the 27-nation bloc's first "associate member”, as she pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Canadian leader Mark Carney.

Ms. von der Leyen told the European Parliament in Strasbourg that as democracies face a "fracture in the international rules-based system", Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together.

"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," Ms. von der Leyen told the Canadian Prime Minister, who was attending her annual keynote speech — drawing a standing ovation in the chamber.

Mr. Carney has been pursuing closer ties with the European Union, as both seek to pivot away from a hostile United States under President Donald Trump.

The first foreign head of government to attend the annual "State of the European Union" speech — before addressing the parliament himself the next day — his visit is meant to act as a catalyst ahead of an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next month.

Ms. von der Leyen said it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader "alliance for the future" and "bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible".

"We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project," she said.

She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security, as other fields of cooperation.

"This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength," she added.

What's in a name

EU treaties do not envision the possibility of becoming an "associate member". But the idea was first floated by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz this year vis-a-vis Ukraine.

Under that plan, which met a cold reception in Kyiv as it pushes for full membership, Ukraine would have been allowed to attend the bloc's summits and have a representative in the European Commission.

It would have also benefited from parts of the EU budget, but without full voting rights.

"We don't really know yet what it means," said Tobias Cremer, a centre-left European lawmaker from Germany and the main sponsor of a March resolution urging stronger EU-Canada cooperation, after Ms. von der Leyen's "associate membership" pitch.

But a closer alliance "inherently" made sense, he added. "Not just because we share values and history but because we share common interests, we share a strategic vision," he told AFP.

Valerie Hayer, the head of the centrist Renew group, envisaged an even broader partnership as she took the floor after Ms. von der Leyen, telling lawmakers Ottawa and Brussels must respond together to tariffs and "trade coercion", and foster university exchanges among other things.

Others were less enthusiastic.

Under EU rules, member states have to approve any form of partnership with a third country and it was unclear how much support Ms. von der Leyen's proposal would receive from capitals.

World.title: India voices concern over attempted drone attack on Mecca
World.content:
India has expressed deep concern over a drone attack reported near Mecca in Saudi Arabia, reiterating its condemnation of attacks on the sovereign territory of the Kingdom and actions that threaten civilian lives and infrastructure.

Responding to media queries, Ministry of External Affairs Official Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India was “deeply concerned” by the incident and stressed the need to protect civilians and critical infrastructure from attacks.

“India reiterates its condemnation of attacks on the sovereign territory of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and of actions that endanger civilian lives and infrastructure,” Mr. Jaiswal said.

“The incident near Mecca is particularly concerning, given the special significance of the city to Muslims across the world,” he said.

India expressed hope for a swift de-escalation of tensions, calling for the restoration of peace and stability in the region.

“We hope for the early restoration of peace and stability in the region,” Mr. Jaiswal added.

Saudi Arabia’s air defences destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca ‌before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, a spokesperson for ​the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said on Wednesday (September 16, 2026), as fighting spreads in ⁠West Asia.

Our response to media queries regarding the drone attack near Makkah ⬇️



🔗 https://t.co/l3qVpApFa3pic.twitter.com/2bXH7fzijo — Randhir Jaiswal (@MEAIndia) September 16, 2026

The drone, intercepted on Tuesday evening (September 15, 2026), was the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca after a ballistic missile launch in July 2017, spokesperson Turki al-Malki said in a statement, and follows ‌a week of attacks from Iran-aligned Houthi fighters that have drawn Saudi Arabia deeper into the war.

Mecca is home to some of the ‌holiest sites in Islam and the focal point of the annual hajj pilgrimage, and ‌its ⁠security was a “red line”, the coalition spokesperson al-Malki said in the statement.

World.title: Telangana Assembly session LIVE Sept 16: Telangana CM says 98.31 lakh acres have to be in prohibited (properties) list
World.content:
The monsoon session of the Telangana Assembly will resume on Wednesday (September 16, 2016), after being adjourned for three days from Sunday (September 13, 2016). The short discussion on the issues related to Section 22A of Registrations Act continued in the House.

Besides K. Sambasiva Rao, other MLAs who spoke on the issues pertaining to Section22A of Registrations Act were Vemula Veeresham, Naini Rajender Reddy, K Shanakaraiah, Naveen Yadav, Ahmed Bin Abdullah Balala and others. Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy begun speaking on the issues in the afternoon.

The Chief Minister listed the extent of lands under various sub-sections of Section 22A, including assignment lands (24,63,940 acres); forest lands (around 42 lakh acres); State and Central government lands (around 29 lakh acres); lands under endowments and waqf (around 5.12 lakh acres); lands attached by various law enforcement agencies such as ED, CBI. All of this totals 98,31,320 acres.

Mr. Reddy said that nearly 98,31,320 acres have to be in the prohibited (properties) list. Not even an inch can be removed from the list. If done, it amounts to injustice to people and giving a chance to encroach forest lands, he said.

The dispute between the government and private entities is pertaining to 3,72,930 acres of private land. However, it is being claimed that one crore acres is under the prohibited properties list, he said.

Also read: Assembly session highlights on September 12, 2026

On Saturday (September 12, 2016), Revenue Minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy spoke at length about the properties under Section 22A.

A short discussion on the effects of El Niño and remedial measures too is scheduled for today.

The subjects on which questions may be asked in the House include career guidance cells for minority students, improvement of public transport in the CURE region and expansion of horticulture crops in the State.

World.title: Tamil Nadu Assembly records establish M.K. Stalin was a political prisoner under MISA during Emergency
World.content:
Historical records of debates on the Justice Ismail Commission Report that took place in the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly as well as Legislative Council (since abolished) in 1978 reinforce that former Chief Minister and DMK president M.K. Stalin was indeed a political detenu under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA) during the Emergency.

The Commission headed by then Madras High Court judge M.M. Ismail was set up during the President’s Rule in May 1977. The Commission was mandated to conduct an inquiry into the incidents of beating and ill-treatment alleged to have taken place in the Central Prison, Madras, during February 1976 to February 1977.

As many as 88 prisoners were detained at the Madras Central Prison under the MISA. Prominent among them were Mr. Stalin, Dravidar Kazhagam leader K. Veeramani, former MLA Arcot N. Veerasamy (later Minister), DMK leader Murasoli Maran, and then MP Chittibabu.

The charge was that several detenus including Mr. Stalin, arrested soon after the dismissal of the M. Karunanidhi Government, were beaten up severely upon their arrival in the prison.

By the time the Commission submitted its report to the Government of Tamil Nadu in September 1977, the AIADMK headed by M.G. Ramachandran (MGR) had taken over the reins of power at the Fort St. George.

On March 31, 1978, a Government resolution was moved by Minister C. Aranganayagam on the floor of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Council to discuss about the Ismail Commission Report on the allegations of attack on the “political detenus”. Mr. Veerasamy spoke at length for more than an hour graphically describing the attack on the MISA detenus inside the prison.

Thereafter elaborate discussions on the report took place in the Legislative Assembly on April 6 and 7. On the second day, then Leader of Opposition and former Chief Minister M Karunanidhi spoke extensively on the arrest of the political party functionaries, following the dismissal of his government on January 31, 1976. The text of his speech, typed by the Assembly stenographers, ran to nearly 15 pages.

Karunanidhi recalled how family members of the MISA prisoners were denied an opportunity to meet them in Madras Central Jail even nearly four weeks after their detention. On February 26, 1976, he had shot off a telegram to Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, which read: “Interview for relatives of MISA detenus of DMK party in Tamil Nadu not yet granted for past 26 days in Madras prison. Reason we reliably understand the detenus are mercilessly beaten inside the prison. MPs, former MLAs and office bearers of DMK party are amongst such detenus so beaten. Request your immediate intervention preventing ill treatment and necessary action to get interview.”

The following day, he had written a letter to the President, explaining about the attack and poor prison conditions. “I do hope that your conscience will not accept the way in which the political prisoners have been treated worser than those who have been convicted for murder. I request you to save the jail birds from torture by the Madras Central Jail authorities,” he wrote.

A day later, Karunanidhi had telephoned Inspector General of Police F.V. Arul and gave him an ultimatum – he would go on a fast outside the jail if family members were not allowed to meet the prisoners by 1 p.m. the next day. It was after this that the authorities allowed them to meet the inmates.

The DMK leader recalled his emotional meeting with his 23-year-old son Mr. Stalin with few words exchanged as the police were watching over the inmates.

Karunanidhi utilised the opportunity in the House to ensure the key extracts from the prison diary of the late Chittibabu, whose health condition had suffered a setback during the assault by prison staff, made its way into the Assembly records.

Referring to the discussion over the diary, Karunanidhi posed in the House: “Before his death, did Chittibabu write the diary anticipating such circumstance would befall him? Don’t we all know Chittibabu? Isn’t Chittibabu our close friend? Doesn’t the Finance Minister [Nanjil] Manoharan know, when we were together [DMK before the split], about how Chittibabu functioned efficiently as Mayor of Chennai and got fame? Didn’t he perform efficiently as an MP who was praised by Anna [C.N. Annadurai]? Are we doubting his diary?.... We need to ponder over this. At the time of penning his notes, Chittibabu could not have anticipated that the Ismail Commission would be constituted. He wouldn’t even have had an inkling that this diary would serve as an evidence. He had merely penned what happened...”

Referring to a demand by CPI(M) MLA Govindarasan to provide a compensation of Rs. 5 lakh to Chittibabu’s family, Karunanidhi said: “Even that is not required. It would be no exaggeration to say that if that great warrior’s diary makes its way to the records of this House, that would be the greatest honour for him.” Thereafter, Karunanidhi read out the key excerpts from the diary including how Surulirajan, a jail warder, had placed his boots on the face of Mr. Stalin, who had fallen on the ground inside the prison cell.

[Other prominent MISA detenus in the country who had maintained a diary of what happened in the jail included the Gandhian leader Jayaprakash Narayan and actor Snehalatha Reddy, who like Chittibabu had died after being released from detention in Bangalore.]

A day earlier, in the Assembly, Durai Govindarajan, the Government Whip, cited the speech of another member, Jebamani (also a MISA detenu), to wonder if the latter was hinting at something deeper when he had said, “a son may face a situation where he would have to take the punishment for the mistakes committed by his father.”

Immediately, former Minister K. Anbazhagan (DMK) intervened, and said it was not proper for the Government Whip to make such statements with inner meaning. Jebamani responded saying he had not made that statement with any ulterior meaning. The Government Whip then said: “I only made a general statement and did not say that it was right to beat up Stalin there (in the cell).”

Not giving up, Anbazhagan contended Jebamani’s speech and Govindarajan’s statement appeared to convey that Mr. Stalin was imprisoned and beaten up because he was the son of the [former] Chief Minister.

World.title: DG ISPR says Makkah defence pact has 'no regional aspirations', intended for collective deterrence
World.content:
Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said that the Makkah Defence Alliance — a tripartite agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye — has no “regional aspirations”, adding that it is intended for collective deterrence.

The military spokesperson made the remarks during an interview on Al Arabiya English’s programme ‘Global News Today’, during a conversation with the host, Tom Burges Watson.

During the show, aired during the early hours of Wednesday, Lt Gen Chaudhry was asked about Pakistan’s commitments under the agreement.

“It formalises Pakistan’s decades-old relationship with the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the brotherly country of Turkiye in the domains of collective deterrence and defence,” he said.

Watson then asked whether the pact was primarily a defensive cooperation or the beginning of a broader strategic alliance. To that, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that the pact was defensive, as its name implied.

“It is defensive. There’s nothing aggressive. There are no regional aspirations. It is collective deterrence,” he said, adding that the agreement was also “complementary”.

Elaborating further, he said the countries part of the alliance had independent relationships with other nations, blocs and alliances.

“So this mutual defence agreement is complementary in nature. It is not competing with any other relationship of these countries,” he added.

At that, Watson asked, “But does it contain any mutual defence obligation?”

In his short reply to the question, Lt Gen Chaudhry remarked, “The text that has been made public by the leadership of the three countries enunciates that very clearly and it’s interpretation is quite clear.”

Asked how Pakistan would respond if one of the countries in the alliance came under attack, he said that the operationalisation of defensive commitments was never made public in any discourse.

“You see, you have multiple other agreements which are defensive in nature, which are committal in nature. But no country comes out and starts sharing its operational details […] What you’re asking is the how part — that how we are going to defend Pakistan against any aggression.

“That is always part of the operational classification and security […] What you’re asking is that how it will be done. It is for the three countries to decide, and it is for them to know and for them to actualise it,” he said.

Specifically asked whether the military spokesperson saw the alliance “complementing or competing” with Pakistan’s relationship with China, Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted that it complemented Islamabad-Beijing ties.

“We need to understand that the Pak-Saudi and the Pak-Turkiye relationship has not come out of the blue. The Chinese understand it. The world at large understands it. That’s how historic these relationships are. We have formalised that.

“Nobody has any problem with that. Everyone understands that this is defensive. Everyone understands it is for maintaining stability and peace in the region. And all the three countries that are part of it, they have a wonderful relationship with China,” he said.

During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked whether he saw the defence agreement becoming a part of the wider, Muslim-world security architecture.

He replied that there was nothing in the pact that stated that it was a Muslim alliance, adding that it was an alliance for regional stability.

“It is not a club that is being made for only Muslim countries,” he said, adding that decisions on its expansion were to be taken by the leadership of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

“This agreement, this alliance can always encompass new, willing partners who also believe in regional peace, stability and security, [and] who have a shared vision of non-aggression, non-interference and collective deterrence.

“But that’s for the leadership of these three countries to decide; the how and when part,” he elaborated.

The joint defence pact was signed on Aug 7 and provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. Its inaugural meeting was held in Istanbul on Aug 31, where it was decided that Pakistan would initially head the alliance’s secretariat for three years.

Since its signing, there has been conversation about the possibility of its expansion, with Turkiye initially suggesting the possibility of Egypt’s inclusion. Though there has been no confirmation from Cairo.

From Pakistan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar clarified soon after the signing that the pact was defensive in nature, with the latter saying that it was also “open to any country in the region” willing to uphold its fundamental principles.

However, when Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjah Haider Khan was asked about possibility of the pact’s expansion during a weekly media briefing last week, he said an expansion was not on the cards at that point.

The three countries first needed to solidify the new organisation before considering opening it to other states with similar threat perceptions and requirements, he explained.

US-Iran mediation and Pakistan’s ‘unique position’

During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was also asked about Pakistan’s efforts to mediate between the United States and Iran and whether the Makkah Defence Alliance complicated Islamabad’s position towards Tehran.

Lt Gen Chaudhry replied such was not the case, adding that the alliance was based on decades-old strategic ties.

“This alliance is a formalisation of that strategic relationship in a peculiar environment,” he said, reiterating that the pact was based on collective deterrence. The defence pact, he said, had no offensive or aggressive element and was purely defensive in nature.

Asked why Pakistan had opted to play the role of a mediator in the ongoing Middle East conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, he succinctly stated, “For regional peace.”

Lt Gen Chaudhry then added that stability stemmed from peace and Pakistan was a proponent of peace in the region. Moreover, he continued, Pakistan had a “unique position” in this case because of its policy of alignment and engagement with countries across the world.

Hence, it could play the role of an “objective arbiter of peace and an honest broker of peace”.

To a question about progress on the mediation front and towards a settlement, Lt Gen Chaudhry explained that one of the prerequisites of good mediation was remaining objective and neutral.

“So it’s not for us as a mediator to start commenting on things that are happening or that are bound to happen,” he said, adding that Pakistan’s political and military leadership had been reaching out to all the parties so that “better sense prevails and, instead of a military solution, we come to a negotiated outcome of this very complex situation”.

Watson then pointed to the possibility of the US and Iran rejecting Pakistan’s proposal and asked whether Islamabad was prepared to continue its mediation in that case.

Lt Gen Chaudhry replied, “Is there any other way of resolving this conflict other than [through] mediation? Is there any other desirable way of doing that?”

He stressed the need for a “negotiated, peaceful outcome”, adding that those who could mediate objectively and sincerely between the two sides must continue their efforts.

Asked whether Pakistan was concerned about the conflict spilling over towards its western frontiers, Lt Gen Chaudhry answered that as far as Pakistan’s borders, territorial integrity and sovereignty were concerned, “we are very confident and very self-reliant on our security”.

There were always concerns of any conflict spiralling horizontally or vertically, he said, adding that not just Pakistan, but the entire world at large was feeling the impact of the conflict.

“So, there are [always] concerns in multiple domains”, but Pakistan was “fully confident of taking care of whatever nefarious designs come out of that towards” it, he said.

Asked whether Pakistan aimed to become a regional mediator or was simply trying to prevent a regional war from reaching its own doorstep, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Pakistan is interested in regional peace and stability, because peace and stability are essential for development, for human development, for prosperity and for the citizens of Pakistan and the region.”

And if the “mediation is for peace, […] and we’ll always be there”.

Prospects of dialogue with India

Watson then came to the brief military conflict between Pakistan and India in May last year, and asked what lessons Pakistan’s military had learned from the episode.

Lt Gen Chaudhry replied that what was more important were the lessons Pakistan and its military taught during that conflict. He said that a military conflict between two nuclear countries, especially neighbours, was “out of question”.

“It’s a sheer, I would say, a sort of mad idea,” he said, adding that Pakistan also showed that India made a “strategic folly” in May last year.

Asked whether he believed India had learned that lesson, Lt Gen Chaudhry replied it was for the Indian side to answer.

“Our job in Pakistan is to keep on reminding them of that lesson,” he said, adding that the other side had a “hubristic mindset” and the Indian military was “deeply politicised”.

In India, he continued, there was a propensity of externalising their internal problems, giving the example of minorities facing oppression.

On the other hand, he said, there was the Kashmir issue, which was an “external problem” that New Delhi wanted to “internalise through repression”.

The military’s spokesperson added that Pakistan continued to give out the message to India that it believed in “peace on equal terms” and that it was a rational and objective player.

Pakistan believes in regional peace, but if India has any “misconceptions about [imposing] regional hegemony through military aggression, results of that would be beyond their imagination”, he warned.

Lt Gen Chaudhry said Pakistan had showed India and the world in May last year that it had the capability and resolve to dominate and control an escalation.

“And we’ll do it again,” he added.

Asked whether there were any realistic prospects of restoring sustained military-to-military communication with India, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Yes, of course.”

He added that communication between the directors general of military operations had remained effective during the May conflict and beyond.

“Communication is always good. We must communicate, we must engage, but that engagement has to be done on equal terms while respecting each other’s integrity and sovereignty,” he said.

To a question about resuming dialogue with India, he said it was for the political leadership to decide. But dialogue, he said, had to be on equal terms.

“Dialogue cannot be, or engagement cannot be to provide a cover for the ongoing state-sponsored Indian terrorism in Pakistan, for the ongoing aggression,” he emphasised.

‘Only successful counter-terrorism campaign in the world’

Coming to Afghanistan, Watson asked about the Pakistani military’s preferred end state with the Afghan Taliban.

“I think the military’s end state is actually part of Pakistan’s end state that the political leadership sets. So, there is no separate military end state.

“So, there are Pakistan’s objectives and desire, which are primarily the domain of the Pakistan’s political leadership and an expression of the will of the people of Pakistan. And what that is that we want — no interference, no terrorism from Afghanistan in Pakistan. So that’s the foundation,” he said.

Asked what options Pakistan considered legitimate for preventing cross-border attacks in case of the failure of diplomacy, Lt Gen Chaudhry said, “Right of self-defence is enshrined in the Article 51 of the United Nations; right of self-defence is given to each nation state of the world.”

He added that the Pakistani state had an obligation to defend the lives, honour and property of its citizens. To that end, “all that is necessary will be done and is being done”.

In this connection, he detailed Pakistan’s counter-terrorism measures and said the country’s counter-terrorism campaign was the “only successful counter-terrorism campaign in the world”.

“Because we are the bulwark state against” terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, he said.

Lt Gen Chaudhry also mentioned that in the current year, 42,000 intelligence-based operations (IBOs) had been carried out and 2,100 terrorists had been killed.

Towards the programme’s end, Watson steered the discussion towards Balochistan, on which Lt Gen Chaudhry said there was no insurgency in the province.

“There’s just terrorism,” he said, adding that the military had clarity on that, tactically and strategically.

He said of the 42,000 IBOs, over 32,000 were conducted in Balochistan and security forces remained engaged in “taking out the so-called proxies who associate themselves with Balochistan and have got nothing to do with it”.

Regarding strategic clarity, he said the government, people of Balochistan and the military understood that the way to deal with terrorism was to kill terrorists and “embrace the people of Balochistan”.

World.title: Weapons dealer among 'JAAC-linked network' caught during intelligence-based operation: Tallal Chaudhry
World.content:
Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry said authorities had traced a “network” allegedly linked to the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), including a weapons dealer.

Addressing a press conference in Islamabad, the minister recalled the government’s move to proscribe the JAAC in Azad Jammu and Kashmir in June. He observed that many questions were raised, including whether the ban was a political decision.

“At that time too, you were told that they were proscribed with great responsibility, based on the evidence that has reached us, investigation into which is underway and many things have surfaced,” he said.

The state minister went on to say that questions were raised about audio clips that surfaced on social media, allegedly linked to the JAAC, and whether they were AI-generated.

He then played a montage of news channels’ reporting on the situation in AJK in recent months, including incidents and footage that the authorities linked to JAAC as well as attacks on security personnel.

“Many of our critics continued to criticise these as well without knowing the facts,” Chaudhry remarked.

The state minister said a “network was captured” during an IBO, which began with tracing a person named Zia. He identified Zia as a resident of AJK who was “working as a weapons dealer for various people for the past eight to 10 years”.

“For the past two years, he has been directly supplying weapons to the closest members of JAAC,” the minister claimed.

He said Zia was arrested during an IBO carried out after security forces were targeted in a firing incident at Kashmir Mor.

Citing information obtained from his mobile phone and subsequent backtracking, Chaudhry said Zia was in contact with Majid, whom he said carried out special tasks for JAAC member Sardar Amaan.

The minister said close ties between Majid and Amaan were “known to everyone who has been part of negotiations on this issue in Kashmir or was in contact with JAAC”.

An audio clip was then played, allegedly of a conversation between Zia and Majid about sending armed men and Dragunov rifles. Chaudhry claimed more information, such as the cost of weapons and the ammunition used, could be presented before the public.

Zia was connected with Zarshad, who used to send weapons from Afghanistan to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Bara, according to the minister.

He then played “one of the audio clips available with intelligence agencies”, allegedly of Zia and Zarshad speaking about various weapons such as Kalashnikovs.

“We have been saying for a while that these people would expose themselves,” Chaudhry said, highlighting that intelligence agencies were noticing them.

He explained the reasoning for the “doubts” against JAAC, noting that 37 of its 38 demands had been “partially or completely agreed upon and implementation had been initiated”, but the group announced a long march “as soon as it was decided to hold elections”.

“The aim was to create an environment in which elections could not take place to reinforce the narrative that someone else makes decisions for Kashmiris,” he asserted.

Recalling the violent incidents in AJK a couple of months ago, Chaudhry stressed there was an “entire campaign with preparation” as Zia had provided many consignments over the past two years.

“We will have to differentiate between political struggle and an armed group,” he declared, criticising “any such movement whose aim is to create doubt about state decisions either through statements or actions or supporting groups that destabilise Pakistan”.

The state minister played a video statement of a man who identified himself as Zia and a resident of AJK’s Sudhanoti district.

He said he had remained affiliated with the senior leadership of JAAC and recalled his communication with Zarshad and Akbar for procuring weapons. The person further said he had been involved in attacks on security forces in AJK.

Govt employee role and ‘political-crime network’

The state minister noted that the question arose of the logistics of supplying the weapons even though security forces were present on the border.

He then said that a government employee named Akbar “played an important role in this”, noting that he had the “cover to carry such items without security forces and hiding them”.

Chaudhry described Akbar as a “carrier”, adding that he was an employee of an “important institution and used to bring all weapons under the cover that no one would check him”.

The minister explained that the weapons network extended from Afghanistan to AJK’s Kotli via KP’s Bara, using local facilitators. He then played an audio clip, allegedly of Zia speaking to Akbar.

“Unfortunately, the political class is also involved in this terror-crime network,” the minister said, contending that “political support” helped fuel stations selling smuggled petrol and the wide use of smuggled vehicles in some districts.

“Many people have stakes in this political-crime network.”

Chaudhry observed that one of the 20 points of the national counter-terrorism drive was to eradicate the “terror-crime network”, which included illegal petrol pumps, narcotics and other activities that provided financial and logistical support to the network.

Referring to Zarshad’s alleged audio, the minister noted it mentioned Rs2.2 million, of which Rs1.1m were paid and some of that amount was transferred via hawala/hundi.

At the outset of his press conference, Chaudhry said about 200 IBOs were carried out daily.

He noted the “role of Afghanistan and the people sitting in Afghanistan in terrorism in Pakistan and efforts to destabilise Pakistan”.

The state minister said there was a “terror-crime network here, which many people call their business but we call it a terror-crime nexus”, adding that it facilitated a plethora of illegal activities, such as smuggling of narcotics, vehicles, petroleum products and supply of weapons from ordinary criminals to large networks.

“This entire terror crime network facilitates the kind of actions that in Pakistan appear as terrorism and actions that are sponsored and managed in an organised manner through our eastern and western borders alike, from those two countries unfortunately.”

World.title: Imran's hospital transfer: SC expresses reservation at fixation of cases before FCC
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court on Wednesday expressed reservations over the Federal Constitutional Court’s (FCC) directive that cases pertaining to PTI founder Imran Khan’s hospital transfer be fixed before the latter, but deferred its own proceedings on the matter for a date after three weeks, observing that propriety demanded deferment.

The FCC had issued the orders on Tuesday, directing the court’s office to requisition from the SC the relevant cases and fix them before it under Article 175-E of the Constitution. The directive was issued on a plea by three Adiala jail inmates seeking relief similar to that provided to Imran by the SC in an August 18 interim order.

A three-judge SC bench, headed by Justice Shahid Waheed and including Justices Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Ishtiaq Ibrahim, took up the pleas on Wednesday.

The judges told Attorney General for Pakistan (AGP) Mansoor Usman Awan that what bothered them was the fixation of the cases before the FCC, as stated in paragraph six of the Sept 15 FCC order.

Justice Waheed also observed that fixing cases before the FCC requisitioned from the SC did not fall under clause 5 of Article 175-E of the Constitution.

Article 175-E, which was inserted in the Constitution through the 27th Constitutional Amendment, empowers the FCC to call for the record of any case and authorises it to decide matters involving major questions of constitutional law.

For his part, the AGP said that the issue required deep analysis and deliberation, following which the bench conceded that the situation was unprecedented as it was the first time the FCC had requisitioned case records from the SC, unlike the usual practice of summoning records from the high courts.

The SC also stated that its Aug 18 directive for the relevant authorities to shift Imran to Shifa International Hospital, a private facility in Islamabad, was made without prejudice to the intentions of the parties.

On a query, the AGP conceded that the SC’s Aug 18 order was in the field but made no assurance when the petitioner’s counsel insisted on its interpretation.

Justice Waheed told the petitioners that the court was leaving the implementation of the Aug 18 directions to AGP, who was not present in the courtroom when the hearing began.

Any other law officer was also not present in courtroom no.5, which was otherwise packed to the capacity.

Subsequently, the court asked for AGP Awan. But it was Additional Attorney General Rana Asadullah Khan who first appeared before the court and read out the FCC’s Sept 15 directives for requisitioning the case record from the SC to the FCC.

The court then retired momentarily, directing that AGP Awan should appear before it.

After almost 35 minutes, when AGP reached the courtroom, the bench wondered whether the Sept 15 FCC order was binding upon the SC.

AGP explained that the FCC had issued the directions by invoking Article 175 E (5) of the Constitution, adding that the tentative jurisdictions in which the two judicial institutions operate have been clearly spelt out under the 27th Constitutional Amendment.

Justice Waheed also read out the questions framed by the FCC in its Tuesday order:

Which courts have the jurisdiction and competence to enforce the fundamental rights under the Constitution? What are the rights that must be afforded to the prisoners under the Constitution and the Pakistan Prison Rules, 1978? What is the scope and extent of obligations of the state with regards to the fundamental rights of the prisoners? What consequences entail if any functionary of the state violates the fundamental rights of the prisoners?

Justice Waheed observed that if fundamental rights were the pivotal point, then fundamental rights were always involved in all cases, be it civil, criminal or even service matters. He added that the requirement for a fair trial under Article 10-A of the Constitution applied to every case.

Justice Waheed also made it clear that the SC could extend any relief to the prisoners under the guiding principles of the Holy Quran and Sunnah – a jurisdiction which the FCC lacked.

AGP Awan, however, contended that the SC’s Shariat Appellate Bench had the jurisdiction to interpret questions under the Holy Quran and Sunnah.

Justice Afghan observed that the bench’s only concern was the further scope of action for the SC in view of paragraph six of the FCC order.

“Both institutions have to co-exist, and both have jurisdiction of their own,” Justice Afghan observed. He said the case record could be requisitioned expressed reservations at the fixation of the cases before the FCC.

Senior counsel Barrister Syed Ali Zafar, who was also present at the hearing, contended that the case transfer “had nothing to do with jurisdiction” and that there was no question of taking away or conferring jurisdiction under Article 175 E(5) of the Constitution.

Advocate Uzair Karamat Bhandari, representing Dr Uzma Khan, in her plea against the alleged violation of the SC’s Aug 18 directive, requested the court to at least issue directions to ensure meetings with the family members and lawyers with the incarcerated leader.

According to the court order, a copy of which is available with Dawn, the court sought the AGP’s “assistance” for the proper course in the proceedings, particularly the extent to which the FCC order is binding on the proceedings.

“This course is considered appropriate so as to avoid any situation that may be inconsistent with the proper functioning of the two apex judicial institutions of the country and, at the same time, to preserve the spirit of judicial comity,” the court observed.

The AGP sought three weeks to consider the matter and prepare his submissions.

Subsequently, the court adjourned the proceedings for a date after three weeks, observing that propriety demanded deferment of the present matter since the SC, in the spirit of the Constitution, could not disregard a judicial order.

World.title: Saudi-led coalition says Houthis targeted Makkah with drone, warns of 'red line'
World.content:
The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthis accused the rebels on Wednesday of targeting the holy city of Makkah, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region.

Fresh fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government has dragged in Riyadh, with the Houthis declaring a maritime blockade on the kingdom and targeting its ships in the Red Sea.

Last week’s lightning offensive saw the group seize control of the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes off the Strait of Hormuz strategic shipping route.

The Houthis swiftly rejected as a “lie” Riyadh’s report that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards Makkah, which attracts millions of pilgrims each year.

“The claims about targeting Makkah are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone,” Hazem al-Assad from the Houthis’ politburo wrote on X.

The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, warning that the security of holy sites was a “red line”.

“The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the Terrorist Houthi Militia,” the coalition said in a statement shared by spokesman Turki al-Maliki.

The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) — a bloc of 57 Muslim countries — condemned the “heinous” attack.

Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Makkah and across swathes of the kingdom’s south, which borders Yemen.

The alerts, including the first one issued in Makkah since the Middle East war erupted in February, came a day after a wave of ballistic missile and drone attacks launched from Yemen wounded 13 people in the kingdom’s south.

Fighting flared in July when the Houthis, who have for years controlled swathes of northern Yemen, launched a large-scale offensive against Yemeni government forces.

The conflict in the Arabian Peninsula’s poorest country has forced 82,000 people to flee their homes since the start of September, according to the United Nations.

Yemen’s permanent representative at the UN, Abdullah al-Saadi, said Yemenis were fighting to restore “national institutions across every inch of their land”, and called on the international community to take action against the Houthis.

PM Shehbaz condemns ‘dastardly and heinous attempted drone attack’

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned in the “strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous attempted drone attack against the Holy Site of Makkah Al-Mukarramah”.

“The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act. There can be no words strong enough to capture the depth of anguish and sorrow felt by us at this reprehensible and unforgivable act,” he wrote in a post on X.

He lauded the “extraordinary vigilance, courage, and professionalism of the Royal Saudi Armed Forces for their swift and heroic action”.

The premier urged “all parties to exercise maximum restraint and to step back from the brink of further escalation”.

“Our region has already suffered far too much from conflict. Dialogue and diplomacy remain the only sustainable path towards peace,” he stressed.

“Pakistan stands unwaveringly, shoulder to shoulder with the brotherly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, in the defence of its sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as for the security and sanctity of the Haramain Sharifain — a duty that every Pakistani carries close to their heart.”

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also condemned the incident, saying that “such a provocative act violates the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the kingdom of Saudi Arabia, gravely offends the religious sentiments of the Muslims worldwide, and threatens regional peace and security”.

“Pakistan stands firmly with the leadership and people of the kingdom of Saudi Arabia in safeguarding the sanctity and security of the Two Holy Mosques, the Haramain Sharifain, and ensuring the safety of pilgrims, citizens and residents,” he said.

‘Hostile and extremist’

On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia and Egypt called for free navigation in the Red Sea following the Houthis’ offensive in the vital waterway.

After meeting in Cairo, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called for “ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation” through the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — which links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, the Egyptian presidency said.

The revival of Yemen’s civil war, dormant since 2022, has left Riyadh rushing to respond.

US media reported last week that the Saudi crown prince made a personal request to President Donald Trump for US intervention, but was turned down.

The Houthis have insisted that there is no threat to navigation in the Bab al-Mandab except for Saudi vessels.

Any attacks in the waterway are likely to make it less attractive to shippers.

Disruption in the strait could cause Egypt to feel the pinch too, as the Red Sea serves as the gateway to the Suez Canal, upon which Cairo relies for crucial foreign revenue.

Canal revenues are currently around half of what they were before the Houthis first started attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023, a campaign they said was in solidarity with Palestinians during Israel’s war on Gaza.

On Tuesday, Qatar warned of dire consequences if Bab al-Mandab was closed, saying it would be “catastrophic for the entire world”.

The Houthis have also targeted oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world’s leading crude exporter, helping push global prices above the $100-a-barrel threshold.

The Saudi-led coalition said it would deal with the attacks “firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom”, and would take “all necessary operational measures to deter this … hostile and extremist approach”.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Tuesday that Saudi Arabia launched 52 airstrikes on Yemen over the past 24 hours, accusing it of targeting civilian sites, including schools and bridges.

But Riyadh’s strikes have failed to reverse the group’s gains.

A US military task force is working to enhance intelligence-sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces as they face attacks, a US official told AFP on Tuesday.

World.title: What's behind the foul smell in Karachi today?
World.content:
Residents of Karachi, particularly those residing near the sea, woke up on Wednesday morning to a foul smell which some described as “fishy”. According to experts, decaying microscopic marine algae and current weather conditions are behind the pungent smell permeating the air.

Muhammad Moazzam Khan, technical adviser on marine resources at World Wide Fund for Nature-Pakistan (WWF-P), said the fishy smell was a result of decomposing microscopic marine algae called phytoplankton — a naturally occurring event.

He explained that when the regional monsoon system ends in mid-September, it results in significant changes in the sea conditions. Consequently, these phytoplankton, found abundantly during the monsoon, begin to decay.

Phytoplankton are found in the upper 100 metres of the sea, where sunlight can penetrate, and are not visible to the naked eye.

The WWF-P expert said this phenomenon — also witnessed in 2024 — often causes a foul smell to permeate the air in the coastal areas. He added that the smell would likely dissipate in a few days.

The Pakistan Meteorological Department’s (PMD) spokesperson, Anjum Nazir Zaigham, and climate change expert Fatima Yamin attributed the scale of the smell to the weather conditions too.

Yamin said a low-pressure area off the coast of India’s Jamnagar was circulating wind around Karachi’s coastline, which was turning into smog because of air pollution.

She added that the combination of smog and the weather conditions was causing the smell to “circulate throughout the city”.

WInd forecast map shows a low-pressure area off the coastline of India, as of 12:50pm PKT on Sept 16, 2026. — screengrab via Zoom Earth

Zaigham also pointed out the low-pressure area and the smog, in addition to the south-easterly wind direction.

He said the air would likely get better by the evening with the sea breeze.

The stench was also reported across the metropolis in October 2024, with Clifton, Defence Housing Authority (DHA), SMCHS, PECHS, Korangi, Orangi, North Nazimabad, Federal B Area (blocks 9 and 10), and Saddar witnessing it strongly.

Asked about possible health risks at the time, ecologist Rafiullah had said that while there was no “concrete” evidence yet, prolonged exposure to the combination of dusty winds and the smell might affect sinusitis.

World.title: Ban on Indian aircraft using Pakistani airspace extended until Oct 24
World.content:
Pakistan has extended its airspace ban for Indian aircraft until October 24, according to a Notice to Airmen (Notam) issued by the Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA).

The previous extension of the ban was set to expire on September 24.

“Pakistan airspace not available for Indian registered aircraft and aircraft operated/owned or leased by Indian airlines/operators, including military flights,” the Notam said.

According to the notice, the extension came into effect at 10:45am on Wednesday and will remain until 04:59am on Oct 24, 2026.

The country’s airspace is divided into two flight information regions (FIRs) — Karachi and Lahore, according to a Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority (PCAA) document from 2022.

Wednesday’s Notam applies to both the Karachi (OPKR) and Lahore (OPLR) FIRs.

India and Pakistan closed their airspaces to each other’s airlines in late April 2025, when tensions between them escalated in the wake of a deadly attack in India-occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam.

On April 24, Pakistan’s top brass had announced a series of measures , including the closure of its airspace to all India-owned or Indian-operated airlines with immediate effect, as it retaliated against New Delhi’s slew of aggressive measures against the country.

New Delhi, without evidence, had alleged that Islamabad backed the Pahalgam attack. However, Pakistan had strongly denied any involvement and offered a neutral probe . The nuclear powers had the fiercest air battle in May, in which Pakistan said it downed seven Indian fighter jets.

Since then, Pakistan has extended the airspace ban several times, forcing Indian carriers to use longer and costlier routes.

For Air India, the country’s only carrier with a major international network, fuel costs rose by as much as 29 per cent and journey times by up to three hours on some long-haul routes, according to a document submitted to Indian officials last October.

The airline, owned by Tata Group and Singapore Airlines, estimated the Pakistan airspace closure’s impact on its profit before tax at $455 million annually — a significant amount given its fiscal 2024-25 loss stood at $439m.

World.title: PM orders implementation of Pims inquiry reccomendations within 3 months
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday directed authorities to implement the short-term measures recommended in an inquiry report into the fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) within three months.

He issued the directives while chairing a meeting on an action plan for improving Pims, where the inquiry report and the performance audit by the Ministry of National Health Services were reviewed, according to a statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

The August 26 fire at a nursery in Pims’ Mother and Child Hospital claimed the lives of 14 newborns. The incident raised concerns over fire safety measures and sparked calls for accountability , with criminal action being ordered against eight officials .

During Wednesday’s meeting, the prime minister directed that the short-term measures in the inquiry report should be implemented within the next three months.

He also emphasised taking “every possible step” to improve the hospital and align it with international requirements. He directed that assistance and recommendations should be sought from the Pakistan Kidney and Liver Institute and Research Centre for the fire safety system.

He also directed that measures to ensure the free provision of medicines and facilities at the hospital be made part of the action plan.

The prime minister called for personnel with strong professional reputations to be employed at the hospital, adding that a comprehensive action plan based on the recommended long-term measures should be formulated.

PM Shehbaz also directed to carry out an audit of Polyclinic Hospital to address irregularities, adding that a plan for its restructuring should also be prepared.

He said that Capital Development Authority (CDA) should ensure the implementation of fire safety measures in all public and private hospitals in Islamabad.

“The CDA and relevant agencies should also conduct fire safety audits of public and private offices and buildings and ensure the implementation of safety measures,” the premier was quoted as saying.

During the meeting, the premier was informed that the performance audit of Pims found only 39.7 per cent compliance against indicators assessed.

It was also informed that immediate implementation was being ensured on 37 proposed measures in light of the investigative report. The meeting was also briefed on short, medium and long-term measures for improving the hospital.

The inquiry committee was formed on PM Shehbaz’s directives on the day the fire occurred. It presented its findings and recommendations in a 43-page report on Wednesday.

The committee said that the deadly blaze was most likely caused by a localised electrical failure, while also calling out the hospital management for systemic and institutional failure that turned the fire into a catastrophe.

The committee, headed by former interior secretary Shahid Khan, said in its report that abnormal localised electrical heating — possibly from excessive current, a high-resistance connection or another localised defect — most probably caused insulation failure and ignition of nearby combustible material.

The report, however, pointed out a “history of known but incompletely closed risks”, citing prior warnings, such as the fire at the nursing hostel in Pims. “Yet those warnings had not been converted into a comprehensive, time-bound and independently verified corrective programme before the nursery fire,” the report regretted.

World.title: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have brought Mideast conflict to 'dangerous juncture', Pakistan tells UN
World.content:
UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan said on Tuesday that Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia had brought the conflict in the Middle East to a “dangerous juncture”, while the United States and China called for restraint and de-escalation in Yemen as renewed fighting and attacks on the kingdom threatened to further destabilise the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.

Speaking at an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council, Pakistan’s Permanent Representative Asim Iftikhar Ahmad condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

“The Houthi military escalation inside Yemen, the continued Houthi attacks against the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the latest military developments along Yemen’s Red Sea coast have brought the conflict to an extremely dangerous juncture,” he said.

He added that the expansion of attacks in and around the Bab al-Mandab Strait represented a “serious escalation”.

“Pakistan condemns, in the strongest terms, all Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” he said, reaffirming Pakistan’s “unwavering support for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and prosperity” of the kingdom.

He said that Pakistan “fully supports Saudi Arabia’s legitimate right”, consistent with the UN Charter and international law, “to take necessary measures to defend its territory, protect its citizens and safeguard its national assets against threats”.

Ahmad warned that continued violations of international law against commercial shipping posed a growing threat to freedom of navigation and international maritime commerce.

“Any attempt to threaten, obstruct, or weaponise the vital waterways will have consequences for international trade and commercial shipping, global supply chains, and energy security,” he said.

He said the relative calm painstakingly maintained in Yemen since 2022 had collapsed, warning that continued escalation risked reigniting a full-scale conflict and drawing Yemen deeper into the wider regional confrontation.

“This must be prevented,” he said, calling for diplomacy to match the gravity of the crisis.

“Diplomacy must assume urgency in proportion to the gravity of this situation,” Ahmad said, expressing Pakistan’s strong support for “the resumption of an inclusive, Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process under United Nations auspices”.

US, China call for restraint

China also called for restraint and a return to negotiations, while stressing that protecting shipping in the Red Sea was a shared international responsibility.

Chinese representative Sun Lei said protecting freedom of navigation required an end to armed conflict and a lasting peace. He urged all parties to exercise restraint and return to negotiations, while calling for a greater role for Gulf countries in mediation and a new security architecture for the Middle East.

The US demanded that the Houthis halt their advances, withdraw from seized territory and cease their attacks.

US representative Jennifer Locetta also called on Iran to end its support for the group, accusing Tehran of arming, funding and directing the Houthis.

“Freedom of navigation underpins the global economy, and the United States is working with our partners to protect it,” she said, adding that the council could not ignore Iran’s role in supporting the Houthis.

Saudi Arabia told the council that the Houthi escalation threatened Yemen, regional security, international trade and global supply chains.

Saudi representative Abdulaziz M Alwasil cited attacks on Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran that injured civilians, as well as renewed attacks on Sept 14 and continued targeting of commercial vessels in the Red Sea.

He said the Houthis and militias supporting them were pursuing a policy of “choking the straits”, holding the international community and global economy hostage.

“Protecting vital waterways is a collective responsibility requiring a firm Council response,” Alwasil said. Saudi Arabia remained committed to de-escalation and peace, he said, while reserving its right to defend its territory and citizens.

Yemen said the Houthi advance towards Bab al-Mandab had transformed the conflict into an increasingly serious regional and international security issue.

Yemeni representative Abdullah Ali Fadhel al-Saadi said his government was responding to Houthi advances along the western coast, with its forces reorganising to regain the initiative and prevent the Houthis from using the coast to threaten international shipping.

He said continued Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and energy infrastructure were part of a broader regional threat, while warning of links between instability around the Red Sea, terrorist groups and trafficking networks in the Horn of Africa.

Al-Saadi called on the council to enforce the arms embargo, disrupt weapons, financing and smuggling networks, support Yemen in restoring authority over its territory and coast, and respond urgently to growing humanitarian needs.

Liberia, speaking on behalf of the three African council members — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Somalia and Liberia — warned that further territorial changes along Yemen’s coast could increase tensions, threaten international navigation and undermine efforts towards a political settlement.

Its diplomat, Lewis Garseedah Brown II, said there was no military solution to the conflict and warned against Yemen becoming an arena for proxy warfare.

For Africa, he said, Red Sea security was particularly important because disrupted shipping and rising freight and insurance costs could translate into higher prices for imported grain, fuel and fertiliser.

Bahrain also condemned the Houthi escalation and attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying the renewed fighting had worsened Yemen’s humanitarian crisis and forced civilians to flee their homes.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.
