World.title: [OPINION] Expanding armies, shrinking peace: Militarization in Southeast Asia
World.content:
These examples of military-led approaches in the region may each temporarily contain dissent, but likely also exacerbate human suffering while failing to reduce either armed or non-armed opposition

Several nations in Southeast Asia have undergone military expansion and increased securitization over the past decade contributing to what many observers describe as a regional arms race.

The ongoing militarization in Southeast Asia, combined with the erosion of the liberal international order and the weakening of democratic and human rights norms, has contributed to a self-reinforcing cycle of violence involving state militaries and domestic armed oppositions.

Rather than addressing the political causes of conflict, military solutions prolong insecurity, intensify armed confrontation, and exacerbate human suffering in conflict-affected communities such as Myanmar, the Philippines and Indonesia.

Myanmar’s sham peace: Promising peace, waging war

After the illegal 2021 military coup overthrew the elected government, military authorities intensified their repression of political expression, launched large-scale counteroffensive operations against armed resistance groups, expanded conscription, and gradually increased both conventional and unconventional aerial attacks on civilian and military targets.

An estimated 90% of Myanmar’s population has been exposed to conflict. Over 3.5 million people have been displaced, while one in three citizens now require humanitarian assistance. The scale of insecurity has transformed Myanmar into one of the world’s most severe humanitarian and protection crises.

The Myanmar military, which is responsible for the vast majority of political violence in the country, has demonstrated little genuine commitment to resolving the political crisis fueling nationwide conflict. Airstrikes and attacks against civilian populations continue despite junta leader Min Aung Hlaing’s 100-day peace plan, killing over 600 between April 20 to July 31.

For the junta, peace talks appear to be less aimed at achieving conflict resolution than at managing threats to its authority and fragmenting opposition coalitions. Dialogue risks becoming a mechanism where the military prioritises regime survival over the pursuit of durable and inclusive peace. Recent China-brokered ceasefires between the military and Ethnic Armed Organisations operating in northern Shan state reflect the military’s longstanding divide-and-rule strategy: neutralising one adversary through ceasefire agreements while intensifying military operations against others.

The Myanmar military faces limited external pressure to change while it is backed by international partners such as China and Russia, which continue to provide it with military equipment and technical assistance, and the junta also benefits from varying degrees of diplomatic engagement from neighboring countries such as India and Thailand.

PH security dilemma: Rejecting dialogue, prolonging conflict

The New People’s Army (NPA), widely regarded as Asia’s longest-running communist insurgency, has been engaged in armed conflict with successive Philippines governments since 1968.

Since President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. declared in July 2024 that the rebellion had effectively ceased, armed confrontations between state forces and insurgents have continued and, in some areas, intensified. April 2026 marked the deadliest month for the insurgency in recent years, with counterinsurgency operations reportedly resulting in 19 deaths, including six civilians. Overall, at least 390 combatants and civilians were reportedly killed in insurgency-related and counterinsurgency violence in 2025 alone.

Separately, Manila has deepened defence and security cooperation with the US and other regional partners amid growing tensions in the South China Sea. Joint military exercises, technology transfers, expanded access to military facilities, and new defence agreements have been justified by the Marcos administration as necessary measures to strengthen deterrence and protect Philippine sovereignty. However, these developments may also contribute to the militarization of areas where insurgent activity persists, including parts of Luzon, potentially complicating local conflict dynamics.

Indonesia’s failure in Papua: Projecting power, not peace

Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto is pushing to project power outside Southeast Asia.

He seeks to transform Indonesia into one of the world’s 10 largest developed economies by 2045 while simultaneously improving military capabilities. Indonesia has also sought to strengthen its international profile by joining US President Donald Trump’s controversial Board of Peace platform. Through these initiatives, Jakarta aims to present itself as a responsible actor committed to international peace and security, supported by a strong defence posture.

Domestically, the administration led by Prabowo Subianto, a former military general, regularly faces strident public opposition to its economic and populist policies and armed resistance in the province of Papua. Prabowo’s flagship “free lunch” program, which many Papuans perceived as facilitating greater military presence and settlement by military families in the region, generated significant opposition. The Indonesian government has deployed thousands of Indonesian Armed Forces and police to Papua since January 2025.

One consequence of the increased security presence in Papua, has been a rise in military operations. According to conflict monitors, state forces have carried out 78 air and drone strikes since Prabowo assumed the presidency in October 2024. A military operation in April 2026 extended beyond active combat zones and struck civilian areas, including a refugee sanctuary previously recognised by both the Indonesian military and the West Papua National Liberation Army in Kambru District, blurring the distinction between combatants and non-combatants. The resulting security deterioration has produced a severe humanitarian crisis, with more than 100,000 people reportedly displaced across Papua as of March 2026.

At the international level, military cooperation and defense ties with foreign governments provide the Indonesian military with access to weapons, training, and logistical support, enabling the continuation of counterinsurgency operations in Papua.

Perpetuating cycles of violence

These examples of military-led approaches in the region may each temporarily contain dissent, but likely also exacerbate human suffering while failing to reduce either armed or non-armed opposition.

Achieving peace requires a fundamentally different approach: prioritising peaceful conflict resolution over military responses, recognising historical injustices, facilitating meaningful dialogue between states and affected communities, providing impartial mediation, addressing long-standing grievances, ensuring accountability and the right to truth, creating conditions for reconciliation, supporting inclusive socio-economic development, and establishing political systems that accommodate diverse interests.

Without at least some of this work, genuine peace will remain out of reach. The relatively successful peace processes in the region, such as those in Aceh, Indonesia, and the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao in the Philippines demonstrate that durable peace requires sustained peace-building efforts even long after formal agreements are reached. – Rappler.com



Su Mon has provided the following: Su Mon is ACLED’s Regional Expert and the 2025 Conflict and Peace Research Fellow at the Australian National University and University of Melbourne. (ACLED is Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Asia Pacific).

World.title: Preventing school violence starts at home, but gov’t must step up
World.content:
SCHOOL SAFETY. Government officials and experts discuss measures to ensure children's safety inside schools during Rappler's 'Civic Circles' on September 10, 2026.

It’s not only empowering parents to participate in their children’s lives, but also ensuring that critical government programs are funded to prevent school violence

MANILA, Philippines – Just this year, fatal shootings rocked the country’s education system, raising questions on the government’s capability to keep children safe, and on the current state of Filipino youth.

In June, three students were killed after their two schoolmates opened fire in Tacloban City. By August, two students died inside a private school in Zamboanga City, including the alleged perpetrator himself.

Other cases of school violence included stabbing, viral security threats, and reports of weapon confiscation.

Who is to blame? Who is responsible? Dr. Princess Gairanod, a child protection specialist from the Philippine Pediatric Society, stressed that systems surrounding children must be examined.

For her, it is essential that every sector of society fulfills their role in ensuring school safety.

“It’s not just a list of things that we tick off. We have to look at the different factors that affect it,” Gairanod said during Rappler’s “Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe?” on Thursday, September 10.

Importance of parents’ involvement

During the panel discussion, Gairanod said parents’ participation in the lives of their children will go a long way to combat youth violence.

As a pediatrician, she teaches parents how to spot warning signs and other sudden changes in children’s behavior, as well as technological practices to protect minors against online harms.

It’s not micromanaging but giving children proper attention.

“If something goes wrong, if someone threatens them (the children) online, then they should be able to feel safe enough to tell parents because parents can escalate the action [to authorities],” Gairanod said.

Play Video

Connecting with parents is also a highlight of local initiatives. For instance, parents in Quezon City have important duties in the QC Safe Schools Whole-of-Community Framework.

“There was already a demand from our parents to have values formation programs. So, the city has developed a five-module program wherein this will be deployed to all our public school parents,” Quezon City Councilor Aly Medalla said.

The program seeks to train parents to reinforce positive values and responsible behavior at home, while also strengthening the partnership with schools to give proper support to children.

Play Video

Unfunded child protection, mental health services in schools

On the part of the Department of Education (DepEd), it recently introduced active shooter drills as one of the ways to educate students and school personnel about emergency situations.

In September, the DepEd revised its protocols to make the drills “trauma-informed,” following recommendations of medical groups. This means that there will be no active threat role players or individuals pretending to be “active shooters” and no weapons during the simulation exercises.

DepEd Director IV Razzel Anne Requesto, who works under the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Governance and Support Services, said students appreciated being taught how to prepare for threats and other incidents.

Other than reaction, prevention is also key. However, the DepEd’s response could be limited next year amid lack of funding for its critical programs to address school violence.

The agency is still lobbying for an increase in its 2027 budget, including injecting P44 million more into its child protection program, particularly to train teachers to detect red flags.

It is also through the program that schools develop their reporting mechanisms for bullying incidents, and the referral system for needed interventions and support.

And while P802 million is already earmarked for the hiring of 1,800 school counselor associates and 221 schools division office counselors next year, this would not be enough to cover all schools in the country. The DepEd is still seeking P13.81 billion more to effectively implement its mental health and guidance counseling program.

“We’ve seen over the past year how we were able to help our learners to understand better their rights and responsibilities, how we can also train and capacitate our parents and our teachers — basically, our entire stakeholder and school community — in terms of how to protect our children,” Requesto said.

“And I believe that more investment in mental health and child protection would be much needed and could help prevent these cases of school violence,” she added.

Play Video

Need for better cybersecurity infra

For the Philippine National Police (PNP), targeting online influences is part of its strategy, as discussions surrounding school violence include nihilistic violent extremism (NVE).

NVE, which is a loose online subculture, glorifies violence without a coherent ideological framework.

This year, authorities have rescued at least 43 minors in NVE-related cases, according to Police Captain Wallen Arancillo, spokesperson for the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group (ACG).

The PNP is ramping up awareness campaigns on NVE networks, as the extremists target minors, specifically vulnerable youth experiencing social isolation and mental health struggles, through online platforms.

Curbing cybercrime would also entail having a better cybercrime infrastructure. Arancillo said the ACG needs upgraded tools, especially on digital forensic investigation, and 2,000 more personnel across the country.

“If you have strong cybersecurity, it would be easier for us and faster for us to investigate, monitor, and trace these cyber threats,” added Arancillo.

Play Video

The experts emphasized that enhanced collaboration among sectors must continue to keep children safe.

But Gairanod also issued this reminder: “Policy is not protection, implementation is.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Why Romblon’s islands deserve more love and attention
World.content:
The sun was up when we arrived at Tablas Island, offering a stark contrast to Metro Manilaâs gloomy August skies. As we made our way to our resort in San Agustin, the coastal highway opened up to endless views of the sea. Itâs a sight that stayed with me, making it feel as if the island itself were saying, âThis is just the beginning.â

The whole trip felt like a reminder to slow down and surrender to Tablasâ quiet yet inviting atmosphere. And with each minute spent on the island, I found myself wanting for more.

❮ ❯

Underrated, laid-back beaches

❮ ❯

Before this Sunlight Air-sponsored trip, Iâd never heard of Tablas, but Bon Bon Beach is now etched in my memory. The entire journey was filled with similarly unforgettable moments. A standout, however, was Bon Bon Beach itself. Ranked number 38 on the 2025 Worldâs 50 Best Beaches list, it offered a truly one-of-a-kind experience.

Bon Bon beach stretches long and wide, ending at its northern tip with the famous sandbar that reaches toward Bang-og, a small, uninhabited island. Unfortunately, the high tide kept the sandbar hidden, so we cut short what could have been a ten-minute walk to the far end. Still, the waters on the southern side of the beach were calm and clear enough to swim in.

We also crossed over to Cobrador Island, which had clear, picturesque waters and a laid-back vibe.

❮ ❯

ð Field Guide Explore more travel stories like this on Rappler's Field Guide! Explore More

Cove Aurelio in Calatrava, on the other hand, was a secluded spot surrounded by towering limestone rock formations that offered an even more intimate escape.

Tucked between limestone islands, Cove Aurelio feels like a private sanctuary. The imposing rock formations create a natural fortress against the open sea.

Heading to the far north end of Tablas Island, we visited Lapus-Lapus beach. The name translates to 'tagos-tagos' in Tagalog, as a giant limestone formation in between the shores create an illusion of two completely separate beaches. Walking through them feels like stepping from one hidden cove right to another. A similar vibe awaits at Binucot beach on the southern coast of Tablas.

Views from one side of the Lapus-Lapus beach... ...to the other hidden side. Binucotâs twin shores await on the southern coast. A similar secluded charm to Lapus-Lapus.

While clear waters and white sand isnât so rare in the country, the true charm of Romblon comes from two things. First, we felt so much more connected to the place because, for the most part, we were the only ones exploring the area while the locals simply went on with their day. Secondly, you canât easily find Romblon food anywhere else but Romblon â and itâs very underrated.

The taste of Romblon

On our way to Odiongan, we asked our guide, Josh Martinez of the Romblon Provincial Tourism Office, about local delicacies we could bring home. His response resonated with me: ââYung mga delicacies ng Romblon, hindi siya basta nai-uuwi, you have to experience them here.â

Over the next four days of our stay there, I found out how right he was.

One dish that stood out was Taghilaw, a savory stew of pork meat, innards, and liver simmered in vinegar and water. When I described it later to a friend, he asked if it resembled Bopis. Taghilaw has a similar texture, but with larger cuts of meat. And unlike the sauteed and oily Bopis, Taghilaw is distinctly soupy.

On the spread Taghilaw Pork meat, innards, and liver stew simmered in water, vinegar, and spices.

Gayabon Fresh taro leaves cooked in coconut milk.

Steamed Vegetables with Balitsaw Fermented shrimp sauteed in coconut milk, served alongside local greens.

Pinangat nak isra Yellowfin tuna cooked slowly in rich coconut milk.

Crispy fried bolinao Breaded anchovies fried golden for the perfect crunch.

For a healthier choice, Inaslom is Romblomanonsâ answer to Northern Luzonâs Dinengdeng or the Tagalog Bulanglang. The locals claimed this dish has at least a hundred variations that every family across the province has its own signature twist.

The version served to us in Odiongan was made with bamboo shoots and corn simmered in a base of hibe (dried shrimp) which filled the dining space with its rich aroma.

As for seafood, the highlight was Sarsa na Uyang (freshwater prawns) over lunch at Cobrador Island. Finely pounded shrimp paste is mixed with shredded coconut, siling labuyo, ginger, garlic, onions, and spices, then wrapped in coconut leaves and boiled in coconut milk. Personally, this would be best enjoyed when topped onto hot, steaming rice.

While these dishes had to be enjoyed on the spot, I did manage to bring home packs of Tipin, a circle-shaped, thin yet crunchy coconut biscuit made by the Romblon-native Shapes Bakeshop. My only regret was not buying more, as they are surprisingly addictive.

Romblon Heritage

To dive into Romblonâs past, we visited one of the twin forts, the Fuerza de San Andres. The forts are located on Romblon Island (an island within the province of Romblon), just a 30-minute motorboat ride away from Tablas.

On the way up the fort, you are greeted by mosaic artworks etched onto the steps. These depict local folklore, including the origin of the provinceâs name from Dublon or Donblon, and the act of a bird warming an egg in its nest.

Built during the Spanish colonial period, Fuerza de San Andres once served as a watchtower to protect the area from Dutch and Muslim invaders. Unfortunately, its twin, Fort Santiago, was destroyed in ruins by Moro pirates centuries ago.

Another notable heritage stop is the San Jose Cathedral. Built in 1644 using limestone, red bricks, and egg-white mortar, this Baroque church is famous for housing the revered image of Nuestra SeÃ±ora del Sto. NiÃ±o de Romblon. You might recognize it from the news, as the centuries-old icon was stolen in 1991 and only returned home in 2013 after more than two decades.

The historic San Jose Cathedral. Built in 1644 using limestone and red bricks. The Baroque facade stands as a testament to Romblon's heritage.

Marble Capital of the Philippines

Romblon is known as the Marble Capital of the country. And true to its title, youâll see it everywhere â from local roads to the provincial capital itself.

We got a glimpse of where it all begins, mined straight from the hillsides. During an impromptu stop at our guideâs house, we saw for ourselves how common raw marble blocks are, as they had some right in their backyard.

❮ ❯

We visited a local workshop to watch raw marble blocks sliced and polished into sleek floor tiles. Meanwhile, local artisans shape the stone into charming trinkets that we couldn't resist picking up at a pasalubong center in Odiongan.

How to get there

Reaching Romblon used to mean committing to an eight-to-ten-hour journey via ferry, or flying into Caticlan and crossing open waters by boat. But an easier route is offered by Sunlight Air.

Through direct flights from Clark International Airport to Tablas Island, Sunlight Air cuts the trip to at least 1 hour and 15 minutes. For travelers coming from Metro Manila, there are car rental services like Hertz or point-to-point (P2P) buses departing directly from Trinoma in Quezon City.

Pulling you back in

Though the monsoon rain kept us from ticking all the places in our itinerary, it left me with a quiet longing to return under sunny skies.

But missing a few spots is only part of why I want to go back. Thereâs something rare that Romblon offers to visitors: a tranquil, unhurried escape free from heavy tourist crowds.

Catching Romblonâs islands in shrouded grey skies reminded me that travel isn't just about admiring a destination at its absolute best. Itâs about learning to appreciate a place for what it reveals, even when it isnât postcard-perfect.

Romblon stole my heart â and Iâm sure it will steal yours too. â Rappler.com

World.title: EU’s von der Leyen backs AI slowdown, to invite frontier labs for talks
World.content:
URSULA VON DER LEYEN. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reacts after delivering the State of the European Union address to the European Parliament, in Strasbourg, France, September 16, 2026.

'I will invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier,' Ursula von der Leyen says

STRASBOURG, France – European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday, September 16, backed calls by leading US AI labs for a pause in the development of the technology, saying she will invite the main frontier AI labs to discuss efforts to tackle the risks.

Von der Leyen’s comments in her annual speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg came amid growing worries about the potential danger posed by artificial intelligence, putting her at odds with US President Donald Trump who has dismissed the AI safety alarm.

The dangers were underscored by Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon who resigned and accused both the company and OpenAI of ⁠racing toward self-improving superintelligence without acting responsibly. He had previously worked at OpenAI.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last week called on AI companies to slow the rate at which they advance model capabilities, drawing the support of both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI.

“As the frontier models become more capable, these risks have come more sharply into focus. Models being developed will allow hacking on a level we never thought possible. And they will soon be in the hands of adversaries who see the world very differently from us,” von der Leyen told EU lawmakers.

She pointed to recent incidents of rogue AI agents and warnings from developers.

“CEOs of the most advanced companies tell us that it is time to slow down on the self-recursive models. To pace the frontier. If the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too,” von der Leyen said.

Von der Leyen said landmark EU rules governing the use of AI adopted recently put Europe in the position to shape global efforts to tackle the risks.

She said Europe will work with like-minded partners such as Canada, the United Kingdom and others to take measures such as model evaluation, verification and AI security.

“I will invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier,” von der Leyen said.

She also proposed a social media ban for children under 13 and no personal accounts for people under the age of 15, saying that platforms have to prove that they are safe for children. She will announce details on Thursday. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Be The Good] Holding space through Civic Circles
World.content:
This is how we show up for our readers, our partners, and the communities impacted by the stories we cover. We hope you can be part of it.

Hi, I’m Jene Pangue, Head of MovePH, Rappler’s civic engagement arm.

During our recent Civic Circles initiative, I stood near one of our workshop tables when a mother quietly reached out to hand me a small, handcrafted whistle. Jennifer shared that her son had experienced bullying at school. Desperate for help, she had reached out to authorities, only to be met with silence.

Finding a community that held space for her story allowed her to feel less alone. That whistle, which she was giving away for free, became a tangible reminder encouraging others in the room to keep speaking up so that no family has to face these struggles in isolation.

Handcrafted ‘Stop Bullying’ whistles given by a mother during our Civic Circles pilot session.

I also met Teacher Mars, a public school educator of 20 years who traveled all the way from Laguna to join us. Despite the heavy demands of her daily work, she was eager to learn how to keep children and schools safe. “Ang teacher ngayon dapat matatag at matibay,” she said. “Ang dami naming ginagawa na labas na sa responsibilidad namin. Pero hanggang kaya, kakayanin.” (Today’s teachers must be strong and resilient. We do so many things that are outside our responsibilities. But as long as we can, we will endure.)

Their stories reflect a broader problem. Across the country, communities are grappling with rising campus violence, critical resource shortages, and a mounting mental health crisis. Teachers are often forced to act as unequipped first responders, while parents navigate painful realities in silence.

To help address these challenges, MovePH envisioned a space where citizens from all walks of life — educators, parents, youth advocates, civil society leaders or ordinary citizens who care — could come together, move beyond online discussions, and co-create actionable solutions.

This is the heart of how Civic Circles came to life.

Our pilot session brought together over 50 in-person participants from child rights groups, academe, local government units, healthcare, law enforcement, and parent associations, alongside hundreds more who joined virtually.

We opened with a panel discussion featuring Quezon City Councilor Aly Medalla, National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group spokesperson Captain Wallen Arancillo, Philippine Pediatric Society Child Protection specialist Dr. Princess Gairanod, and Department of Education (DepEd) Director IV Razzel Anne Requesto. They underscored that boosting funding and strengthening systemic responses are essential to creating lasting safety.

The panelists also highlighted the importance of active parental involvement, localized safety frameworks, trauma-informed drills, expanded mental health support, and enhanced cybersecurity capacity. You can watch the full panel discussion here.

Building on these insights, participants rotated across four action station circles to translate ideas into practical steps.

Their recommendations include the following:

boosting campus security through parent-teacher capacity building;

strengthening psychosocial care through regular counseling, parent internet safety orientations, and safe spaces — alongside commitments to expand licensed support and referral system;

tackling systemic violence via interagency policy collaboration; and

mitigating digital safety risks through community-wide awareness campaigns on parental control tools and cybersecurity advocacy.

We thank our co-organizers, CyberGuardiansPH, and Mental Health Youth Hub. Their technical expertise, support, and dedication to youth well-being were essential in bringing this multisectoral and trauma-informed space to life.

To ensure these conversations extend beyond event-day, participants and community members can stay connected and join upcoming initiatives through our education chatroom on the app.

MovePH will continue working alongside our partner groups and volunteers to consolidate these commitments into actionable briefs or community toolkits that concerned citizens like Jennifer and Teacher Mars can bring directly to their schools, homes, and local councils.

Is there a specific commitment or solution from this session that you would like to support? Or a topic you think we should tackle in our next Civic Circles?

We are just getting started, and we would love to have you with us.

Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe? Organized in partnership with CyberGuardiansPH and Mental Health Youth Hub, this pilot initiative tackles rising school violence and digital risks

When school violence happens, the whole community needs to listen Psychologists say young Filipinos need safe spaces to be vulnerable without judgement



Psychologists want us to rethink what we ask about school violence Rather than neatly condense all the violence and trace it to one root cause, psychologists choose to ask the difficult questions about each individual case.

[Inside the Newsroom] The least we can do covering school shootings The least we can do as a newsroom is to cover responsibly, to the best of our judgment and abilities, and not add to the grief, especially of families who are experiencing the loss and of the affected communities

– Rappler.com

Be the Good is a newsletter that comes out every other Wednesday. We deliver updates straight to your inbox on how journalism and communities can work together for impact.

To subscribe, follow the #FactsFirstPH movement or visit rappler.com/newsletters.

World.title: Saudis pound Yemen as Houthis solidify gains in new theater of Middle East war
World.content:
Iran-aligned Houthi fighters pose next to a captured vehicle following what the source described as an attack on Saudi-backed forces in the location given by the source as al Jawf governorate, Yemen, in this screengrab taken from a video released by Houthi Military Media on September 15, 2026.

Traders say a prolonged closure of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply

Saudi warplanes pounded Yemen, the Houthis said on Wednesday, September 16, as the Iran-backed fighters solidified their gains after a lightning advance that has extended Tehran’s reach in the Middle East war and further disrupted global oil supplies.

In a sign of the worsening conflict in a new theatre, the United States tightened its travel warning for Saudi Arabia, banning government employees from travelling within 20 miles of the Yemen border.

The Houthis, who since last week have swept through Yemeni towns along the Red Sea coast and seized islands in the Bab el-Mandeb strait at its mouth, released battlefield video overnight of fighters seizing armoured vehicles from Saudi-backed forces. Warplanes flew overhead and huge explosions billowed into the sky from desert dunes.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Houthis had shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet. No immediate evidence was presented and Saudi officials did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.

Saree said the Saudis had carried out as many as 450 air strikes on Yemen this week. Officials in the Saudi-backed government that controls southern Yemen have acknowledged that their forces and those of Saudi Arabia were conducting air strikes on Houthi positions, though Riyadh itself has not confirmed them.

The Houthis have fired repeatedly into Saudi Arabia over the past week causing alarms over cities in the south and west. An attack blamed on Iran-aligned fighters in Iraq last week also knocked out Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, the main route used to divert exports away from the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

Riyadh said its air defenses had shot down a Houthi drone south of Mecca on Tuesday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, an attack it said crossed a “red line” of threatening shrines sacred to all Muslims. Houthi spokesperson Saree denied the group had targeted Mecca, and said the Saudi reports were a set-up for propaganda purposes.

Danger of global energy supply shortage worsening

The extension of the war into Yemen threatens to worsen the global energy supply shortage caused by the six-month-old US-Israeli war on Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The price of Brent crude hovered around $108 a barrel on Wednesday, close to its highest level since May. The politically sensitive average retail price of diesel fuel in the United States hit another all-time high above $6.30 a gallon for the first time.

Traders say a prolonged closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply. Saudi Arabia has not said when operations might resume, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Tuesday that crude oil should be flowing through the pipeline within days.

Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015. The conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in recent years, but reignited when the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in July and fired at southern areas in the kingdom. Violence has intensified sharply this month when the militant group pushed back forces aligned with the Saudi-backed internationally recognised Yemeni government.

Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman phoned US President Donald Trump last week seeking military support, which so far has been limited to intelligence aid.

The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in 2025, but halted that campaign after reaching what President Donald Trump described as a ceasefire with the group.

Trump now faces a dilemma of whether to stand by and risk the Houthi advance worsening the global energy crisis, or provide more direct military support to the Saudis and risk extending the costly US intervention to another theater. – Rappler.com

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

World.title: Prosecution to call Sebastian Duterte to witness stand in VP Sara’s trial
World.content:
The prosecution wants to ask Sebastian Duterte about Davao City hall's dealings with Gencorp, of which the Vice President is a stockholder

MANILA, Philippines – The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte will call her brother, Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, to the witness stand.

The impeachment court on Wednesday, September 16, granted the prosecution’s request to compel the attendance of the younger Duterte on September 23.

“In broad strokes, we remember that in the SALNs (Statements of Assets Liabilities and Net worth), it was mentioned that among the companies she has financial interest… is Gencorp,” prosecution spokesman Jay Tolosa said.

“We want to know, in his capacity as mayor of Davao, if Gencorp has dealings with the city government of Davao,” he added.

The younger Duterte was not initially identified as a witness by the prosecution team in its pre-trial brief, although it is not precluded from asking him to testify as among the unnamed, reserve witnesses.

The development comes a day after Rappler published an exclusive report detailing how Gencorp cornered P15 million in food and catering contracts from the PhilHealth Davao Regional Office and Davao City Hall between 2022 and 2025.

Sara, who is a stockholder of the company, was already vice president at the time.

The Constitution bars a vice president’s participation in any business, and the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Official instructs them to divest their shares from any private business enterprise within 60 days from their assumption. – Rappler.com

World.title: Experts Highlight Investment and Coordination Priorities for Middle Corridor
World.content:
ASTANA – The Middle Corridor is gaining strategic importance as countries across Central Asia and the South Caucasus seek to strengthen trade connectivity and diversify transport routes between Asia and Europe, experts said during a Sept. 15 British-Kazakh Society (BKS) Trade Group webinar on Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan-Middle Corridor Investments, Operations & Trade.

The webinar brought together experts from Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and the United Kingdom (UK) to discuss investment, operations, regional cooperation and the corridor’s development.

“The Middle Corridor is really maturing politically faster than it’s maturing operationally,” said Assylbek Nurgabdeshov, Assistant Professor of Strategy and director of Strategy Postgraduate Programs at Edinburgh Business School, Heriot-Watt University.

He noted that the route remains a multimodal system involving railways, ports, ferries and road networks across several jurisdictions. Improving coordination among the countries involved is therefore essential to its development.

“Reliability is the key aspect” for companies considering the route, Nurgabdeshov said, stressing the importance of predictable operations and long-term sustainability.

According to Nurgabdeshov, the UK could contribute through financial, legal and institutional expertise rather than directly building the corridor.

“UK’s main role will be to shape how it functions rather than to build the corridor,” he said.

Ahmad Alili, director of the Caucasus Policy Analysis Center in Baku, described the Middle Corridor as a “geopolitical necessity,” arguing that closer cooperation between the South Caucasus and Central Asia will become increasingly important.

He pointed to growing contacts between Azerbaijan and Central Asian countries, including cooperation in transport, trade and other areas, as part of a broader regional integration process.

Arzu Abbasova, research analyst at the Royal United Services Institute’s Center for Finance and Security, said geopolitical developments have made connectivity a strategic issue extending beyond trade.

“The war in Ukraine, the uncertainty in Iran, in the maritime trade routes, and the competition around the critical minerals and technology and supply chains have all made this connectivity very much of a strategic issue rather than a purely commercial one,” she said.

The experts also discussed digitalization, Caspian Sea infrastructure and Kazakhstan’s use of alternative routes for oil exports.

Nurgabdeshov stressed that cooperation should take precedence over competition among countries along the route.

“Let’s work on collaborating rather than on competing with each other,” he said.

World.title: Experts: Geopolitical Volatility Reshapes Kazakhstan’s Energy Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s energy security is increasingly tied to diversified supply routes, modern electricity infrastructure and deeper regional connectivity, while green hydrogen could open a new industrial opportunity if the country can turn its resource potential into commercially viable projects, experts said at the third Regional Central Asian and European Decarbonization Forum on Sept. 16.

The Energy Security in Volatile Geopolitics panel highlighted a fundamental shift in what energy security means. For Kazakhstan, it is no longer only about securing sufficient supplies of oil and gas, but also about developing multiple energy sources, strengthening electricity networks and creating alternative routes to regional and international markets.

“Dependency on single routes is not a good thing,” said Sanzhar Zharkeshov, deputy Energy Minister of Kazakhstan, stressing the need to diversify energy routes while expanding alternative electricity sources.

The country is pursuing nuclear power alongside renewable energy. At the same time, expanding renewables requires greater flexibility in the electricity system. Zharkeshov said Kazakhstan’s new legislation requires renewable energy projects to include battery storage.

“You can’t count on natural gas forever for balancing and manoeuvring power. We have to have a reliable battery storage system,” he said.

This highlights a key challenge for the energy transition: adding generation capacity alone is not enough. Transmission networks, storage and regional interconnections will determine how effectively new electricity can be integrated and delivered.

Building the infrastructure before demand peaks

Azerbaijan’s Deputy Minister of Energy Orkhan Zeynalov said stronger electricity links between Central Asia, Azerbaijan and Europe could provide additional resilience and flexibility.

He said that regional infrastructure should be developed with future demand in mind rather than based solely on current volumes, comparing energy connections with highways that need to be built ahead of traffic growth.

“Tomorrow, the biggest risk is not having this infrastructure,” Zeynalov said.

Plans for a green energy corridor linking Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan are part of this emerging regional approach. Greater interconnection could allow countries with different renewable-generation patterns to exchange electricity and provide additional routes to European markets.

The discussion also linked the growth of artificial intelligence to a potentially sharp increase in electricity demand. Zharkeshov said this could change the economics of different energy technologies, making it less relevant to view them as competing alternatives and more important to develop them in parallel. He argued that stronger demand could, in turn, help improve the economic case for hydrogen.

“There will be no battle between the energy sources. We’ll have to throw everything at it so that we can meet the demand. And that will drive the economic feasibility of hydrogen as an energy source,” he said.

Green hydrogen: from strategy to a market

Green hydrogen illustrates both Kazakhstan’s potential and the challenges of developing new energy technologies.

Zharkeshov identified metallurgy, chemicals, ammonia production and refining as potential applications, notably in sectors that are difficult to decarbonize. However, he acknowledged that production costs remain a major obstacle.

“One of the challenges we’re seeing in hydrogen is the price, the break-even price,” he said.

Kazakhstan has significant wind and solar potential that could support renewable hydrogen production. But the next question is whether this potential can be converted into projects with buyers and viable business models.

Hendrik Meller, program director of H2-diplo at the German Society for International Cooperation (GIZ), told The Astana Times that the clearest milestone over the next five years would be an operating or near-operating project with a committed buyer.

“In five years it would be great to have a project in operation or close to operation, producing green hydrogen, with a clear offtake customer to cater to,” Meller said.

He suggested that Kazakhstan could initially focus on domestic applications rather than relying entirely on exports, including replacing grey hydrogen at refineries and using green hydrogen in fertilizer production. Other applications, such as green steel and sustainable aviation or maritime fuels, could develop as the market matures.

Meller said the immediate practical step is to engage with project developers and technology providers to advance existing hydrogen projects and determine where they can secure an offtake agreement.

“I think that’s something where we have to bring businesses together,” he said.

Critical raw materials add another opportunity

For the European Union, Kazakhstan’s importance extends beyond energy to critical raw materials, connectivity and industrial processing.

EU Ambassador to Kazakhstan Aleška Simkić stressed that developing new technologies requires a long-term investment perspective.

“We have to invest now in order to have long-term benefits, even though it’s not commercially viable,” she said.

Simkić noted that 21 of the 34 critical raw materials the EU identified as important for its green transition are present in Kazakhstan. But she emphasized that cooperation should move beyond extraction.

“We actually want the processing and technologies to be here, locally managed and dealt with,” she said.

This could allow Kazakhstan to capture more value from its mineral resources while helping Europe diversify supply chains.

Taken together, the discussion suggests that Kazakhstan’s energy advantage will depend less on the scale of its resources alone and more on its ability to connect them to modern infrastructure, regional markets and higher-value industries.

The key indicators to watch will be progress on electricity interconnections, battery storage, grid modernization, critical-minerals processing and, particularly, the emergence of a green hydrogen project with a real buyer. If those elements begin to materialize, Kazakhstan’s energy transition could move from a collection of strategies and potential projects towards a more integrated regional energy and industrial model.

World.title: Kazakhstan Highlights New Stage of Nuclear Development at IAEA Conference
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is entering a new stage of nuclear sector development, focusing on nuclear energy, science, medicine and high-tech industry, Deputy Chairman of the Agency for Atomic Energy Gumar Sergazin said at the 70th session of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) General Conference on Sept. 15.

“Atom, placed at the service of peace, science and humanity, can become not a source of fear, but a source of energy, progress and hope,” Sergazin said, outlining Kazakhstan’s priorities in the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

He said Kazakhstan’s nuclear agenda is guided by the newly approved Strategy for the Development of the Nuclear Industry until 2050. The strategy envisages a national nuclear cluster bringing together energy, industry, science, education and high-tech manufacturing, the agency’s press service reported on Sept. 16.

Sergazin also highlighted Kazakhstan’s role in global nuclear supply chains and the country’s contribution to nuclear fuel security through the IAEA Low Enriched Uranium Bank hosted in Kazakhstan.

International cooperation remains a key priority. A Roadmap signed in 2026 to expand Kazakhstan-IAEA cooperation through 2036 covers nuclear energy, nuclear medicine, science, safety and workforce training.

The national statement also highlighted the 35th anniversary of the closure of the Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site. Kazakhstan reaffirmed its commitment to nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation and called for the early entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty.

Kazakhstan said it remains committed to strengthening its strategic partnership with the IAEA and advancing the peaceful use of nuclear energy for energy security, science, medicine and sustainable development.

World.title: One Plant Tripped in Kyrgyzstan, Four Countries Go Dark
World.content:
What the August 14 Blackout Revealed About Central Asia’s Shared Power System

The Almaty metro stopped, and the traffic lights went dark at around 14:37 local time on Aug. 14. The trigger occurred in Kyrgyzstan’s Toktogul Hydropower Plant, where two generating units had tripped, taking roughly 600 MW off the Central Asian grid during one of the year’s highest demand peaks. Within minutes, consumers across Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan lost power.

Reuters reported simultaneous outages across the region that afternoon, and investigators later traced the trigger to the loss of two 300 MW units at Toktogul. Kyrgyzstan’s Energy Ministry acknowledged the technological failure on August 17 while disputing responsibility for what followed in neighboring states. By then, emergency protection had already isolated Kazakhstan’s southern zone from the Central Asian unified power system to prevent a wider collapse, at the cost of outages across the region’s largest cities.

The individual infrastructure fault matters less than the overarching problem it reveals. A trip at one plant in one country reached millions of consumers across four countries, carried there by an aging electricity system already under strain from climate stress, rapidly growing demand, and thin regional coordination. All while Central Asia is positioning itself as a destination for digital infrastructure, including hyperscale artificial intelligence data centers that consume hundreds of megawatts of continuous power, matching an entire city’s demand.

Yesterday’s Grid Running Today’s Central Asia

Central Asia inherited an interconnected grid made for a different era. Under the Soviet Union, the five republics were designed to operate as a single integrated power system rather than as independent national grids, relying on a carefully balanced seasonal exchange. In summer, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan exported hydropower from snowmelt and reservoir releases. In winter, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan supplied coal and gas generation so upstream countries could conserve water.

After the 1991 collapse, coordination weakened because of commercial disputes, underinvestment, and Turkmenistan’s 2003 decision to disconnect and operate synchronously with Iran.

Consequences arrived in the winter of 2007 and 2008, when extreme cold, low water, and suspended supplies from neighbors left Tajikistan to freeze under subzero temperatures. Uzbekistan then withdrew from the regional system altogether in December 2009, exposing the absence of planning to manage such cross-border emergencies. Since then Uzbekistan returned to the grid, and Cooperation has improved considerably, but much of the underlying infrastructure has not.

Although melting glaciers and varying river flows erode hydropower availability, water was not this year’s problem.

Kyrgyzstan’s Energy Ministry estimated the Toktogul reservoir has enough water to support normal turbine operation through autumn and winter. The failure came instead from temperature stress beyond the climate the system was designed for. Extreme summer temperatures pushed demand toward seasonal peaks in several countries at once, reducing transformer cooling efficiency. As equipment temperatures approached safety limits, protection systems disconnected generators to prevent damage. Heat, combined with high energy use, caused high-voltage conductors to expand and sag, raising the risk of a line fault. When Toktogul abruptly lost 600 MW, the deficit spread through the grid and overloaded other parts of the network.

What Needs Investment

The system that lets Kyrgyz hydropower turn on the lights in Kazakhstan also lets a Kyrgyz fault turn them off. Kazakhstan remains reliant on Russian imports at system peaks, and plans to expand its own generation and end those imports by 2027. But that does not solve the infrastructure problem. Large portions of the region’s power plants and transmission infrastructure were built decades ago and are approaching the end of their effective life. This requires investment in asset renewal, control systems, and reserve capacity.

Basic asset renewal involves rehabilitating aging thermal and hydropower plants, replacing overloaded transformers and substations, and modernizing the high-voltage lines that carry power between them.

Fortunately, control system modernization is already underway in Tashkent’s Coordination Dispatch Center “Energiya,” the operational heart of Central Asia’s grid, with World Bank support. Modern dispatch depends on real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and automated contingency analysis to detect instability before it becomes an outage. Still, many of these capabilities remain limited within the existing regional system.

Expanding regional reserve capacity is crucial to preventing a repeat of August 14 by buffering the loss of a large generating unit. The Forecast Balance for 2026–2032 is often cited to show that generation will outpace consumption by 2032. But that measures energy over a year, not capacity at the hour of peak load, and on that measure, the roughly 3 GW deficit never closes.

Storage can close part of that gap, and it has already been tested. Uzbekistan’s Energy Ministry credited recently installed energy storage systems with limiting the domestic impact of the August 14 disturbance, and Kazakhstan is moving in the same direction. A draft law would establish capacity market auctions in which developers bid to provide guaranteed availability.

Efficiency remains the cheapest option at scale. Improved efficiency frees up capacity that would otherwise have to be built and increases gains from new generation. Modernizing industrial equipment, insulating old buildings, and upgrading aging heating and cooling systems lower stress at seasonal peaks and can postpone expensive investment in new capacity.

Data Centers Arriving Ahead of the Grid

Kazakhstan is trying to capitalize on the global shift into the AI era, and the commitments are growing quickly. Under the Digital Qazaqstan strategy approved by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in June 2026, NVIDIA and Firebird.ai signed a $10 billion package based in Ekibastuz’s Data Center Valley, and the UK-based consortium JMOT04 signed a memorandum to build a 200 MW facility paired with a 250 MW gas-fired plant to power it. Signed agreements already amount to roughly 650 MW of new load, and talks with Nasdaq-listed SuperX AI Technology over a 1 GW project would more than double that.

The location is a risk. The zonal tables from Kazakhstan’s Forecast Balance for 2026–2032 show the Northern Region, containing Ekibastuz, in official surplus, and the Southern Region, containing Shymkent and Almaty, in heavy deficit. Shipping power from North to South closes this gap, turning the North’s official surplus into an actual deficit. Thus Kazakhstan’s data center buildout is sited in a zone that only looks like it has power to spare.

According to S&P Global, Kazakhstan’s grid underinvestment is a returns problem, as years of tariff policy oriented toward keeping consumer prices low disincentivized private investment through low returns and unpredictable prices. A recent amendment now runs tariffs through a commission that includes the owner of Samruk-Energo, Kazakhstan’s largest power generator, which may make tariff decisions more sympathetic to producer economics.

The JMOT04 arrangement is the one worth repeating. New large-scale data centers should be required to invest in dedicated generation, storage, and substations rather than drawing on the existing public grid. A facility that brings its own power does not drain the surplus the South is already counting on. On that condition, Ekibastuz becomes the right site rather than the wrong one, and Kazakhstan can use the AI boom to attract the generation investment it needs regardless.

The Need for an Operating Agreement

World Bank projections estimate that electricity demand across Central Asia could triple by 2050, driven by population growth and rapid economic development. Technological investment alone is unlikely to eliminate the risk. The region also needs renewed political agreement on how the interconnected system should operate during normal and emergency scenarios. Normal operations should include transparent plans for cross-border flows, joint investment planning, and coordinated emergency protocols.

Central Asia’s interconnection is also a major strength, enabling it to pool diverse energy resources across borders. The task for the coming decade is to strengthen this grid together. August 14 served as an unplanned stress test, and power returned within hours. Why a local fault crossed four borders remains an open question about the system, not the plant. Every year of delayed investment raises the probability that the next local failure becomes a regional one.

The authors are Sobir Kurbanov and Amel Metjahic, experts and fellows at Nightingale Int. network.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans Cross-Border QR Payments With 11 Countries
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is working to launch cross-border QR-code payments with 11 countries, including China, the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and India, Deputy Governor and Digital Transformation Adviser of the National Bank Binur Zhalenov said at a Sept. 15 government briefing on the development of the digital assets ecosystem.

According to Zhalenov, separate road maps have been developed with each country to integrate national payment systems and establish cross-border QR payments.

“Among the countries we are working with, there are 11. I will not list all of them, but they include China, the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, we signed a memorandum last week, the Kyrgyz Republic and India. We have a corresponding road map with each of these countries,” Zhalenov said.

QR payment pilot with China planned for 2026

The timeline for launching the service will vary depending on the country. Testing and pilot projects with some partners are expected to begin before the end of 2026. China is among the countries where such testing is planned this year.

If the pilot is successful, Kazakh citizens could be able to use the mobile application of any bank in Kazakhstan to make QR-code payments in China as early as next year.

“If testing and piloting go well, next year Kazakh citizens will have the opportunity to pay through the application of any bank using QR in China, and vice versa,” Zhalenov said.

The National Bank expects the pace of integration to differ across partner countries. While some systems could be connected next year, others may require up to two years to complete the necessary technical and regulatory work.

“When we have a clearer picture regarding all 11 countries or other countries that may be added, we will certainly provide a separate communication,” Zhalenov said.

World.title: Tokayev Calls for New Chapter in Kazakhstan–South Korea Ties, Signs $19 Billion in Deals
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and South Korea signed commercial agreements worth $19 billion during President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s state visit to Seoul on Sept. 15, with both sides seeking to expand cooperation in investment, industry, urban development and cultural and humanitarian ties, Akorda reported.

“Our goal is the comprehensive development of bilateral relations,” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said during talks with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.

Speaking about the outcome of his visit, Tokayev highly assessed the current state and prospects of cooperation between the two countries.

“As for bilateral relations, during this visit, commercial agreements worth $19 billion were signed. We are satisfied with our work with Korean investors and are ready to continue working with them. There are good plans for the construction of hotels, an oil refinery and urban development. Particular attention is paid to strengthening cultural and humanitarian ties,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev also highlighted the high level of coordination between Astana and Seoul on the international stage, noting that the two countries share common positions on global sustainable development and security.

“Our states share common positions on issues of global sustainable development and security,” Tokayev said.

Lee reaffirmed South Korea’s commitment to further deepening bilateral cooperation, pointing to the growing alignment of the two countries’ foreign policy priorities.

“The Republic of Korea and Kazakhstan are broadening the scope of their external cooperation and pursuing pragmatic diplomacy focused on national interests and tangible results. Kazakhstan is an important partner for us in the area of economic security. The country is not only rich in energy and natural resources, but also has significant potential in promising high-tech industries,” Lee said.

He added that South Korea was ready to support the modernization of Kazakhstan’s industrial sector by leveraging its advanced industrial and digital technologies.

“Amid an increasingly unpredictable international environment, our two countries should strengthen cooperation by bringing together our respective strengths and capabilities and actively creating new opportunities for mutually beneficial growth,” Lee said.

President Tokayev expressed gratitude to Lee for the invitation to visit South Korea, describing the country as a strategic partner of Kazakhstan. He noted the longstanding ties of friendship and mutual understanding between the two peoples, as well as close cultural and humanitarian links, stressing that there are no contradictions or disagreements between Kazakhstan and South Korea.

He said the two countries are pursuing ambitious projects across a range of sectors and highlighted the importance of the Kazakhstan-Korea business forum held in Seoul with the participation of representatives of the two countries’ business communities. Among the projects discussed was the further development of Alatau City, which Tokayev described as an important initiative for Kazakhstan.

“The provisions concerning the status of this city have been incorporated into the Constitution. Korean companies will be provided with all legal guarantees. More than 120,000 ethnic Koreans live in Kazakhstan. All conditions have been created for them, and they are active members of our society,” Tokayev said.

He also highlighted the historical significance of General Hong Beom-do, a Korean independence movement figure whose remains were returned from Kazakhstan to South Korea in 2021. Tokayev said he was well acquainted with Hong Beom-do’s history and described him as a hero and patriot. He noted that preserving the general’s memory and returning his remains to South Korea demonstrated mutual understanding between the two countries.

“It is remarkable that even after more than a hundred years, the Korean people have not forgotten their general. Bowing to his memory, we returned his remains to his homeland, thereby fulfilling our civic duty,” Tokayev said.

Lee warmly welcomed Tokayev and emphasized the importance of his visit to Seoul. He thanked Kazakhstan for the decision to return Hong Beom-do’s remains and expressed appreciation for the way ethnic Koreans were received in Kazakhstan.

“We are grateful for your decision to return the remains of General Hong Beom-do, who played a special role in the history of Korea and in protecting the Korean people during difficult times. Korean citizens were warmly welcomed in Kazakhstan at the time. We are grateful to you and the Kazakh people for this,” Lee said.

The two presidents said they were ready to cooperate long-term and provide comprehensive mutual support when needed. Following the talks, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and South Korea and giving it new practical substance.

Earlier, Tokayev met with South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong-sook, congratulated her on her recent appointment, and wished her success in the post. Tokayev said Kazakhstan-South Korea relations are developing steadily within the framework of their strategic partnership, with numerous mutually beneficial initiatives being implemented. South Korea is among Kazakhstan’s top 10 trade and investment partners, while more than 1,000 joint ventures with Korean capital operate in Kazakhstan.

“However, there are still many important tasks ahead of us. Therefore, I am confident that, working together as one team, we will successfully implement all the plans we have outlined,” Tokayev said.

President Tokayev said Kazakhstan had created favorable conditions for business and investment, including for small and medium-sized enterprises alongside major Korean corporations. He noted the role of the Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic and Scientific-Technical Cooperation and the Business Council, as well as the bilateral legal framework supporting cooperation.

Tokayev thanked Han Seong-sook for taking part in the roundtable of Kazakh and Korean business representatives and expressed confidence that the agreements signed during the event would contribute to expanding bilateral ties.

He also said his upcoming talks with Lee were intended to open a new chapter in the history of Kazakhstan-South Korea relations.

Tokayev outlined several priorities for further government cooperation, including a target to double bilateral trade turnover.

“It is important not only to increase volumes, but also to qualitatively change the structure of trade and expand the range of goods with high added value. Therefore, I consider it highly relevant to develop a Comprehensive Program for Trade, Economic and Investment Cooperation between Kazakhstan and Korea for 2027-2030,” the President said.

He also proposed preparing a separate roadmap for industrial cooperation, incorporating the most promising localization projects and initiatives to export products to third-country markets.

Tokayev reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s commitment to comprehensive strengthening of its partnership with South Korea.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans $60 Million Tokenization Pilot for Alatau City Projects
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to tokenize up to $60 million in real estate and logistics projects by the end of 2026, launching its first major test of digital assets as a new source of financing for the economy, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said at a Sept. 15 government meeting.

The plans include up to $50 million for the Iconic Tower complex and $10 million for the Birlik logistics center in Alatau City in the Almaty Region. Both are expected to be issued through the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange’s digital infrastructure.

Kazakhstan also plans to link its nationwide regulatory framework with the separate regimes of the Astana International Financial Centre and Alatau City, creating what officials describe as a single digital asset market.

Under that model, authorities are considering a regional payments and settlement hub with Binance. Suleiemenov said the project would involve establishing a Binance legal entity in Kazakhstan and obtaining a top-tier payment organization license, potentially allowing the hub to serve clients across the Commonwealth of Independent States, Eastern Europe and Asia, Suleimenov said.

The projects are part of a 65-measure plan approved by the government on Sept. 15 to expand Kazakhstan’s regulated digital asset market.

Kazakhstan plans to tokenize major infrastructure projects, real estate and commodity assets to attract investment. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed the National Bank to compile a priority list of assets for tokenization and establish rules intended to protect investors.

“The digital assets sector is a completely new area of Kazakhstan’s economy. The basic conditions for the development of the digital assets market have already been established. We are now in the process of forming a comprehensive ecosystem,” Bektenov said.

“We have major infrastructure projects, real estate, commodities and other assets. Tokenization can be used to attract additional financing for these projects,” he added.

The government seeks to attract investment and bring more cryptocurrency activity into the regulated economy under the new plan. It also calls for expanding the use of the digital tenge, exploring digital instruments for cross-border payments and developing a more tightly regulated cryptocurrency-mining industry.

The National Bank expects the initial pool of tokenized assets to include government securities, corporate bonds, real estate, infrastructure projects and mineral deposits. Suleimenov called on the Finance Ministry, Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund, Baiterek Holding, KASE and the Central Securities Depository to prepare the first large-scale issuances.

What is tokenization

Tokenization records rights to an asset on a digital ledger. It can divide assets such as real estate, infrastructure or corporate debt into smaller digital units that investors can buy and trade. Supporters say the technology could accelerate transactions, reduce administrative costs and make investments previously dominated by large institutions accessible to a wider range of investors.

Larry Fink and Rob Goldstein of BlackRock have compared tokenization’s current development to that of the internet in 1996, noting that the technology could advance more quickly than many expect. They do not expect it to replace conventional finance soon, but envision the two systems gradually converging.

They portrayed that transition as a bridge being built from two sides: traditional financial institutions on one side and stablecoin issuers, fintech companies and blockchain networks on the other.

Global trends

The World Economic Forum describes 2026 as a “defining moment for digital assets.” It said clearer regulation, wider institutional adoption and greater interoperability are moving blockchain beyond experimentation and into the infrastructure supporting digital financial markets.

Tokenized real-world assets remain a small part of the global digital asset market. Boston Consulting Group estimates that around $30 billion in such assets are publicly visible, compared with roughly $3 trillion in cryptocurrencies and $300 billion in stablecoins. Under the firm’s more expansive scenarios, tokenized assets could represent nearly 16% of global investable assets by 2035, although the outcome would vary considerably by asset class.

According to Suleimenov, the digital assets market now has approximately 750 million users worldwide. Stablecoin transaction volume reached $50 trillion in 2025, while the market for tokenized assets expanded 12-fold over the past three years.

“Three major trends have emerged globally. The first is a shift from prohibition and observation toward licensing, supervision and common international standards. The second is the integration of digital assets with banks, payment infrastructure and capital markets. The third is a move toward practical applications,” Suleimenov explained.

Digital assets are increasingly used for cross-border payments, custody services and the tokenization of real and financial assets.

“Kazakhstan’s objective is to create a competitive, regulated market, with transactions, liquidity and capital concentrated within the country,” he added.

Steady progress

Suleimenov said Kazakhstan began building a regulated digital asset market in 2022. Then, it allowed cryptocurrency exchanges licensed by the Astana International Financial Centre to work with local banks. The parliament followed with a digital assets law in 2023.

By the end of 2025, AIFC-based providers had processed $10.6 billion in transactions and attracted approximately 215,000 users, according to figures cited by Suleimenov. The framework, however, remained limited to the financial center and did not cover the wider domestic market.

The National Bank expanded its approach in July 2025 by launching a regulatory sandbox where companies could test digital asset products under its supervision.

“The sandbox now includes 34 projects across 14 areas. Among them are stablecoins, tokenization, cryptocurrency exchanges, custody and services connecting cryptocurrencies with conventional currencies,” Suleimenov said.

Legislation that took effect on May 1 extended regulation nationwide and formally recognized digital financial assets, including stablecoins and tokenized real and financial assets. It also introduced licensing requirements for tokenization platforms, cryptocurrency exchanges and exchange services. Suleimenov described it as Central Asia’s first comprehensive nationwide regulatory framework for digital assets.

A presidential decree in July expanded the effort by seeking to establish a fully-fledged digital assets industry, encouraging the transition of digital asset transactions to the country’s regulated ecosystem and launching the tokenization of the economy and diversifying sources of financing for the economy.

Key figures

The National Bank has authorized the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange to operate platforms for issuing and trading digital assets. Its digital platform has recorded 34,000 transactions worth 20.5 billion tenge (US45.9 million) in an exchange-traded fund linked to bitcoin futures.

Three newly introduced cryptoasset ETFs have generated 650 transactions worth one billion tenge (US$2.2 million), according to Suleimenov.

Three licensed cryptocurrency exchange operators have also processed around two billion tenge (US$4.5 million) during their first two months of operation, while five more companies are seeking licenses.

Yerkegali Yedenbayev, chief authorization and fintech officer at AIFC’s Astana Financial Services Authority, said Kazakhstan’s citizens are estimated to hold around one million cryptocurrency wallets worldwide, suggesting that much of their trading still takes place through foreign platforms.

He said the center’s regulated digital asset providers currently serve nearly 270,000 clients, up from 53,000 in 2023.

“Today, there are 35 providers operating in the AIFC that offer services in the digital assets sector. Among them are 11 digital asset exchanges, including Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, and Bybit, the fourth-largest crypto exchange. In addition, there are 16 investment service providers and eight payment organizations, including three stablecoin issuers,” Yedenbayev said.

“While the volume of transactions in the licensed market reached $320 million in 2023, this figure reached $10.5 billion by the end of last year. In the first half of this year, the volume of transactions reached $5.5 billion. Thus, in a short period of time, the regulated market has grown more than 30-fold,” he said.

Digital tenge

The newly adopted plan also calls for wider use of the digital tenge, the central bank’s digital currency. Unlike cryptocurrencies, it is issued by the National Bank.

Bektenov instructed the Finance Ministry and the National Bank to examine its use in government procurement, corporate transactions and programmable contracts, which could automate payments when predetermined conditions are met.

“Unlike cryptocurrencies, the digital tenge is a centralized digital currency issued by the National Bank and is therefore legal tender. Its use should improve the efficiency of public spending and support the development of digital financial services. Digital contracts could help automate payments in government procurement and corporate transactions,” he said.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, Binur Zhalenov, deputy governor of the National Bank of Kazakhstan (NBK), said the digital tenge has the potential to transform how money moves. Most of the real-world use cases of digital tenge will be related to government spending, including public procurement and social spending.

What needs to be done

Suleimenov said the plan’s success would depend on competitive tax rules, more targeted compliance controls by banks and a sufficient supply of high-quality assets for tokenization. He said concerns involving an individual transaction or customer should not result in banks freezing all accounts held by a licensed digital asset provider.

The concern echoes findings reported earlier. Ainur Zhanturina, founder of RISE Research, said limited access to banking services was the principal barrier identified in the organization’s survey and interviews with Kazakhstan’s digital asset companies.

“Many banks are unwilling to work with companies in this sector, viewing them as higher-risk clients, which complicates transfers and account management,” Zhanturina said.

Сryptocurrency mining

While the digital tenge and tokenization are intended to expand Kazakhstan’s financial infrastructure, the plan also addresses a more established and energy-intensive part of the digital asset industry: cryptocurrency mining.

Kazakhstan has 76 licensed cryptocurrency miners and five accredited mining pools, with around 470,000 pieces of mining equipment registered with the government, said Vice Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Gizzat Baitursynov.

The country’s mining pools reported producing approximately 3,600 bitcoins in 2025, four times the volume recorded in 2023. According to Baitursynov, tax revenue from the industry rose to 22.4 billion tenge (US$50.1 million) in 2025 from nine billion tenge (US$20.1 million) two years earlier.

Bektenov said Kazakhstan should focus on regulating energy consumption and taxation rather than simply expanding mining capacity. He instructed officials to examine the use of gas- and coal-fired generation to supply mining centers.

“According to international studies, by the end of 2025, our country had entered the world’s top 10 in terms of its share of global Bitcoin mining. Now, our priority should no longer be focused on the quantitative growth of mining capacity,” said Bektenov.

He emphasized that the policy should focus on creating a more effective operational model that ensures control over energy consumption, transparent taxation, and the industry’s integration into the global digital economy.

“It is necessary to establish a fully-fledged digital mining industry comprising exchanges, digital instruments, tokenization, asset storage, and payment solutions,” he added.

World.title: Tokayev Calls for Doubling Kazakhstan-South Korea Trade, Expanding Industrial Ties
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for Kazakhstan and South Korea to double bilateral trade and deepen cooperation in advanced manufacturing, critical minerals, energy, transport, artificial intelligence and other high-value sectors. Speaking at the opening of the Kazakhstan–South Korea business roundtable in Seoul on Sept. 15, Tokayev said bilateral trade exceeded $3 billion last year and could be doubled through joint efforts by the two governments and businesses.

“This visit provides a good opportunity to consolidate the progress achieved and give new impetus to bilateral cooperation,” Tokayev said.

He also emphasized that Kazakhstan and South Korea had built strong relations over the past three decades based on mutual respect, trust and friendship. According to him, South Korea is now among Kazakhstan’s major trade and investment partners, with Korean companies playing an increasingly prominent role in the country’s economy.

Korean companies have invested more than $12 billion in Kazakhstan, while more than 1,000 companies with Korean capital operate in the country, including Samsung, Kia, Hyundai, Lotte, Doosan Enerbility and Shinhan Bank.

Industrial partnership enters a new stage
