World.title: Kyrgyzstan proposes joint specialist training with South Korea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 16. Kyrgyzstan has proposed establishing specialized training centers and developing joint educational programs with South Korea.

According to the press service of the President of Kyrgyzstan, President Sadyr Japarov made the statement on September 16 during a special session of the business summit held as part of the first Central Asia–Republic of Korea Summit in Seoul.

"Sadyr Japarov proposed establishing specialized training centers, developing joint educational programs and supporting technology startups," the statement said.

The President noted the importance of human capital development as one of the promising areas of cooperation.

Furthermore, Sadyr Japarov highlighted the Kyrgyzstan is interested in training specialists based on the needs of modern sectors of the economy, as well as developing technology startups.

He also emphasized the potential of combining South Korea’s expertise in artificial intelligence, digital platforms and innovation with Central Asia’s human capital.

World.title: Kazakhstan seeks Korean investment in Middle Corridor infrastructure
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 16. Kazakhstan President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed that South Korean companies participate in the development of infrastructure projects along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) or Middle Corridor.

According to the press service of the Kazakh president, Tokayev made the proposal during the Central Asia - Republic of Korea Business Summit.

He said the expansion of transport connectivity is becoming increasingly relevant, noting that Central Asia's geographic location creates significant opportunities to strengthen transport and logistics links across Eurasia.

"The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route plays an important role in this regard, a significant part of which runs through Kazakhstan. Currently, this route accounts for around 85% of all overland transportation between Asia and Europe," Tokayev said.

According to the President, container transportation along the Middle Corridor increased by 36% last year, while an 18% increase was recorded in the first eight months of this year.

"We plan to increase the route's capacity from 6 million to 10 million tons over the next two years. We propose that Korean companies take an active part in the development of infrastructure projects along this route. To this end, the Government of Kazakhstan will form a portfolio of investment projects for Korean partners," Tokayev said.

Tokayev also emphasized the importance of developing cooperation in critical materials. According to him, Kazakhstan has significant deposits of critical minerals and rare earth metals.

"We produce copper, chromium, titanium and many other elements that have been identified by the Korean Government as priority strategic resources. Given Korea's advanced technological experience, we propose forming a pool of targeted full-cycle investment projects covering geological exploration, extraction, deep processing and production of critical materials," the President said.

World.title: Uzbek Tashkent region, Chinese firms target new manufacturing projects
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 16. Uzbekistan’s Tashkent region held talks with major Chinese manufacturers on establishing new production facilities, localizing industrial products and introducing advanced technologies.

This was reflected in the statement by the Tashkent regional government, following the Tashkent Region Investment Cooperation Exchange Forum in Hangzhou, organized as part of a working visit by a delegation from the region led by Governor Zoyir Mirzayev.

Representatives of major Chinese manufacturing and industrial companies participated in the forum, discussing potential projects in Tashkent region and opportunities to use the area as a production base for markets across Central Asia.

The forum brought together Goldpro New Materials, Hangzhou Cable, Hangzhou COCO Healthcare Products, Hangzhou Oxygen Plant Group and Sicher Elevator for talks on prospective investment projects.

The discussions covered the localization of wear-resistant steel products, high-voltage electrical cables and optical communications products, as well as the production of industrial and specialty gases.

The sides also explored cooperation on air-separation equipment and the introduction of modern energy technologies.

“Tashkent region is ready to expand practical cooperation with Chinese companies, localize modern technologies and create new production capacities oriented toward both the domestic and regional markets,” the regional administration said.

The forum focused on establishing production with greater local content and creating opportunities for companies to export manufactured goods to Central Asian markets.

The participation of Chinese manufacturers also provides opportunities for Tashkent region to attract technologies and expertise in areas ranging from advanced materials and electrical equipment to industrial gases and energy-related technologies.

Several cooperation agreements were signed with companies at the conclusion of the forum, according to the regional administration.

The agreements are expected to support the implementation of new investment projects in Tashkent region, expand local production capacity and strengthen the region’s export potential.

The forum was held as part of the Tashkent region delegation’s broader business engagement in China, aimed at developing direct contacts with Chinese companies and identifying new investment and industrial cooperation opportunities.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan and South Korea sign 10 documents following business summit
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 16. Ten documents were signed between participants of the Kyrgyzstan–Republic of Korea business summit in Seoul.

According to the press service of the President of Kyrgyzstan, this was mentioned on September 16 during a special session of the business summit held in Seoul as part of the first Central Asia–Republic of Korea Summit.

"More than 30 domestic companies and around 50 Korean companies participated in the event. Ten documents were signed between them following the business summit," the statement said.

The business summit was held under the theme “Future Cooperation between the Republic of Korea and Central Asia for Growth and Innovation.”

More than 30 Kyrgyz companies and around 50 Korean companies participated in the event.

President of Kyrgyzstan Sadyr Japarov described the meeting as the beginning of a new practical chapter in relations between the countries and called for moving from discussions to the implementation of concrete joint projects.

Meanwhile, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov is participating in the first Central Asia–Republic of Korea Summit in Seoul on September 16–17. The summit brings together the leaders of South Korea and the five Central Asian countries — Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan — marking the first elevation of the Korea–Central Asia dialogue to the leaders’ level. The meeting is focused on expanding cooperation in areas including trade and investment, industry, energy, transport, digitalization, technology and human capital.

In recent years, bilateral contacts have also focused on attracting Korean investment and technology to Kyrgyzstan and strengthening cooperation in infrastructure and industrial development.

The current summit provides a regional platform for Kyrgyzstan and South Korea to discuss practical areas of cooperation and potential joint projects, while Seoul is seeking to further institutionalize and expand its engagement with the five Central Asian countries.

World.title: Canada in the EU and other takeaways from State of European Union
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has laid out her bold vision for a strengthened, revitalised, united Europe and has invited a new name to the party: Canada.

Ms von der Leyen covered a large range of topics in a 73-minute annual "state of the union" address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, leading off with the opening line from Charles Dickens' Tales of Two Cities, which she said also described the world today.

"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times," she said.

Here are five key takeaways from her speech.

Oh, Canada!

Ms von der Leyen said the European Union was opening the door for Canada to become its first associate member.

"We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible," she said.

"So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU."

Mark Carney received a standing ovation from the European Parliament. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

Ms von der Leyen walked up to and embraced Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who she had invited to the address, after mentioning Canada's "associate membership" and he received a standing ovation from the chamber.

It will be up to the 27 EU member states whether Ms von der Leyen's proposal goes ahead.

The US-Canada 'divorce' The US and Canada are often referred to as North American cousins, but the family feud has turned bitter as their trading relationship falls apart.

The EU has historically resisted such types of flexible alliances that have no legal status.

EU members were lukewarm in reacting to Germany's proposal in May of associate membership for Ukraine as a stepping stone to full membership.

New security council

The European Commission chief also pitched setting up a "European Security Council" with countries including Britain and Ukraine, as the continent grapples with the threat from Russia.

"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," Ms von der Leyen said.

"This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play.

"This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."

Russia and Ukraine continue strikes on energy The US president declared both sides would refrain from striking energy-related targets as petrol and diesel prices rise.

Europe is grappling with what it calls a campaign of "hybrid attacks" by Moscow aimed at undermining support for Ukraine, including recent attacks on Lithuania, Denmark and a Russian strike on the Ukraine–Poland border that just missed a train carrying diplomats, including former British prime minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt.

"We should be under no illusions about what is happening here: hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats," Ms von der Leyen said.

"Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook.

"We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents: Those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security."

The European Commission president said she wanted to establish an "emergency security protocol" that would allow any EU member state to convene urgent talks in case of crisis.

'Strongest ever' support for Ukraine

While the EU is struggling to counter Russian activities, Ms von der Leyen pledged that the bloc would ramp up support for Kyiv as Russia steps up bombardments ahead of the winter.

"We will give our strongest-ever support to Ukraine over the toughest winter of the war," she said.

"Together with our partners, we will provide humanitarian aid and reinforce Ukraine's supplies of power and heating."

Ursula von der Leyen has invited Canada to become the first associate member of the European Union. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

Ms von der Leyen backed plans to jointly "develop with Ukraine an affordable, modular missile-defence system".

She said that Europe would also step up its efforts to develop its own key military capabilities, pledging a "new European instrument for strategic enablers".

Strengthened trade and manufacturing

Ms von der Leyen said she would like Europe to build "an alliance for the future, to create a common prosperity" and economic security.

"We will work on intelligent manufacturing," she said.

"We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases.

"We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project."

While Ursula von der Leyen was laying out her vision, animal rights activists demonstrated outside the European Parliament. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

She said the EU would work on energy critical minerals and batteries, on AI, quantum, cyber and economic security.

"This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strengths," Ms von der Leyen said.

Slow down on AI and social ban for kids

Despite calling for more European technological advances, Ms von der Leyen said she supported the recent calls from tech leaders for a slowdown on AI.

Last week, AI researcher Jacob Coxon quit tech company Anthropic, saying those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".

Anthropic researcher says AI 'could kill us all' A researcher for AI developer Anthropic has quit the company and is one of a growing number of AI experts to call on the industry to slow down.

And earlier this week, AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton and Anthropic's Dario Amodei both called for a global slowdown in AI development.

"Models being developed will allow hacking on a level we never thought possible," Ms von der Leyen said.

"And they will soon be in the hands of adversaries who see the world very differently from us."

She pointed to recent incidents of rogue AI agents and warnings from developers.

"CEOs of the most advanced companies tell us that it is time to slow down on the self-recursive models, to pace the frontier," Ms von der Leyen said.

"If the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too."

Landmark EU rules governing the use of AI adopted recently put Europe in the position to shape global efforts to tackle the risks, Ms von der Leyen said.

She said Europe would work with like-minded partners such as Canada, the United Kingdom and others to take measures such as model evaluation, verification and AI security.

"I will invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier," von der Leyen said.

She also proposed a social media ban for children under 13 — similar to Australia's world-first ban for kids under 16 — and no personal accounts for people under the age of 15, saying that platforms have to prove that they are safe for children.

ABC/Reuters/AFP

World.title: Former Kosovo president Thaci sentenced to 25 years' prison for war crimes
World.content:
Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci has been found guilty of war crimes, including murder, torture and illegal detention by the Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

Thaci, 58, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes committed as top commander of the ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the territory's violent break from Serbia in the 1990s.

The tribunal said he was guilty of the murder of 96 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces by Kosovo Liberation Army forces during the conflict.

He was also convicted of arbitrary illegal detention of 385 people, torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of about 50.

The court said Thaci had "actively participated in and encouraged crimes".

"The scale and nature of the crimes committed were very serious," presiding judge Charles Smith said.

"The so-called intelligence on which many of these victims were arrested, detained and killed was little more than unverified rumours. Based on that information, victims were called and described as spies and collaborators and violently treated."

Thaci had denied all charges.

Supporters gather in Pristina

Supporters of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci protested after he was found guilty. (Reuters: Valdrin Xhemaj)

The ruling was closely watched in Kosovo and Serbia, where the legacy of the 1998-99 conflict and Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence remain a source of tension between ethnic Kosovo Albanians and Serbs.

Thaci remains a revered figure for many Kosovo Albanians, while the tribunal itself is deeply unpopular in Kosovo.

In Pristina, Kosovo's capital, thousands of people watching the verdict on a big screen booed the verdict and chanted "Thaci, Thaci" as some burst into tears.

One billboard showed the faces of the defendants, which read: "In the name of the people you are declared innocent".

Albania's Prime Minister criticised the verdict with a picture posted on social media of a circle of barbed wire across a map of Europe and one word: "Unbelievable".

Former Kosovo leader pleads not guilty on war crimes The former president and three others charged led a pro-Kosovo guerilla faction during the break-up of Yugoslavia.

Prosecutors had sought a 45-year sentence against Thaci and three other former top commanders of the KLA.

But the three-judge panel dismissed six charges of crimes against humanity.

However, they ruled that Thaci and his co-accused were part of a joint criminal enterprise, with a common plan to take control of Kosovo politics following its independence by targeting political opponents.

Thaci's lawyers had argued the accusations were unfounded, amounted to an attempt to rewrite history and there was no evidence to directly link Thaci to any of the alleged crimes..

Reuters

World.title: Perth city 'landmark' sign badly damaged by fire at Yagan Square
World.content:
A popular sign at tourist attraction Yagan Square in the heart of the Perth CBD has been badly damaged in a fire, as authorities investigate its cause.

Yagan Square's social media account announced the news in a statement this evening.

"Farewell to an icon," the post read.

"Today, we share the news that the PERTH Sign at Yagan Square was badly damaged by fire.

"For eight loyal years, it has been the backdrop to countless photos, cultural celebrations and memorable Perth moments.

The sign, pictured prior to the fire. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"It has well and truly earned its place as one of our city's most-loved landmarks."

The square's social media account invited users to share their favourite photos of the sign, with social media users expressing their sorrow and devastation.

Blaze quickly extinguished

The fire was reported to the Department of Fire and Emergency Services at 2:30pm today, and extinguished by 2:50pm.

A worker at a nearby bar told the ABC he saw the fire once it had already started.

He said there were plenty of people around until security moved onlookers away.

Once firefighters arrived, he said the flames were extinguished within less than five minutes.

A closer look at the sign shows blackened areas where the fire has been put out. (ABC Radio Perth: Ashleigh Davis)

Development WA, which manages and maintains the square, said it would not comment on the incident as it was an active fire investigation.

Yagan Square is described as a transit area for thousands of city workers and Perth residents, situated between the Perth CBD and the city's Northbridge entertainment precinct.

It is surrounded by bars and restaurants, the new multi-million-dollar Edith Cowan University city campus, Perth Underground train station and Perth Busport.

The square is named after the 19th century Aboriginal warrior Yagan, and was officially opened in 2018, costing taxpayers tens of millions of dollars.

World.title: Pyne warns AI could be 'means of human race's destruction'
World.content:
Former Labor leader Bill Shorten and former Coalition defence minister Christopher Pyne have joined the chorus for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence (AI).

Both issued blunt warnings on 7.30 about the damage AI could do if guardrails are not introduced as Mr Shorten compared AI to nuclear weapons and called for an AI version of the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NNPT).

That treaty was introduced in 1970 to stop the spread of nuclear weapons, promote peaceful use of nuclear energy and pursue negotiations towards disarmament.

"I think the more that we hear from the CEOs and the chief officers of these frontier laboratories of AI, I cannot help escape the conclusion that we may have built nukes with opinions," Mr Shorten told 7.30.

"This is a marvellous technology, but until we can regulate it, we need to slow down.

"What we're seeing at the cutting edge of AI laboratories is actually a technology which doesn't appear to need humans to make decisions. Once you eliminate human oversight, there's no guarantee that what we're designing will actually make decisions in the best interest of humanity."

Mr Shorten said he was not suggesting that building data centres or infrastructure was a problem but that generative AI needed more human oversight.

It was a sentiment Mr Pyne, who now holds a number of positions as a strategic advisor and consultant, including for the defence industry, echoed.

"AI has tremendous opportunity for the human race It has the capacity to make our lives much, much better, not just from a health perspective, but many others," Mr Pyne said.

Former Liberal MP Christopher Pyne runs lobbying firm Pyne & Partners. (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

"But there is an inherent danger.

"Obviously human beings are the smartest being on the planet, we have dominion of the globe because we might not be the strongest, we might not be the fastest, but we're the smartest.

"And we've created something that's actually smarter than us and with regenerative self-improvement is going to get much smarter and much quicker than we ever can.

"So we could have actually created the means of the human race's destruction.

" I'm not saying next week or in 10 years, but I think you would be a brave person to predict that the human race will dominate the globe in 500 years from now. "

Pressed if that was something he expected, Mr Pyne pulled back.

"I'm an optimist. I think it will all be OK in the end, but we wouldn't want to underestimate what we've done," he said.

An AI non-proliferation treaty?

With that warning the pair were asked what could be done to bring the rapid development of AI under control.

It is the same question those in the industry have been facing.

CEO and Co-Founder of Anthropic Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown on AI advancement. (Reuters: Denis Balibouse)

First AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.

That sparked a deluge of calls to slow it down from Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI", Anthropic boss Dario Amodei, OpenAI head Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns xAI.

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Mr Amodei wrote in a post on his personal website.

Given the nuclear comparisons made earlier, Mr Shorten was asked if an AI version of the NNPT was needed.

"Dario [Amodei] has proposed a plan, which does involve independent verification," Mr Shorten said.

"It does involve, as technologies are being developed, that you have external observers like we have the International Atomic Energy Agency.

"So I do think it does need global action and I don't think we can afford, in Australia, to say the problem is someone else's.

"As a middle power we can help lead this debate, but it's pretty interesting that you have the technology leaders, the private sector saying, 'hey, we need help here. We need regulation'.

"So I do think there is some analogy between the proliferation of nuclear weapons and the proliferation of AI and maybe some of the solutions that were used for nuclear weapons need to be put into place here."

Mr Pyne agreed and while he said AI was a race between the US and China, he suggested that guardrails were necessary to prevent potential rogue actors from being involved.

"China and the United States are locked in a competition over AI for different reasons and it could be very dangerous," he told 7.30.

"But by the same token, we as humans need to live on this planet and we need them to come to an agreement that the rest of the world can then fold into."

Cutting immigration is 'economic self-harm'

With the issue of immigration dominating the political agenda after One Nation released their policy earlier in the week it was put to the two former senior politicians as to what should be done.

Tony Burke was due to outline Labor's migration policy last month, but postponed the speech. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Shorten, who is the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Canberra, acknowledged the government had work to do but cautioned them against acting too harshly, especially when it comes to mooted changes to policy around international students.

"We don't need to be in a bargaining auction in a race to the bottom about the lowest possible number," he told 7.30.

"We need migrants for this country to do well. Migrants tend to pay, as a group they're more likely to pay tax."

He said that cutting international student numbers would become a potential economic nightmare.

"If some people are overstaying their visas, by all means clamp down but economic self-harm when it comes to cutting international students is a real problem.

"It's international students whose fees cross-subsidise us being able to support Aussie kids. It's international students' fees who allow us to be able to fund research, which the nation wouldn't otherwise get.

Bill Shorten, is currently Vice-Chancellor at the University of Canberra. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

"And in regional Australia ... if you take out international students, there will be job losses.

"So governments have got to have a migration debate, but it's not going to save a government or an opposition."

Asked for his take on the issue, Mr Pyne said "migration has built this country".

"Everything Bill said about international students is right.

"Saying that we're going to start curtailing international students is definitely an act of self-harm.

"Politicians need to do is actually start standing up for migration, a population that is sustainable and explaining the benefits that this brings.

"Australia is so powerful internationally because of its multiculturalism and all the people in Australia who do business with the countries that they came from or their grandparents came from because of the knowledge they have, the skills they gain, the language commonalities.

"These things are not something that we should be embarrassed about."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Ninth person charged over fatal house party attack on 21yo man
World.content:
Police have charged a ninth person with murder over the death of a 21-year-old man at a Logan house party in July.

Jongkuch Kur Jongkuch died on August 1, days after being allegedly assaulted by a group of people at an out-of-control house party at Bahrs Scrub.

The Redbank Plains man was discovered unconscious with critical head injuries on Orchard Avenue just after 2am on July 26.

Last month, police charged eight teenagers aged between 17 and 19 with his murder.

The 21-year-old Redbank Plains man was found unconscious with critical head injuries on Orchard Avenue. (ABC News: Meghan Dansie)

On Wednesday, detectives charged a ninth person, a 17-year-old Inala boy, with murder.

Police have alleged the teenagers who fatally attacked Mr Jongkuch came to the party armed and "prepared to inflict harm" on the people there.

The 17-year-old arrested this week will face the Beenleigh Children's Court on Thursday.

Police acknowledged the assistance of residents, community leaders and representatives who encouraged members of the community to come forward with information throughout the investigation.

World.title: 'Very disappointing': Indigenous group reacts to NSW land law change
World.content:
Changes to a law allowing the transfer of government land into Indigenous ownership have passed NSW parliament, creating barriers to land claims a peak body has described as "regression".

Aboriginal Land Councils can claim unused or unoccupied Crown land, or land held by the state government on behalf of the public, under the Aboriginal Land Rights Act.

The amendments enable the lands minister to retrospectively convert an invalid or defective lease on Crown land into valid one by marking it as in-use.

It is this new power that the NSW Aboriginal Land Council (NSWALC) believes diminishes the original "intent" of the legislation.

"The minister can, by the stroke of a pen, make a decision that certain land claims are now not on the table," council chair Raymond Kelly said.

"That is a real regression."

Unresolved claims date back decades

The government first proposed the bill in March, deferring it for further community consultation and winding back some of the changes.

Lands and Property Minister Steve Kamper said at the time the amendment aimed to address "edge cases" in which community assets became claimable due to technical errors.

There are more than 43,000 unresolved land claims in the state, some dating back to the 1980s.

"We've been following the law to the letter and it is the law that is now taking a serious dent," Dr Kelly said.

NSW Aboriginal Land Council chair Raymond Kelly says the new laws are a "regression". (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

He said it would now reduce the council's ability to dispute decisions made by the government.

"If we don't agree with the minister's take, it makes it more difficult for us to then put a position for the community forward."

Premier Chris Minns described the law as "hugely important," but said its "structure" needed to be altered.

"If the community land is transferred out of government ownership to other forms of ownership, either its use can be changed ... for example, from a tennis club to housing, or the rent can go up," Mr Minns said.

" We could lose an enormous amount of community land in our state. "

Club evicted after 'poorly worded legislation'

Paul Francis has managed the Love'n Deuce tennis club in Naremburn on Sydney's lower north shore for the past 40 years.

It was Crown land until the state government transferred it to the Metropolitan Local Aboriginal Land Council four years ago.

'Common sense': Aboriginal land council hails High Court win The High Court of Australia has ruled in favour of the La Perouse Local Aboriginal Land Council, affirming its claim on disputed land in Sydney's Paddington.

Love'n Deuce has now been evicted from the site, which Mr Francis partly puts down to "poorly worded legislation".

He said the club was not part of the land transfer decision in 2022, and managers like himself were unable to correct inaccuracies in the claim.

"The site was portrayed as being a private club and you had to be a member of the club, we don't have any memberships here, the whole site is open to the public," he said.

Mr Francis said the lease had been granted to new tenants, Racquet Club.

"We weren't aware of any tender going out and the next thing we knew, we got the eviction notice," he said.

"I think if the [new] legislation had been in place we wouldn't be having the dramas we're having today, no doubt."

'We're not going to sit idle'

Indigenous groups say the legislation erodes Aboriginal land claims processes. (ABC News: Amelia Searson)

The Naremburn tennis club is the kind of "edge case" the state government says it wants to avoid, however, what that term refers to is not clear to the NSWALC.

"What are we talking about in terms of these edge cases? That's the difficulty here because we can't see into that," Dr Kelly said.

He said he looked forward to sitting down with Mr Kamper to gain some clarity on the phrase.

"When we're dealing with hypotheticals, this is where the hysteria gets carried away," Dr Kelly said.

"This is where that concept of 'land grab', 'ungrateful', these things injure people, these statements, they injure our people and it continues to happen time and time again."

Dr Kelly said the consultation period for the law changes was "forced" and "short", but the NSW Aboriginal Land Council was open to further discussion.

"Clearly the ball is in the court of the government right now. They know full well our position," he said.

Charles Lynch says the NSWALC will "continue to stand up". (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Councillor Charles Lynch said despite the legislation change being "very disappointing," NSWALC was committed to moving forward.

"What we want to assure people is today is a new day and we're not going to sit idle," Mr Lynch said.

"We will continue to stand up every day and move forward in achieving what we've set out to do."

World.title: Domestic violence offenders to face harsher penalties under new laws
World.content:
Domestic and family violence offenders who breach protection orders will face harsher penalties under new proposed laws from the Queensland government.

It comes after the premier was forced to rule out changes to the definition of a domestic and family violence (DFV) victim for Police Protection Directions (PPDs).

The orders allow police to issue immediate directives for perpetrators to not commit DFV against someone, or face fines or jail.

Legislation expected to be introduced on Thursday will create new offences for the repeated contravention of a PPD, or a Domestic Violence Order (DVO).

It would increase the duration of a PPD from 12 months to three years, and the maximum penalty for breaching an order from three to five years.

An electronic ankle monitoring pilot for high-risk DFV offenders will be expanded statewide, and a requirement introduced for courts to consider fitting a device as part of a DVO.

Police Minister Dan Purdie said the changes were about trying to ease the workload of police.

A trial requiring high-risk DFV offenders to wear an electronic ankle monitor will be expanded statewide. (Supplied: QPS)

"We're going to make sure that we expand it, and we give police the powers that they need to rapidly protect victims and get to that next victim sooner."

The changes are expected to remove many of the barriers police face in issuing PPDs, which can force them to go to court to implement an order.

PPDs have been criticised by some experts, with evidence previously showing police mis-identified who the perpetrator and victim were in DFV incidents in around a third of call-outs.

Calls to change DFV victim definition

Queensland Police Union president Shane Prior was supportive of the changes to PPDs and urged the government to go further.

He said he would be advocating for the government to change the definition of a DFV victim to only include intimate partner relationships when concerning police orders.

Queensland Police Union president Shane Prior has urged the government to go further. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"That's the priority because right now, we've got a situation in the state where informal care disputes and family arguments are being pulled into this one remit, and it just ensures it enters the queue like everything else," he said.

"And we've got victims of intimate partner violence in the state waiting in the queue for a police response."

Asked about changes to the definition on Wednesday morning, Mr Purdie left the door open but said it wasn't "on my desk at the moment".

"It is certainly something that we certainly won't be turning away from in the future," he said.

Evidence shows police mis-identified who was the victim and perpetrator in around one-third of call-outs. (ABC News: Ashleigh Stevenson)

"Where the police are spending six hours to take out a protection order on two adult brothers who are having a fight over the Xbox, maybe that focus should be put back on those intimate partner relationships."

Mr Purdie claimed it was a change those in the DFV sector had raised with him and later ruled out any changes to the definition.

None of the several experts in the space the ABC spoke to said they had been consulted on any change to the definition.

The opposition interrogated the issue during parliament.

"Will the premier rule out narrowing the meaning of relevant relationships as defined in the Domestic and Family Violence Prevention Act," Labor leader Steven Miles asked in the House.

"The answer is yes," Premier David Crisafulli responded.

DFV sector experts are expected to be briefed on the changes by the government on Thursday.

World.title: Australia's 43-year MotoGP streak continues with Senna Agius signing
World.content:
There will be a full-time Australian rider in motorcycle racing's premier class for the 43rd consecutive year with 21-year-old Senna Agius signing on to race for KTM Tech3 next year.

The Sydneysider currently sits fourth in the Moto2 standings after placing 10th in 2025.

He has four grand prix wins in Moto2, including at the Circuit of the Americas in the United States and Jerez in Spain earlier this season.

He won his home Moto2 grand prix at Phillip Island last year, and will be in MotoGP for next year's maiden Australian Grand Prix at the new Adelaide street circuit.

Agius has signed on for KTM Tech3, which has former F1 team principal Guenther Steiner has the team's chief executive.

"Today a lifelong dream of mine has come true, reaching MotoGP," Agius said.

"So many years of hard work have gone into this moment and I'm incredibly grateful to Guenther and everyone at Tech3 for believing in me and giving me this opportunity.

"I can't wait to repay their faith. I know the challenge ahead, but I'm ready to learn, work hard, and become the best version of myself with this team."

Australia has had a full-time rider in the premier class since 1985.

In the modern era of grand prix motorcycle racing, which began in 2002 when 500cc two-stroke bikes were replaced with 990cc four-stroke engines, Agius will become the 11th full-time Australian rider.

He will also be the only Australian on the grid next season, with Jack Miller ending his 12-year MotoGP stint and moving to World Superbikes in 2027.

Sydney are highly unlikely to be returning to the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne if they qualify for next week’s grand final. Related Article AFL 2026 Suspended Swans to foot their own legal bills under AFL rules Four of the players – Heeney, Warner, Blakey and Jordon – are persons of interest in a police investigation from the night after three women alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent. World.title: ‘Is that news to you?’ Liberal apparatchiks listed as Toplace creditors
World.content:
Two Liberal Party operatives accused of washing illegal political donations through their companies are listed as creditors wanting to claw back more than $2 million from disgraced developer Jean Nassif, whose company Toplace collapsed in 2023 with debts of at least $1 billion. The Independent Commission Against Corruption heard on Wednesday that lobby firms run by ex-Liberal powerbroker Christian Ellis and his business partner Jeremy Greenwood are listed as creditors in documents provided to the public inquiry by insolvency firm DVT, the administrators appointed after Toplace folded. Jeremy Greenwood is a person of interest in this inquiry. Sitthixay Ditthavong Counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, told the commission that Beckington, which Ellis and Greenwood co-founded, and JPG Advisory, Greenwood’s firm, appear as creditors in publicly available documents. Dwyer said Ellis had claimed that Beckington was owed $1,433,000 by Toplace and Greenwood’s company JPG Advisory appears as a creditor owed $721,700.



“Is that news to you?” Dwyer asked Greenwood as he gave his final day of evidence to the commission. “Yeah, I definitely haven’t put in a form, sorry, it might be those outstanding invoices, but I’ve never submitted anything,” Greenwood said. Related Article Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny as it happened: Jeremy Greenwood returns to witness box after Jean Nassif slams Elliott, Chandler in chaotic appearance Greenwood, Ellis, and former right-wing powerbroker Charles Perrottet allegedly shared in $2 million from Nassif in return for political outcomes. The commission has heard that the money was washed through Beckington, with some being used to pay for Liberal Party recruitment and branch stacking. Greenwood told the commission on Wednesday that the reason for his inconsistent invoicing to Toplace and large-sum payments from Nassif was because of the chaotic way the fugitive property developer did business.



Dwyer had been trying to extract an explanation about why there was no written agreement to show how much Nassif owed Greenwood in outstanding payments. “You’ve met him now, it’s how Jean does business,” Greenwood said, adding it was “regrettable” that he did not have clearer agreements in writing because Nassif would often take months to pay a retainer. Jean Nassif appeared before the ICAC from Beirut. ICAC In an erratic appearance, Nassif dialled into the commission from his bedroom in Beirut on Monday and Tuesday, where he maintained that all he wanted from Greenwood and Ellis was their help with his stalled development projects. “I was not involved with paying politics to get my projects approved,” Nassif said. “If they did any corrupt work, I am not involved with it. I was not aware of it.”



Greenwood also denied giving “ridiculous” evidence when he told the commission that he paid consultant Anita Perrottet for her advice on deterring children from vaping. The former Liberal staffer told the commission on Wednesday that it was not relevant that Anita Perrottet’s children were aged under five when he paid her to provide “a mum’s perspective” on kids vaping. Anita Perrottet gave “a mum’s perspective” on vaping, the ICAC has heard. ICAC The commission has previously heard there were no emails reflecting any work done by Anita Perrottet for Greenwood, nor any phone records showing direct calls between them, despite Anita being paid $660,000 over two years for “strategic advice”. Dwyer asked Greenwood how old Anita Perrottet’s children were when she was paid for her thoughts on deterring children from vaping.



“I don’t know,” Greenwood responded. “I don’t think it’s of relevance.” Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny ‘No one can make me shut up!’: Fugitive Jean Nassif melts down at ICAC Dwyer said Perrottet’s children were aged two and three at the time of her advice. “Did she give you a mum’s perspective on deterring under-fives from vaping?” Dwyer asked. “No,” Greenwood said. Dwyer responded: “Your evidence is ridiculous; can I suggest to you that Anita Perrottet contributed to a debate that had been the subject of professional reports … for many years before you say you brought Anita Perrottet on board.”



Greenwood disagreed. Greenwood has repeatedly maintained that Anita Perrottet gave all her strategic advice verbally. He told the corruption inquiry that it was not standard practice in government relations consulting to keep records of hours worked or specific work done. The commission heard that, at one point, Macquarie Consulting invoiced for $82,120 for “project consulting fees”, plus GST. “Isn’t this just a way of you distributing the money that’s come in from Jean Nassif that’s intended for Charles Perrottet?” Dwyer asked. “No,” Greenwood said. World.title: LNP insider hopes to become Brisbane’s youngest councillor
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council LNP insider hopes to become Brisbane’s youngest councillor William Davis September 16, 2026 — 8:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Taylor Hull will run for the LNP in the Brisbane City Council ward of Holland Park at the 2028 election, as Krista Adams plans to stand down after almost two decades in local government. If she wins, the 25-year-old adviser to state treasurer David Janetzki could become the city’s new youngest representative. She would still be older than Calamvale councillor Emily Kim was when elected in 2024, or Chandler councillor Ryan Murphy when he was elected in 2012. Taylor Hull, who will replace Krista Adams as the LNP candidate for Holland Park, with Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner. Hull unsuccessfully ran for the seat of Toohey at the 2024 state election.



Living in Mount Gravatt East, she holds a business degree from the Queensland University of Technology and previously sat on the lord mayor’s Youth Advisory Council. “I’ll spend the time between now and 2028 listening to locals, learning from [former deputy mayor Adams], and working hard to earn the community’s support,” Hull said in a statement. Her CV also includes volunteering through her local Rotary Club and mentoring women beginning careers in finance. The LNP insider could find herself at City Hall before 2028. Parties are permitted to parachute candidates into wards without a byelection if retiring councillors choose to leave in the final stages of their term. Before the last election, this happened in the Hamilton and Paddington wards, and Adams could do the same.



At the 2024 election, Labor attracted a swing of just over 1 per cent in the Holland Park Ward, with the LNP winning about 53.7 per cent of the two-party-preferred vote. Labor confirmed it was yet to open its own nominations for the ward. Holland Park councillor Krista Adams says she still has plenty to do before standing down in 2028. Brisbane Times In a statement, its council leader, Jared Cassidy, said Hull would not be an effective advocate for the community. “It’s remarkable that the LNP have chosen an adviser for the state treasurer that delivered Queensland’s first credit rating downgrade since 2009 as their candidate,” he said.



“Just as the current councillor has done for almost 20 years, this new LNP councillor will just be a mouthpiece for the LNP regime.” Adams is resigning after almost two decades on council, having served as deputy mayor and as a senior member of civic cabinet. This year she was appointed to the boards of Tourism and Events Queensland and Economic Development Queensland. “After many years representing Holland Park Ward, there’s a lot of local knowledge and experience I want to share with Taylor,” Adams said in a statement. “I’m looking forward to introducing Taylor to all the community groups, local businesses and residents I’m incredibly lucky to work with.



“There’s still plenty I want to get done before 2028 and my focus remains firmly on delivering for Holland Park Ward.” Labor is adamant it can secure a swing towards it in 2028. The Greens also believe they can significantly increase their ward count. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner has confirmed he will run for re-election, while Cassidy said he was also mulling a tilt for the top job. World.title: Fans face price hikes and ticketing shake-up for Melbourne Grand Prix
World.content:
Four-day tickets to the Australian Grand Prix will increase again in 2027 for people who want guaranteed access to the Albert Park circuit. The Australian Grand Prix Corporation (AGPC) has announced a new ticketing structure for the April event, including a membership offering and the addition of a sprint race. Australian F1 driver Oscar Piastri greets fans at Albert Park. Formula 1 via Getty Images Where a four-day general admission pass costs $425 - an extra $40 above what it was this year - people who pay an extra $275 for an Albert Park Circuit Club Membership will be granted entry 30 minutes early, as well as discounts on merchandise and priority renewal access each year. For $1370, grandstand members will get reserved seating in a grandstand of their choosing and a member welcome pack.



Those who pay top dollar - at least $2185 - will get a reserved seat in the Premium Members-only Brabham Grandstand across all four days. For those who only want to attend the big race on Sunday, there’s also a price increase of $10 to $220. Melbourne will host the third round of the 2027 Formula 1 season from April 1-4 at Albert Park, with a major addition to the weekend schedule.



On Wednesday evening, the AGPC confirmed the inclusion of a high-speed, 100km sprint race ahead of Saturday’s qualifying session, giving the top eight drivers a chance to score extra championship points. The news comes after the FIA, the international governing body for world motorsport, announced an increase in the number of sprint races from six to 10 for the 2027 F1 World Championship. Australia, Japan, Monaco, plus the season finale in Abu Dhabi will all get their first taste of the sprint format. Introduced in 2021, the sprint race was designed to increase fan engagement and add more action to typical race weekends. However, the format is controversial, with some F1 fans complaining about the lack of pit stops and overtaking, arguing the race is often predictable.



AGPC chief executive officer Travis Auld heralded the sprint race as an “exciting addition for fans” and said the Friday and Saturday sessions would offer “more on-track action than ever before.” “We’re also excited to launch the Albert Park Circuit Club membership program and today’s announcement brings us another step closer to next year’s event,” he said. “We can’t wait to welcome fans back to Albert Park Circuit.” AGPC chief executive officer Travis Auld welcomed the addition of a sprint race. Eddie Jim Over the past four years, many F1 fans have taken to social media to air their frustrations on rising ticket prices, with many voicing concerns around being “priced out” of the sport.





At the time, Auld said the AGPC had aimed to “strike a balance between keeping tickets accessible while continuing to enhance the fan experience and respond to the record level of interest.” Members’ tickets for the Australian Grand Prix go on sale midday October 1, with general public tickets on sale October 6. Greenwood also denied giving “ridiculous” evidence when he told the commission that he paid consultant Anita Perrottet for her advice on deterring children from vaping. The former Liberal staffer told the commission on Wednesday that it was not relevant that Anita Perrottet’s children were aged under five when he paid her to provide “a mum’s perspective” on kids vaping. Anita Perrottet gave “a mum’s perspective” on vaping, the ICAC has heard. ICAC The commission has previously heard there were no emails reflecting any work done by Anita Perrottet for Greenwood, nor any phone records showing direct calls between them, despite Anita being paid $660,000 over two years for “strategic advice”. Dwyer asked Greenwood how old Anita Perrottet’s children were when she was paid for her thoughts on deterring children from vaping.



“I don’t know,” Greenwood responded. “I don’t think it’s of relevance.” Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny ‘No one can make me shut up!’: Fugitive Jean Nassif melts down at ICAC Dwyer said Perrottet’s children were aged two and three at the time of her advice. “Did she give you a mum’s perspective on deterring under-fives from vaping?” Dwyer asked. “No,” Greenwood said. Dwyer responded: “Your evidence is ridiculous; can I suggest to you that Anita Perrottet contributed to a debate that had been the subject of professional reports … for many years before you say you brought Anita Perrottet on board.”



Greenwood disagreed. Greenwood has repeatedly maintained that Anita Perrottet gave all her strategic advice verbally. He told the corruption inquiry that it was not standard practice in government relations consulting to keep records of hours worked or specific work done. The commission heard that, at one point, Macquarie Consulting invoiced for $82,120 for “project consulting fees”, plus GST. “Isn’t this just a way of you distributing the money that’s come in from Jean Nassif that’s intended for Charles Perrottet?” Dwyer asked. “No,” Greenwood said. World.title: LNP insider hopes to become Brisbane’s youngest councillor
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council LNP insider hopes to become Brisbane’s youngest councillor William Davis September 16, 2026 — 8:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Taylor Hull will run for the LNP in the Brisbane City Council ward of Holland Park at the 2028 election, as Krista Adams plans to stand down after almost two decades in local government. If she wins, the 25-year-old adviser to state treasurer David Janetzki could become the city’s new youngest representative. She would still be older than Calamvale councillor Emily Kim was when elected in 2024, or Chandler councillor Ryan Murphy when he was elected in 2012. Taylor Hull, who will replace Krista Adams as the LNP candidate for Holland Park, with Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner. Hull unsuccessfully ran for the seat of Toohey at the 2024 state election.



Living in Mount Gravatt East, she holds a business degree from the Queensland University of Technology and previously sat on the lord mayor’s Youth Advisory Council. “I’ll spend the time between now and 2028 listening to locals, learning from [former deputy mayor Adams], and working hard to earn the community’s support,” Hull said in a statement. Her CV also includes volunteering through her local Rotary Club and mentoring women beginning careers in finance. The LNP insider could find herself at City Hall before 2028. Parties are permitted to parachute candidates into wards without a byelection if retiring councillors choose to leave in the final stages of their term. Before the last election, this happened in the Hamilton and Paddington wards, and Adams could do the same.



At the 2024 election, Labor attracted a swing of just over 1 per cent in the Holland Park Ward, with the LNP winning about 53.7 per cent of the two-party-preferred vote. Labor confirmed it was yet to open its own nominations for the ward. Holland Park councillor Krista Adams says she still has plenty to do before standing down in 2028. Brisbane Times In a statement, its council leader, Jared Cassidy, said Hull would not be an effective advocate for the community. “It’s remarkable that the LNP have chosen an adviser for the state treasurer that delivered Queensland’s first credit rating downgrade since 2009 as their candidate,” he said.



“Just as the current councillor has done for almost 20 years, this new LNP councillor will just be a mouthpiece for the LNP regime.” Adams is resigning after almost two decades on council, having served as deputy mayor and as a senior member of civic cabinet. This year she was appointed to the boards of Tourism and Events Queensland and Economic Development Queensland. “After many years representing Holland Park Ward, there’s a lot of local knowledge and experience I want to share with Taylor,” Adams said in a statement. “I’m looking forward to introducing Taylor to all the community groups, local businesses and residents I’m incredibly lucky to work with.



“There’s still plenty I want to get done before 2028 and my focus remains firmly on delivering for Holland Park Ward.” Labor is adamant it can secure a swing towards it in 2028. The Greens also believe they can significantly increase their ward count. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner has confirmed he will run for re-election, while Cassidy said he was also mulling a tilt for the top job. World.title: Fans face price hikes and ticketing shake-up for Melbourne Grand Prix
World.content:
Four-day tickets to the Australian Grand Prix will increase again in 2027 for people who want guaranteed access to the Albert Park circuit. The Australian Grand Prix Corporation (AGPC) has announced a new ticketing structure for the April event, including a membership offering and the addition of a sprint race. Australian F1 driver Oscar Piastri greets fans at Albert Park. Formula 1 via Getty Images Where a four-day general admission pass costs $425 - an extra $40 above what it was this year - people who pay an extra $275 for an Albert Park Circuit Club Membership will be granted entry 30 minutes early, as well as discounts on merchandise and priority renewal access each year. For $1370, grandstand members will get reserved seating in a grandstand of their choosing and a member welcome pack.



Those who pay top dollar - at least $2185 - will get a reserved seat in the Premium Members-only Brabham Grandstand across all four days. For those who only want to attend the big race on Sunday, there’s also a price increase of $10 to $220. Melbourne will host the third round of the 2027 Formula 1 season from April 1-4 at Albert Park, with a major addition to the weekend schedule.



On Wednesday evening, the AGPC confirmed the inclusion of a high-speed, 100km sprint race ahead of Saturday’s qualifying session, giving the top eight drivers a chance to score extra championship points. The news comes after the FIA, the international governing body for world motorsport, announced an increase in the number of sprint races from six to 10 for the 2027 F1 World Championship. Australia, Japan, Monaco, plus the season finale in Abu Dhabi will all get their first taste of the sprint format. Introduced in 2021, the sprint race was designed to increase fan engagement and add more action to typical race weekends. However, the format is controversial, with some F1 fans complaining about the lack of pit stops and overtaking, arguing the race is often predictable.



AGPC chief executive officer Travis Auld heralded the sprint race as an “exciting addition for fans” and said the Friday and Saturday sessions would offer “more on-track action than ever before.” “We’re also excited to launch the Albert Park Circuit Club membership program and today’s announcement brings us another step closer to next year’s event,” he said. “We can’t wait to welcome fans back to Albert Park Circuit.” AGPC chief executive officer Travis Auld welcomed the addition of a sprint race. Eddie Jim Over the past four years, many F1 fans have taken to social media to air their frustrations on rising ticket prices, with many voicing concerns around being “priced out” of the sport.





At the time, Auld said the AGPC had aimed to “strike a balance between keeping tickets accessible while continuing to enhance the fan experience and respond to the record level of interest.” Members’ tickets for the Australian Grand Prix go on sale midday October 1, with general public tickets on sale October 6.
