If it has water tanks: Dirty-water tanks should be cleaned after each mopping run of your vacuum. Clean water can stay filled in the station.

Make sure to review your robot vacuum’s manual for any other steps the manufacturer recommends you take regularly to keep the vacuum running for as long as possible. Many brands also have replacement parts, so you can swap out individual pieces like brushes without needing an entirely new vacuum.

Did Robot Vacuums Just Get Banned?

The Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, announced in late July that foreign-produced advanced robotic devices will now be included on the FCC’s Covered List. That list includes communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States, and as of this week, that includes robot vacuums (and similar devices like robotic pool cleaners and lawn mowers). While it won’t ban any models already on the market that have FCC approval, we’ll likely see a huge decline in available new models after this year. Models made in the US will be fine, but future vacuums from popular brands like Dreame, Eufy, Roborock, and more will be affected.

This comes from an interagency body in the White House executive branch called the National Security Determination, which determined that automated robotic devices are a security risk due to the data they collect, which could be used for surveillance and be remotely commandeered by “malign actors.” While the initial documentation describes humanoid robots and a recent case of a humanoid robot’s cybersecurity vulnerability to be remotely taken over, the official description of these robot devices will include robot vacuums and any devices meeting the following criteria:

Tech.title: How Self-Driving Cars Might Change Crash Testing Forever
Tech.content:
In a video posted on X, a Tesla enthusiast hops into what was once the driver’s seat of a new matte gold Cybercab. “Once” because the vehicle, which officially hit the streets earlier this month as part of Tesla’s Robotaxi ride-hail service, doesn’t have a steering wheel or brake pedals.

For the person in the front seat, this opens up new possibilities. Eat, game, watch, work. Or doze. To help you catch some z’s, the enthusiast demonstrates that the Cybercab’s seats can recline. “You can really go back,” he says. “You can really just sleep here.”

Or maybe don’t. In the official Cybercab rider guide, Tesla says passengers in its autonomous vehicles should keep their seat backs reclined no more than 35 degrees from vertical, with their seatbelts snug across their hips and their feet flat on the floor. Doing so “reduces the risk of injury in a collision or sudden stop.” (Tesla did not respond to WIRED’s questions for this story.)

Safety researchers say Tesla’s right here. In fact, passengers sitting in less-than-standard positions in any car are more likely to get hurt in a crash, even with their seatbelts fastened. According to US federal safety data, 42 people killed in traffic crashes in the past decade were identified as “seat back not in normal upright position, seat back reclined.”

That’s likely an undercount. After a crash, “it's really hard to identify people who are sitting out of position,” says Becky Mueller, a senior research engineer at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety. Crashes move human bodies, and emergency responders work quickly to extricate hurt people from damaged vehicles. Very few are noting, or even have a way to note, exactly how victims were sitting before or during a crash.

Field data for reclined occupants is sparse, according to a spokesperson for the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the federal vehicle safety regulator. But the emergence of self-driving cars like the Tesla Cybercab has nudged governments to take a fresh look at an older, dangerous issue.

“NHTSA decided to explore reclined occupants as a starting point for automated vehicle occupant safety based on the potential that occupants may choose to ride in a reclined posture if driving was no longer necessary,” the spokesperson wrote in a statement to WIRED.

A fresh look could take years. The vehicle safety standards automakers must meet today generally assume that vehicle occupants are seated upright, with their seatbelts across their hips. Airbags are configured for people sitting in this way, and the dummies used in crash tests have inflexible pelvises, which means they physically can’t slouch. To create new safety standards, studies must be proposed, funded, completed, and analyzed. Afterward, the government collects public comments from all comers.

“That’s the big excuse: ‘Oh, we can't revisit this regulation because it's such a hassle to open it back up, to go through the whole process,” Mueller says. Autonomous vehicles are finally convincing regulators “to open up some of these archaic rules and make modifications—maybe modifications that can help modernize regulations for other vehicles, too. It’s a good time to make sweeping changes.”

Crashing Out

Photograph: Smith Collection/Getty Images

Seatbelts are designed to be worn around upright, forward-facing bodies. So when a reclining body, or one sitting sideways, gets into a traffic crash, the seatbelt doesn’t do what it’s devised to—it tightens around the soft belly instead of the hard, bony pelvis.

Tech.title: Boox Launches the Palma 3 E-Reader
Tech.content:
It's that time of year: The weather's finally starting to cool off, Halloween decor has taken over most of the stores, and tech companies are dropping their fall launches. Last week was Apple's annual September iPhone event, and last night another tech launch hit the books, though this one's a little more niche. (Though I'd still say folding smartphones are in their early days.)

If you're a fan of e-paper devices that use E Ink, a technology that mimics the appearance of ink on paper, you've probably stumbled across Boox's wide range of E Ink digital notebooks and tablets. One of Boox's most popular models is the smartphone-sized Palma, and the company just announced its third-generation Palma along with two other new products.

Here are all three products released last night and what’s available to shop now (and which one I'm most excited to test as WIRED's resident E Ink device tester).

Boox’s New Generation

Courtesy of Boox

Boox launched three new E Ink products: the Boox Note Air6 C ($580), Note Mini C ($580), and the Palma 3 ($340).

The Note Air6 C is a new addition to the Note Air line I've previously tested for my guide to the best digital notebooks. These are essentially E Ink Android tablets that come with a stylus, making them an excellent choice for a powerful digital notebook. That remains true with the Note Air6 C, which will run on Android 16 for an even more tablet-style user interface and apps. The C stands for color, since this model has a color screen with a 10.3-inch Kaleido 3 color display. The Note Air6 C also has new firmware that adds Dual Notes so you can annotate two documents side by side. There are also several AI features, including a meeting and audio insights feature and a document summary. Out of the three devices announced, the Boox Note Air6 C is the only one available right now.

The Boox Note Mini C will cost the same as the larger Note Air6 C, but it has a smaller, 8.52-inch screen. It uses the same Kaleido 3 color display but is designed for more on-the-go work and for holding the device in one hand compared to the larger Air6 C. The Mini C and Air6 have fairly similar specs when it comes to power—both models have an octa-core processor, 6 GB of RAM, and 64 GB of storage. You can expand that storage on both devices up to 2 TB with a microSD card. Overall, it's more about size than it is power if you're choosing between them, but the Note Mini C is not on sale yet. Boox says it's coming soon.

Tech.title: China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
Tech.content:
For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China, and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous, tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down.

“Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier.”

China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don't believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal.

“The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it's being treated from a position of equals."

Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies.

“His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI. “Which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.”

Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”)

The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained.

When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fear-mongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.”

The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power.

Tech.title: Forget the iPhone Duo — the First iPhone Had More Hype and a More Shocking Price
Tech.content:
I’ve been reviewing the iPhone since 2020 and wasn’t even working at CNET when the original iPhone launched in 2007. Fortunately, Kent German and Donald Bell were, and their wonderfully written review of the first iPhone shows off the pair’s thorough testing.

“The iPhone is noteworthy not for what it does, but how it does it,” wrote German and Bell.

As CNET waits to test Apple’s newest devices, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, it’s insightful to revisit our review of the first iPhone, especially since the company’s announcement of its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, seems to be swirling in the same mix of hype, wonder and shock that German and Bell so artfully navigated in 2007.

Is it easy to use? Certainly. Does it live up to the stratospheric hype? Not so much. Kent German and Donald Bell

Remember, back then, touchscreen phones and smartphones we nowhere as common as they are now.

“Is it easy to use? Certainly. Does it live up to the stratospheric hype? Not so much. Don’t get us wrong, the iPhone is a lovely device with a sleek interface, top-notch music and video features, and innovative design touches,” said German and Bell. “But a host of missing features, a dependency on a sluggish EDGE network, and variable call quality — it is a phone after all — left us wanting more.”

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s most innovative and expensive phone. Patrick Holland/CNET

And while there are a lot of reactions around the iPhone Duo’s $2,000 starting price, CNET wasn’t a fan of the first iPhone’s $499 starting price. German and Bell thought $499 was “a lot to ask for a phone that lacks so many features and locks you into an iPhone-specific two-year contract with AT&T.”

If you’re keeping track, that $499 price works out to about $800 in today’s dollars. Another way of looking at it: You could buy roughly two and a half original iPhones for the price of one iPhone Duo. But in 2007, most phones before the iPhone cost $100 to $150. Even with an AT&T contract, you still had to pay $200.

Read our 2007 review of the first iPhone. Click below to read German’s revisit of the first iPhone review on its 15th anniversary in 2022.

Tech.title: How to Bring Siri AI, or Siri Classic, to Your iPhone in iOS 27
Tech.content:
You’d be forgiven if you thought that the iOS 27 update, which Apple released on Monday, Sept. 14, only brought Siri AI to your device. Apple’s Worldwide Developers Conference was largely focused on the digital assistant, prompting some readers to reach out to me and ask what to do if they don’t want to leap into Siri AI.

For the record, iOS 27 does bring more than just Siri AI, to your device though a lot of the upgrades are under the hood. The good news is that you don’t have to enable Siri AI on your device if you don’t want to.

The iOS 27 upgrade doesn’t automatically put Siri AI on your iPhone. You have to enable it, which involves signing up for a waitlist. So if you don’t want Siri AI but want to download the update, there’s a path for that. I’ll walk through all the different scenarios: enabling Siri AI, disabling Siri AI and bringing back the old-fashioned Siri.

Enabling Siri AI in iOS 27

Once you update to iOS 27, you have to 

Tap Settings. Tap Siri. Tap Try New Siri.

Then follow the onscreen prompts, and you’ll be enrolled in the waitlist. Your iPhone will notify you when you’ve been accepted, but be aware: That could be a few minutes, hours or longer. I waited a couple hours during the beta process, but some folks on Reddit waited much longer.

Once accepted, you can start using the new digital assistant, and you’ll get a new Siri AI app on your home screen.

Disable Siri AI in iOS 27

If you do get access to Siri AI and want to turn it back off, here’s how to do that.

Tap Settings. Tap Siri. Tap Turn Off Siri near the bottom of the menu. Tap Turn Off Siri again in the popup menu.

The pop-up menu that appears right before you turn off Siri AI details all the features that will be limited or not functional if you go through with this change, including not being able to start conversations in Siri AI.

While I understand Apple wanting to highlight the centerpiece of its new operating system, I don’t like the full-screen double confirmation for disabling Siri AI. I disabled a few other features, including Sensitive Content Warnings, to see if a similar menu popped up and none did, and disabling or restricting Siri on older iOS versions opened a much smaller pop-up asking if you’re sure. I appreciate additional confirmations for irreversible decisions, like resetting a device, but the full-screen confirmation felt more like an unnecessary guilt trip.

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Luckily, you’re not stuck between using Siri AI and not using Siri at all. There’s a third option that lets you use the old version of Siri, minus the AI. Here’s how to enable it.

Bring Siri Classic back to your iPhone in iOS 27

Once you’ve gained access to Siri AI, there’s only one way I’m aware of that allows you to gain access to the pre-iOS 27 Siri, called Siri Classic, without resetting your device to a previous backup. First, you have to turn Siri AI off, following the above steps. From there:

Tap Settings. Tap Siri. Tap Turn On Siri. Tap Use Siri Classic. Tap Continue.

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Now Siri will be just Siri and not Siri AI. If you want to enable Siri AI later — like after Apple hammers out some bugs — you can do so by going to Settings > Siri > Try Siri AI (Beta) > Continue.

Remember, Siri AI is still in beta so Apple will likely update and improve it with future updates.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and everything iOS 26 brought to your device.

Tech.title: This $26 Sliding Pizza Peel Promises to Improve Your Launches, but Does It?
Tech.content:
Chances are, if you own a pizza oven, have stood near a pizza oven or have uttered the words “pizza oven” in the vicinity of your phone, it’s likely that the almighty algorithm has delivered up a steady stream of pizza oven accessories, from pizza oven stands to sizzler platters to pizza peels in every style and shape.

If you have cursed in the vicinity of your phone while trying to launch a pizza into your pizza oven without inadvertently creating a calzone, chances are even better that Big Internet Brother has targeted you for a sliding pizza peel. If, after dozens of practice launches, you haven’t mastered the art of the traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel, even with all-powerful semolina flour gliders, you may be very tempted by the ease promised by such a tool as a sliding pizza peel.

The Best Pizza Ovens, Tested by CNET See at CNET

But is it worth it? Or is it just the Temu-niverse capitalizing on your desire for a homemade pizza that doesn’t come with a side of anxiety and despair? Reader, the temptation was too strong. I checked one out, and here’s the lowdown on what you can expect from a sliding pizza peel.

How does a sliding pizza peel work?

A sliding pizza peel costs $30 to $40 on Amazon. Pamela Vachon/CNET

A sliding pizza peel is essentially a lightweight wooden pizza peel with a manual conveyor belt attached. Rather than thrusting a stationary peel under your entire pie, you only need a small edge of maneuverability to start. Once the sliding peel gets a little purchase on the raw pizza dough, you pull the cloth slide toward you by its handle while pushing the wooden board underneath.

To launch the pizza with a sliding pizza peel, reverse the process: Use the handle on the cloth glider to push, sliding the pizza into the oven while pulling the sturdy board out from underneath it.

Cloth, you say? Well, not exactly. The conveyor mechanism moves like fabric, but think of it more like a nonstick baking mat. Many are made of woven fiberglass with a polytetrafluoroethylene coating, which is nonstick but still grips enough to hold raw or cooked pizza dough. It’s frankly like a flimsier Silpat or not unlike an oilcloth table covering.

PTFE, in case you’re wondering, is related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. Yes, we’ve worked hard to avoid PFAS; however, the material’s pliability doesn’t encourage chipping, and it is also replaceable. The wooden board itself admittedly also spares every expense without the heavy lifting required of other wooden pizza peels — this is made from raw, lightweight bamboo.

Sliding pizza peel best practices

I practiced with naked dough. Pamela Vachon/CNET

While a sliding pizza peel may seem like a cure-all, if, like me, you adore what your pizza oven offers but still struggle with pizza peel mechanics, it does require some practice of its own — and some caution. As with more traditional pizza peels, it cannot undo other mistakes, such as poorly constructed, too warm pizza dough or an overloaded pie. You can still calzone-ify your pizza, even with a sliding pizza peel.

Unlike a traditional pizza peel, which lets you push and pull simultaneously, the sliding pizza peel’s primary handle is also very short, meaning you kind of have to get (uncomfortably) close to the mouth of the oven to use it.

The fact that none of these seemingly magic wands are produced or branded by any major pizza oven manufacturer should serve as a bit of a caution. (The pizza oven manufacturers probably just want you to become a bona fide pizzaiolo, confidently employing the legitimate tools of the trade; they are clearly not trying to encourage the use of these cheap devices.)

Various sliding pizza peels are purportedly heat-resistant up to a certain temperature (which varies). Many pizza ovens, however, can reach temperatures much hotter than those sliding peels are designed for.

Loading a raw pie into the oven is one of the trickiest parts of at-home pizza making. Pamela Vachon/CNET

More than one user on various online pizza oven forums reported that the nonstick belt of a sliding pizza peel melted onto the hot pizza stone. Others, however, called the device an absolute game changer. Either way, using a sliding pizza peel requires you to launch quickly, which again requires practice, probably best done outside your actual pizza oven. (Your oven-oven with a removable pizza stone? A much lower-stakes practice arena.)

My experience with a sliding pizza peel

Because of the peel’s modest length, you have to get uncomfortably close to the oven during launch. Pamela Vachon/CNET

I have been an enthusiastic pizza oven user since one came into my life, but I still haven’t mastered the mechanics of either a traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel. I slightly prefer metal, but either way, pizza attempt number one always results in a folded disaster. My crime, apparently, is wanting the kind of thin pizza crust a 20-year-old New Yorker demands. The thinner the pizza, the harder to launch.

I can attest that the sliding pizza peel did make it easy to pull the pizza off the cutting board where I shaped the dough and applied toppings. Despite feeling cheaply made, the mechanics are inarguable. I achieved a crust thinness I truly couldn’t with the other models.

While you have to get close to the heat to deposit it, I haven’t earned any burns or scars from trying. Repeated launches in a very hot pizza oven also didn’t seem to affect the fabric slide, but then again, I was prepared to move extremely fast to avoid a crisis — and to get away from the heat.

Success, if not exactly centered. Pamela Vachion/CNET

In case it merits saying, a sliding pizza peel is entirely unnecessary for pulling pizza out of a pizza oven. In fact, I would caution against it since it really relies on setting the peel down on the pizza stone, never mind the fact that you really have to get your hand inside the oven in the starting position for pulling a pizza onto it. Once a pizza is fully cooked and the dough is sturdy, even a thin pizza can be collected with a more traditional pizza peel anyhow.

A traditional pizza peel is still best for pulling pies from the oven. Pamela Vachon/CNET

The verdict on a sliding pizza peel? Proceed with caution. And practice.

Ultimately, the average price of sliding pizza peels available online is about $30. Even with mixed reviews, it’s a fairly low-stakes gamble to see whether one improves how often you use your big-ticket pizza oven.

Tech.title: T-Mobile Is the First Carrier to Support Apple’s iPhone Handoff, but It’ll Cost $5 a Month
Tech.content:
The new iPhone Handoff feature in iOS 27 is a clever idea: If you have two iPhones, you can use either one with a single phone number — the system automatically activates your number on whichever phone is unlocked. And like Apple’s Handoff to Mac and iPad, your texts, calls, voicemails and Find My location follow you, too.

At launch, however, the feature is supported only by T-Mobile in the US, and the carrier is charging $5 a month to use it. And while Verizon support is expected by the end of the year, according to Apple, AT&T appears to be sitting this feature out for now.

iPhone Handoff is similar to what the Apple Watch has done with data for a few generations, where taking off one watch and putting on another automatically switches all of your information, such as activity tracking, to it. For example, some people use one watch during the day — perhaps the rugged Apple Watch Ultra — and switch to a slimmer, older Apple Watch at night, allowing the first to charge for the morning.

But replicating that behavior to the iPhone requires coordination with cellular providers. Each phone’s eSIM needs to be configured for iPhone Handoff by a carrier, and service needs to switch cleanly on the network side.

Ironically, the Apple Watch gets left out of the iPhone Handoff transaction: Your watch remains paired with just one watch, communicating with it via Wi-Fi or cellular (if that’s an option). “If neither is available,” Apple writes, “calls, messages, notifications, certain health and fitness features, Siri AI or other app experiences relayed from your paired iPhone may not be available.”

In its press release about offering the iPhone 18 Pro, T-Mobile writes, “iPhone Handoff is available on any iPhone with iOS 27 via iPhone settings and ready to use from day one on the new iPhone 18 Pro lineup and iPhone Duo. T-Mobile is introducing the feature at $5/month.”

When I reached out to T-Mobile asking about the charge, a spokesperson wrote via email, “The $5/month charge reflects the added service that powers the experience on both devices.”

While iPhone Handoff appears to seamlessly switch your eSIM just by picking up the phone you want to use, it’s not yet clear what else is different with this process versus just transferring your eSIM manually using your iPhone’s settings menu.

Notably absent from Apple’s news was the other major US carrier, AT&T. I contacted a spokesperson there to learn more about the company’s plans for the feature, but it sounds like it’s not a priority.

“While we see that there could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” the spokesperson replied, “our focus remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” They then pointed to “existing eSIM activation and transfer options across compatible devices.”

In addition to T-Mobile, iPhone Handoff is currently supported by Telekom in Germany. The UK carrier EE will also support the feature later this year, according to Apple.

A Verizon representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Samsung Goes to Couples Therapy to Unpack iPhone-to-Android Tension
Tech.content:
Change can be challenging in a relationship, even when you know it’s for the best. Samsung’s new Switchers ad campaign acknowledges that challenge, particularly when it comes to switching from iPhone to Android.

Playing on classic therapy talking points, Samsung recruited celebrity clinical psychologist Orna Guralnik to help couples overcome fear, discomfort and anxiety about exploring something new — in this case, purchasing a device outside Apple’s ecosystem.

Guralnik helms the documentary TV series Couples Therapy, which follows real-life couples as they attend regular therapy sessions. The show is in its fifth season on Showtime and Paramount Plus.

Launched on Monday, days after Apple announced its own foldable, the iPhone Duo, the Switchers campaign particularly plugs Samsung’s new Galaxy Z foldables. It features celebrity pairs with real relationships, including Ciara Miller and Dylan Efron from The Traitors; Carl Schmidt and Aniya Harvey from Love Island; and football icons Nick Foles and Clay Matthews.

What Switchers gets right

Rather than demoing Samsung’s latest foldable phones in a spec-heavy pitch, the six ads cleverly frame the purchase decision as an emotional one. In each 30-second commercial, the Galaxy phone appears as the centerpiece of a common relationship issue, masked as a worry that arises when switching smartphones. By the end, the concern is resolved when Guralnik presents one of Samsung’s attractive features that makes the transition, well, less painful.

Samsung’s ad campaign does more than just entertain — it effectively taps into a very relatable psychological attachment we often have to our phones. It’s common to stick with a device because it’s familiar and predictable in a rapidly changing world, much like we lean on established patterns in long-term romantic relationships. Guralnik, known for tackling such issues with deep insight and compassion on the show, lends these ads credibility.

While Samsung’s campaign shows off Galaxy Z and S series phones — including the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra and S26 Ultra with a privacy display — it doesn’t demand or bully you into switching from iPhone to Android. It just asks that you remain curious about what’s out there.

Problem, meet solution

The Switchers campaign uses a mix of humor, cultural commentary and sympathy. When one partner in the couple is worried about losing existing data, the solution is Samsung’s Smart Switch, a data transfer feature that moves iOS contacts, photos, messages, apps and settings to Android using a simple QR code. No more fear of abandonment.

The sessions also highlight a deeper operational hurdle: cross-platform messaging friction, such as incompatible emoji reactions and the limitations of green text bubbles between Android and iOS. In response, Guralnik says there’s “no need to shame green bubbles anymore” and proposes using rich communication services, also known as RCS, which enable consistent communication across different brand ecosystems. Communication saves the day.

When a partner worries about losing the freedom to easily share files and photos with other Apple users, Samsung’s wireless file-sharing service Quick Share offers a remedy, because it’s now compatible with AirDrop. Everyone needs validation.

Making the switch

Samsung says people are, in fact, making big changes — or one could say, breaking up with their time-honored smartphone.

In its press release, the company reported that 30% of Galaxy Z Flip 8 buyers switched from a competing brand. Samsung’s latest foldables seem to be the draw, as the Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra accounted for 23% and 12% of buyers who switched, respectively, outperforming the Z Fold 7.

Foldable or flippable phones aren’t unique to Samsung. Motorola has its 2026 Razr, Google has its Pixel 10 Pro Fold, and now Apple has the iPhone Duo. Each has its own set of features, specs and prices, but their collective presence on the market demonstrates that people are willing to make a shift. Maybe it’s because they also crave the flip phones of years gone by. In times of tumult, nostalgia can offer just as much comfort as familiarity.

Tech.title: Today’s NYT Strands Hints, Answers and Help for Sept. 16, #927
Tech.content:
Looking for the most recent NYT Strands puzzle answers? CNET publishes daily answers and hints for The New York Times Mini Crossword, Connections, Connections: Sports Edition and Strands puzzles.

Strands is like a word find game, but without the list of words to find. Sometimes I see the theme and begin recognizing the answers right away. But for those times when I can’t seem to manage this, there’s a loophole: Strands lets you make as many words of four or more letters as you want. For every three of those words you find, the puzzle will highlight one of the answers. You’re still going to have to unscramble that answer, though, which can be very tough.

I go into depth about the rules for Strands in this story.

Today’s puzzle has a fun category, with some lively words. They’re pretty easy to unscramble once you pick up on the theme. Read on for hints and all the answers.



Hint for today’s Strands puzzle

Today’s Strands theme is: Hard not to notice.

If that doesn’t help you, here’s a clue: Showy or glitzy.

Clue words to unlock in-game hints

Your goal is to find hidden words that fit the puzzle’s theme. If you’re stuck, find any words you can. Every time you find three words of four letters or more, Strands will reveal one of the theme words. These are the words I used to get those hints, but any words of four or more letters that you find will work:

CASE, CHIN, STIR, SHACK, HACK, LACK, LACE, LACY, TRICK, RICE

Answers for today’s Strands puzzle

These are the answers that tie into the theme. The goal of the puzzle is to find them all, including the “spangram,” a theme word that reaches from one side of the puzzle to the other. When you have all of them (I originally thought there were always eight, but learned that the number can vary), every letter on the board will be used. Here are the nonspangram answers:

JAZZY, VIVID, BRIGHT, FLASHY, VIBRANT, STRIKING

Today’s Strands spangram

The completed NYT Strands puzzle for Sept. 16, 2026. NYT/Screenshot by CNET

Today’s Strands spangram is EYECATCHING. To find it, start with the E that’s the first letter on the top row, and wind down, over, and then down again.

Quick tips for Strands

#1: To get more clue words, see if you can tweak the words you’ve already found, by adding an “S” or other variants. And if you find a word like WILL, see if other letters are close enough to help you make SILL, or BILL.

#2: Once you get one theme word, look at the puzzle to see if you can spot other related words.

#3: If you’ve been given the letters for a theme word, but can’t figure it out, guess three more clue words, and the puzzle will light up each letter in order, revealing the word.

Tech.title: PS Plus Gets a Diverse Lineup for September With WWE 2K26, RuneScape: Dragonwilds and More
Tech.content:
It’s September 2026, and the avalanche of quality games is already underway with Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Star Wars Zero Company and Marvel’s Wolverine. The big game releases will continue to happen weekly until Nov. 19, when Grand Theft Auto 6 releases, but this month, PS Plus subscribers are getting a mix of action, fantasy and a sprinkle of quirky games added to the service.

PS Plus, which is Sony’s version of Xbox Game Pass, offers a large, constantly expanding library of games. Subscribers can choose from the Essential, Extra and Premium tiers, each with unique perks and benefits. Starting at $11 per month, the plans give subscribers access to games and rewards, and each month, subscribers can play a handful of new games at no additional charge.

If you’re a PlayStation Plus Extra or Premium subscriber, you can grab these games now.

RuneScape: Dragonwilds

Set on the forgotten continent of Ashenfall, RuneScape: Dragonwilds is a cooperative survival RPG where players must gather resources, craft gear, build shelters and develop their skills to survive a land filled with dangerous creatures. The adventure combines classic RuneScape lore with survival mechanics and a new fantasy setting. Players can unlock abilities and spells as they progress, while quests lead them through a hand-crafted world filled with familiar enemies and new threats. At the center of the adventure is a confrontation with the fearsome Dragon Queen.

RuneScape: Dragonwilds is available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers on Tuesday.

WWE 2K26

WWE 2K26 puts hundreds of WWE Superstars and legends at your fingertips, combining wrestling simulation with a variety of ways to play out your own version of WWE history. The massive roster includes modern stars alongside icons from the Attitude Era, while Showcase mode focuses on CM Punk and explores alternate versions of his career. Players can also rewrite wrestling history through fantasy scenarios, allowing them to revisit famous rivalries and imagine how things might have unfolded differently. It’s a wrestling game built around both authenticity and fan-driven fantasy.

WWE 2K26 is available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers on Tuesday.

Ball x Pit

A ruined city, a bottomless pit and an army of monsters set the stage for Ball x Pit, a fast-paced fantasy roguelite built around frantic combat and progression. Players descend through increasingly difficult levels while using magic-infused projectiles to battle enemies and overcome obstacles. Between runs, they can develop new ammunition and resources, recruit additional heroes and work toward rebuilding the destroyed city of New Ballbylon. Its combination of arcade-style action, randomized challenges and character progression gives each attempt a different feel as players push deeper into the pit.

Ball x Pit will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Sept. 22.

Date Everything!

When a woman loses her customer service job to AI, a mysterious gift gives her a bizarre new career path: dating the objects in her own house. Date Everything! turns the traditional dating simulator into a comedic adventure where magical Dateviator glasses bring everyday items to life. Each object has its own personality, story and relationship path, and your choices can lead to friendship, romance or conflict. The game blends visual novel storytelling, relationship management and comedy, with a huge cast of voiced characters hidden among the furniture and appliances around your home.

Date Everything! is already available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers.

Slitterhead

Set in the neon-soaked streets of Kowloon, Slitterhead is a horror action-adventure that follows Hyoki, a mysterious entity without a physical body or memories. His goal is to hunt Slitterheads, monstrous creatures that disguise themselves as humans. Combat revolves around manipulating blood and working alongside special humans known as Rarities, who can help Hyoki infiltrate dangerous groups and take down enemies. As the investigation unfolds, players uncover the mystery surrounding Hyoki and the creatures haunting the city. The result is a dark blend of supernatural horror, action and investigative storytelling.

Slitterhead will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Sept. 22.

Ninja Gaiden: Ragebound

Ninja Gaiden: Ragebound brings the classic series into a modern 2D action-platformer, combining the fast combat and lore of the original games with ideas inspired by the newer 3D entries. When the barrier between the human and demon worlds breaks, Hayabusa Village is overrun while Ryu Hayabusa is away. Young ninja Kenji Mozu must step up and defend his home from the invading forces. Developed by the team behind Blasphemous, Ragebound emphasizes precise movement, aggressive combat and challenging enemies in a stylish side-scrolling adventure.

Ninja Gaiden: Ragebound will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Sept. 29.

Dungeons of Hinterberg

Corporate burnout takes Luisa to the Austrian Alps, where a quiet vacation town hides a network of mysterious dungeons. Dungeons of Hinterberg mixes action-adventure gameplay with puzzle solving, exploration and social simulation. Players can snowboard across snowy landscapes, climb mountains, explore the countryside, and tackle dungeons filled with magical abilities and unusual challenges. Time spent in town is just as important, allowing Luisa to build friendships with locals and fellow adventurers. The result is a colorful fantasy adventure that balances combat and exploration with brain-teasing puzzles and character-driven downtime.

Dungeons of Hinterberg will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Sept. 29.

Sniper Elite: Resistance

Set behind enemy lines in occupied France, Sniper Elite: Resistance follows SOE agent Harry Hawker as he works with the French Resistance to stop a devastating Nazi superweapon. The third-person shooter emphasizes stealth, tactical combat and the series’ signature long-range sniping, giving players considerable freedom in how they approach missions. Multiple targets and different infiltration and extraction points encourage experimentation rather than a single path through each level. The campaign can also be played cooperatively, adding another layer to its mix of methodical shooting, reconnaissance and tactical action.

Sniper Elite: Resistance will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Sept. 29.

Mega Man X Command Mission

Mega Man X Command Mission puts the robot hero and his allies in the middle of a dangerous conflict over Giga City. Unlike the series’ traditional run-and-gun platformers, this adventure is a turn-based RPG, allowing players to assemble a team and combine their abilities during battles. X is joined by familiar characters, including Zero and Axl, along with new allies, as they tackle more than 50 missions. Side quests, powerful bosses and team-based combat add depth to the futuristic story, making it a notable genre shift for the Mega Man X series.

Mega Man X Command Mission is currently available for PS Plus Premium subscribers.

Metro Redux

Metro Redux combines two atmospheric first-person shooters set in a post-apocalyptic Russia where survivors live in underground stations after a devastating nuclear war. Players take control of Artyom, who ventures through the Metro tunnels and eventually into the poisoned world above while confronting mutants, hostile survivors and a growing threat to humanity. The games emphasize tense exploration, resource management, stealth and gunplay, with limited supplies making every encounter dangerous. Blending survival horror with immersive storytelling and first-person action, Metro Redux creates a bleak underground world where survival is never guaranteed.

PlayStation Plus subscriptions start at $11 a month See at Sony

For more on PlayStation Plus, here’s what to know about the service. You can also check out other games on PlayStation Plus and games on Xbox Game Pass.

Tech.title: Samsung Is Fast-Tracking Galaxy Z TriFold 2 After iPhone Duo Reveal, According to Leaks
Tech.content:
Foldable phones have never exactly been a powerhouse segment of the handset market, despite being flashy pieces of technology – but when Apple enters the fray, public interest is sure to follow.

Now that the iPhone Duo has been revealed, and following strong early sales for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra, Samsung is looking to fast-track a competing device, according to known leaker Lanzuk.

A successor to the Galaxy Z TriFold has reportedly been under development for months, with detailed patents painting a picture of what we might expect from the new phone – it could be wider and shorter and might include a slot for the S Pen stylus.

But Samsung is now reportedly considering an accelerated release timeline, which could mean the next Galaxy Z TriFold will launch in late 2026 or early 2027. Previous reports indicated that the phone would likely be slated for a late 2027 release.

The first Galaxy Z TriFold had an expensive, limited release in the US. The phone was available starting in January, and despite a commanding starting price of $2,900, it sold out quickly before being discontinued three months later. It felt like a more experimental product in Samsung’s mobile lineup, but a second TriFold might signal a more serious commitment to this design.

According to Lanzuk, Samsung wants to produce the new TriFold handset at a “nearly identical” price, despite rising hardware costs. If people are willing to turn out in droves for the high-end iPhone Duo configurations – some of which cost more than $3,000 – this could prove to be a more competitive market niche than ever before.

A Samsung representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

It’s worth noting that the iPhone Duo hasn’t officially hit the market yet and won’t do so for another month. All the online buzz in the world isn’t worth anything if the new foldable phone doesn’t sell well, so Samsung may be watching how the market reacts to the Duo before reallocating any development resources.

The Galaxy Z TriFold 2 has reportedly been under development for some time, so a shift in plans may signal renewed urgency and confidence in the market segment.

The iPhone Duo will be released on Oct. 23 with a starting price of $1,999.
